Crop yield impact assessment using crop simulation model involves various processes. The critical data inputs for running the simulations are daily weather, soil parameters and crop management details.8,9 Figure 1 Jasmine cultivations and flower bud collections in different parts of Tamil Nadu. There are various sub modules inside crop simulation models. The major modules are land module, management module, soil module, and weather module, and soil-plant-atmosphere module. Some models utilize mass balance principles to simulate the carbon, nitrogen, and hydrologic processes and transformations that occur within agro- ecosystems.9–12 Crop development proceeds through a series of growth stages based on photo thermal time or heat unit accumulation from planting to harvest.13–17 There is a wide gap and lack of regional crop simulation modeling for floriculture crops and further impact studies on its productivity focusing at local scale. It is necessary to have research studies focusing on micro and macro climatic influence on quality and quantity of flower yield .Higher temperatures may pose significant negative impacts on flower development in the purview of climatic variability and change. In tropical environment, high temperature exposure above the threshold level eventually affects the quality and the quantity of the flower buds eventually weeds infest the area and pests proliferate. Vagaries in precipitation patterns augment the likelihood of short-run crop failures and long-run production declines. Not only temperature and rainfall, but relative humidity also plays a major role in the new leaf production, the leaf expansion, the leaf area duration, the flower initiation, the flower development, the pollination, the maturity etc. Thermal stress during the most sensitive plant developmental stages may impede photosynthesis and thus its flower yield. Winter season (December to February) is a dormant season for flower crops especially Jasmine. The farmer requires polyhouses for getting sustained income and flower production. Literature reviews shows that much of this research has addressed the consequences of warming for and distributional shifts in plants. In contrast, relatively little is known about the physiological responses of perennial plants and insect pollinators to climate warming and, in particular, how these responses might affect plant-pollinator interaction networks and flower yield directly or indirectly in a changing climatic condition. Crop simulation modelers should look into the multi thronged mutualistic interactions happens among pollinators, flowers, and climate and incorporates it in scope of the modeling processes. This approach should lead to a new urge in crop simulation research overcoming the limiting scope for simulating pollinator and flower interactions in flower crop especially on the plant responses to which include altered flower, nectar, and pollen production, could modify floral resource availability and reproductive output of pollinating insects. The production of floral scent, nectar, and pollen can also be affected by temperature. Conclusion Understanding the local changes with respect to climate necessitates better adaptation and future management especially for the vulnerable low lying coastal areas in the developing countries who has 50% of its workforce engaged in agriculture. It is the responsibility of the scientific community to disseminate the climate change knowledge through a Top down approach method, will help all the stakeholders including decision makers in furthering researches and policy formulations. Acquiring local level authentic information on future plausible climate change and its impacts on flower productivity will facilitate implementing site specific adaptation options in this sector. Gundumalli Sushree Choudhury, Jatindra Nath Das, Chitta Ranjan Mohanty, Bijaya Kumar Mishra and Arun Kumar Das DOI: https://doi.org/10.22271/chemi.2020.v8.i2i.8833 Abstract A research on standardization of method of packaging to extend shelf life of Jasminum sambac CV. Gundumalli was conducted in College of Agriculture, Odisha University of Agriculture and Technology, Bhubaneswar during 2015-16. The experiment was laid out in FCRD with two factors in three replications, with 16 treatment combinations. Observations were recorded on the visual quality in terms of freshness index, flowers opening index, colour retention index, and shelf life of flowers and the physiological parameters associated with the postharvest quality of flowers, namely, moisture content, relative water content, physiological loss in weight. The flowers treated with 4% boric acid, packed in 60-micron polyethylene bags without ventilation and stored under 7 0C significantly extend the shelf life to 168.33 hours with highest freshness index (87.45%), maximum colour retention index of (92.68%), and lowest flower opening index (10.57%), highest moisture content of (75.82%) and lowest physiological weight loss percent (0.35%) on 48 hours after packing. Keywords: Jasmine, sucrose, boric acid, NAA, packaging method, polythene bags, micron thickness Introduction Flower is the symbol of beauty, love and tranquility, flower conveys the message of love, joy and affection. Flowers are used by people to express their first feeling one for other. In beautification, flowers are one of the main ingredients since the beginning of history and its importance has not yet diminished but rather increased as time proceeds. Among the commercial flowers grown in India the most important are roses, carnation, gerbera, orchid, chrysanthemum, jasmine, marigold, aster etc. Among the different kind of flowers, Jasmines take uninumero position because of their elegant star like attractive flowers, rich fragrance, multifaceted aesthetic utilities, high exportable value and earning lucrative income for the flower growers. “Think of fragrance, think of jasmine” such is the special attraction of this white coloured and fragrant flowers that has a pride of place in the heart of every women (Mundhe,2012) [11]. Jasmine (Jasminum sambac Ait.) is the oldest of fragrant flowers cultivated by man and belongs to the family “Oleaceae”. The genus jasminum comprises around 300 species which are dispersed throughout warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa, the Pacific region and many other tropical and subtropical countries. About 40 species are native of India (Bhattacharjee, 1980) [1]. Among the large number of Jasminum species existing, only three species (J. sambac, J. grandiflorum, J. auriculatum) have attained importance in commercial cultivation in India. (Rimando, 2003, Green and Miller, 2009) [5]. The cultivar Gundumalli belongs to the group J sambac. The flowers are used for various purposes, viz., making garlands and bouquets, for religious offerings, etc. These are also used for production of essential oils in the form of ‘concrete’ and ‘absolute’ used in cosmetic and perfumery industries. These flowers have good demand for export due to its attractive fragrance. The flowers are very delicate and show signs of wilting with abrupt loss of fragrance within 24 -36 hour after harvest. One of the major problems faced by exporters is lack of suitable packaging technology for export. Presently, Jasmines are grown for fresh flower trade with obsolete technologies and lack of improved method of harvesting, packing, storing and transporting. Under normal condition, Jasmine flowers do not retain for more than a day and show a sign of ~ 599 ~ International Journal of Chemical Studies http://www.chemijournal.com browning or rotting of petals on the second day of harvest with an abrupt loss in fragrance. Krishnamoorthy (1990) reported that packaging is a fundamental tool for post harvest management of highly perishable commodities and adequate packaging protects the produce from physical, physiological and pathological deterioration during transport and marketing and enhancing their shelf life by retaining their attractiveness. Even if two per cent wastage of horticultural produce is reduced from the production centers to the market, there will be a saving of rupees 100-200 crores per year in India (Ramana et al., 1988). Therefore, a study was undertaken to assess the feasibility of Postharvest Treatments on Quality and shelf life of flowers of Jasminum sambac cv. Gundumalli. Materials and Methods The experiment was carried out at the Department of floriculture and landscaping, College of Agriculture, Odisha University of Agriculture and Technology, Bhubaneswar. Fully developed fresh flower buds of uniform size, shape and milky white colour, were used for the study. Fifty numbers of fresh flower buds of uniform size were treated with the chemicals and surface dried. Then the treated flowers packed in polythene bags of 40, 60-micron thickness and 20cm*12cm dimension without vents and heat sealed. These bags were stored under room temperature or cold storage conditions. The temperature and relative humidity of the cold room were 7 °C and 80-85% respectively. The experiment design followed for this study is FCRD with two factors. So, all total 16 treatment combinations and each treatment replicated as thrice. The treatments comprised of four different Chemical treatments (C1: Sucrose 4%, C2: Boric acid 4%, C3: NAA 100ppm, C4: Water ) and packed in four different Packaging method (P1:Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, P2:Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, P3:Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, P4: Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature ) So all total 16 treatment combinations are : T1 :Sucrose 4%+ Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C T2:Sucrose 4%+Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T3:Sucrose 4%,+ Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T4: Sucrose 4%,+ Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T5: Boric acid 4% + Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T6:Boric acid 4% + Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T7:Boric acid 4%+ Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T8: Boric acid 4% + Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T9: NAA 100ppm+ Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T10: NAA 100ppm + Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T11: NAA 100ppm + Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T12:NAA 100ppm+ Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T13:Water+ Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T14: Water + Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C, T15: Water + Packed in 40micron polythene bags and Stored under room temperature, T16: Water+ Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C. The visual flower quality parameters namely, freshness index, flower opening index, colour retention index, and shelf life were recorded based on hedonic scale scoring as per Madhu (1999) [8]. Physiological parameters namely moisture content (MC), relative water content (RWC), physiological loss in weight (PLW). All the observations were recorded on the 24th,48thhours after packing. Standard procedure of Sukhatme and Amble (1985) [18] was adopted for statistical scrutiny of data Results and Discussion Visual flower quality parameters Data pertinent to the flower quality parameters recorded in the present study are presented in Table 1, Figures1-3. Among the different treatments imposed, treating flowers with Boric acid 4%, packed in 60micron polythene and stored under 7 0C (T6) recorded the highest freshness index (98.35, 87.45%) on the 24th, 48th hours after treatment respectively. The lowest freshness index (87.71, 55.12% respectively) was observed in (T15) i.e. flowers treated with water and packed in 40micron polythene and stored under room temperature. The lowest flower opening index (3.59, 10.57% respectively) 24th,48th hours after treatment respectively was observed in the treatment (T6) i.e. Boric acid 4% and packed in 60-micron polythene and Stored under 7 0C. Maximum flower opening index (11.35, 33.72% respectively) was observed in (T15). The maximum colour retention index of flowers was observed when the flowers subjected to Boric acid 4% and packed in 60micron polythene and stored under 7 0C (T6) with the values being (100, 92.68%) 24th, 48th hours after treatment respectively. The minimum colour retention index of 76.77, 49.21% respectively was observed in (T15) i.e. flowers treated with water and packed in 40micron polythene and stored under room temperature. The longest shelf life of flowers (168.33 hours) was recorded in the treatment T6i.e. Boric acid 4% and packed in 60-micron polythene and Stored under 7 0C. The shortest shelf life (60.75 hours) was observed in(T15) i.e. flowers treated with water and packed in 40micron polythene and Stored under room temperature. Boric acid has been used as a mineral salt that could increase the osmotic concentration and pressure potential of the petal cells, thus improving their water balance and longevity in cut flowers as reported by Vanmeeteren, (1989). This might be due to treatment of boric acid is an antisense agent. Burzo et al. (1998) [4] reported that the brown colouration and loss of fragrance might be due to the accumulation of flavins and other phenolic substances in flower cell vacuoles. The phenol accumulation was also found to be minimum with normal colour retention and fragrance in the packed flowers than the control In agreement with the present finding, the potential of boric acid in prolonging the postharvest life of flowers has been reported earlier in jasmine by (Mukhopadhyay et.al 1980, Binisundar, 2011, Jawaharlal et.al 2012, Manimaran et.al, 2018) [10, 6, 9] in crossandra by Bhattacharjee, (2002) [2], in carnation by Serrano et al., (2006) [16]. Flower physiological parameters The data presented in Table 2and Figure4 revealed that the highest moisture content of flowers was observed when the flowers subjected to Boric acid 4% and packed in 60-micron polythene and stored under 7 0C (T6) with the values being (81.94, 75.82%). on the 24th,48th hours after treatment respectively. The lowest moisture content (55.13, 34.71% respectively was observed in (T15) i.e. flowers treated with water and packed in 40micron polythene and stored under room temperature. The lowest physiological weight loss percent (0.10%, 0.35% respectively) was observed in the treatment T6 i.e. Boric acid 4% and packed in 60-micron polythene and Stored under 7 0C.on the 24th,48th hours after treatment respectively. The highest physiological weight loss percent (2.69%, 6.95% respectively) was observed in (T15) i.e. flowers treated with water and packed in 40-micron polythene and stored under room temperature. Increased PLW leads to decline in fresh weight of flowers, which expresses visually as symptoms of wilting of flowers, as reported in carnation (Nichols, 1966) [12] and Rosa damascena (Sharma, 1981) [17]. Relative water content of flowers manifests water status of petals. It is obvious that when moisture content is higher and weight loss is lower, relative water content stays high. Similar evidence has been reported in gladiolus, wherein a decrease in RWC of petals caused the dehydration of tissues and in turn wilting, as reported by Zahed Hossain et al., (2006) [21]. This might be due to maintenance of optimum humidity temperature and proper balance of CO2 and O2 concentration under refrigerated condition which in turns slows down the process of respiration and evapotranspiration and ultimately reduced the PLW. The results are in close agreement with the findings of Nirmala and Venkatesh Reddy (1993) [13] and Yathindra et al. (2018) [20]. Conclusion From the present investigation, it may be concluded that post- harvest treatment of Jasminum sambac flowers, with 4% boric acid and Packed in 60micron polythene bags and Stored under 7 0C proved effective for improving the flower quality with a high freshness index, colour retention index, high moisture content and low physiological loss in weight. Flowers in this package can be kept fresh for a longer period with a shelf life of 168.33 hours. text: Plant Science Today, ISSN 2348-1900 (online) Introduction The genus Jasminum belonging to the family Oleaceae comprises of around 200–300 species out of which 40 species are found to occur in India (1). The species Jasminum grandiflorum L. commonly called as 6321/royal jasmine, Spanish jasmine and Sicilian jasmine, is one of the most important fragrant traditional flower, native to South Asia and is traditionally grown for its fresh flowers in the Arabian peninsula, East and Northeast Africa, the Yunnan and Sichuan regions of China, Thailand, Sri Lanka and Philippines. In India, its commercial cultivation is extended in Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and some parts of Bihar and West Bengal for its flowers and buds, for making garlands, flower strings veni and for religious offerings. This royal jasmine has a rich history of medicinal and cosmetic uses. Research on this plant has focused on its potential therapeutic properties, including anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, antioxidant and wound-healing effects as well as its traditional uses in treating various ailments. Additionally, it's a significant source of essential oils used in perfumery and cosmetics. In Europe and Mediterranean countries, jasmine flowers are used in large scale exclusively for extraction of essential oils. Apart from domestic consumption, India is the largest exporter of jasmine oil in the world accounting for over 40 % of total world export and Tamil Nadu is the leading producer and exporter of jasmine flowers to other countries. Owing to its wide range of uses, the demand for jasmine flowers is growing day by day. Since, high yielding varieties are not available for cultivation to the farmers, which arise an urgent need for development of high yielding varieties/hybrids in jasmine. The success of a crop improvement programme is highly dependent on the genetic diversity present among the available genotypes. But there is only limited variability exists in Spanish jasmine, as it is propagated vegetatively. Hence for developing improved varieties with novel floral traits, breeding programmes that increases genetic variation is highly needed to improve the yield and yield contributing traits of jasmine. In the recent years, mutation and molecular breeding methods offers sound and attractive choice for plant breeders to develop desired traits in plants. Upgrading the well-adapted plant varieties by improving a few desirable traits is the principal strategy in mutation breeding (2). The process of induced mutation can be performed either physically or chemically and it is very effective in the production of natural genetic resources for the formation of mutation in plants. Plant Science Today. 2026; 13(sp2): 1-19. https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.10713 Abstract The present investigation was carried out to identify the high yielding mutants in pink and white pitchi ecotypes of royal jasmine (Jasminum grandiflorum L.), based on vegetative traits viz., number of primary and secondary branches, internodal length, number of leaves, leaf length and leaf width as well as flowering traits viz., days to flowering, number of flowering cymes/branch, flower bud length, corolla tube length, bud girth, flower diameter and 100 flower bud weight than control. Based on high phenotypic coefficients of variation (PCV) and genotypic coefficients of variation (GCV), selection can be affected for the traits viz., flower yield per plant, number of secondary branches per plant, number of flowering cymes/branches, plant height, internodal length, stem girth, number of primary branches per plant, leaf length, leaf breadth and 100 bud weight. High heritability for all the 16 traits and high genetic advance in 13 traits were observed whereas, the genetic advance was moderate for corolla tube length, days to flowering and flower bud length indicating additive gene effects and selection will be very effective when these traits are considered. The correlation results are in desirable direction for flowering cymes, plant height, secondary branches and 100 bud weight, hence these traits can be given more preference during selection. This extensive growth habit of morphological as well as reproductive growth traits may be due to mutation, that finally increased flower yield. Six mutants viz., PPM-12, PPM-72, PPM-96, PPM-115, WPM-2 and WPM-25 of pink and white pitchi were identified as the best and promoted to advanced yield trials, for confirmatory results on yield and flowering traits. Keywords: economic traits; elite mutants; genetic studies; pink and white pitchi; royal jasmine SOUNDARYA ET AL 2 https://plantsciencetoday.online the mutation efficiency decide the success of mutation breeding. The phenotypic variation is largely in response to the environment particularly the temperature which implies on the development of mutants (3). The most effective technique for the creation of morphological and genotypic variability in plants is induced mutation. Therefore, like other crop plants, mutation breeding would be a successful tool to generate genetic variation for breeding new varieties. Keeping this in view, the present investigation on phenotypic characterisation and genetic variability assessment was carried out to identify the high yielding promising mutants of M1V3 generation evolved through mutation breeding of pink and white pitchi of royal jasmine. Materials and Methods The experiment was conducted at the Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu (Latitude of 11°00’ N, longitude of 77°00’ E and an elevation of 412 m above mean sea level), India during 2020–23. The released cultivar J. grandiflorum cv. CO.1 (pitchi), commonly called as pink pitchi, released during 1980 is a clonal selection from the germplasm collection maintained at Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU), Coimbatore and J. grandiflorum cv. white pitchi, is a region-specific cultivar of jasmine popularly cultivated in the southern districts of Tamil Nadu were used as the plant materials for mutagenic treatments. Terminal cuttings (13–15 cm long with 3 pairs of nodes) were irradiated with 10, 15, 20 and 25 Gy of gamma rays at the dose rate of 5000 rad/min in gamma chamber - 1200 available at Centre for Plant Breeding and Genetics, TNAU, Coimbatore. After irradiation, the treated cuttings were planted in polybags filled up to 3/4th of the height with rooting medium consisting of red soil + farmyard manure + sand (1:1:1) and the top 1/4th with sand along with untreated cuttings as control for comparison. Another set of cuttings treated with EMS (25, 30, 35 and 40 mM). After shade drying, the cuttings were incubated in respective concentrations of ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) solutions at room temperature (1 hr) andthen rinsed with running tap water for 1 hr to wash out the chemical residues. The cuttings were then planted into polybags filled with the rooting medium. The mutagenised M1V1 population was screened for deviation in the various traits in comparison with the control plants, with respect to vegetative growth and flowering parameters. Analysis was carried out to find out mean, range, standard error, coefficient of variation using MS Excel, 2010. The M1V1 generation plants of J. grandiflorum cv. white pitchi were further raised for the next vegetative generation namely, M1V2 through vegetative propagation using terminal stem cuttings and placed under poly-tunnels with average temperature of 28–30 °C and relative humidity 80 % to induce rooting. After root formation, the M1V2 putative mutants were transferred to grow bags filled with potting mixture and then maintained in field for evaluation of various growth parameters and economic traits that contributing to flower yield. The M1V3 generation of the mutant genotypes were raised through vegetative propagation of the M1V2 generation plants with semi-hardwood cuttings rooted under poly-tunnels with average temperature of 28–30 °C and relative humidity 80 %. The M1V3 generation plants were replanted in larger grow bags filled with potting mixture after root development and the rooted cuttings were transplanted to the field for assessing the growth, flowering and quality characteristics. A total of 156 genotypes (128 mutants of pink pitchi and 26 mutants of white pitchi derived using gamma rays and EMS and two check varieties pink pitchi and white pitchi) were evaluated for 3 seasons from 2020–23 in randomized block design (RBD) with 2 replications. Each entry was raised with a spacing of 2 × 2 m. All recommended package of practices were followed under irrigated condition. Observations recorded for various quantitative traits at vegetative stage viz., plant height, number of primary branches, number of secondary branches, number of leaves/plant, leaf length, leaf width, internodal length, stem girth and at flowering stage viz., days to 50 % flowering, number of flowering cymes, flower bud length, corolla tube length, flower bud girth, 100 flower bud weight, diameter of open flower and flower yield, were subjected to statistical analysis using TNAUSTAT. Phenotypic and genotypic coefficients of variation (PCV and GCV) were calculated (4). Broad-sense heritability (H2), representing the proportion of phenotypic variance attributable to genotypic differences, were estimated (5). Furthermore, the expected genetic advance, expressed as percentage of the mean (GAM), was determined (6). Results and Discussion The derived putative mutants of Pink and White Pitchi cultivars were evaluated for three seasons and studied for various phenotypic traits, mean performance, variability, heritability, genetic advance, correlation and path analysis for various vegetative and flowering traits of economic value in order to identify the desirable mutant genotypes with stable performance across the seasons and the results obtained are discussed hereunder. The analysis of variance (ANNOVA) indicated the presence of substantial amount of variation among the genotypes for all the studied traits (Table 1, 2). Mean performance of the mutant genotypes for various economic traits In any crop improvement programme, the genotypes are primarily evaluated based on their phenotypic values. Best genotypes are generally identified based on their higher per se performance, the main selection criterion in many breeding programs. The mutant genotypes that recorded higher mean than the check variety pink pitchi and white pitchi were considered as superior genotypes for vegetative traits (Table 3) and for flowering traits (Table 4). Heritability acts as a gauge for the transmissibility of traits to the subsequent generation (20). The variation must be highly heritable and the traits selected should have more variation with high heritability and genetic advance and to some extent moderate variability with high genetic advance can be considered during selection. Heritability along with genetic advance is very much useful in estimating the influence of environment. Genetic advance refers to the improvement in the mean genotypic value of selected plants over the base population. In the present study, higher estimate of broad sense heritability (more than 60 %) was exhibited by all the genotypes for all the traits and the heritability range was between 71.50 % in corolla tube length and 99.00 % in plant height, number of secondary branches per plant, internodal length and number of leaves per plant. Selection based on simply inherited and highly heritable yield attributes is most effective and reliable approach as compared to direct selection on yield itself. Understanding the nature and extent of association of different yield components with yield and inter relationship among themselves is an essential prerequisite for the formulation of breeding procedure for effective improvement of yield and its components. The aim of correlation studies is primarily to know the suitability of various characters for indirect selection. Correlation studies provide information on the nature and extent of association between any two metric traits and it will be possible to bring about genetic improvement in one trait by selection of the other. The correlation between characters may exist due to various reasons such as pleiotropy, genetic linkage and association of loci or blocks of loci governing variability for different characters located on same chromosome. The extent of observed relationship between two characters is known as phenotypic correlation. Phenotypic correlation among traits is influenced by genotype and environment. Genotypic correlation is usually attributed to pleiotropy and measure the association due to additive and additive x additive gene action and phenotypic correlations measure the environmental deviation together with the non-additive gene action (25). Study of inter relationships of the yield components among themselves besides their correlation with yield itself would be more revealing and useful as correlation between any two characters is influenced by other inter related characters. In the present study, a high magnitude of genotypic correlations compared to the corresponding phenotypic correlations indicated that there was a strong inherent genetic association between the various characters studied and the expression of traits was sensitive to environmental fluctuation. The phenotypic correlation is reduced by the significant interaction of environment and this may confirm the considerable role of environment in modifying the total expression of genotypes (Table 6). Path analysis Flower yield is an interaction of many mutually associated component characters hence change in any one component may disturb the other component. Correlation coefficients help in determining the yield component however they do not provide an exact picture about the relative importance of direct and indirect influence of each component characters towards yield. Path coefficient analysis furnishes the cause and effect of different yield components which would provide better index for selection rather than correlation coefficients. Studies on correlation of characters along with their relative direct and indirect effects on yield are of immense value in selection of superior genotypes from the population (31). Direct effect of yield components on flower yield per plant Among all the traits studied, number of flowering cymes (0.378), number of primary branches (0.197), flower diameter (0.119) and 100 bud weight (0.118) displayed positive direct effects on total flower yield per plant therefore for increasing total flower yield per plant, these traits can be given most preference while going for selection. The highest negative direct effect on total flower yield per plant was exhibited by days to flowering (-0.171), flower bud length (-0.082) followed by corolla tube length (-0.020), stem girth (-0.017) and internodal length (-0.014) suggesting that these traits are not considered while going for selection to flower yield. At the phenotypic level, the flowering cymes (0.266), secondary branches (0.177) followed by primary branches (0.162) exhibited highest direct effect on total flower yield per plant. Negative direct effect was revealed by days to flowering (-0.133), stem girth (-0.032), flower bud length (-0.022), leaf breath (-0.017), internodal length (-0.010) followed by corolla tube length (-0.004) (Table 7, Fig. 5). Indirect effect of yield components on flower yield per plant The parameter number of flowering cymes exhibited positive indirect effect through plant height, primary branches, secondary branches, leaves per plant, leaf length, days to flowering, flower diameter and 100 bud weight and negative indirect effects through stem girth, internodal length, flower bud length, flower bud girth, corolla tube length. The character 100 bud weight revealed positive indirect effect through plant height, primary branches, secondary branches, leaves per plant, leaf length, days to flowering, flowering cymes and flower diameter. Days to flowering showed negative indirect effects through plant height, primary branches, secondary branches, leaves per plant, leaf length, leaf breadth, flowering cymes, flower diameter, flower bud girth and 100 bud weight. Hence, the above results showed that for increasing total flower yield per plant, characters like flowering cymes and 100 bud weight can be given most preference while going for selection. This might be due to more growth habit of some of the genotypes resulting in higher proportion of morphological growth as well as reproductive growth due to mutation that finally resulted in increased flower yield. These results are in conformity with the earlier reports in chrysanthemum (30–32). Conclusion The mutant genotypes derived from the pink and white flower ecotypes of Jasminum grandiflorum L. in M1V3 generation that expressed distinct variations through mutation for plant growth and different traits contributing to yield were selected on comparison with the control of pink and white pitchi. The study confirmed the reliability of the selection for the investigated traits contributing for flower yield and based on the yield performance, 6 mutant genotypes viz., PPM-12, PPM-72 (ethyl methanesulfonate (EMS) derived mutants), PPM-96 and PPM-115 (gamma ray derived mutants) of pink pitchi and two EMS derived mutant genotypes WPM-2 and WPM-25 of white pitchi were identified as the best mutants. text: Plant Science Today, ISSN 2348-1900 (online) Introduction Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton, commonly known as Arabian jasmine, is a floriculture crop of immense cultural and economic significance, particularly in India where it plays an integral role in religious ceremonies, garland manufacturing, perfumery industries and essential oil extraction (1). India's jasmine cultivation occupies approximately 27000 ha, yielding 272000 MT annually, with Tamil Nadu leading national production at 172000 MT from 17000 ha (2). The global jasmine trade, valued at approximately USD 500 million annually, depends critically on maintaining flower quality during long-distance transportation (3). Despite its commercial importance, jasmine cultivation and marketing face significant post-harvest challenges that threaten long -term sustainability and profitability. The inherently perishable nature of jasmine flowers results in rapid quality deterioration, with shelf-life ranging from 2.7 days under conventional storage to 4.16 days with advanced packaging technologies (such as chitosan- based biodegradable films and optimised cold chain systems) (4). The broader horticultural sector experiences post-harvest losses of 20–30 % due to inadequate handling practices, highlighting substantial post-harvest risk for perishable ornamental crops (3). Traditional packaging systems predominantly rely on non- biodegradable materials, particularly expanded polystyrene (EPS), which contribute to environmental degradation while failing to provide optimal preservation conditions (5). The environmental crisis associated with conventional plastics has become increasingly severe, with European markets alone producing 25 million tonnes of plastic waste annually while achieving only 30 % recycling rates (6). Nearly 99 % of conventional plastics originate from non-renewable petrochemical sources, contributing to persistent pollution, greenhouse gas emissions and resource depletion throughout extended product lifecycles (7). Evaluation of mycelium foam packaging for quality preservation of Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton during long-distance transport. Plant Science Today. 2026; 13(sp2): 1-9. https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.13853 Abstract The floriculture industry faces increasing pressure to adopt sustainable packaging solutions while maintaining product quality during long- distance transportation. This study evaluated 4 packaging materials-expanded polystyrene (EPS), mycelium foam, coir-lined carton and aluminium foil-lined carton-for preserving Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton flowers under ice gel conditions (4-6 °C) over 48 hr. Visual, physiological and biochemical parameters were assessed using a completely randomized design (CRD) with 5 replications. Mycelium foam packaging demonstrated consistently higher performance across all quality metrics: highest freshness retention (71.54 % at 48 hr vs. 63.43 % for EPS), colour preservation (77.82 % vs. 68.71 %), extended shelf life (4.12 vs. 3.83 days) and superior moisture retention (49.91 % vs. 40.43 %). Physiological parameters confirmed mycelium superiority with minimum physiological loss in weight (3.59 % vs. 4.65 % for EPS). Biochemical analysis revealed maximum total carbohydrate retention (63.50 mg/g vs. 58.54 mg/g in EPS) and phenolic content (39.94 mg/g vs. 28.26 mg/g in EPS) at 48 hr, indicating suppressed respiration and enhanced antioxidant capacity. The porous hygroscopic structure of mycelium foam provided optimal humidity regulation and thermal buffering (0.04 W/m·K) while offering complete biodegradability within 30-45 days. This study demonstrates that mycelium foam can serve as an effective bio-based alternative to conventional EPS packaging for jasmine flower export, simultaneously enhancing post-harvest quality and environmental sustainability. Keywords: biodegradable packaging; floriculture; jasmine export; mycelium foam; sustainable packaging MOHAMED ET AL 2 https://plantsciencetoday.online use plastic applications across international markets, while consumer purchasing preferences demonstrate clear shifts toward environmentally responsible products (8). These converging pressures-regulatory mandates, consumer demand and corporate sustainability imperatives-create urgent imperatives for the floriculture sector to transition toward biodegradable packaging alternatives. Jasminum sambac presents particularly complex post- harvest challenges, as its delicate white flowers and intense fragrance are accompanied by exceptionally demanding preservation requirements. The flowers exhibit extraordinarily rapid senescence processes characterised by immediate moisture loss, accelerated enzymatic browning and deterioration of essential oil content that directly impacts market value (9). Conventional storage methods demonstrate severe limitations, restricting shelf life to approximately 24–48 hr under ambient storage conditions without cold chain support, while international export markets routinely require 48–72 hr transportation periods with stringent quality maintenance standards throughout the cold chain (10). Recent advances in biodegradable packaging materials have opened new possibilities for sustainable floriculture. Mycelium- based bio composites, manufactured through controlled fungal cultivation on agricultural waste substrates, achieve thermal conductivity values of 0.038–0.05 W/m·K, approaching EPS performance benchmarks while offering complete biodegradability and carbon sequestration benefits (11). Coir pith-based materials utilize abundant coconut processing waste to create naturally structured packaging with inherent cushioning properties and humidity regulation capabilities (12). Aluminium foil-lined carton systems represent transitional approaches combining renewable cellulose-based substrates with metallic barrier properties for enhanced thermal performance (13). Research on jasmine post-harvest management has demonstrated potential for significant improvements through technological interventions. Chitosan-glycerol based biodegradable packaging extended J. sambac shelf life to 4.16 days compared to 2.7 days in untreated controls (4). Export-oriented packaging systems combining boric acid treatment with aluminium-foil lined containers and gel-ice achieved 42.88 hr shelf life with improved freshness and colour retention (14). However, the development of biodegradable packaging specifically optimised for the Ramanathapuram Gundumalli variety for long-distance market transportation remains an urgent priority. This study evaluated the efficacy of three eco-friendly packaging materials-mycelium foam, coir-lined carton and aluminium foil-lined carton-as sustainable alternatives to conventional expanded polystyrene (EPS) packaging for jasmine string flowers under gel-ice cold conditions, assessing their performance across visual, physiological and biochemical parameters to establish viable solutions for the international flower export industry. Materials and Methods Plant material and experimental location The experiment was conducted at the Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, Horticultural College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University, Coimbatore (11°00'57.3" N, 76°55'52.3" E, 457 m above mean sea level) during June 2025. Fresh J. sambac cv. Ramanathapuram Gundumalli flowers were harvested during morning hr (05:00–06:00 hr) from field -grown plants following optimised microbial inoculant treatments (Methylobacterium radiotolerans JSM15 + potassium-solubilising bacteria). Only uniform, unopened flowers with consistent bud size were selected, with flowers exhibiting physical damage, pest infestation, or over-maturity rigorously excluded. Each experimental unit contained 100 g of freshly harvested jasmine string flowers. Experimental design and treatments The experiment employed a completely randomized design (CRD) with 4 packaging treatments and 5 replications, with 2 experimental units per replication (total n=40 packages). The treatments comprised: T₁ - Expanded polystyrene (EPS) packaging (control); T₂ - Mycelium foam packaging; T₃ - Coir pith-lined carton packaging; T₄ - Aluminium foil-lined carton packaging. All packaging materials maintained standardised dimensions (20 cm × 15 cm × 8 cm) to ensure comparable conditions. Packaging material specifications EPS packaging (T₁): Conventional expanded polystyrene with 2.5 cm thickness, density 0.02 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 0.033 W/ m·K, sourced from commercial packaging supplier, Coimbatore . Mycelium foam (T₂): Bio-fabricated mycelium foam derived from agricultural waste substrates (Pleurotus ostreatus cultivated on rice straw), 2.5 cm thickness, density 0.15 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 0.04 W/m·K, laboratory-grown following the protocol of Sivaprasad et al. (15). Briefly, rice straw substrate was sterilised by autoclaving (121°C, 30 min), then inoculated with P. ostreatus oyster mushroom spawn under sterile laminar-flow conditions and packed into acrylic moulds (20 cm × 15 cm × 8 cm) sealed with perforated cling wrap. Moulds were incubated at 28 °C and 70–80 % relative humidity for 7–10 days until complete mycelial colonisation was confirmed visually. Growth was arrested by oven- drying at 80–100 °C for 2–3 hr. Finished panels were demoulded, inspected for structural integrity and trimmed to final packaging dimensions (Fig. 1 and Plate 1A–C). Coir-lined carton (T₃): Processed coir pith with natural binding agents, 1.5 cm thickness, density 0.18 g/cm³, thermal conductivity 0.05 W/m·K, sourced from Coconut Development Board, Tamil Nadu. Aluminium foil-lined carton (T₄): Corrugated cardboard (3 mm, 3- ply) with aluminium foil inner lining (0.01 mm thickness), sourced from packaging materials supplier, Coimbatore . Pre-treatment and packaging protocol Fresh jasmine flower buds were sorted for uniformity, with damaged or over- mature buds removed. Pre-cooling was performed by soaking flower buds for 10–15 min in cold water (4–6 °C) containing 4 % boric acid a concentration established as optimal for jasmine post -harvest quality preservation by Jawaharlal et al. (14). The flower buds were strung with gentle handling to avoid mechanical injury. Exactly 100 g of pre-cooled jasmine strings were weighed using digital balance (±0.01 g accuracy) and packed in small boxes (14 × 7 × 4 cm dimension) lined with food-grade butter paper. Flower boxes were placed in respective packaging materials with gel-ice packs (ThermaFreeze New Jersey, USA) layered between flower boxes, with aluminium foil and butter paper preventing direct gel-ice contact. Gel-ice to product ratio was maintained at 1:2 (w/w). Each 3 Plant Science Today, ISSN 2348-1900 (online) package was sealed using food-grade adhesive tape and stored under ambient conditions (temperature 28–32 °C, relative humidity 60–70 %) for 48 hr to simulate long-distance export conditions. Visual parameter assessment Freshness index (FI): Flowers were scored based on turgidity, petal necrosis, wilting and browning using a 7-point scale (7 = all buds turgid, 1 = fully wilted). FI calculated as: FI was calculated as: FI = [(7×X₁) + (6×X₂) + (5×X₃) + (4×X₄) + (3×X₅) + (2×X₆) + (1×X₇)] / [(X₁ + X₂ + X₃ + X₄ + X₅ + X₆ + X₇) × 7] × 100, where X₁–X₇ represent flower counts in each score category (16). Colour retention index (CRI): Flower colour development scored using 9-point scale (9 = bright white, 1 = completely brown). CRI = [(9×X₁) + (8×X₂) + ... + (1×X₉)] / [(X₁ + X₂ + ... + X₉) × 9] × 100 (16). Shelf life: Number of days until 50 % freshness retention threshold (16). Physiological parameter measurements Moisture content: Fresh and dry weights (70 °C oven-drying) were recorded. Moisture content (%) = [(Fresh weight - Dry weight) / Fresh weight] × 100 (17). Physiological loss in weight (PLW): PLW (%) = [(Fresh weight Day 1- Weight Day 2) / Fresh weight Day 1] × 100. Biochemical parameter estimation Total carbohydrates: Estimated using anthrone method (18). Approximately 100 mg fresh weight of petal tissue per sample was hydrolysed with HCl, neutralised with sodium carbonate and colour development by anthrone reagent measured at 630 nm, expressed as mg glucose/g sample. Colour retention index (CRI): Flower colour development scored using 9-point scale (9 = bright white, 1 = completely brown). Results Visual quality Mycelium foam packaging (T₂) maintained the highest freshness index at 48 hr (71.54 %), exceeding EPS control (63.43 %) by 12.8 %. Colour retention was superior in mycelium packaging (77.82 %) compared to EPS (68.71 %), representing a 13.3 % improvement. Shelf life extended to 4.12 days with mycelium foam versus 3.83 days for EPS-a 7.6 % increase. Coir-lined and aluminium foil-lined cartons showed substantially poorer performance (Table 1). Physiological parameter Mycelium foam maintained the highest moisture content at both 24 and 48 hr, with a progressive decline observed across all treatments. At 48 hr, mycelium foam recorded 49.91 % compared to EPS (40.43 %), coir-lined (29.85 %) and aluminium foil-lined cartons (26.24 %). Physiological weight loss was minimised in mycelium packaging (3.59 %) versus EPS (4.65 %), representing a 22.8 % reduction (Table 2). Biochemical parameters Total carbohydrate content declined progressively in all treatments from 24 to 48 hr. Mycelium foam (T₂) showed the slowest rate of decline, retaining 8.5 % more carbohydrate than EPS at 48 hr. The T₃ and T₄ exhibited substantially greater losses (Table 3). Total phenolic content followed a similar declining pattern. Mycelium foam (T₂) retained 41.3 % more phenolics than EPS at 48 hr, while T₃ and T₄ showed the steepest declines, indicating greater oxidative stress under those packaging conditions (Table 3) (Fig. 2 and 3). The fungal mycelium network creates interconnected micro-pores (15–50 µm diameter) that facilitate controlled water vapour diffusion, preventing desiccation while avoiding condensation- induced microbial proliferation (21). MOHAMED ET AL 6 https://plantsciencetoday.online The thermal properties of mycelium composites (thermal conductivity 0.04 W/m·K) provide effective insulation approaching EPS performance (0.033 W/m·K) while offering superior breathability (22). The controlled gas permeability prevents accumulation of CO₂ and ethylene while ensuring adequate O₂ supply, thereby suppressing fermentative pathways that accelerate deterioration (23). This mechanism explains the 8.5 % higher carbohydrate retention and 41.3 % higher phenolic content observed in mycelium- packaged flowers, indicating suppressed respiratory substrate depletion and enhanced antioxidant capacity. Comparison with alternative materials While EPS provides thermal insulation, its hydrophobic closed-cell structure prevents moisture regulation, leading to quality loss (24). The lack of breathability causes ethylene accumulation, accelerating senescence. Coir-lined carton showed intermediate performance with natural cushioning and humidity regulation, but lower density and higher thermal conductivity resulted in inadequate temperature buffering and accelerated moisture loss (25). Aluminium foil-lined carton performed poorest across all parameters. The impermeable metallic barrier trapped heat and moisture, creating anaerobic conditions conducive to fermentative metabolism and microbial proliferation (26). Physiological and biochemical implications The significantly higher carbohydrate retention in mycelium- packaged flowers (63.50 mg/g vs. 58.54 mg/g in EPS at 48 hr) indicates suppressed respiratory metabolism, as carbohydrates serve as primary energy substrates during post-harvest senescence (27). The moderated oxygen availability through mycelium pore structure likely shifts metabolism toward more efficient aerobic pathways while preventing excessive respiration rates that deplete energy reserves (23). The enhanced phenolic content in mycelium packaging (39.94 mg/g vs. 28.26 mg/g in EPS) suggests that the packaging microenvironment supports antioxidant defence mechanisms. The exceptional colour retention in mycelium packaging (77.82 % vs. 68.71 % in EPS at 48 hr) directly correlates with reduced enzymatic browning and oxidative pigment degradation. Polyphenol oxidase and peroxidase activities, which catalyse browning reactions upon cellular breakdown, are suppressed under the stable microenvironment conditions maintained by mycelium foam (28). The stable humidity prevents desiccation-induced cellular collapse while the breathable structure minimises oxidative stress, collectively preserving petal chromatic quality. Environmental and commercial implications Mycelium foam offers compelling environmental benefits. The material achieves complete biodegradability within 30–45 days under composting conditions, contrasting with centuries-long EPS persistence (29). Production utilises agricultural waste substrates, achieving carbon sequestration while valorising waste streams (30). Life cycle assessments of mycelium-based packaging demonstrate substantially lower environmental impacts across global warming potential, eutrophication and fossil fuel depletion categories compared to petroleum-based plastics (31). The 7.6 % shelf-life extension enables expanded market access for jasmine exports to more distant international markets without quality compromise. Implementation considerations Commercial adoption requires addressing several considerations. Current production costs exceed EPS by approximately 40–60 %, though economies of scale and increasing EPS regulatory restrictions are narrowing this differential. The 7–14-day production timeframe for mycelium cultivation necessitates production planning aligned with jasmine harvest schedules. Quality standardisation represents another challenge, as mycelium composite properties vary with substrate composition and cultivation parameters (32). However, ongoing advances in mycelium manufacturing are progressively improving process control and product consistency (33). Conclusion Mycelium foam packaging demonstrated clear superiority over conventional expanded polystyrene and other eco-friendly alternatives for preserving Jasminum sambac during long-distance transport, achieving 12.8 % higher freshness retention, 13.3 % better colour stability, 7.6 % extended shelf life, 23.5 % improved moisture retention and markedly higher preservation of carbohydrates and phenolics at 48 hr. Its porous hygroscopic structure provides effective humidity regulation, gas exchange control and thermal buffering (0.04 W/m·K), while offering complete biodegradation within 30-45 days-simultaneously addressing product quality and environmental sustainability objectives. These findings support adoption of mycelium foam as a viable bio-based replacement for expanded polystyrene in floriculture export packaging. Future research should focus on scale-up economics, substrate optimisation and performance validation across diverse export route durations and temperature profiles. Horticultural University in Andhra Pradesh, aimed at assessing the impact of different pruning dates and foliar applications of FeSO₄, ZnSO₄ and MgSO₄ on the physiological, biochemical and yield characteristics of Jasminum sambac cv. CO.1 Gundumalli. The experimental design utilized was a Factorial Randomized Block Design that included four distinct pruning dates alongside four micronutrient treatments. The interaction between the timing of pruning and the levels of micronutrients had a significant effect on all examined traits. Specifically, the treatment P₁M₃ (pruning on December 25 combined with foliar applications of FeSO₄, ZnSO₄ and MgSO₄ at a concentration of 0.5% each) achieved the highest values for relative water content (88.17%), leaf area (28.03 cm²), chlorophyll content (61.79 SPAD units), total phenols (3.62 mg g⁻¹), soluble protein content (13.84 mg g⁻¹) and flower cymes per plant (957.00). These findings suggest that conducting pruning on December 25 followed by monthly applications of FeSO₄, ZnSO₄ and MgSO₄ at a rate of 0.5% is an effective strategy to enhance physiological efficiency and optimize flower yield in J. sambac cv. CO.1 Gundumalli. Keywords: J. sambac, foliar micronutrients, physiological traits, pruning date, flower yield Introduction Jasmine (Jasminum sambac Ait.) represents a significant commercial loose flower crop in India, esteemed for its beautiful and fragrant blossoms which are utilized in religious rituals, garlands, hair accessories, as well as in the perfume, cosmetic and essential oil sectors. The success of flower production is heavily reliant on effective crop management practices, with pruning being particularly crucial. This process entails the removal of older shoots to encourage vigorous new growth, enhance light availability and air circulation, decrease disease prevalence, and improve flowering outcomes (Gibson, 1984; Anderson, 1991) [3, 2]. Prior research has indicated that performing pruning during December or January leads to notable improvements in both growth and flower yield for J. sambac. However, the ideal timing for pruning can differ based on cultivar and agro-climatic factors (Singh and Moe, 1980; Pal and Bose, 1981; Pawar et al., 2019; Khanchana and Jawaharlal, 2019) [16, 10, 12, 6]. In addition to pruning, balanced nutrition is critical for enhancing plant growth, flowering capabilities, and flower quality. Among secondary and micronutrients, elements such as iron, zinc and magnesium are essential for processes including chlorophyll production, photosynthesis enhancement, enzyme activation, auxin generation, protein metabolism, carbohydrate conversion, and pollen development (Wallihan et al., 1958; Thorne, 1957; Shukla et al., 2009; Mengel and Kirkby, 2001; Marschner, 2012) [20, 19, 14, 9, 8]. A lack of these nutrients can negatively impact plant development and flower output. While there has been considerable research into the individual impacts of pruning and nutrient management separately, knowledge regarding their combined effects remains scarce. Consequently, this study was conducted to assess how varying pruning dates alongside foliar applications of iron, zinc, and magnesium influence the physiological characteristics and yield of J. sambac cv. CO.1 Gundumalli. Horticultural University, located in Venkataramannagudem. A Factorial Randomized Block Design (FRBD) with two replications was employed for the experiment. The first factor involved four different pruning dates (P1, P2, P3, and P4), while the second factor included four levels of micronutrient applications (M1, M2, M3, and M4). This distinct variety is noted for its increased yield of nine-budded cymes per plant, demonstrating greater productivity compared to the traditional Ramanathapuram Gundumalli variety. Rooted cuttings aged ten months were transplanted into the main field with a spacing of 1.2 x 1.2 meters. Pruning was conducted according to the established schedule up to a height of 50 cm above ground level, followed by monthly foliar applications of micronutrients post-pruning. Regular observations were made on the pruned plants over two years (2024-25 and 2025-26), during which data were collected regarding various physiological leaf parameters such as Relative Water Content (RWC) (%), leaf area (cm²), chlorophyll content (measured in SPAD units), total phenol content (mg g⁻¹), soluble protein content (mg g⁻¹) and yield metrics like the number of flower cymes per plant. The data analysis was performed using ANOVA methods as described by Panse and Sukhatme (1985) [11]. Among the pruning dates, P₃ recorded the highest mean chlorophyll content (53.78 SPAD units), followed by P₂ (51.82 SPAD units) and P₁ (48.77 SPAD units), whereas the lowest value (38.31 SPAD units) was observed under P₄. The interaction effect was significant, and the maximum chlorophyll content (61.79 SPAD units) was recorded in P₃M₁, whereas the minimum (36.93 SPAD units) was observed in P₄M₄. The trend for total phenols was similar. Among the pruning dates, P₃ registered the highest mean phenol content (2.79 mg g⁻¹), followed by P₂ (2.47 mg g⁻¹) and P₁ (2.35 mg g⁻¹), whereas P₄ recorded the lowest value (1.78 mg g⁻¹). The highest total phenol content (3.62 mg g⁻¹) was observed under P₃M₁, whereas the lowest (1.72 mg g⁻¹) was recorded under P₄M₄. The pooled results presented in Table 3 showed that soluble protein content were significantly influenced by pruning dates, micronutrient strengths and their interaction. Among the pruning dates, P₃ recorded the highest mean soluble protein content (12.27 mg g⁻¹), followed by P₂ (11.79 mg g⁻¹) and P₁ (11.28 mg g⁻¹), whereas the lowest value (9.59 mg g⁻¹) was recorded under P₄. The superior performance of P1M3 suggests that optimal pruning combined with balanced foliar nutrition enhanced physiological efficiency and metabolic functioning. Relative water content, an indicator of plant water status and cellular hydration, was higher under P1M3, reflecting improved water uptake, efficient translocation and maintenance of cellular turgor. Magnesium aids in osmotic regulation, while zinc helps to preserve membrane stability and stomatal function, collectively improving tissue water retention. Elevated RWC sustains physiological processes and delays dehydration. Zahed et al. (2006) [21] in gladiolus and Thamaraiselvi (2009) [18] in J. sambac linked higher tissue water content with better physiological performance and delayed senescence. Significantly greater phenol content as recorded under P1M3 might be due to enhanced secondary metabolism stemming from favourable nutritional and physiological conditions. Phenolic compounds act as antioxidants and protectants against oxidative stress. Micronutrients serve as cofactors for enzymes in the phenylpropanoid pathway, promoting phenol biosynthesis. Sanjay et al. (2010) [13] in mango and Kaushik et al. (2020) [5] in peach reported increased total phenols with improved canopy management and pruning. Soluble protein content was found to increase with every increase in micronutrient levels, peaking under M3. This might be due to improved nitrogen assimilation, enzyme production and protein metabolism. Zinc regulates enzymes involved in protein synthesis, iron participates in nitrate reduction and amino acid formation; and magnesium supports ribosomal function and protein assembly. Hence, optimal micronutrient application could encourage greater soluble protein accumulation in leaves. Kumaresan et al. (2017) [7] recorded similar increases in soluble proteins in J. sambac under treatments that enhanced physiological efficiency. Srividhya et al. (2021) [17] also reported higher nitrate reductase activity and protein content following foliar micronutrient application in jasmine. Praneeth Kumar2 1Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, College of Horticulture (SKLTSHU), Rajendranagar, Hyderabad, India 2Floricultural Research Station, (AICRP), Rajendranagar, Hyderabad, India 3Department of Fruit Science, College of Horticulture (SKLTSHU), Mojerla, Wanaparthy District, India *Corresponding author A B S T R A C T Introduction Jasmine (Jasminum sambac L.) Oleaceae member which is a very important commercial loose flower crop in South India. The white fragrant flowers of jasmine are symbol of purity, eternal love, nobility and also symbolizes the beauty of a girl and are usually offered to God for worshiping. Hence, these are preferably planted in Hindu temple gardens and Moghul garden for their quality of serenity. Pruning helps in rejuvenation and encouraging growth of new healthy shoots to bear more flowers. Besides pruning exogenous application of chemicals in jasmine will also result in enhancing growth and flowering. However, the selection of suitable chemicals, dosage and time of application certainly manipulate the growth towards profitable yields of flower crops in A field experiment was conducted at Floricultural Research Station, Agricultural Research Institute, Rajendranagar, SKLTSHU, Hyderabad during 2019-2020 to study the influence of certain chemicals on flower induction, flowering, quality and yield in Jasmine (Jasminum sambac). The experiment was laid out in Randomized Block Design (RBD) with nine treatments and three replications. Results of the experiment revealed that, the plants treated with 0.5 % Thiourea significantly reduced days taken for flower initiation (27.6 days) and influenced to increase number of cymes per plant (137.6), number of flower buds per cyme (5.0), number of flower buds per plant (688.30), the flower quality parameters like length of flower bud (22.56 mm), length of corolla tube (13.30 mm) and width of flower buds (9.62 mm), were also recorded maximum in 0.5 % thiourea. Weight of 100 flower buds (28.03 g), flower yield per plant (192.90 g), flower yield per month in plot (1.153 kg) and flower yield for three months in plot (2.35 kg) were also found superior in 0.5 % thiourea. Besides the natural phytohormones, a group of off season flower inducing chemicals modifies the plant in its growth and developmental behaviour without inducing phytotoxic or malformative effects. It has been reported that the demand for jasmine is increasing due to its unique fragrance but there is a huge demand supply gap of fresh flowers during off season. During the off season the cost of flower increases 10 times than normal season. The balance of production during lean and peak season should be maintained by different horticultural techniques and one of important practice is application of flower inducing chemicals. Thiourea is a nitrogen and sulphur containing compound and is used for its growth promoting attributes in plant biology under different environmental conditions and it is known to have great roles in oxidative stress tolerance and modification of gene expression, regulation and induction of signaling mechanisms (Ratna Kumar et al., 2016). Thiourea, accumulates carbohydrate in plant body which leads to early flower bud initiation as well as bud opening, later which results in lengthening of flowering span (Sainath, 2009). Nitrobenzene is a combination of nitrogen and plant growth regulators, extracted from seaweeds that act as plant energizer, flowering stimulant and yield booster (Aziz and Miah, 2009). Foliar application of nitrobenzene leads to quick absorption and influences the biochemical pathway of the plants to uptake more nutrients from the soil. It also increases nutrient use efficiency thus improves vegetative growth. Further, it also induces profuse flowering and helps in regulation of flowers (Mithila et al., 2012). Similarly, Humic and fulvic acids are called humin materials widely consist of a part of soil organic matter (65-70%) these organic complexes are found naturally in soil (Mackowiak et al., 2001). These humin materials affect the soil properties and physiological properties of plants due to carboxyl (COOH–) and phenolic (OH–) groups (Schnitzer, 1992) which increase plant growth, early flower induction and yield. In the view of the above facts, the present investigation has been taken up to study the influence of various chemicals on flowering aspects of jasmine (Jasminum sambac L.). Materials and Methods The present study was conducted during 2019-2020 at Floricultural Research Station, ARI, Rajendranagar, SKLTSHU, Hyderabad. The experiment was laid out in Randomized Block design with three replications and nine treatments. Pruning was done at a height of 45 cm above the ground level during last week of September the cultivar taken in the study was Gundumalli. After pruning, fertilizers were applied at the rate of 60:120:120g NPK per plant in 2 splits (1/2 N+ full P: K at pruning and remaining 1/2 N was applied after first flush of flowering). Crop was irrigated depending upon the requirement. The pruning operation was done in seven years old plants manually with pruning shears. Foliar application of Nitrobenzene 200 ppm (T1), Nitrobenzene 300 ppm (T2), Humic acid 0.25% (T3), Humic acid 0.5% (T4), Fulvic acid 0.25% (T5), Fulvic acid 0.5% (T6), Thiourea 0.25% (T7), Thiourea 0.5% (T8), Control Water spray (T9) was done until their leaves were completely wet to the point of run off. Spraying was done in two intervals at 30 and 60 days after pruning. The data was collected monthly wise for all the parameters from January to March. Results and Discussion Effect of chemicals on number of days taken for flower initiation The results indicated in Table 1 shows significant differences in initiation of flowering due to chemical sprays. Foliar application of T8 Thiourea 0.5 % induced significantly early flowering (27.6 days) which was significantly followed by thiourea 0.25 % (29.6 days) whereas, the treatment Control (T9) recorded late initiation of flowering (53.0 days) as compared to all other treatments. These results might be due to the fact that plants treated with thiourea have built up sufficient food reserves at initial stages due to suppression of apical dominance, increased number of leaves and mobility of photosynthates from source to sink. This reserve food has been utilized for reproductive purpose with a restriction on vegetative growth which decreases days to flowering (Nandhini et al., 2018) This trend is in concurrence with the findings of Kalicharan, (2012) in Moringa and Jutamanee et al., (2009) in Jasmine. text: Plant Science Today, ISSN 2348-1900 (online) Introduction Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) is one of the most valued aromatic flowering plants, renowned for its captivating fragrance and ornamental appeal. The term ‘Jasmine’ originates from the Persian word Yasmyn, meaning fragrance. Belonging to the family Oleaceae, the genus thrives predominantly in warm and subtropical regions. India serves as a significant centre of diversity, housing nearly 40 indigenous Jasminum species, of which about 20 are cultivated extensively across South India (1). Jasmine holds immense commercial importance serving the floricultural, perfumery, cosmetic and pharmaceutical industries (2). India’s total jasmine cultivation area reached 27.49 thousand hectares, with 272.80 thousand metric tonnes production during 2023-2024 (3). Among major producing states, Tamil Nadu led with 17.10 thousand hectares and 172.05 thousand metric tonnes, followed by Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka. Other states such as West Bengal, Bihar, Kerala and Telangana also contributed to the national output (3). Vegetative and floral quality traits largely influence yield variation among jasmine genotypes. Vegetative parameters such as plant height (PH), number of branches (NB), leaf size (LS) and internodal length (IL) play a vital role in determining the overall vigor and yield potential of jasmine plants (4). These morphological traits influence light interception, photosynthetic efficiency and the number of flowering shoots (5). Variation in vegetative growth among Jasminum genotypes reflects their genetic adaptability to environmental conditions and management practices. Plant Science Today. 2026; 13(sp1): 1-12. https://doi.org/10.14719/pst.12676 Abstract Integrated comparative studies combining morphology, sensory attributes and aroma profiling in Jasminum auriculatum genotypes are limited, hindering the identification of superior types for commercial and perfumery use. The current study aimed to evaluate the morpho- physiological traits, floral quality and aroma profile of three J. auriculatum genotypes, CO.2 Mullai, Muthu Mullai and Pacha Mullai to identify superior types for commercial cultivation and perfumery applications. The field experiment was conducted at the Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU), Coimbatore, during 2023–2025, using a randomized block design (RBD) with five replications. All vegetative and floral parameters showed significant genetic variability. Among the genotypes, CO.2 Mullai recorded the maximum height (157.5 cm), longest buds (3.11 cm), highest flower yield (FY) (2437.6 g plant-1) and the highest concrete recovery (0.287 %), proving to be the best. As part of the sensory evaluation using a nine-point hedonic scale, CO.2 Mullai achieved the highest total acceptability (mean score = 2.17), mainly owing to its strong, pleasant scent. Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry analysis revealed 19 volatile compounds across different genotypes, with CO.2 Mullai showing linalool (3.62 %), caryophyllene (5.51 %) and acetic acid methyl ester (12.98 %) as the main contributors to its floral scent. Muthu Mullai had more α-farnesene (6.26 %) and linalool (4.82 %), while Pacha Mullai exhibited the highest acetic acid methyl ester (30.21 %) content. The combination of morphological, sensory and metabolite data led to the conclusion that CO.2 Mullai was the genotype with the highest FY, fragrance quality and concrete recovery. However, Pacha Mullai remains noteworthy for its green buds and distinct floral scent, which hold emerging market appeal. These attributes collectively determine market value and consumer preference (6). High-yielding cultivars with desirable flower morphology, fragrance intensity and postharvest longevity are crucial for sustainable production. In Jasminum auriculatum, known locally as Mullai, the growth behaviour, flower quality and adaptation to stress conditions contribute to differences in yield potential and market acceptability (7-9). Thus, identifying genotypes that combine high productivity with superior floral traits is essential for varietal improvement and commercialization. Beyond floral morphology, the chemical composition of floral scent is a defining characteristic of jasmine quality. The essential oil extracted from freshly opened flowers contains a complex mixture of volatile compounds, such as benzyl acetate, linalool, indole, methyl anthranilate and cis- jasmone (10). A comparative gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) profiling of J. auriculatum genotypes revealed chemotypic diversity and enabled differentiation of cultivars based on essential oil composition (11). Such profiling is invaluable for selecting high-quality aromatic types, for breeding programs targeting enhanced fragrance and for quality assurance in perfumery and pharmaceutical applications. Considering the above aspects, the present investigation was undertaken to evaluate the vegetative and yield performance of different J. auriculatum genotypes and to characterize their GC- MS-based aroma profiles. The study aims to identify promising genotypes combining superior growth, flower yield (FY) and essential oil composition that are suitable for large-scale commercial cultivation and crop improvement programs. Materials and Methods The present investigation on J. auriculatum genotypes was conducted at the Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, Horticultural College and Research Institute, Tamil Nadu Agricultural University (TNAU), Coimbatore (11°02′ N, 76°57′ E; altitude 426.72 m above mean sea level (MSL)) during 2023– 2025. The experimental field consisted of sandy loam soil with a pH of 8.69 and an electrical conductivity of 0.33 dSm-1. Three genotypes of J. auriculatum namely, CO.2 Mullai, Muthu Mullai and Pacha Mullai were selected for evaluation based on their commercial importance, flower quality and local adaptability. The plant materials were obtained from the Jasmine germplasm plot maintained at the Department of Floriculture and Landscape Architecture, TNAU, Coimbatore. The meteorological data for the study period were obtained from the Agro Climate Research Centre, TNAU, Coimbatore (Supplementary table 1). The mean annual temperature was 24.8 °C, with the highest (36.2 °C) recorded in April and the lowest (19.2 °C) in December. Relative humidity ranged from 47.6 (March) to 88.1 % (July). Rainfall was highest in May (11.33 mm), while sunshine duration was longest during March–April (10 h day-1) and shortest in July (3.3 h day-1). Assessment of growth and yield parameters Vegetative parameters, including PH, number of primary and secondary branches were measured. Internodal length, leaf length (LL), width and thickness were measured using digital calliper. Flower parameters, including flower bud weight, FBL, CTL, BG and OFD and yield parameters, namely FY per plant, SL and concrete yield, were measured. The total fresh FY from each plant was recorded daily and averaged for FY per plant. Shelf life was determined as the number of hr during which ≥ 50 % of flowers remained fresh under ambient conditions. Concrete yield was determined by solvent extraction (12). Fifty grams of freshly harvested flowers were extracted in a Soxhlet apparatus using food -grade hexane as solvent. The distillation process continued for five cycles, each lasting 30 to 45 min for solvent evaporation and condensation, until the extraction of concrete from the flowers. Sensory analysis of fresh flowers A sensory evaluation of J. auriculatum flowers was conducted to assess the human-perceived fragrance and visual quality of the genotypes. Freshly harvested flowers from all three genotypes (CO.2 Mullai, Muthu Mullai and Pacha Mullai) were taken early in the morning and presented to a panel of 30 evaluators comprising flower vendors, consumers and perfumery experts at the Coimbatore Corporation Flower Market, Tamil Nadu. Along with three J. auriculatum genotypes, the popular J. sambac cv. Ramanathapuram Gundumalli with higher perceived fragrance and J. multiflorum cv. White Kakada with lower perceived fragrance levels were included for comparison. The evaluators rated four sensory attributes, namely, floral scent intensity, floral scent likeliness, flower colour appeal and overall appeal, using a 9-point hedonic scale where 1 = extremely low/least liked and 9 = extremely high/most liked (Table 1) (13). Volatile metabolite profile of J. auriculatum genotypes Approximately 100 g of freshly opened flowers (with calyx and corolla) were collected early in the morning before 9 AM and sealed in glass containers to prevent volatile loss. Samples were analysed within 4 hr of harvest. The oven temperature was programmed from 40 °C (3 min hold) to 80 °C at 10 °C min-1, then to 120 °C at 15 °C min-1 and finally to 180 °C at 10 °C min-1 (2.33 min hold).
