These samples were analyzed for chemical properties such as pH, EC, available nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. 3.9.1 Soil pH Soil pH was determined in soil : water (1:2.5) suspension by using a digital pH meter (Jackson, 1973). 3.9.2 Electrical conductivity (EC) After measuring the pH, the supernatant solution was used for measuring the electrical conductivity using a conductivity bridge and expressed in dS/m. 3.9.3 Available nitrogen It was determined by alkaline potassium permanganate method. Soil samples were added with excess alkali and potassium permanganate solution. The ammonia evolved was absorbed in boric and was titrated against standard acid (Subbaiah and Asija, 1956). 3.9.4 Available phosphorus The available phosphorus in the soil was extracted using the Brays-I reagent (0.03 N ammonium fluoride in 0.025 N HCl). The available P in the extract was estimated by chlorostannous reduced molybdophosphate blue colour method by taking OD at 660 nm in a spectrophotometer (Jackson, 1973). 3.9.5 Available potassium The available potassium in the soil was extracted with neutral normal ammonium acetate solution and determined using a flame photometer (Elico model CL361) (Jackson, 1973). 3.10 MICROBIOLOGICAL ANALYSIS 3.10.1 Estimation of microbial population in the rhizosphere of jasmine grown in the experimental plot Sample collection Soil samples were collected from each treatment plot after pruning of jasmine plants and before imposing the treatments (i.e. at the initial stage) and at 90 DAP i.e., before applying second dose of fertilizers. The samples were analyzed for total bacteria, fungi, actimycetes by using nutrient agar, MRBA and Kuster’s agar media respectively. The samples collected at 90 DAP were analyzed for P-solubilizers free living, N2 fixers, Trichoderma and fluorescent pseudomonads on TCP medium, Norris N-free medium, TSM and King’s B medium, respectively. 3.10.2 Estimation of microbial load in lignite based biofertilizers All the biofertilizers used in the experimentation were analyzed for their respective microbial loads as done in 3.8.1. Azospirillum biofertilizer culture contained 5.0 x 107 cfu/g population, PSB culture – 4.7 x 107 cfu/g, Trichoderma culture – 3 x 105 cfu/g and P. fluorescens culture – 4.6 x 107 cfu/g. 3.10.3 Testing the compatibility of microbial inoculants The microbial inoculants viz., Azospirillum sp. (ACD-15 and ACD-20), phosphate solubilizer (Pseudomonas striata). Pseudomonas fluorescens (WGUK 327(2) and Trichoderma viridae were purified by four way streaking and tested for compatibility amongst themselves before using them in the experimentation following the dual culture assay. 3.10.4 Enzyme activities 3.10.4.1 Dehydrogenase activity Dehydrogenase activity in the soil samples were determined by following the procedure as described by Casida et al. (1964). Ten grams of soil and 0.2 g CaCO3 were thoroughly mixed and dispensed in test tubes. To each tube was added one ml of 3 per cent aqueous solution of 2, 3, 5-triphenyl tetrazolium chloride (TTC), one ml of one per cent glucose solution and eight ml of distilled water which was sufficient to leave a thin film of water above the soil layer. The tubes were stopped with rubber cork and incubated at 30°C for 24 hrs. At the end of incubation, the contents of the tube were rinsed down into a small beaker and a slurry made by adding 10 ml methanol. The slurry was filtered through Whatman No. 50 paper. Repeated rinsing of soil with one ml methanol was continued till the filtrate ran free of red colour. The colour sampled was measured at 485 nm against a methanol blank using Graphicord Shimadzu UV visible spectrophotometer (model UV-240). The concentrations of formazan in soil samples were determined by referring to a standard curve prepared by using graded concentration of formazan. The results were expressed as µg of triphenyl formazan (TPF) formed g-1 soil per day. 3.10.4.2 Urease activity The procedure adopted to determine the urease activity of soil was essentially the same as adopted by Pancholy and Rice (1973) except that the ammonia liberated due to hydrolysis used in the reaction mixture was determined by nesslerization as described by Jackson (1973). Ten grams each of freshly collected soil samples were placed in 100 ml capacity Erlenmeyer flasks to which one ml toluene was added and allowed to stand for 15 minutes to permit complete penetration into soil. Each of these flasks were added with 10 ml of phosphate buffer (pH 6.7) and 10 ml of 10 per cent urea solution. For control flasks, urea solution was replaced by equal quantity of distilled water. The contents of the flasks were well shaken for five minutes and incubated at 30°C for 24 hrs. After incubation, the contents of the flasks were filtered through Whatman No. 42 filter paper. The remaining soil in the flask were added with 15 ml of 1 N KCl solution shaken for five minutes and filtered. The volume of the total filterate was made upto 100 ml in a volumetric flask using distilled water. The amount of ammonia present in the filterate was determined by nesslerization. One ml filtrate of each sample was transferred to a 20 ml volumetric flask to which two ml of ten per cent sodium tartarte solution and 0.5 ml of Nessler’s reagent were added. The volume was made upto 20 ml with distilled water. The yellow colour developed after 30 minutes was measured at 410 nm using Graphicord Shimadzu UV-visible spectrophotometer (model UV 240) against the reagent blank. 3.10.4.3 Phosphatase activity Phosphatase activity of soil samples was determined by following the procedure of Evazi and Tabatabai (1979). One gram of soil sample was placed in a 50 ml Erlenmeyer flask to which 0.2 ml toluene followed by 4 ml of modified universal buffer (pH 7.5) were added. One ml of P-nitrophenol phosphate solution made in modified universal buffer was added to the flasks and contents of the flasks were mixed by swirling for two minutes. The flasks were stoppered and incubated at 37°C for one hour. After incubation, one ml of 0.5 M CaCl2 and four ml of 0.5 M NaOH were added to the flask, swirled and filtered through Whatman No. 42 filter paper. DISCUSSION In the universe of flowers used for their fine precious scent used in perfumes, no other blossom stands alone as ubiquitous as jasmine, with the possible exception of rose. Commercial floriculture, particularly cultivation of jasmine is being taken up by large number of farmers. Jasmine is a perennial crop and requires heavy doses of chemical fertilizers which further increase with the age of the plant. In the recent past, more interest is evinced about sustainable agriculture. Escalating cost of inorganic fertilizers and the environmental pollution that they cause when applied in excess have called for the use of natural resources as a supplementary source to achieve targeted agricultural production. The use of cost effective and ecofriendly biofertilizers, replacing a part of the recommended inorganic fertilizer, is one of the steps towards sustainable agriculture and is necessary in jasmine cultivation also whose nutrients requirement is very high. The combined application of chemical, bio and organic fertilizers may be useful in the production of quality flowers as well. Hence, in this regard, field experiments were laid out on the University farm as well as on a farmer’s field to study the effects of biofertilizers at different doses of chemical fertilizers on yield and quality of jasmine flowers. The results obtained are discussed in this chapter. 5.1 EFFECT OF BIOFERTILIZERS ON PLANT GROWTH PARAMETERS OF JASMINE The biofertilizer consortium used consisted of Azospirillum sp. (ACD-15, ACD-20) a free living N2 fixer, Pseudomonas striata, a P-soluiblizer, P. fluorescens (WGUK 327(2)), a plant growth promoting rhizobacterium and Trichoderma viridae, a phytohormone producing fungus. Different levels of recommended NPK i.e. 100 per cent, 75 per cent and 50 per cent were tested with and without biofertilizer application. In general, various growth parameters like plant height, number of branches, number of leaves, plant canopy and leaf area were improved due to the application of biofertilizers in combination with chemical fertilizers in field experiments, both on the University farm and the farmer’s field. Biofertilizer application enhanced plant height at all stages of growth compared to chemical fertilizer application alone. And, the highest plant height was observed in the plants receiving 100 per cent NPK + biofertilizers (T4 treatment). Similar trend was observed even in the experiment on the farmer’s field. Increased cell elongation and cell multiplication due to enhanced nutrient uptake by plants following inoculation of Azospirillum and P-solubilizing bacteria (PSB) probably caused the increased plant height (Preethi et al., 1999). This can also be attributed to the production of plant growth promoting substances in the vicinity of roots by the inoculated microorganisms. Azospirillum ACD-15 and ACD-20 strains, used in our study, produced copious amounts of IAA and GA (Amitha and Savalagi, 2004). Plant growth promoting factors like IAA, GA and cytokinin like substances are also known to be produced by PSB (Gowda, 2004 and Jagadish, 2006) and fluorescent pseudomonads (Suneesh, 2004; Indira and Bagyraj, 1997). And, IAA is known to be involved in root initiation, cell division and cell enlargement (Salisbury, 1994). Inoculation technology, which encourages proliferation of pre-selected efficient microorganisms in association with crop plants is known to enhance plant growth and nutrient uptake. In the recent past, it has been documented that inoculation with more than one microorganism benefits crops by enhancing the synergistic action of the associates in growth and nutrient uptake (Subba Rao et al., 1985). Significant increase in plant height and spread due to combined application of Azospirillum, PSB and inorganic fertilizers has been reported earlier in crossandra (Narashima Raju and Haripriya, 2001) and gundumalli (Manonmani, 1992). Similar results were obtained by the application of Azotobacter + PSB + VAM in Valeriana jatamansi (Salathia, 2005) and gladiolus (Srivastava and Govil, 2005) as well. Although non-significant, in general, biofertilizer application increased the number of jasmine branches per plant, in the farmer’s field experiment. T6 (50% RDF + biofertilizer) was on par with T1 (100% RDF), indicating a saving of cost on NPK fertilizers by 50 per cent (Fig. 9). This could be explained by the activities of the inoculants viz., nitrogen fixation, release of Pi from insoluble phosphates, production of phytohormones etc. with simultaneous uptake of nutrients by the inoculated plants. PGPS produced by Azospirillum are known to be involved in breaking of apical dominance, resulting in higher number of branches (Parvatham et al., 1989). Although non-significant, number of leaves and plant canopy and leaf area were higher in plants treated with biofertilizers along with chemical fertilizers when compared to chemical fertilizers alone. This may be due to better availability of nutrients and congenial conditions created, in the vicinity of root zone by the biofertilizers to absorb more nutrients, besides production of bioactive substances by Azospirillum (Dhanpal et al., 1978). In the farmer’s field experiment, number of leaves in T6 was on par with that of T1 indicating T6 as a promising treatment. The leaf area of the plant plays an important role in photosynthetic activity, as it intercepts more of radiant energy from sunlight. The maximum leaf area in jasmine was observed due to application of biofertilizers along with different levels of NPK fertilizers. A leaf area of 10.23 cm² per plant was recorded in T6 treatment (50% RDF + biofertilizer) which is on par with T1 (100% RDF) with 9.44 cm² per plant. Increased leaf area in these treatments could be attributed to enhanced cell division and cell elongation by the production of bio- active substances produced by Azospirillum, PSB, P. fluorescens and T. viridae. Inbar et al. (1994) reported growth promotion in cucumber and pepper seedlings due to inoculation with Trichoderma harzianum. The results of the experiment showed that the inoculation of biofertilizers significantly influenced the quality parameters of jasmine flowers. Treatment of plants with biofertilizers had a significant effect on various floral characteristics viz., time taken for bud initiation, days taken for first flowering and 50 per cent flowering, stalk and petal length and shelf life of flowers (Plate 5). Plants receiving 50 per cent recommended dose of NPK fertilizer + biofertilizers took significantly lesser number of days for bud initiation (108.5 days), first flowering (115.00 days) and 50 per cent flowering (150.83 days) in comparison to T1 (100% RDF) (Fig. 9). Significantly higher stalk and petal length were produced in treatment T6 (50% RDF + biofertilizer) as compared to 100 per cent NPK. Thus substituting NPK fertilizers by biofertilizers to the extent of 50 per cent (Fig. 10). Similar observations were made in the farmer’s field also. The significant increase in these floral characters might be due to the production of auxins by microbial inoculants which brought about an increase in cell division and cell elongation as observed by Preethi et al. (1990) in rose and Velmurugan (1998) in African marigold. The cell enlargement which occurred as a result of plasticitiy of cell wall is known to reduce wall pressure around the cell wall and, therefore, pressure caused by osmotic forces in the vascular sap led to entry of water in to the cell. This results in cell enlargement and thereby improves floral characters (Padmadevi et al., 2004). Similar effects of Azospirillum and PSB on tuberose spike length of have been reported by Swaminathan et al. (1999) and Wange et al. (1995). Parvatham and Vijayan (1989) observed that Azospirillum treated bhendi plants flowered earlier, produced higher number of flowers and ultimately the number of fruits. They attributed the increase in flowers and fruits to the vigorous vegetative growth resulting from increased activity of phytohormones produced by Azospirillum. Increase in fruit length, girth and volume could be due to the increased photosynthetic activity which, in turn, might have favored an increased accumulation of dry matter and also efficient partitioning of photosynthates towards the sink. In jasmine, flowers having higher diameter are preferred. The treatments tested differed significantly with respect to flower diameter. Flower diameter in plants treated with 50 per cent RDF + biofertilizers (T6) was on par with T1 treatment. This may be ascribed to early breaking of apical dominance followed by easy and better translocation of nutrients to flowers, which are brought about by the activity of beneficial microorganisms in the biofertilizer formulations. Another fascinating observation was the significant influence of biofertilizers the post harvest behaviour of jasmine flowers. Besides saving NPK, biofertilizers improved shelf life of loose flowers (Fig. 9). The highest shelf life of loose flowers (52.67 h) was recorded in T5 (75% RDF + biofertilizers). This accounts to 33.34 per cent increase over T1 (100% RDF). Further T6 treatment (50% RDF + biofertilizers) was on par with T1 treatment (100% RDF). Similar beneficial effects of biofertilizers and vermicompost on shelf life have been reported in marigold (Anuradha et al., 1990; Mashaldi, 2000). Inoculation of jasmine plants with biofertilizers had a significant impact on flower yield. An average 10 per cent increase in flower yield were obtained due to biofertilizers at different levels of NPK tested. Plants receiving 75 per cent RDF + biofertilizers yielded about 5 per cent higher than plants receiving 100 per cent RDF. And, 50 per cent RDF + biofertilizers treatment (T6) resulted in flower production on par with 100 per cent RDF (T1), showing a saving of chemical fertilizers by 50 per cent (Fig. 9). The increase in number of flowers may be explained by the role of Azospirillum though atmospheric nitrogen fixation, better root proliferation, uptake of nutrients and water, higher leaf number and area. Higher photosynthesis enhanced food accumulation which might have resulted in better plant growth and subsequently higher number of flowers per plant and hence, more flower yield per plant. Besides this, increase in flower yield may be attributed to increased availability and uptake of phosphorus (Kundu and Gaur, 1980). And, the beneficial effects of Pseudomonas fluorescens might have played a secondary role in increasing the flower yield. Plate.5. An increase in the activities of all the enzymes was noticed, as the age of the plants was increased up to 90 DAP. The treatment T6 (50% RDF + biofertilizers) exhibited significantly higher enzymatic activities at all stages and in all enzymes, when compared to T1 (100% + RDF) (Fig. 12). Thus, the treatment T6 (50% NPK + biofertilizer) could be rated as the best treatment combination. It promoted the rhizosphere colonization of general groups of microorganisms as well as functionally important microorganisms, leading to higher enzymatic activities resulting in enhanced nutrient uptake which led to increased growth, yield and quality of jasmine flowers. The findings of the present field experiments have clearly brought out the positive effects of biofertilizers on yield and quality of jasmine. The application of biofertilizer consortium consisting of Azospirillium, Pseudomonas striata, bacteria Psuedomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma viridae has promoted growth and yield of jasmine flowers, enhanced NPK content in leaves and improved floral characteristics including shelf life. Biofertilizer application along with 50 per cent NPK fertilizers was as effective as 100 per cent NPK fertilizer application in all the parameters. SUMMARY AND CONCLUSIONS Field experiments were conducted one each on the University Farm and a farmer’s field at Chigateri village, Harapanahalli Taluk, Davanagere District. The effect of biofertilizers on growth, yield, quality and nutrient content in Jasmine were assessed in presence of different levels of chemical fertilizers. The biofertilizers used included the lignite based cultures of Azospirillum, Pseudomonas striata, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma viridae. The salient features of the findings are outlined below. 1. Biofertilizer application enhanced various growth parameters at all stages of growth compared to chemical fertilizer application alone. 2. Application of biofertilizers along with 50 per cent NPK brought about results on par with 100 per cent NPK fertilizer with respect to chlorophyll content, floral characteristics such as days taken to 50 per cent flowering, number and weight of flowers per plant, diameter of flowers, ten flower weight and flower yield per plant and shelf life of flowers, indicating replacement of NPK chemical fertilizers to the extent of 50 per cent. 3. Biofertilizer application improved chlorophyll content by 4.7 per cent when compared to 100 per cent RDF. 4. Inoculation of biofertilizers influenced the post harvest behaviour of jasmine flowers. Besides saving NPK, biofertilizers improved shelf-life of the loose flowers by over 33 per cent when compared to 100 per cent NPK treatment. 5. Flower diameter and stalk length which govern the quality were increased by 8.6 per cent and 11.2 per cent respectively due to T6 treatment, 50 per cent RDF + biofertilizers. 6. T6 treatment improved jasmine petal length by 13.4 per cent when compared to T1. 7. T6 treatment substituted 50 per cent NPK without sacrificing flower yield. 8. Biofertilizer application improved the total microbial population in the rhizosphere by several times. T6 treatment resulted in the highest colonization of N2 fixers, P- soluiblizers, P. fluorescens and T. viridae in the rhizopshere of jasmine when compared to all other treatments. 9. In addition to 50 per cent savings on chemical fertilizers, About 10 per cent increase in flower yield was obtained due to T6 treatment. 10. T6 treatment exhibited significantly higher enzymatic activities at all stages and in all enzymes when compared to T1 treatment (100% RDF). Thus, the field experiments have indicated that the application of biofertilizer consortium has brought about positive effects on vegetative growth, yield, quality and shelf- life of jasmine and rhizosphere microbial population. Its application along with 50 per cent NPK chemical fertilizers was as effective as 100 per cent NPK fertilizer application in all the parameters, indicating a net saving of chemical fertilizers by 50 per cent. JAYAMMA 2008 Dr. K. S. JAGADEESH MAJOR ADVISOR ABSTRACT Field experiments were conducted one each on the University Farm and a farmer’s field at Chigateri village, Harapanahalli Taluk, Davanagere District to study the effect of biofertilizers on growth, yield, quality and nutrient content in Jasmine with different levels of chemical fertilizers. The biofertilizers used included the lignite based cultures of Azospirillum, Pseudomonas striata, Pseudomonas fluorescens and Trichoderma viridae. Biofertilizer application enhanced various growth parameters at all stages of growth compared to chemical fertilizer application alone. Application of biofertilizers along with 50 per cent NPK brought about results on par with 100 per cent NPK fertilizer with respect to chlorophyll content, floral characteristics such as days taken to 50 per cent flowering, number and weight of flowers per plant, diameter of flowers, ten flower weight, flower yield per plant and shelf life of flowers, indicating replacement of NPK chemical fertilizers to the extent of 50 per cent. Biofertilizer application improved chlorophyll content by 4.7 per cent, shelf-life of the loose flowers by over 33 per cent when compared to 100 per cent NPK treatment. Flower diameter, stalk length and petal length were increased by 8.6 per cent, 11.2 per cent and 13.4 per cent respectively due to T6 treatment (50% RDF+biofertilizers). Biofertilizer application improved the total microbial population in the rhizosphere by several times. T6 treatment resulted in the highest colonization of N2 fixers, P-soluiblizers, P. fluorescens and T. viridae in the rhizopshere of jasmine when compared to all other treatments. In addition to 50 per cent savings on chemical fertilizers, about 10 per cent increase in flower yield was obtained due to T6 treatment. T6 treatment exhibited significantly higher activities of urease, dehydrogenase and phosphatase at all stages when compared to T1 treatment (100% RDF).

The treatments were comprised of the ten combinations of organic manures and inorganic fertilizers i.e. T1 - Recommended dose of fertilizer (RDF), T2 - RDF +Azotobacter+ PSB, T3- 75 % RDF + Azotobacter + PSB, T 4 - 50 % RDF + Azatobacter + PSB, T 5- 100 % N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB, T6 - 100 % N (Cow Dung Slurry) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB, T7 - 100% N (Farm Yard Manure)+ remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter + PSB, Ts - 50 % N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of NPK through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB, T9 - 50 % N (Cow Dung Slurry) + remaining dose of NPK through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB and T1o - 50 % N (Farm yard manure) + remaining dose of NPK through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB. The experiment was laid out in randomized block design with three replications. The results obtained in the present investigation indicated that, the productive shoot planr1, number of days for initiation of leaves primary shoor1 , leaf area, weight. of 100 flower buds (51.15 g), number of flower buds planr1 (611.33), flower yield (23.15 q ha-1), diameter of flower bud (mm), mean corolla tube length (1.07 mm), length of flower bud excluding corolla tube length (0.97 em) ) were found maximum under the treatment T2 with application of RDF + Azotobacter + PSB. Whereas number of days for emergence of first flower bud (78.67 days) and 50 per cent flowering (91.00 days) were recorded minimum in treatment T2 with application of RDF + Azotobacter + PSB and it was at par with treatment T 5 receiving 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB. In case of number of days for longevity of intact flower (1.31 days), flower bud index (1.1 0), shelf life of flower (0.96 days) and oil content in fresh flower (0.41%) were found maximum under the treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB. In case of the maximum nutrient content like total N, P, K and S from flower and leaves and soil physical property i.e. lowest bulk density and highest maximum water holding capacity were found in treatment T5 receiving 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers+ Azotobacter+ PSB. Similarly, soil chemical properties i.e. pH, EC, ·organic carbon, calcium carbonate, available N, P, K and S content and micronutrients Cu, Fe, Mn and Zn were also studied. There was decrease in pH, EC and calcium carbonate whereas, increase in organic carbon, available nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and sulphur content and micronutrients Cu, Fe, Mn and Zn in soil and highest values were recorded due to application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter + PSB in treatment T 5. Though the treatment Ts was more but it was at par with treatment Te (FYM instead of vermicompost) and treatment T7 (cow dung slurry instead of vermicompost) for nearly all the parameters. Therefore, from the above findings it can be said - that, application of vermicompost or FYM or cow dung slurry, biofertilizers along with inorganic fertilizers increases yield and yield attributing .v characters as well as improve fertility and productivity of soil i.e. maintain soil health. Therefore integrated nutrient management is best for productivity and sustainability of soil health. Jasmine flowers have been used to flavour tea for many centuries by the Chinese. The flowers are also edible and have a sweet taste. Recommended dose of phosphorus (240 kg ha.1) and potassium (120 kg ha"1) were applied uniformly through chemical fertilizers to each treatment plot immediately after pruning. The recommended dose of nitrogen required for jasmine i.e. 120 kg ha·1 was applied as a control treatment. Half dose of nitrogen was applied immediately after pruning of the plants 29 and the remaining half dose of nitrogen was applied 30 day after pruning. The nitrogen content of organic manures was calculated after analysing vemicompost, cow dung slurry and farm yard manure and according to nitrogen content exact dose of each organic manure to supply recommended dose of nitrogen was decided and applied to each plot as per the treatment. Cow dung slurry was prepared by mixing 20 kg fresh cow dung in 200 lit water+ 4 lit fresh cow urine + 2 kg jaggery + 1 kg gram flour and allowed it to decompose up to 4 days by stirring the mixture once a day and then the fresh slurry was applied once in 15 days interval from pruning up to flower bud initiation. Well decomposed farm yard manure, vermicompost and biofertilizers were obtained from Horticulture section, College of Agriculture, Nagpur. Azotobacter and PSB were applied to the soil @20 kg ha·1 each by mixing with organic manures. The organic manures, biofertilizers and inorganic fertilizers were applied 15 em deep in rings and 15 em away from the main stem. FYM, vermicompost and biofertilizers were applied once after pruning. The experiment was laid out in Randomized Block Design with 10 treatments and 3 replications. The technique of random sampling was adopted and treatment wise five plants were selected from each plot for recording various observations from all the replications, and results are summarized as below. 1. The maximum number of productive shoot planr1 (26. 75), maximum number of days for initiation of leaves primary shoor1 and leaf area were recorded in treatment T2 with application of RDF + Azotobacter+ PSB. 2. The minimum number of days for emergence of first flower bud (78.67 days) and 50 per cent flowering (91.00 days) were recorded in treatment T2 with application of RDF +Azotobacter+ PSB and maximum number of days for longevity of intact flower (1.31 days) were recorded in treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB. 3. The yield contributing characters like weight of 100 flower buds (51.15 g), maximum number of flower buds planr1 (611.33) and flower yield (23.15 q ha"1) were found maximum under the treatment T2 with application of RDF + Azotobacter+ PSB, but it was at par with treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical 73 fertilizers+ Azotobacter+ PSB and yield percent decrease by 2.77 over the control. 4. The better flower quality in terms of length of flower bud (em) was found maximum under the treatment T1 with application of recommended dose of fertilizer (RDF), diameter of flower bud (mm), mean corolla tube length (1.07 mm), length of flower bud excluding corolla tube length (0.97 em) were found maximum under the treatment T2 with application of RDF + Azotobacter + PSB, whereas flower bud index (1.1 0), shelf life of flower (0.96 days) and oil content in fresh flower (0.41 %) were found maximum under the treatment T 5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter+ PSB. 5. The nutrient content in flowers N (1.66%), P (0.44%) and K (1.65%) were also significantly maximum in treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB and S {1.20%) was found maximum under the treatment Te with application of 100% N (Cow Dung Slurry)+ remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers + Azotobacter + PSB. However the maximum nutrient content in plant N (2.42%), P (0.27%), K (2.24%) and S (0.97%) were recorded in treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB. 6. The lowest bulk density (1.20 Mg m-3) and highest maximum water holding capacity (51.60%) were recorded in treatment T5 with application of 100% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers+ Azotobacter+ PSB. 7. The lowest value of pH (7.05), EC (0.15 ds m-1) and CaC03 (3.16%) and highest value of organic carbon (5.97 g kg-1 ) were recorded in treatment T5 with application of 100% N 74 (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB. 8. The highest content of availability of nitrogen (354.51 kg ha"1), phosphorus (18.89 kg ha·\ potassium (321 .00 kg ha"1) and sulphur (13.21 kg ha-1) in soil after harvest of jasmine were recorded in treatment T 5 with application of 1 00% N (Vermicompost) + remaining dose of P and K through chemical fertilizers +Azotobacter+ PSB. INTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the important group of flowering plants cultivated on commercial scale and is highly esteemed for its fragrant flowers. In India, it is specially appreciated where most of the people have a love for fragrant flowers. The word jasmine has been derived from Persian word "Yasmin" meaning fragrance. The scent emitted by jasmine is so well liked that the word jasmine has become synonym for fragrance. For the past many centuries, jasmines have adorned the gardens of Central Asia, Afghanistan, Iran, Nepal and many other tropical and sub-tropical countries. Jasmine belongs to the family Oleaceae. Genus Jasminum comprises of about 300 species which are dispersed in the warmer parts of Asia, Africa, Europe and Pacific region (Bhattacharjee, 1980). More than 40 species have been identified in India and about 20 species are identified in South India and some are under cultivation (Watt, 1890). Most of the species of jasmines are native to India and have their origin in the Southern foot hills of the Himalaya (Bailey, 1947). Jasmines are cosmopolitan in distribution being found in cultivation under a wide spectrum of climatic conditions ranging from warm humid region of coastal plains upto an elevation of 1300 meters above mean sea level. Jasmine has now an international acclaim due to its wide adaptability to varied climatic conditions, geographical zones and seasons. They are invariably found growing in almost every house, particularly in South India. Jasmines are grown on a commercial scale in Belgium, France, Italy, Morocco, Algiria, North Africa, Spain and Egypt. 2 In India, it is commercially cultivated in large scale in states of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Kerala, West Bengal and in Andhra pradesh. It is estimated that in India jasmine occupies an area of more than 6630 hectares, contributing substantially to the national economy. India exports flowers to South East Asian countries {Sri Lanka, Singapore and Malaysia) and of late to the Gulf countries. In Karnataka, jasmine occupies an area of 1707 hectares with an estimated production of nearly 4438 tonnes of fresh flower and ranks first among the commercial flower crops of the state followed by chrysanthemum and marigold (Anon.,1998). It is mainly grown in Bangalore, Bellary, Chitradurga, Mysore, Dharwad, Gadag, Belgaum, South Kanara, North Kanara and in Kolar districts. Of the different species cultivated in South India, the most commonly cultivated ones are Jasminum sambac Ait.(Gundumallige), Jasminum auriculatum Vahl.(Sooji mallige) Jasminum grandif/orum L. (Jaji mallige) and Jasminum multiflorum Andr. (Kakada). These are extensively grown for their loose flowers. In Karnataka, J. sambac and J. auriculatum are more common and are very popular due to their pleasant fragrance and superior quality.In India fresh flowers of jasmine are highly valued and are used for making garlands, bouquets, veni, gajra and for decorating hairs of woman and for various religious and marriage ceremonies. The products of jasmine are an important natural raw materials in the perfumary industry. Jasmine concrete is the most commonly extracted product of jasmine. It is used as such in making perfumed hair oils, preparations of absolute and hand kerchief perfumes. In addition, it is used in toiletaries, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, food essences, chewing tobacco, dental preparations and confectioneries. France and Italy are the major producers of jasmine concrete and also have the largest 3 markets for the products. Its different parts of plant such as leaf, stem, bark, root and seeds are used for medicinal purpose. In order to meet the ever Increasing demand for fresh flowers, efforts are being made to increase the production through the expansion of area under jasmine and evolving high yielding varieties supplemented by improved ec'otechniques. Though, the quality of flower is primarily a varietal trait, it is c-eatly influenced by climate and agrotechniques followed. Among the EC'otechniques, nutrition is the main factor which influence the quality and yield c: jasmine under any agroclimatic condition. Boodley (1975) considered quality to be function of nutrient level. Toxic level of nutrients adversely affect the c jality of ornamental plants and flowers. The appropriate fertilizer requirements of jasmine under Ghataprabha command area of North Karnataka are not exactly known. Judicious fertilizer aoplication not only produce higher yields, but also optimise the cost of cultivation. Tr,3 present fertilizer recommendation seems to be very high which reflect directly cn cost of production. Further overuse of these synthetic fertilizers and chemicals poses problems of environmental pollution with potential hazards to flora and fauna and also on human beings. in view of escalating cost of fertilizer and their hazardous polluting effects on environment there is growing awareness in the farming community about the alternative agricultural system, known as biological farming or organic farming or Low External Input Sustainable Agriculture (LEISA). In jasmine cultivation, fertilizer cost alone adds a major per cent to the annual cost of cultivation. Green revolution is the resultant of intensive agriculture with the extensive use of chemical fertilizers. The intensive agriculture practices boost the production to meet the demand of growing population, especially of the third world. There was no thought about its hazardous adverse effects in the long run on the soil health in general and on the environment in particular. Farmers are showing inclination to revert back to traditional farming with least usage of synthetic fertilizers. Various research groups are now working to find out the alternative system in crop production with an aim to study these farming systems which have long term durability and sustainability. One such area of study has been the production and utilization of organic wastes. Change over from chemical to organic farming is effected by harnessing vermiculture biotechnology. Earthworms are considered as agents to restore the soil fertility from the times of Arisrotle,who called earthworms "The intestine of earth." Earthworm physically an aerator,a crusher, a mixer and chemically a degrader, biologically it decomposes various organic wastes. The degradation of organic wastes by earthworm is known as "Vermicomposting . The importance of vermicomposting was known since ancient times. However, it was Darwin {1881) who for the first time stressed the importance of earthworm through his classical publication, "Formation of vegetable mould through the action of earthworm". Though Nedham et al. (1959) gave the methodology for culturing earthworms, its rearing as a technology was developed by Canadians in early 70's. During this period, first vermicomposting was attempted in Holland and Canada. Later on, the vermicomposting has spread to other countries. The potential of earthworm and vermiculture in India for worm compost was realised in early 1980's with the advent of vermiculture biotechnology. Only a few promising exotic species of earthworms viz., Pherltima escavatus, Eisenia foetida and Eudn'lus euginae were successfully cultured to produce vermicompost and worm meal in India. The vermicompost is rich in macro (N, PjOg and KjO) and micro nutrients (Fe, Bo, Zn, Mo etc.), vital plant promoting substances, humus farming substances, humus forming microorganisms and nitrogen fixers (Garvilov, 1962 and Bano etaL, 1987). In India, recently it has been found that use of vermicompost in some vegetable crops (tomato, carrot, brinjal), flowering plants (salvia, zinnia, china aster etc.), fruit crops (grape, banana, pomegranate) and in field crops (paddy, sugarcane, barley etc.) with increased yield both qualitatively and quantitatively with less disease and pest incidence. Thus, vermiculture is gaining importance in farming system. There is no information with respect to use of vermicompost and in situ vermiculture on the productivity of jasmine. So keeping in view all the above aspects, present study was undertaken with the following objectives. 1) To standardize the nutritional requirement of jasmine. 2) To study the effects of organic, inorganic fertilizers and in situ vermiculture on growth and flower yield of jasmine. 3) To study the interaction effects of inorganic fertilizers and organic manures on growth and flower yield of jasmine. Similarly, rose, marigold and ixora respond very well to the application of vermicompost (Patnaik, 19921. Vermicompost effect was on par with FYM and chemical fertilizers in six ornamental plants viz. balsom, zinnia, celosia, marigold, lady's lace. In most of the flowering plants studied, a signifioant increase in fiowering was observed when chemicals were added in small proportions with even reduced quantity of vermicompost. Effects on plants applied with vermicompost (2.5 to 5 tonnes /ha) and supplied with 50 to 75 per cent of the recommended dose of fertilizer and m situ vermiculture (2 lakh worms/ha) adoption without any fertilizer were comparable with those of full dose of recommended fertilizers plus recommended dose of FYM in china aster (Kulkarni, 19941. This indicates the possibility of reducing the application of chemical fertilizers upto 25 to 50 per cent and completely eliminate the use of chemical fertilizers by adopting the in situ vermiculture. The net returns were little less in in situ vermiculture treatment compared to treatments having fertilizers with FYM, but it will have a long run effect on the fertility level of the soil as earthworms will be remaining in the field for longer period and there is no need of applying the worms in forth coming seasons. Nutritional requirement is one of the key factor which governs the growth and development of plants. The natural deposits of nutrients in soils are inadequate to meet the demands of the plants in context of increased pressure for maximizing the productivity. Further, continuous growth of crops depletes the fertility of the soil. Therefore, it becomes essential to supplement artificial sources of nutrients in the form of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium and other minor nutrients to the soils. To realise the capacity of plants, it is necessary to determine the rate at which the nutrients are absorbed by plants and utilized for production purpose. The efficiency of the plants to absorb and assimilate the nutrients depends on several factors and differs with agroclimatic conditions in which they grow. The present chapter highlights on the indepth review of work carried out on the nutrition in jasmine, supplemented with information on other related ornamental crops. 2.3 Importance of nutrition and nutrient supply to flower crops Growth, development and yield are functions of many factors such as genetic make up of the plants, the prevailing climatic conditions and the nutrient status of the soil and its availability. Altering the nutrient status to suit the plants need is one of the way to exploit the genetic potential of the plant, thereby enhancing the production (0 Rourke, 1962). It has been established by many workers that nutrient requirement of different flower crops are not consistent.Mengel (1969) stated that, nutrient supply should be adjusted to the specific requirement of plants during the various stages of growth to attain maximum levels of yields. An interruption in plant nutrition even for a short period has a negative effect on the yield, this cannot be corrected later by nutrient supply. There is a need for adjustment of nutrient supply to meet the specific requirements of plants during various growth stages to maximize the yields. MATERIAL AND METHODS The present investigation was carried out in the "Floriculture Unit" Kittur Rani Channamma College of Horticulture, Arabhavi, University of Agricultural Sciences,Dharwad during 1996-97 and 1997-98. Two experiments were carried out to study the effect of organic, inorganic fertilizers and in situ vermiculture on growth and flower yield of jasmine. Planting was done by planting one plant per pit on 18th September 1996. Light irrigation was given soon after planting. Fertilizer application Treatments were imposed as per the programme. The first split was given three months after planting (last week of December) and second was given 6 months after the first dose application (1st week of July). Application of vermicompost Vermicompost obtained from the Agricultural Research Station, Sankeshwar, University of Agricultural Sciences,Dharwad and Farmers Training Centre, Arabhavi was pooled and applied as per the treatment levels in full doses at the time of treatment imposition. Then the volume of the supernatant made upto 10 ml using DMSO. The absorbance of the extract was measured at 645, 663 and 653 nm using DMSO as blank in spectrophotometer. The total chlorophyll, chlorophyll 'a' and chlorophyll 'b' contents were calculated by using the formula given below. Gross returns Gross returns was worked out by multiplying the treatment yield with the sale price of flowers. Net returns Net returns was worked out by deducting the total cost from the gross returns. Benefit Cost Ratio Benefit cost ratio was worked out by dividing the gross returns with the total cost. Additional cost Additional cost was worked out by adding the cost of fertilizers and application spent for each treatment over and above the control. This was worked out only for J.sambac Ait. Additional returns Additional returns was worked out by multiplying the additional yield with sale price of the flowers. This was worked out only for J.sambac Ait. Additional benefit Additional benefit was worked out by dividing the additional return with additional cost. This was worked out only for J.sambac Ait. The cost of inputs to calculate all the above said parameters are presented in appendix IV and V. 3.17 Statistical analysis and Interpretation of data Statistical analysis of data was carried out by following the Fisher's analysis of variance technique as given by Panse and Sukhatme (1967). DISCUSSION V. DISCUSSION The whole complex of crop production and the resultant yield on profitable basis is based entirely on a balanced nutrition under congenial agroclimatic conditions. Importance for better growth and development of flower production and quality flowers has been recognized by several workers (Lunt and Kofranek, 1958; Joiner, 1967; Raman 6t a/., 1967 and Arora and Saini, 1976). The results of this investigation entitled "Effect of organic,inorganic fertilizers and in situ vermiculture on growth and flower yield of Jasmine" are discussed in this chapter. 5.1 Effect of organic, inorganic fertilizers and in situ vermiculture on growth and flower yield of Jasminum sambac Ait. With the increasing cost, coupled with adverse effect of chemical fertilizers and pesticides on the non target biota and environment, it has become very much necessary to establish an alternate strategy to cut down the fertilizer input so as to reduce cost of cultivation and also to reduce the environmental pollution. In this aspect efforts have been made to study the effects of organic fertilizers on growth and production of various crops and has been well documented. Vermiculture is going to be one of the alternative answer to the above said problems (Kale et ai., 1991; Barve, 1992; Desai, 1992 and Gunjal and Nikkam, 1992). In the present investigation, efforts were made to study the effects of vermicompost either alone or in combination with inorganic fertilizers and in situ vermiculture on growth and flower yield in J. sambac Ait. 128 5.1.1 Growth parameters Vegetative growth is the best measure in terms of plant height, number of primary, secondary and tertiary branches, girth of primary and secondary branches, number of leaves, total leaf area and chlorophyll content etc. In the present studies, the plants supplied with vermicompost along with 50 per cent recommended dose of fertilizers or only vyith recommended fertilizers (120:240:240 g NPK/plant) were taller, sturdier and produced more number of branches. Effect and advantages of chemical fertilizers have been well documented by previous workers in many crops like jasmine (Muthuswamy and Pappiah, 1976 a,b and 1979; Natarajan and Rao, 1980; Kumar and Gill, 1983; Pal et a!., 1984 and 1985; Kulkarni, 1992 and Maruthiprasad and Patil 1992a and 1992b), rose (Mukhopadhyaya et a!., 1989 and Damke and Bhattacharjee, 1995), Dahlia (Singh et a!., 1996), helichrysum (Sharanabasappa et aL, 1990) and china aster (Maheshwar, 1977; Ramachandra, 1982; Mantur, 1988 and Ravindra, 1998). In addition to supply of nutrients, vermicompost has role in improving the soil conditions like drainage, aeration and water holding capacity (Bhandari et a!., 1967; Noble et aL, 1970 and Lee, 1985). Further, when it is applied along with the chemical fertilizers, it presents the nutrients in most available farms (Kale et aL, 1987). This made it possible for the plants grown in treatments having both vermicompost and chemical fertilizers to grow and put up luxurious growth in terms of plant height, girth and number of branches (Plate-8, 9, 10 & 11). This could be due to increased protein synthesis with I2y increased uptake in vermicompost incorporated plots as reported by Tomati et at. (1990). On the other hand , the plants in control (Plate-7) were poor in vegetative growth with less number of primary branches, indicating the importance of nutrients in the growth and development of plants. Similarly, role of vermicompost in enhancing the components of vegetative growth like plant height, stem girth, number of branches, number of leaves, leaf area etc., have been reported by many workers in different crops (Khan, 1966; Edward and Lofty, 1978; Altanvinyte and Zimkuvine, 1985; Kaleefs/., 1987and 1991; Vadirajefa/. 1992; Jadhav, 1994; Kulkarni, 1994; Kolhar, 1995; Patil 1995 and Mannikeri, 1997). Plant spread was better in the plants supplied with vermicompost alone (either at 2,4 and 8 kg per plant) or in combination with fertilizers and recommended dose of fertilizers plus recommended dose of FYM and also in situ vermiculture plants. The increase in plant spread in these plants could be attributed to the increased production of primary, secondary and tertiary branches. On the other hand, the control plants which were weak in their growth had less spread as they could produce less branches. Even though, the production of leaves per plant was found non significant, the total leaf area per plant (m^) and chlorophyll content were influenced by various treatments. The highest leaf area and chlorophyll contents were recorded in the plants supplied with vermicompost either at 2,4 or 8 kg per plant along with 50 per cent recommended dose of fertilizer and recommended dose of fertilizer plus recommended dose of FYM per plant, in situ vermiculture (at ICQ worms/plant) plants also recorded more number of 130 leaves, leaf area and chlorophyll content (Chlorophyll 'a', chlorophyll 'b' and total chlorophyll content). This Increased number of leaves was due to Increased number of branches in all above said treatments as there was positive correlation between number of branches and number of leaves and leaf area. Similar results were reported by Kulkarni (1992) in J. grandiflorum L. and Maruthi Prasad and Patil (1992a) in J. auriculatum with respect to chemical fertilizers and Vadiraj et al. (1992) in cardamom and Kulkarni (1994) in china aster with respect to vermicompost and in situ vermiculture. 5.1.2 IM.P.K. content in leaves and soil The N,P and K content in leaves were higher in all the treatments as compared to that of control plants. However, the influence in N, P and K content in leaves were significant in plants which received recommended dose of fertilizer plus recommended dose of FYM, only recommended dose of fertilizer and vermicompost along with 50 per cent recommended dose of fertilizer and in in situ vermiculture. This increased content of N,P and K in leaf tissue in above said treatments might be due to the richness of vermicompost with respect to humus forming microbes, nitrogen fixers and PjO^ content and its nature of improving the physico-chemical properties of the soil. Apart from that when the vermicompost is applied along with chemical fertilizers, it presents the nutrients in most available forms (Kale eta!.. 1987). This led to increased uptake and accumulation of nutrients in the leaf tissues. Role of vermiculture in the uptake of nutrients has been established by previous workers (Barley and Jennings, 1959 and Mackay eta!., 1962). 131 The available N, P and K content in soil were higher in all the treatments as compared to that of control plants. However, the influence on available N,P and K contents in soil was significant in plots which received recommended dose of fertilizer plus recommended dose of FYM, only recommended dose of fertilizers and vermicompost along with 50 per cent recommended dose of fertilizers. This increased content of available N, P and K in soil in the above said treatments was due to the application of higher levels of nutrients. The increased NPK content in plots which received only 50 percent recommended dose of fertilizer and vermicompost could be attributed to the richness of vermicompost with respect to humus forming microbes, nitrogen fixers and PjO^ content and its nature of improving the physico-chemical properties of soil. Apart from this vermicompost presents nutrients in most available forms (Kale et al., 1987) which lead to increased availability of nutrients In the soil. These results are in confirmity with the findings of Barley and Jennings (1959). Role of vermicompost in maintaining the soil health has been well documented by Edward and Lofty (1978), Lee (1985) and Gunjal and Nikkam (1992). 5.1.3 Flowering, flower bud characters and flower yield 5.1.3.1 Commencement of flowering Generally fertilizers at their optimum levels, promote vegetative growth and delay flowering, while deficient nutrition causes stunted growth and early flowering. However, these were statistically on par with each other. Benefit cost ratio was minimum in the plants which received recommended dose of fertilizer plus recommended dose of FYM. The lowest benefit cost ratio in plants which received recommended dose of fertilizer plus recommended dose of FYM was due to the highest cost of cultivation for which the cost of fertilizers was the major contributing factor. The benefit cost ratio was medium in plants which received 50 per cent of recommended dose of fertilizers plus vermicompost either at 2 or 4 kg per plant. This is because of the highest gross return obtained in these treatments. Even though the benefit cost ratio was medium, the additional benefit was very high in plants which received 50 per cent recommended dose of fertilizer plus vermicompost either at 2 or 4 kg per plant. This high additional benefit was due to highest additional returns over the control plants. The primary factors responsible for obtaining an economic yield in any crop, are the genomic constitution of the crop, climate, soil, nutrition and cultural manipulations and their interactions. Importance of balanced nutrition and nutrient requirement in jasmine has been stressed by many workers (Muthuswamy, 1975; Natarajan and Rao, 1980; Pal et al., 1984 and 1985; Kulkarni, 1992 and Maruthiprasad, 1991). Future line of work 1) Experiments have to be continued for another two to three years in order to get stabilized yields, since they are of perennial nature. 2) Nutritional requirement may be workedout for other commercial species of jasmines since they are known to vary in their requirements, uptake and utilization of nutrients. 3) Greater emphasis has to be given for the in situ vermiculture by maintaining optimum moisture level throughout the year. 4) Weed management studies have to be carried out since it is a major hurdle in cultivation of jasmine. 5) Pruning techniques have to be standardized with respect to time and extent of pruning for different species of jasmine. In the second experiment, the growth parameters which were influenced mostly by N were optimum in lower levels of N, but luxur-iant in higher levels at the cost of flowering. The nutrient combination of 60:120:120 of per plant of NPK along with 20 kg FYM per plant was found optimum to achieve the optimum growth and flower yields in the first two years of planting in Jasminum auricuiatum Vahl.

INTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the important group of flowering plants cultivated on a commercial scale and is highly esteemed for its attractive and fragrant flowers. Think of fragrance, think of jasmine they say. Such is the special attraction this, multi-coloured, multi-seasoned flower that has a pride of place in the heart of every woman. The starry bright white is the common variety that is grown extensively in India. In the south, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have grown this crop on a commercial scale. ‘Mysore Mallige’ is world famous. In Madurai district of Tamil Nadu, the jasmine dominates the lives of not only the ordinary small farmers but even the flight schedules of the Indian Airlines have to be adjusted to the delicate demands of this ‘Queen of Flowers’ to reach it to different parts of the country. It is now transported to distant places, thanks to the air freight facility that is available to the cultivators of Jasmine. The Jasmine belongs to the family Oleaceae, the term Jasmine is derived from an Arabic word ‘Jessamine’ (Bailey, 1947) and also on old Persian name ‘Yesmyn’ meaning fragrance. The genus jasmine comprises of about 300 species which are dispersed through warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Pacific region (Bhattacharjee, 1980). About 43 species are found in Indian subcontinent, but commercially only the following four species are important. 1. Jasminum sambac Ait. 2. Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. 3. Jasminum grandiflorum Linn. 4. Jasminum multiflorum Roth. Since, time immemorial, Jasmine is considered as a spritual flower of India. The Japanese call it the flower that heralds the spring. In India, this flower is a winter and summer favourite. Different species are grown in gardens as shrubs and climbers. Several species and varieties are grown on a large scale in different states for loose flower production. Jasminum species find a very important place in the perfume industry. The concrete of Jasminum grandiflorum has worldwide acceptance and there is an increasing demand in the international market for essential oil extracted from Jasminum auriculatum and J. sambac, the smell of Jasmine oil is not familiar outside India. Jasmine oils are used extensively in the manufacture of cosmetics, soaps, confectionary perfumes, perfumumed tobacco, syrups, aerated water, ointments, disinfectants and detergents. Flowers are used for making garlands, hair adornments of women, religious and social functions. The different plant parts like leaf, stem, bark, root, seed and fruit are also used for medicinal purpose (George and Watt, 1980). Besides the edible uses of the plant are also reported by Tanaka (1976). The fragrance of jasmine flower cannot be imitated by any of the known synthetic aromatic chemicals (Bhattacharjee, 1980). In India, Jasmine cultivated throughout the country over an area of about 12,000 ha both in plains and hills upto 3,030 m. However, large chunks of areas under jasmine flower production are in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka with 5,203 and 4,010 ha of land, respectively. In India, the flowers are generally harvested when the buds are well developed but still unopened. The buds are in great demand for both fresh market and concrete extraction. The best known species among jasmines is Jasminum sambc Ait. and several varieties of this species viz., Arabian or Tuscan. Jasmine (Grand duke of Tuscassy, Motia, Mogra, Malligae and Kodai Mullai (Bhattacharjee, 1980) are commercially cultivated. The species has several synonyms viz., J. fragrans, J. sambac Rorb. Mogram sambac Laik. etc. In Karnataka, they are known as Mysore mallige, Mangalore or Udupi mallige depending upon the place of cultivation and Gundu or Dundu mallige, Yelu-suttina mallige depending upon the morphology of the flower specially number of whorls of petals. One of the important cultural operations in Jasmine is pruning which is done to regulate the growth in untidy bushes and promote profuse flowering. Variations in respect of quality and quantity of flower have also been observed with different dates of pruning. Regulation of flowering in jasmine has great practical values due to seasonal nature of flowering and peak productivity in certain months of the year which remain as major problems in Jasmine flower production. So, making the plant to flower throughout the year would be certainly desirable as it offers advantages to both growers and consumers. Nutrition is also one of the important factors. Judicious application of manure and fertilizers are inevitable for getting higher yields. In order to meet the ever increasing demand for fresh flowers, efforts are being made to increase the area under jasmine, to develop high yielding varieties and improved agro- techniques, cultivation aspects such as pruning, nutrients management and plant density. Practices have been standardized under Coimbatore, Madurai and Bangalore condition. But no such work has been undertaken for transitional conditions of Dharwad even though the area under this crop is increasing in this region. Hence, the present investigation was undertaken in order to know the standardization of time of pruning and nutrition on growth and yield of Mangalore mallige with the following objectives. 1. To standardize the time of pruning of Mangalore mallige under transitional tract of Northern Karnataka. 2. The preventing climatic conditions and the nutrient status of the soil and its availability, altering the nutrient status of the soil to suit the plants need is one of the ways to utilize the maximum genetic potential of the plant thereby enhancing the productivity (O’Rourke, 1962). Judicious and balanced fertilizer application along with adequate amount of water is known to result in the overall improvement in the quality of flowers and total flower yields in many flower crops (Elongorm, 1975 and Mentrova et al., 1976). It has been established that the nutrient requirement by many of the flowering crops are not consistent. Hence, the nutrient supply should be adjusted to the specific requirements of plants during the various stages of growth to attain maximum levels of yield (Mengel, 1969). He has also observed that an interruption in plant nutrition even for a short period has a negative effect the yield and this cannot corrected later by nutrient supply. He stressed the need for adjustment of nutrient supply to the specific requirements of plants during various growth stages to obtain maximum levels of yield. Mentrova et al. (1976) also gave a similar opinion. Tayama et al. The average maximum temperature 37.40C was observed in the month of April. 3.4 SOIL OF THE EXPERIMENTAL SITE The soil of the experimental site was red sandy loam soil. There were 12 treatment combinations comprising of three levels of dates of prunings and four levels of fertilizer. Time of pruning (at an interval of 15 days) P1 – Early pruning = Pruning in the last week of November P2 – Early mid pruning = Pruning in the second week of December P3 – Late pruning = Pruning in the last week of December Four fertilizer levels : F0 – No fertilization F1 – 100:200:200 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant F2 – 120:240:240 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant F3 – 140:280:280 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant Treatment combinations 1. P3F3 3.5.1.3 Pruning The bushes were pruned according to the date schedule to a level of 60 cm above the ground level (Plate 2a and 2b). 3.5.1.4 Manures and fertilizer application The FYM was applied at the rate of 20 kg per plant. The manure and fertilizers were given or applied in 15 cm deep in rings and 30 cm away from the main stem. The urea, superphosphate and muriate of potash formed the sources for nutrient element. DISCUSSION The factors responsible for an economic yield and in a plant are the genotype, climate, soil cultural manipulations and their interactions. Maximum yield is obtained when favourable conditions are provided for a crop. In addition to these factors, pruning time and nutrition also play a prime role in deciding the growth and ultimately yield in the jasmine crop. Pruning is one of the important cultural operations in the cultivation of jasmine. A knowledge on this aspect is of paramount importance to manipulate the plants physiology, which may eventually lead to the maximum production. Importance of balanced nutrition and nutrient requirement in Jasmine has been recognized by many workers (Muthuswamy and Pappiah, 1976; Nandakumar, 1976 and Natarajan and Rao, 1980; Anon., 1983 and Bhattacharjee, 1983 and 1985). The present study is specially conducted to know the best time of pruning as well as optimum nutrient requirement and their effects of flower in Mangalore mallige (J. sambac). The results of this investigation are discussed in this chapter under the following heads. 5.1 Effect of time of pruning 5.2 Effect of nutrition 5.3 Effect of time of pruning and nutrition 5.1 EFFECT OF TIME OF PRUNING 5.1.1 Growth parameter The pruning times expressed significant results in respect of number of sprouts per plant at 14, 21 and 28 DAP. It is confirmed that the sprout formation was completely stopped after 28 DAP. The varied pruning treatments significantly influenced the sprout number per plant at this stage. The number of sprouts in pruning at second week of December (P2) significantly recorded the more number of sprouts (194.12) than P3 and P1 (188.00 and 173.00). Similar type of observations were made by (Sumangala, 1997) in J. sambac. The more the number of branches of sprouts, the more will be flower yield as the flowering area increases. Thus, it appears that the flower yield depended on number of sprouts. Similar observation was noticed by Bhattacharjee (1984) and Sumangala (1997 in J. grandiflorum and J. sambac. Different pruning dates imparted significant difference in the length of the primary shoot at all the stages of plant growth. At 60 days after pruning, the length of the primary shoot was more P2 (155.42 cm) recorded followed by last week of December (149.83 cm). The shoot length was significantly lower when pruned at last week of November. The length of the primary shoot is important which will determine the number of secondary laterals and leaves. More the length of primary shoot more will be the flower yield (Anon., 1978-79). The primary shoot length had highly positive correlation with flower yield. Similar observation made in chrysanthemum in respect to height (Rachayanavar, 1983) and Sumangala (1997) in J. sambac. Pruning dates exhibited non-significant influence in respect of basal diameter of the stem at all the stages of growth (Table 3). Similar observations were made in Jasminum sambac under West Bengal (Anon., 1982-83) and in Dharwad conditions (Sumangala, 1997). The number of leaves per primary shoot was significantly influenced by the time of pruning at all the stages of plant growth (Table 4). The present study confirms the findings of Subramaniam and Shanmugavelu (1980) in J. auriculatum. Leaf area per plant was significantly influenced by pruning dates at all stages of growth. Significantly higher leaf area was observed in P2 over all other pruning dates. All the pruning dates differed significantly among themselves with pruning P1 (last week of November) had the lowest leaf area (51.25 cm2) per shoot. The more leaf area per plant in P2 may be due to higher number of branches per primary shoot. Conversely the lesser leaf in P1 and P3 may be due to lesser number of branches. Thus, the higher leaf area per plant was promoted increased photosynthetic activity in the leaves and thereby increasing the final flower yield (as in P2). The decreased flower in P3 and P1 probably due to lesser rate of photosynthetic activity because of smaller leaf area. Similar observations were recorded by Rachayanavar (1983) in chrysanthemum and Sumangala (1997) in J. sambac. Varied pruning dates did not significantly influenced the number of secondary laterals per primary shoot at 120 days after pruning. However, at 180 DAP, P2 registered more number (9.28) of secondary laterals followed by P1 (8.34) and P3 (8.32). Similar observations were made by (Anon., 1982-83. Productive shoots per plant were significantly influenced by the time of pruning P2 had significantly highest number of productive shoots (191.56) than P1 and P3 (173.81 and 173.50), respectively. The higher yield in P2 may be due to more number of productive shoots which would have helped directly to bear more number of flowers. 5.1.2 Yield parameter Commencement of flowering was significantly shortest (50.31 days) with December last week of pruning. Early pruning took maximum duration (58.37 days) for flowering. The yield parameters like length of the flower bud (Table 9), diameter of the flower bud (Table 10), length of the flower bud excluding corolla (Table 12) and flower bud index (Table 13) were not significantly influenced by time of pruning at both stages of harvest. Similar results were mentioned in respect to length and diameter of the flower bud (Anon., 1982-83 and Sumangala, 1997) in J. sambac. The corolla length was significantly influenced by pruning timings at 135 days after pruning (Table 11), P2 significantly had more corolla length (1.98 cm) than P1 and P3 (1.78 and 1.75 cm) respectively. The highest flower yield in P2 may be due to more corolla length. Hundred flower weight was significantly influenced by pruning timings at 135 days after pruning (Table 14). December second week pruning (P2) significantly registered higher flower weight (9.59 g) over P1 and P3 (9.32 and 9.55 g) eventhough the weight of 100 flower was non-significant at 195 days after pruning. The P2 recorded more weight (8.20 g) than the P1 and P3 (8.15 and 8.12 g, respectively). Thus, it appears that the highest flower yield in P2 might have contributed to more weight of flowers. However, the weight of 100 flower did not significantly influence due to pruning timings under West Bengal conditions (Anon., 1982-83) in J. auriculatum and J. sambac. This difference may be due to agro-climatic influence. Pruning times significantly influenced the number of flowers per plant. The P2 significantly registered highest number of flowers per plant (13061.88) than P3 and P1 (10812.50 and 10598.44). The highest flower yield in P2 was due to more number of flowers per plant. The moderate flower yield in P3 was mainly due to moderate number of flowers. It is confirmed that the more number of flowers was responsible for increased flower yield (Anon., 1982-83). The number of flowers per plant had highly significant influence on flower yield. Similar results have been obtained by Nalawadi (1982), Rachayanavar (1985) and Sumangala (1997) in marigold, chrysanthemum and J. sambac, respectively. Difference pruning timings significantly influenced the flower yield per ha basis. The P2 significantly recorded the highest yield (5580.20 kg/ha) than P1 and P3 (4423.78 and 4545.81 kg/ha). The marked increase in flower yield in P2 was due to suitable time of pruning. Mangalore Mallige RATIKANATH 2005 Dr. V. S. PATIL Major Advisor ABSTRACT An experiment was conducted to find out the optimum time of pruning and nutrition in Jasminum sambac var. Mangalore mallige during 2004-05 in the New Orchard, Division of Horticulture, Main Agricultural Research Station, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad. The experiment was laid out in two factorial Randomized Block Design with 12 treatment combinations comprising of three different dates of pruning viz., early pruning (pruning in the last week of November), early mid pruning (pruning in the second week of December), late pruning (pruning in the last week of December) and four levels of fertilizers viz., F0 (No fertilization), F1 (100:200:200 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant), F2 (120:240:240 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant), F3 (140:280:280 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant). The study pointed out that among the different dates of pruning, the pruning on early mid December (P2) encountered better vegetative growth that resulted in highest yield (5580.20 kg/ha) than P1 and P3 (4423.78 and 4545.81 kg/ha) while P1 adversely affected the yield. Among the different levels of fertilizer F2 level recorded highest flower yield (5634.15 kg/ha). The performance of other fertilizer level F1 and F3 also differed with each other (5367.69 and 5003.44 kg/ha). From the study, it could be summarized that the higher yield can be obtained by pruning during early mid December and application of fertilizer level F2 (120:240:240 g of NPK + 20 kg FYM/plant), may be recommended for maximum productivity of Mangalore mallige.
