Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton (English Name: Jasmine, Arabian Jasmine; Family: Oleaceae; Synonym: Nyctanthes sambac L., Nyctanthes undulata L.), Locally known as ‘Mogra’ in Hindi and Marathi. It is also known as Full (Arabic), Beli or Bel (Bangladesh), Sampaguita (Spanish), Mallika (Sanskrit), Juhi Mahli (Oriya), Kampupot, Melati putih (Malay and Indonesian Language), Kampupot (Tagalog), Maliepuwu (Telugu), Mallikaipu (Tamil), Dundu Mallige (Kannada), Kaliyan (Urdu), Pikake (Hawaiian), Sampaguita (Philippines), Yasmin (Persian), Mo li hua 1 (Transcribed Chinese), Jasmin d'Arabie (French) and Bogarim (Portuguese), The jasmine belongs to the family oleaceae, the term jasmine is derived from an arabic word ‘jessamine’ (Bailey, 1947) and also an old Persian name ‘yesmyn’ meaning fragrance. The genus Jasminum is reported to include about 64 species (Anonymous, 2011), out of which 40 are indigenous to the Indian subcontinent (Irulappan, 1994). Jasmine plants are of great economic valuu as a field crop for the florist, landscape, medicinal and pharmaceutical industries (Green and Miller, 2009). Mostly, jasmine plants are grown in houses and gardens for ornamental purposes, and flowers are to make garlands. However, there are a few species with fragrant flowers. Among these species, J. sambac, J. grandiflorum and J. auriculatum are commercially cultivated for oil extraction or perfumery industries (Rimando, 2003 and Green and Miller, 2009). Jasminum sambac is an evergreen, shrubby vine growing up to 3 m high with shiny, pointed and very decorative leaves (Shu, 2008). The leaves are opposite or in whorls of three, simple ovate, 4 to 12.5 cm long and 2 to 7.5 cm broad. The flowers are produced in clusters of 3 to 12 together, strongly scented, with a corolla 2-3 cm diameter with 5-9 lobes. The different plant parts like leaf, stem, bark, root, seed and fruit are also used for medicinal purpose (George and Watt, 1980). Besides the edible uses of the plant are reported by Tanaka (1976). Packaging jasmine flowers in polyethylene bags with no ventilation extended the shelf life for 3 days {Jasminum sambac) to beyond 7 days {Jasminum multiflorum) but, when the shelf life of non packed control flowers were just one day (Jasminum sambac), two days {J. multiflorum) (Nirmala, 1991). The fragrance of jasmine flower cannot be imitated by any of the known synthetic aromatic chemicals (Bhattacharjee, 1980). In India, Jasmine absolute is a viscous clear yellowish brown liquid possessing a delicate odour of fresh jasmine flowers. The essential oil in flowers is 2 extracted through effleurage which is widely used for production of Jasmine attars in India (Sharma et al, 1980). The usual yields are 0.30-0.35 per cent concrete and 45- 55 per cent absolute. The approximate composition of jasmine flower oil obtained by effleurage is benzeyl acetate 65.0 per cent, d-linalool 15.5 per cent, linalyl acetate 7.5 per cent, benzyl alcohol 6.0 per cent, jasmone 3.0 per cent, indole 2.5 per cent and methyl anthranilate 0.5 per cent Benzyl benzoate, geraniol, nerol, terpineol, famesol, nerolidol and p-cresol are also present in traces (Nigam and Misra, 1980). Its white, intensely perfumed flowers appears in light clusters that contain a small amount of essential oil. The essential oil of jasmine is called “otto” or “attar of jasmine”; it contains over 100 constituents but the main chemical components responsible for the aroma. (Lawrence, 1977). Jasmine oil has a wide range of medicinal applications and can be used in perfumery, soaps, flavorings and the cosmetic industry (Lawless, 1995). Jasmine oil is famous for the treatment of dry, greasy, irritated and sensitive skin. Other reported medicinal uses include soothing irritating coughs, alleviating muscular pain and treating sprains (Prabuseenivasan et al, 2006). Therapeutically, jasmine oil is used as an antidepressant, antiseptic, antispasmodic, sedative and uterine tonic (Kang and Kim, 2002). However, the yield and quality production of flower is low which need to be increased by adopting horticultural techniques. Plant nutrition plays an important role for enhancing yield and quality in jasmine. Nitrogen is one of the major components of nucleic acid, co-enzymes ana cell membranes and it is involved in many of the metabolic processes viz., cell division, photosynthesis, protein synthesis and expansion of shoot and root growth in plants and has active role during vegetative growth. Phosphorus is an important constituent of nucleoproteins, involved in high energy transfer compounds such as ATP and plays a key role in energy transfer in the metabolic processes. Potassium functions mainly on regulation and maintenance of electrochemical equilibrium in cells and 3 other compartments and regulation of enzyme activities. It also involved in carbohydrate metabolism, protein synthesis, regulation of activities of various essential elements, adjustment of stomatal functions and water relations. Micronutrients like iron and zinc are essential for plant growth and metabolism. Iron is necessary for the synthesis of chlorophyll, though it actually does not enter into its composition. Iron starved plants develop chlorosis in the young leaves and the veins remaining green. Zinc in the ionic form (Zn**) or in form of a complex with a chelating agent e.g., EDTA, is taken up by the plants. Salts or complexes of zinc can easily absorbed directly through leaves. Hence, it is used for correcting zinc deficiency. According to Stout (1962), “If plants are considered as biological machines, their bodies are constructed from macro-elements, their working parts consist of proteins and enzymes revolving about N atoms and the ‘Micronutrients’ provide the special lubricants required for a variety of energy transfer mechanisms within the plants”. This statement from a scientist, who was in India involved in identification of Mo as essential micronutrient, succinctly portrays the importance of micronutrients in plant metabolism. In the 20th Century, revolution in crop yield increase began with the discovery of micronutrients starting with iron (Fe) in 1868, and ending with molybdenum (Mo) in 1938. Intensive agriculture, with the extensive use of chemical fertilizers, which is the resultant of green revolution, boosted up the production to meet the increasing population. But, there {was no thought about hazardous adverse effects in the long run on the soil health in general and environment in particular. In view of the escalating cost of chemical fertilizers and their harmful polluting effects on the environment, there is growing awareness in the farming community about the -alternative agricultural system. Therefore, deterioration of soil health, stagnation in productivity, insecurity of quality and other environmental hazards has 4 come before the scientific community as big challenges, necessitating new research avenues. Integrated systems of agricultural production are less dependent on high inputs of energy and synthetic chemicals and more dependent on intensive management rather than conventional mono- cultural systems. The strategy of integrated nutrient management (INM) is receiving increased attention, aimed at reducing the dependence of chemical fertilizers and at the same time increasing the effectiveness of organically Supplied nutrients as opined by (Swindale 1990). Total organic farming may be a desirable proposition for improving the quality of agricultural produce. It may not be possible to maintain the quality of the produce in commercial agriculture, where mostly the stress will be given mainly on yield. It is impossible to meet the nutrient requirement of the crops, exclusively through the organic farming. Under these circumstances, integrated soil fertility management practices involving judicious combination of organic manures and chemical fertilizers seems to be a feasible option for sustainable agriculture on a commercial and profitable scale. In addition, they are eco-friendly, easily available and cost effective. Therefore, emphasis is now focused on the use of organic manure such as farm yard manures. Inorganic fertilizers The recommended dose of fertilizers (100 kg N, 50 kg P & 50 kg K) were applied as per the treatments Fertilizers were applied in the form of urea, single super phosphate and muriate of potash as a source of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, respectively. Micronutrients Micronutrients were applied in the form of Z11SO4 and Fe2S04. The recommended dose of micronutrients 20 kg/ha for both zinc and iron. Applied around each plant in a circular band (about 30 cm away and in 15 cm deep furrows), to the plot of given treatment. 25 3.8 Intercultural operation The plots were kept free from weeds by periodic hand weeding. Weeding was given in order to keep the plots clean and to have good aeration. 3.9 Irrigation Irrigations were given at an interval of 8-10 days depending on the soil moisture status and climatic condition, throughout the period of experimentation. 3.10 Loosening of soil Light digging of soil was carried out at fortnightly interval to keep the soil porous and aerated. 3.11 Plant protection Timely and suitable plant protection measures were given to protect the experimental plants from the attack by pests and diseases. Plants were sprayed with 0.1% copper oxychloride soon after pruning. And there was a mild attack of thrips on crop. These pests were controlled by spraying monocrotophos 0.1 per cent at a 15 days interval throughout the period of experimentation. 3.12 Harvesting The buds were harvested daily in the morning. The plant height was measured by meter scale from ground level to the growing tip of the observational plants. 3.13.1.2 Length of shoot (Sin) Length of shoot was recorded at 30 days interval starting from 30 day after application of different nutrients up to 150 days of crop growth. Lengths of shoots were measured by meter scale, from initiation point of shoot to the growing tip. 3.13.1.3 Spread of the plant (cm) The spread of plant was measured in both the direction east west and north south at 30 days interval from 30 days after application of different nutrients to 150 days of crop growth with the help of meter scale. 3.13.1.4 Girth of shoots (cm) Girth of shoots of plant was recorded by Vernier Caliper 50 cm above ground level. 3.13.1.5 Number of leaves per plant To find out the average number of leaves plant"1 under various treatment all the leaves of observational plants were counted and the average per plant was worked out. 27 • -tv* 3.13.1.6 Leaf area (cm2) The leaf area was calculated with the help of leaf area meter machine. THESIS ABSTRACT The present investigation was carried out on, “Effect of different nutrients on growth, flowering and yield of mogra {Jasminum sambac L.) Cv. Bela.” at Department of Horticulture, Marathwada Krishi Vidyapeeth, Parbhani (Maharashtra) in Kharif season during the year 2011-2012. The experiment was laid out in randomized block design with seven different treatments and three replications. The Bela variety of mogra was selected for present study. The materials used in the experiment were farm yard manure, urea, single super phosphate, murate of potash, zinc sulphate (ZnS04), and ferrous sulphate (FeS04). FYM were applied in the soil @ 20 t/ha immediately after pruning. Inorganic fertilizers used were urea, and murate of potash. Recommended source of fertilizer was 100:50:50 kg NPK/ha. Micronutrients ZnS04 and FeS04 recommended dose were applied 20 kg/ha. Among all treatments T6 RDF (100:50:50 kg/ha) + FYM (20 t/ha) + ZnS04 (20 kg/ha) + FeS04 (20 kg/ha) was found to be superior in growth attributes viz. plant height (154.33 cm) number of leaves per plant (2043.23), length of shoots (106.65), maximum number of shoots (primary and secondary) (30.67 and 519.93), leaf area per plant, girth of shoots, diameter of flower, shelf life of flower buds. In yield attributes, T6 (RDF + FYM + Zn + Fe) was found to be superior and obtained high yield of 806.40 g per plant, 16.13 kg per plot and 56.00 q per hectare. In respect of soil parameters superior results were observed in treatment T6 RDF (100:50:50 kg/ha) + FYM (20 t/ha) + ZnS04 (20 kg/ha) + FeS04 (20 kg/ha) available nitrogen, phosphorous, potassium, iron, organic carbon, soil pH and electrical conductivity. However, available zinc and CaCOa were observed significantly maximum in T7 (Control). Hence, in all the growth, flowering and yield attributes treatment T6 RDF (100:50:50 kg/ha) + FYM (20 t/ha) + ZnS04 (20 kg/ha) + FeS04 (20 kg/ha) was found to be superior over all the treatments. PRASANTH University : SRI KONDA LAXMAN TELANGANA STATE HORTICULTURAL UNIVERSITY ABSTRACT The present investigation “Studies on effect of different chemicals on induction of flowering and postharvest methods on shelf life of Jasmine (Jasminum sambac L.) was carried at Floricultural Research Station, ARI, Rajendranagar, during 2019-2020. The field experiment was conducted in Randomized Block Design in three replications and nine treatments and two Laboratory experiments were conducted in Complete Randomized Design with 12 treatments of pre- treatment chemical dipping other with six treatments of packaging studies. In experiment one, among the treatments, thiourea 0.5 % registered significantly best results for all parameters studied which were in increasing trend from January to March. Significantly lesser number of days for flower initiation (27.6 days), maximum number of flower buds per cyme (5.0), maximum number of cymes per plant of (137.6), maximum number buds per plant of (688.30), maximum length of flower bud of (22.53mm), maximum length of corolla tube (13.30 mm), maximum width of flower bud was recorded with (9.62 mm), maximum mean weight of 100 flower buds (28.03 g), maximum flower yield per plant (192.90 g), maximum flower yield per month in plot was observed highest in (1.153 kg/plot), maximum flower yield for three months (2.351 kg/plot) was recorded in thiourea 0.5 % in the month of March. In experiment two consisted of preservative chemicals which were used as postharvest pretreatment, the results on physiological and biochemical changes during the storage period of Jasmine cv. Gundumalli revealed that, among the treatments first best results were obtained in boric acid 4 % with minimum weight loss (47.33 %), minimum per cent of browning (55.30 %), maximum freshness index (59.90 %), minimum flower opening index (45.73 %), maximum shelflife (36.5 hr) followed by GA3 200 ppm. In third experiment, combined effect of postharvest pretreatments and packaging material were studied and results showed that, minimum weight loss (2.52 %), minimum percent of browning (34.30 %), maximum freshness index (71.35 %), minimum flower opening index (42.47 %), maximum shelf life of (96.15 hr) was registered in 4% boric acid + 250 gauge polyethylene. From the current study that it can be concluded that, the flowering parameters in Jasmine Cv. Gundumalli can be successfully induced and enhanced by foliar application of thiourea 0.5 %. Further postharvest pretreatment chemicals like boric acid 0.4 % and GA3 200 ppm enhances the shelf life. The combinational effect of 4% boric acid + 250 gauge polyethylene as pre-treatments and packing material can be used to extend the storage life of jasmine flower buds Cv. Gundumalli. 1 Chapter I INTRODUCTION Jasmine (Jasminum sambac L.) a member of Oleaceae and a very important fragrant loose flower consisting of about 200 species which are mainly shrubs and climbers. In South Indian states it is extensively cultivated as traditional loose flower. According to Bailey (1947) the term jasmine is probably derived from the Persian name “Yasmyn” and Arabic word “Jessamine” meaning fragrance. The white fragrant flowers of jasmine are symbol of purity, eternal love, nobility and also symbolizes the beauty of a girl. It is usually offered to God for worship. Hence, these are preferably planted in Hindu temple gardens and Moghul gardens. Since, immemorial time, Jasmine is considered as spiritual flower of India. Jasmine is cultivated commercially for its fresh flowers and it is used for various purposes viz., decorating hair by women, religious offerings etc. It is also used for extraction of jasmine concrete which is used in cosmetics and perfumery industries. Jasmine oil has a wide range of medicinal applications and is used in perfumery, soaps, flavouring and cosmetic industry. It is documented that, more than 2000 species are known in jasmine and among 40 species have been identified in India. For commercial cultivation in South India 20 species are recommended and the best known species among jasmine is Jasminum sambac and several varieties of this species like Motia, Mogra, Malligae and Kodai Mullai, Gundumalli, Ramanthapuram Gundumalli are commercially cultivated (Bhattacharjee, 1980). In India, Jasmine is cultivated throughout the country. It is estimated that it occupies an area of about 3674.83 ha with an annual production of 22048.26 tonns which is worth of Rs 80-100 million per year income (NHB., 2018-2019). Major regions play vital role in Jasmine sambac absolute market are North America followed by Europe and China. In India major marketing regions are Tamil Nadu with the production of 10.14 tonns per ha. In Telangana, the area of cultivation is about 0.297 thousand ha, with the production of 1.239 tonns (NHB., 2018-2019). 2 Jasmine require temperature of 27–32°C during day time and 21–27°C at night is ideal for good flowering. In off season temperature between 15 and 17°C during night shuts the flowering for a week (Leonhardt et al., 2002). Low winter temperature causes ultrastructural cellular changes in single whorled cultivars of Jasminum sambac and reduction in quality of flower (Su and Wang, 2001). Pruning (physical intervention) is a cultural operation being followed in jasmine. It is a useful method since antique times for restarting growth of plants (Parsons, 1956). As a result of pruning, number of new shoots get increased which resulted in increased flower quality by activation of physiological activity. Plant growth and differentiation are regulated by phytohormones that presumably exert their influence on particular metabolic reactions in the target tissue via receptor molecules. As pruning helps in rejuvenation and encouraging growth of new healthy shoots to bear more flowers. Besides pruning exogenous application of chemicals in jasmine will also result in enhancing growth and flowering. However, the selection of suitable chemicals, dosage and time of application certainly manipulate the growth towards profitable yields of flower crops in general and jasmine in particular during the off season. Besides the natural phytohormones, a group of off season flower inducing chemicals modifies the plant in its growth and developmental behaviour without inducing phytotoxic or malformative effects. It has been reported that the demand for jasmine is increasing due to its unique fragrance but there is a huge demand supply gap of fresh flowers during off season. During regular season, the cost of flowers is between Rs. 40 to 120 per kg. During the off season the cost of flower increases 10 times than normal season. This results in scarcity during the lean season and glut during the peak season creating a wide fluctuation in price. The balance of production during lean and peak season should be maintained by different horticultural techniques and one of important practice is application of flower inducing chemicals. The longevity of flowers depends on two distinct stages, the first stage is flower bud growth and development to full opening and the second stage is maturation, senescence and wilting. Hence, handling techniques have to first promote growth process in the first stage and retard metabolic process leading to senescence at the second stage. Measures such as harvesting at optimum maturity, handling with minimum injury, reducing microbial infection through proper 4 sanitation, maintaining optimum storage conditions leads to enhanced shelf life and postharvest quality of flowers. Jasmine flowers are delicate and loose its elegance after harvesting, flowers are treated with different chemicals to increase shelf life, chemicals like antioxidants, biocides and floral preservatives etc helps in retaining membrane turgidity and impose antisenescence effects during aging thereby increases shelf life of the flowers. Boric acid, a mineral salt that increases osmotic concentration which improves water balance and longevity of flowers (Van meeteran, 1989). Besides, Ascorbic acid an antioxidant also increases the vase life of flowers by increasing water uptake, reducing the respiration rate and ethylene production (Hatami et al., 2010). Similarly, Salicylic acid is applied as preservative solution which delays the process of senescence in flowers by activating antioxidant enzymes and inhibition of ethylene synthesis (Edrisi et al., 2012). Benzyl adenine, can increases shelf life of flowers by improving membrane permeability, delay lipid peroxidation and decreases ions leakage in cell (Abd El Aziz, 2007). Packaging is a tool for controlling flower quality in the distribution chain. Apart from preventing mechanical damage, the package serves as a barrier between the conditions inside and outside the package. It protects the flowers from unfavourable outside conditions and enables a micro climate to develop inside the package (Nowak and Rudnicki, 1991). The main purpose of packing is to store long periods by maintaining keeping quality of flowers with controlled rate of transpiration during transportation and storage. Since, Jasmine flowers are delicate and highly perishable, they need great attention through advanced technologies in packaging to keep them fresh to consumer’s satisfaction. Hence, the ideal packaging technology needs to be developed for jasmine flowers to extend shelf- life (Bhattacharjee, 1997). The effect of pruning has considerable influence both on vegetative growth and flower production. Appropriate level of pruning is very essential for inducing productive growth and to ensure high quality and productivity of flowers. Pruning in jasmine is considered to be the most important crop management practice responsible for flower regulation and production planning. Pruning serves the purpose of forcing the strongest shoot, bud to break in growth. Further, it keeps the jasmine in proper shape and size. Another important purpose served by pruning is to allow light and air to reach the center of the plant and encourage flowering. Hence, removal of the wood on which the flowers were produced will encourage the growth of a new healthy shoots which bear more flowers than old branches. Postharvest losses in traditional loose flowers is high due to high respiration rate and delicate nature. The main objective of the post-harvest studies in traditional loose flowers to minimize these losses by adopting various techniques such as postharvest chemical treatments, different packaging methods and cold storage conditions depending upon different marketing strategies. Effect of pruning on flowering and flower yield. 2.1.1. Jasmine. Muthuswami et al. (1975) conducted an experiment on pruning aspects of Jasminum sambac Ait. var. Single mogra and reported that pruning promoted quantum of flower buds per shoot over unpruned plants. CONCLUSIONS The major conclusions drawn from the present investigation are as follows: Among all the treatments, foliar application of thiourea at 0.5 per cent concentration recorded least number days for flower initiation (27.6 days) and superior in all flowering and quality parameters. Similarly, maximum flower yield for three months per plot (2.35 kg) was also recorded in thiourea 0.5 per cent. The flower buds pretreated with boric acid 4 per cent recorded maximum shelf life (36.5 hour). In the packaging experiment, the flower buds pretreated with boric acid 4 per cent and packed in 250 gauge polyethene bag, recorded maximum shelf life (96.15 hour). FUTURE LINE OF WORK 1. Off season induction of flowering in jasmine is very important for higher returns, role of novel bio stimulants of amino acids, protein hydrolysates and sea weed extracts may also be studied. 2. India is also focusing on export of essential oils extracted from traditional flowers like Jasmines and Roses. The essential oil extracted from Jasmine is highly priced for its aromatic property with the added asset of being compatible with many other reputed floral scents which has made it a highly preferred commodity in the western world. India has a sizable base for jasmine concretes and otto’s which have earned the country a place in woridtrade. India has a natural advantage for large scale production in jasmine concrete production because of favorable climate and cheap labour availability during the most part of the year. Jasmines are commercially important flowers, cultivated mainly for fresh flowers and concrete extraction. Fresh flowers are used in garland making, in places of worship and for hair adornments. The flowers can also be used for extraction of essential oil and products like Jasmine oil, butter, attar and jasmine water etc. 1 INTRODUCTION The term Jasmine is derived from Arabic word Jessamine' (Bailey, 1947) and also persian name Yesmyn’ meaning fragrance. The Jasmine belongs to family Oleaceae’ and the genus Jasminum comprises of about 300 species which are dispersed through warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Pacific region (Bhattacharjee, 1980). About 43 species are found in Itidian sub-continent, but commercially only the following four species are important. 1. Jasminum sambac Ait 2. Jasminum auricuiatum vahl 3. Jasminum grandifiorum Linn 4. Jasminum multiflorum Roth In India, Jasmine is cultivated through out the country over an area of about 8 ,000 hectares, both in plains and on hills up to 3,030 m, contributing substantially to the national economy. The annual flower production is worth over Rupees 8-10 crores. In India the flowers are generally harvested when the buds are well developed but still unopened. The buds are in great demand for both fresh market and concrete extraction. The best known species among Jasmines is Jasminum sambac Ait, and several varieties of this species viz., Arabian or Tuscan jasmine (Grand duke of Tuscassy), Motia, Mogra, Malligae and Kodi mullai (Bhattacharjee, 1980) are commercially cultivated. The species has several synonyms viz., J. fragrans, J, sambac Rorb, Mogram sambac. laik, etc. In Karnataka they are known as Mysore mallige, Mangalore or Udupi mallige depending upon the place of cultivation and Gundu or Dundu mallige, Yelu-suttina mallige etc. depending upon the morphology of the flower. One of the important cultural operations in jasmine is pruning which is done to regulate the growth in untidy bushes and to promote profuse flowering. Variations in respect of quality and quantity of flower have also been observed with different dates of pruning. Regulation of flowering in Jasmine has great practical value due to seasonal nature of flowering and peak productivity in certain months of the year which remain as major problems in Jasmine flower production. So making the plant to flower throughout the year would be certainly desirable as it offers advantages to both growers and consumers. In commercial cultivation, plant density varies from place to place and also depends upon the species cultivated and the soil conditions. In order to meet the ever increasing demand for fresh flowers, efforts are being made to increase the area under jasmine, to develop high yielding varieties and improved agro-techniques. Cultivation aspects such as planting density, nutrient management and pruning practices have been standardized under Coimbatore, Madurai and Bangalore conditions. But no such work has been undertaken for transitional conditions of Dharwad, even though the area under this crop is increasing in this region. The species has several synonyms viz., J. fragrans, J, sambac Rorb, Mogram sambac. laik, etc. In Karnataka they are known as Mysore mallige, Mangalore or Udupi mallige depending upon the place of cultivation and Gundu or Dundu mallige, Yelu-suttina mallige etc. depending upon the morphology of the flower. One of the important cultural operations in jasmine is pruning which is done to regulate the growth in untidy bushes and to promote profuse flowering. Variations in respect of quality and quantity of flower have also been observed with different dates of pruning. Regulation of flowering in Jasmine has great practical value due to seasonal nature of flowering and peak productivity in certain months of the year which remain as major problems in Jasmine flower production. So making the plant to flower throughout the year would be certainly desirable as it offers advantages to both growers and consumers. I Plant density is also one of the important factors which determines ultimate quantum of production. In commercial cultivation, plant density varies from place to place and also depends upon the species cultivated and the soil conditions. In order to meet the ever increasing demand for fresh flowers, efforts are being made to increase the area under jasmine, to develop high yielding varieties and improved agro-techniques. Cultivation aspects such as planting density, nutrient management and pruning practices have been standardized under Coimbatore, Madurai and Bangalore conditions. But no such work has been undertaken for transitional conditions of Dharwad, even though the area under this crop is increasing in this region. Hence the present investigation was undertaken in order to know the effect of plant population and time of pruning on growth and flower yield of Jasmine (Jasminum sambac Ait with the following specific objectives; 1. To standardise the time of pruning of jasmine under transitional tract of Karnataka. 2. To find out the effect of spacing of Jasmine in relation to pruning. 3. To find out the effect of time of pruning and spacing on leaf chemical constituents (N, P and K). 4 Keview of Citemtme Pruning is an important horticultural practice, the knowledge of which is essential for the cultivation since pruning affects many aspects of growth and productivity. The constituents were in the range of 1.64 to 2.20 per cent in case of N, 0.65 to 0.82 per cent in case of P and 2.48 to 2.95 per cent in case of K among different treatments. 57 Discussion The results of the experiments carried out to find out the optimum level of plant population and time of pruning on growth and yield of Jasmine are discussed under the different headings given below; 5.1 EFFECT OF PLANT POPULATION Commercial viability of yield levels without affecting the quality of flowers is governed by optimum plant population in a given area. The present investigation revealed that the plant population has significant influence on both growth and yield characters in Jasmine. It was observed that plants spaced under wider spacing (2x3 m) have excelled all lower spacings regarding growth as well as yield per plant. The length of the primary shoot recorded under wider spacing is higher compared to other spacings. This may be due to better exposure to light and ample moisture and nutrition. The extensive growth of primary shoot in widely spread plants enhanced the number of sprouts per plant, and associated number of laterals per primary shoot. This increased the over all number of productive shoots per plant. The number of productive shoots directly determines the flower number and the yield. The results also revealed that the plants with wider spacing produced the highest number of leaves per primary shoot and maximum leaf area per shoot. Nambison et al. (1968) also made similar V DISCUSSION observations. The interaction studies highlighted best yield performance with wider spacing when associated with early-mid pruning practice. The better exposure would have probably accounted for this. The plant would have accumulated higher levels of total polysaccharides due to higher photosynthetic activity. This would have resulted in vigorous growth of shoots which might have ultimately influenced the yield. Although per plant yield in widely spaced plants was higher, the overall yield on hectare basis was higher in closely spaced plants. This is on account of the fact that plant population per unit area is higher in closely spaced plots. However, the yield parameters like 100- flower bud weight and flower bud diameter values were high with medium (2x2 m) spaced plants. This may be ascribed to the reason that plants under medium spacing have utilised optimum quantity of nutrients, moisture and air. From the flower grade point of view and its economical value there on, the flowers raised in medium spaced plots would have higher economic value. 5.2 EFFECT OF PRUNING The pruning is one of the important cultural operations in the cultivation of Jasmines. A knowledge on this aspect is of paramount importance to manipulate the plants physiology which may eventually lead to the maximum production In the present investigation, a significant influence of time of pruning is observed on increase in different growth parameters like 59 number of sprouts, length of primary shoot, number of productive shoots and number of leaves. The effect was more marked when the plants were pruned at mid-December (Cf: Table. 1,3,4,5,6). The basis for this could be the total polysaccharide content may be more in the plants of J. sambac pruned in December (Sidda and Rai, 1988) might have favoured the vigorous growth of the plant. The higher vegetative growth in early- mid (18-12-95) pruned plants, influenced the flower yield. Raman (1973) reported a positive correlation between the vigour of the plant and yield of certain varieties in J.sambac. In the present study also it was observed that the plants which yielded higher were vigorous in growth. Production of new shoots is a continuous process and flowers are borne on current seasons shoots. Therefore, it is obvious that any increase in length of new shoot and their production would augment the flower production. The plants pruned on December 18^^ produced numerous vigorous shoots which resulted in increased flower production. This increased length of primary shoot would have favoured more number of leaves. However, from the interaction studies it was evident that higher yield/plant can be obtained when wider spacing (2x3 m) was associated with early-mid pruning practice. Because of wider spacing, there is an increased absorption of nutrition under favorable climatic conditions that prevailed during the period of early-mid (18-12- 95) pruning which might have enhanced the photosynthetic activity. This situation favoured vigorous growth of plants and obviously more number of leaves. The increased number of leaves inturn, would have increased 60 perception of flowering stimulus accounting for higher number of flower buds and consequently higher yield. Similar views were held by Muthuswamy et al. (1973) in J.sambac. Nagabawa and Hirari (1959) observed that larger branches produced higher flower buds than the smaller ones in Fiju kaki. The increase in length of primary shoot, more number of productive shoots per plant and more number of leaves in response to pruning in the present study confirms the findings of Sambandamurthy et al. This may be attributed to climatic differences. The highest yield obtained in mid-December pruned plants may be attributed to the highest mean weight per hundred flower buds and increased number of flowers per plant which inturn increased flower yield. These attributes have contributed towards the highest total yield. On the other hand, the lowest yield observed in early pruned plants could be related to the least values recorded in respect of above mentioned characters. However, the foregoing results may be beneficial to the growers to stagger the flower production in Jasmine. From the foregoing discussion, it may be seen that it is necessary to findout the effects of pruning at different heights in furture investigation. Similarly, since December pruning has found to be more favourable, the studies of present kind can be tried during November to January period. 62 Summary The investigation on effect of plant population and time of pruning on growth and yield in Jasminum sambac Ait. was carried out at the Floriculture Unit of New Orchard of Department of Horticulture, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad during 1995-96. The studies consisted of two aspects, viz., finding out the suitable plant population for better yields and finding out the optimum time of pruning for promoting growth and yield of flowers. There were in all 12 treatment combinations with 4 different dates of pruning, viz., Early pruning (8-12-1995), Early-mid (18-12-1995), Late-mid (28-12-1995) and Late pruning (8-1-1996) and 3 spacing levels, namely, narrow spacing (2x1 m or 5000 plants/ha), medium spacing (2x2 m or 2500 plants/ha) and wider spacing (2x3 m or 1667 plants/ha) laid out in 2-Factorial Randomised Block Design. The salient findings of the study are summarised below. 1. Among the three different spacing levels tried, narrow spacing recorded the highest yield (4095.26 kg) per hectare against the medium and wider spacing due to higher number of sprouts per unit area. 2. Although the yield per hectare was highest in narrow spacing, yield per plant was more in wider spacing, caused by increase in length of VI SUMMARY primary shoot, higher number of sprouts, higher number of productive shoots and higher number of leaves. This is followed by the medium spacing which gave higher yield per plant next in order. 3. Regarding flower quality, the study revealed that diameter of flower bud and 100 flower weight were maximum under medium spacing level of 2x2 mts. 4. With regard to pruning, highest length of primary shoot, highest number of sprouts, number of laterals, highest number of productive shoots and more number of leaves were obtained when early-mid pruning (18-12-95) was effected as against lowest values in this regard when pruning was done earlier (8-12-1995). 5. The highest 100 flower bud weight was recorded when the plants were pruned at 18th December 1995 as compared to earlier or later pruning. 6. The plants pruned on 18th December (Early-mid) recorded highest yield of flowers (4069.41 kg/ha). 7. The yield next in the order (2817.70 kg/ha) was in late-mid pruned plants (28-12-95). However, early pruning (8-12-95) adversely affected the yield. 8. The peak period of flowering for all the treatments was observed during the period of May to July. 64 9. None of the chemical constituents viz., nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium were influenced by different dates of pruning or plant population. In the overall conclusion, it may be summarised that the narrow spacing (2x1 m) resulted in highest average yield per hectare. Regarding pruning, the highest yield of flowers was obtained when plants were pruned on 18th December (Early-mid), which may be recommended as optimum time of pruning for Jasminum sambac Ait. 65 Keferences ANONYMOUS, 1962, Rose Annual, National Rose Society, Great Britain. ABSTRACT The present investigation entitled '"Effect of spacing and nitrogen levels on growth, yield and flower quality of jasmine , -:Do-.J,} <- (Jasminum sambac Ait.) Cv. LMogra ' was conducted during, July-'98 to July-'99 in plot E-8 of Regional Horticultural Research Station, Gujarat Agricultural University, Navsari. Twelve treatment combinations consisting of four spacings viz., 1.0 x 1.0 m (SI), 1.5 x 1.0 m (S2), 1.5 x 1.5 m (S3) and 2.0 x 1.5 m (S4) and three levels of nitrogen viz., 90 g (NI), 120g (N2) and 150 g (N3) per plant were tried in Randomized Block Design with factorial concept. All the treatments were replicated thrice. Among the various spacings, the spacing S3 (1.5 x 1.5 m) recorded the maximum number of primary shoots, East-West plant spread, flower bud length and N-content in plant, while wider spacing 54 (2.0 x 1.5) recorded the maximum North- South plant spread, number of flower buds and flower bud yield per plant and K-content in plant. The maximum number of flower buds, flower yield per hectare and P-content in plant were recorded under closer spacing SI . (1.0 x 1.0 mi. The application of 150 g nitrogen per plant (N3) produced significantly the maximum East-West plant spread, leaf area, total leaf area per plant, number of flower buds and flower yield per plant as well as per hectare. The application of 150 g nitrogen per plant (N3) also recorded significantly the highest N, P and K-content in jasmine plant. Interaction effect of spacing and nitrogen levels also found to be significant for most of the characters. The interaction S2Nl recorded significantly the maximum East-West plant spread and flower bud length, whereas, the maximum North-South plant spread was recorded in interaction S4Nl. The interaction S4N2 recorded significantly the maximum leaf area and total leaf area per plant while the interaction S4N3 recorded significantly the maximum flower bud diameter, Nand P-content in plant. The maximum corolla tube length and K-content were found under interactions SlN2 and S3N2, respectively. The interaction effect of spacing and nitrogen levels on flower yield was found to be non-significant. The highest net income with the highest cost-benefit ratio recorded under S 1 N3 combination. From the yield and economic point of view, it could be . ' ·jJ .... 6L. inferred that the jasmine (Jasminum sambac Ait.) Cv. l,Mogra' should be planted at 1.0 x 1.0 m distance (10,000 plants/ha) and fertilized with 150 g nitrogen per plant. Nitrogen should be applied in three equal splits i.e . 15 days after pruning, one and half month after pruning and three months after pruning. Apart from this 60 g each of phosphorus and potash per plant should be applied after pruning along. with farm yard manure at the rate of 20 tons per hectare. • Dr. N. L. Patel M.Sc.(Agri.) INTRODUCTION I INTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the oldest fragrant flowers to be cultivated by man . The word Jasminum has been derived from the Persian word "Jas-Minum" meaning fragrance . The genus Jasm;num belongs to the olive family Oleaceae. It consists of about 90 species . • About 40 species are reported to be occurred in India. Out of these species, with scented flowers, only three are mostly cultivated for their cut flower and extraction of perfume, these • are : Jasmillum sambac Ait, Jasminllm grandi/lorum L. and Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. According to survey conducted by Kolavalli in \988, jasmine is grown in nearly 6385 hectares in India. An annual production of flowers worth Rs. 80-100 million (Muthuswamy and Abdul Khader, 1986). It is estimated that 12,500 kg of cut flowers of different kinds of jasmine are sold everyday in important cities (Randhawa and Mukhopadhyay, 1986). The flowers of jasmine are highly estimated by the perfumer, owing to the delicacy and sweetness of its odour. Mostly jasmine flowers are used for worship. A large quantity of some species is also consumed for extraction of essential oils. There is hardly any high-class floral perfume of oriental origin, which does not contain at least a small percentage of jasmine flower oil. It gives smoothness and elegance to the perfume combinations. The international market prices of jasmine concrete and absolute, in which forms the jasmine oil is commercially produced are, said to be around ,, 2 Rs. 12,OOO/kg and Rs. 19,000/kg, respectively. Jasminum sambac Ait. contains 0.14 % to 0.19 % concrete (Muthuswamy and Abdul Khader,1986). There are also some important species of jasmine like, J. arborescens L., J. calophyJlum Vahl.. J. flexile Vahl.. J. humile L. and J. pubescens Willd. The successful commercial cultivation of this crop is depend on many factors such as climate. soil, soil fertility. irrigation. fertilization, plant density per unit area, season of growing etc. Among these, plant spacing and fertilization especially nitrogen have major effect on plant growth and development. These two factors have a great impact on the ultimate production of flowers. Plant density not only influences the growth and development but also plays an important role in production and quality of flower. This also varies according to cultivar, place, soil type and time of planting. In jasmine, proper spacing between plants is required for better growth and development of plant and thereby higher flower yield. Nitrogen plays a key role in growth and development of jasmine plant. Many researchers have reported that deficiency of nitrogen reduces plant growth and yield. Although, in Gujarat. Jasminum sambac Ait. Cv. 'Mogra' is not grown on commercial scale, and so also information on various cultural operations is lacking. Perhaps, this is the reason why farmers are reluctant to grow this crop. Therefore. it is essential to generate 3 'information that can be passed on to growers who are interested to take this crop whose scope is increasing nearby cities and big towns as it is used for garlands, chaplets and for religious offering. Therefore, keeping the above points in view, an attempt has been made to study the "Effect of spacing and nitrogen on growth, yield and flower quality of jasmine (Jasminum sambac Ail.) Cv. ' Mogra m at Regional Horticultural Research Station, Gujarat Agricultural University, Navsari Campus, Navsari, with the following major objectives. I. To know the effect of nitrogen on growth, yield and flower quality of Jasminum sambac Ail. Cv. ' Mogra' . 2. To know the effect of plant density on growth, yield and flower quality of Jasminum sambac Ail. Cv. 'Mogra'. 3. To know the interaction effect of nitrogen and spacing on growth, yield and flower quality of Jasminum sambac Ail. Cv. 'Mogr.' . 4. To study the economics of flower production of Jasminum sambac Ail. I 5.2 5.3 5.4 5.1 5.1.1 Effect of spacing Effect of nitrogen Interaction effect of spacing x nitrogen Economics Effect of spacing Effect of spacing on growtb attributes The plant spacing is a very important factor responsible for the growth of plant when other inputs are adequately supplied. Spacing had no significant effect on plant height because pruning at equal height might be reduced competition for space among plants under different treatments. • • The response of different spacing treatments to vanous otber growth attributes of jasmine Cv. 'Mogra' namely number of primary shoots and plant spread in E- Wand N-S directions were found to be significant. 62 The results showed that the maximum number of shoots was recorded in spacing S3 (1.5 x 1.5 m). This increase in number of branches might be due to lesser competition for space, light and nutrients among the plants under wider spacing and this helped the plant to produce more number of shoots. Different levels of spacing significantly influenced the spread of plant. Maximum spread of plant in E-W direction was observed in S3 spacing. This may be due to maximum number of shoots per plant in S3 spacing. The maximum spread of plant in N-S direction was recorded in wider spacing S4 (2.0 x 1.5m) being 137.27 cm. However, it was statistically at par with S2 and S3 spacings. These results are in line with the findings of Pal e/ al. (1984) in Jasmil1um auriculalum L. Var. 'Single' and Pal el al. (\985) in Jasmil1um sambac Sol. Var. 'Khoya'. Total leaf area per plant was not affected by spacing. Total leaf area depends on the size of individual leaf and number of leaves per plant. Since both the above characters were not affected by spacing, the total leaf area remained unchanged under different spacings. 5.1.2 Effect of spacing on flower bud quality The flower bud quality under different spacing was almost not change except flower bud length, which was higher under S3 (1.5 x I. 5 m) spacing. This may be due to better vegetative growth under this treatment. 5.1.3 Effect of spacing on yield of flower bud Yield of flower bud per plant was significantly higher in wider spacing S4 followed by S3 and S2 and minimum in closer spacing SI. This increase in the yield of flower buds per plant in wider spacing (S4) was due to better vegetative growth in wider spacing. After successful vegetative phase only, the plant could step into reproductive phase successfully, which resulted in better yields. These findings are also supported by Nambisan et al. (\978) in Jasminum sambac Ail. Cv. 'Gundumalli', Pal el al. (1984) in Jasminum auriculalum Cv. 'Single' and in Jasminum sambac Cv. 'Khoya' during 1985 and Patel and Singh (1995) in Jasminum sambac Ail. Cv. 'Mogra'. Though the yield of flowers per plant was higher in wider spacing, the total yield of flowers per hectare was significantly maximum in closer spacing S I and was decreased with increase in spacing. This increase in the yield of flower buds per hectare in closer spacing was due to the fact that the plant population per unit area was greater in closer spacing SI (10000 plants/ha) than S3 (6666 plants/ha) and S" (3333 plants/ha). Therefore, tbe production of flowers per unit area was increase in plot having larger plant population The lesser number of flower per plant and that of higher per unit area under higher density of planting were also responsible for lower yield per plant and higher yield per hectare respectively under closer spacing. Similar results were also reported in Jasmillum sambac by Nambisan el al. (\978), Pal et al. (\9114) and Patel and Singh (1995) and in Jasmillum auriculalum by Pal el al. (1985). Total number of flower buds per plant was significantly higher in wider spacing 54 followed by S3 and S2 and minimum in SI spacing. This was due to lesser competition among plants in wider • spaclllg, which leads to the better availability of nutrients, and light ~ .. - 64 resulted in better vegetative growth of plant, thereby, increasing the number of potential sites where flower could be developed . 'Mogra' namely plant spread in East-West direction, leaf area and total , leaf area of plant. The highest level of nitrogen N3 (150 g/plant) recorded significantly maximum plant spread in East-West direction, leaf area and total leaf area. There was an increase in E- W spread of plant with increased nitrogen levels, The highest plant spread under N3 treatment indicated that the optimum requirement of jasmine plants for nitrogen is met by 150 g N per plant and this might have caused better spread of plant. In chrysanthemum. 66 The result showed that there was increase in total leaf area of plant with the increased application of nitrogen. The highest level of nitrogen N3 (150 g/plant) produced significantly maximum flower bud yield per plant, flower bud yield per hectare, number of flower buds per plant and number of flower buds per hectare. By applying sufficient quantity of nitrogen, the plants can put forth better vegetative growth, which ultimately leads to higher yield. In present investigation higher nitrogen produced the plant with large size leaf and with higher total leaf area which resulted in higher photosynthetic rate consequently the plant receiving more nitrogen produced more flowers. Cv. 'Mogra'~ was carried out during the year 1999-2000 in Block No-E 8 of Regional Horticultural Research Station, Gujarat Agricultural University, Navsari Campus, Navsari. During the investigation, treatment effects were studied on plant height, number of primary shoots, plant spread, number of leaves per plant, leaf area, total leaf area per plant, flower bud length and diameter, corolla tube length flower bud yield, number of flower bud per plant and hectare and plant nutrient (N, P, K) content. The experiment was laid out in Factorial Randomized Block Design with three replications. There were four spacings viz., 1.0 x 1.0 m (SI), 1.5 x 1.0 m (S2), 1.5 x 1.5 m (S3) and 2.0 x 1.5 m (S4) and three nitrogen levels viz., 90 g per plant (NI), 120 g per plant (N2) and 150 g per plant (N3) for one flowering season. Thus in all there were twelve treatment combinations under the experiment. 6.1 Growth attributes The jasmine plants planted at the spacing S3 (1.5 x 1.5 m) produced the maximum number of shoots per plant (20.02) with maximum spreading habit in East-West direction while wider spacing S4 (2.0 x 1.5 m) recorded the maximum spread in North-South direction. The plant height, number of leaves per plant and leaf area were not affected by different spacings. The plants receiving the 71 highest level of nitrogen N3 (I SO g/plant) had more tendency to grow in East-West direction and had higher total leaf area contributed by larger size of leaf. The interaction S4N2 recorded the maximum individual as well as total leaf area per plant. 6.2 Flower quality The flower quality in terms of bud length, bud diameter and corolla tube length almost remained unchange under different spacing and nitrogen levels except spacing S3 which produced the larger flower bud. The interaction effect was not consistent for different flower quality characters. The maximum flower bud length, bud diameter and corolla tube length were recorded under S2NI, S4N3 and SlN3 interactions, respectively. 6.3 Flower bud yield Effect of spacing and nitrogen levels on production of jasmine flower bud was found to be significant. Production of flower bud per plant was increased while that of per unit area decreased with decrease in plant population. The wider spacing S4 (2.0 x 1.5 m) recorded significantly the maximum number of flower buds and 72 flower bud yield per plant. Whereas, closer spacing Sl (1.0 x 1.0 m) recorded significantly the maximum numher of flower buds and flower bud yield per hectare. Application of higher dose of nitrogen N3 (1 SO g/pant) recorded significantly the maximum N, P and K content in jasmine plant. The interaction effect of spacing and Dltrogen levels was also found to be significant. Bengaluru June, 2017 (Chidananda Muddaiah Hirematha) BIONOMICS AND CONTROL OF RED SPIDER MITE, Tetranychus lombardinii BAKER AND PRITCHARD (Acari: Tetranychidae) INFESTING Jasminum spp. CHIDANANDA MUDDAIAH HIREMATHA ABSTRACT The crimson spider mite, Tetranychus lombardinii infested jasmine crop, more particularly Jasminum sambac in 11 districts of Karnataka. In Bangalore, J. sambac harboured more number of mites (12.72 mites/twig of 6-8 leaves) compared to J. multiflorum & J. grandiflorum (10.39 to 10.95). Mite activity showed gradual increase from August onwards recording a peak of 23.24 mites in Nov. followed by low intensity peaks (10-11mites) in Feb. & April. Mite development in the laboratory was faster (24.85 - 8.74 days for female; 24.26 to 7.37 for male) as rearing temperature increased from 20℃ to 35℃. Life cycle was shortest (7.37 days for male & 8.74 for female) at 35℃. Life cycle was shortest (7.62 to 22.37 days for male; 9.04 to 23.86 for female) on J. sambac at all temperature (20℃- 35℃) & relative humidity (71-88%) conditions. Longevity, oviposition period, fecundity and sex ratio declined (22.61 to 7.96 days, 18.68 to 4.27 days, 49.24 to 16.12 eggs/female and 1:13.6 to 1:4.3) as rearing temperature increased from 20℃ to 35℃. Mite also preferred J. sambac for reproduction vis-a-vis J. multiflorum & J. grandiflorum. Life table data were generated at four constant rearing temperatures on Jasminum spp. Intrinsic rate of natural increase, rm (female offsprings/female/day) was relatively high when reared between 25℃ & 30℃ (0.153 to 0.191 & 0.165 to 0.189, respectively). Relative toxicity of acaricides (based on LC50 values) to T. lombardinii was, Hexythiazox (0.11ppm)> Fenpyroximate (0.14)> Fenazaquin (0.42)> Fenpropathrin (0.56)> Buprofezin (0.83)> Spiromesifen(0.95)> Dicofol (1.49)> Propargite (4.49)> Diafenthurion (8.80). The Order of field residual toxicity (based on LT50 values) was, Spiromesifen (17.12 days)> Fenazaquin (14.54)> Fenpyroximate (14.08)> Propargite (13.98)> Dicofol (13.63)> Hexythiazox (12.92)> Buprofezin (12.52)> Fenpropathrin (12.43)> Diafenthiuron (11.73). family Tetranychidae comprises of more than 1305 species under 70 genera and two subfamilies, Bryobinae & Tetranychinae. Majority of members of subfamily Tetranychinae are soft bodied and brightly coloured (red, green, yellow and orange). They produce silk from glands opening on the tarsus of pedipalps and use it for webbing. In view of global importance of tetranychids, Spider Mites Web” is providing comprehensive current information on every documented species including distribution, host plants, reference literature since 1758 etc. (Migeon et al., 2010). Spider mites damage all types of economically important cultivated crops like field crops, vegetable crops, fruit crops, ornamental & flower crops and medicinal & aromatic plants (Vacante, 2015). In recent times many of our cultivated crops are being damaged by spider mites, owing to many reasons. Recently, Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard was observed to cause noticeable damage to cultivated species of Jasminum around Bangalore (Anonymous, 2016) and globally this mite has nearly 126 host plants now (Migeon & Dorkeld, 2006- 2017). T. lombardinii was first reported and described by Baker & Pritchard from cotton crop in African region in 1960. Further, Meyer and Rodriguez in 1966 included Jasminum nudiflorum, as a host for this mite from South Africa. Meyer (1981) reported severe damage of T. lombardinii on some South African crops such as banana and papaya, particularly during summer season. In India, T. lombardinii has been reported on Gossypium herbaceum (Banerjee, 1965) and Indigofera tinctoria (Gupta, 1985) from Assam. Jasmine is an ornamental shrub and economic flower crop under botanical family Oleaceae and is highly prized for its fragrant flowers and essential oil, more commercially used in perfume industry. Cultivated species of Jasminum are Jasminum sambac, Jasminum multiflorum, Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum auriculatum. Jasmine crop is infested and damaged by many pests such as bud worm, gallery worm, erineum mite etc. (Byatnal, 2002; Rajakumar et al., 2005b). Very recently Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard has been reported as an emerging spider mite pest causing considerable damage to commercially cultivated species of Jasminum and no literature is available either on occurrence or damage of T. lombardinii on jasmine. However, for comparison, information available on the biology, ecology and control of spider mite species under genus Tetranychus on economically important crops, particularly flower crops is reviewed and presented in this Chapter. 2.1. Occurrence of Tetranychus lombardinii on Jasminum spp. Tetranychus lombardinii was first reported and described in 1960 by Baker and Pritchard from cotton in the African region. Further in 1966, it was recorded on Jasminum nudiflorum by Meyer and Rodriguez from South Africa. Byatnal (2002), who carried out a survey on insect and mite pests of Jasminum spp. in Dharwad and Raichur area in Karnataka reported bud borer, blossom midge and two spotted spider mite Tetranychus urticae Koch as serious pests of Jasminum sambac and J. multiflorum, while J. auriculatum was found damaged more by eriophyid mite, Aceria jasmini. Bud borer incidence was more during flowering period and spider mite was damaging the crop almost throughout the year. Zeity (2015), while studying tetranychid mite fauna from 95 host plants in major agroecosystem covering 17 districts of Karnataka recorded 46 species. Of them, Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard was recorded from Jasminum sambac in Bangalore. (2005b) studied the seasonal activity of red spider mite, T. urticae on jasmine crop in Raichur district. The mite incidence was maximum during first week of May with 9.36 mites/leaf followed by 8.50 mites/leaf during last week of April. There was low/no mite population during third week of November, due to non- availability of foliage as a result of pruning of the crop. Later mite population appeared during summer season and the highest mite population was noticed in March-May period on account of dry weather conditions; also no mite population was observed during January – February. Meena et al. (2013) studied the influence of abiotic factors on the incidence of two spotted spider mite, T. urticae on orchid. From January onwards the mite population gradually increased and peaked to 22.98 mites/10cm2 leaf area by first fortnight of December. Roopa (2005) reported that spider mite appeared much earlier on summer crop of brinjal as compared to kharif and rabi crops. The population reached peak twice i.e., July II week (14.20 mites/4 cm 2 leaf area) and Nov. III week (28.73 mites). Maximum and minimum temperatures were positively correlated with two spotted spider mite population build-up on grape crop. The highest population density (22.11- 25.45 mites/cm2 leaf area) was observed between March and April 2005, when the ambient temperature was between 35º and 37.3ºC (Sekhar et al., 2008). 2.3. Bionomics and control of red spider mite, Tetranychus lombardinii ….. infesting Jasminum spp. 15 III MATERIAL AND METHODS Investigations on population dynamics, developmental biology, reproduction attributes and life table parameters of T. lombardinii infesting Jasminum crop and relative toxicity of selected acaricides against T. lombardinii under laboratory and field conditions (for residual toxicity) were carried out in the Acarology unit of Department of Agricultural Entomology UAS, Bangalore during the period 2016-17. The methodologies followed and techniques adopted for carrying out various studies are presented hereunder. 3.1 Occurrence of Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard on Jasminum spp. in Karnataka A roving survey was conducted in major jasmine growing areas of Karnataka to know the occurrence of spider mite Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard on Jasminum spp. From each of the locations such as Bangalore (IIHR, GKVK- UAS & UHS), Bilagi (Bagalkot dist.), Belagavi, Muddebihal (Bijapur dist.), Melur (Chikkaballapur dist.), Dharwad (UAS Campus), Haveri, Balagere (Kolar dist.), Agalkera (Koppal dist.), Malavalli (Mandya dist.), Eklaspur (Raichur dist.), leaves from jasmine plants were sampled and observed under stereo-binocular microscope in the laboratory. The mite population including eggs and active stages of the mite was recorded as the number per twig of 6 - 8 leaves of Jasminum sambac & J. multiflorum and as number per bipinnate compound leaf of J. grandiflorum. Good number of both male and female adult specimens was slide mounted and the taxonomic identification was confirmed as T. lombardinii using both morphological characters and molecular data (by DNA sequencing and BLAST analysis). 3.2 Population fluctuation of Tetranychus lombardinii on Jasminum spp. under Bangalore conditions Jasmine (J. sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum) crop at IIHR Campus (Hessaraghatta) and GKVK Campus (UAS& UHS) was used for mite population dynamics study. The plant samples consisting of twigs with at least 6-8 leaves for J. sambac, J. multiflorum or a bi-pinnate compound leaf for J. grandiflorum were collected 16 Chidananda Muddaiah Hirematha, M.Sc. (Agri.) 2017 from 3 spots each from top and bottom canopies to record the mite population. Leaf samples with proper label were brought to the laboratory in polyethylene bags and observed under stereobinocular microscope to record the number of spider mites (eggs and motile stages) as well as associated natural enemies, if any. With such sampling, observations were recorded at fortnightly interval at all the locations mentioned above from August 2016 to June (IFN) 2017. Maximum and minimum temperatures, relative humidity, rainfall, bright sunshine hours, wind speed and evaporation data of these locations were made used to study their effects, if any on mite abundance or activity. 3.3 Collection, purification and mass culturing of T. lombardinii in the laboratory Spider mite infested leaves of Jasminum from IIHR and GKVK Campus at Bangalore were brought to the laboratory in separate polyethylene bags. Fifty teliochrysalis females (quiescent deutonymph) along with 1 to 2 attending males were randomly picked from infested leaf sample and transferred on to separate 2.5cm X 2.5cm jasmine leaf disks, placed on wet cotton wad in 6” inches Petri plates and allowed for colonization for at least 10-15 days. Excised leaf disk technique was followed for rearing and maintaining mite culture in the laboratory (Plate 2). Later one female and one male from each of these leaf bits were slide mounted using Hoyer’s medium for taxonomic identification. Leaf disks with T. lombardinii mite individuals were pooled and used as a pure starter culture for further culturing on J. sambac leaves placed on wet foam in polyethylene trays measuring 30cm X 25cm X 6cm and this mite culture was used for various biological and toxicological studies. 3.4 Comparative development and reproduction of T. lombardinii on Jasminum spp. at different temperature and humidity conditions The life history of T. lombardinii was studied at four different constant temperatures, 20±1℃, 25.3℃ (lab. temperature during October- November 2016), 30±1℃ and 35±1℃ on leaves of Jasminum spp. (J. sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum) with 16h:8h L:D conditions in a BOD incubator. The corresponding relative humidity conditions recorded at these study temperatures were, 83-88%, 71-74%, 73-77% and 74-79%. Plate 2. Jasminum auriculatum was found either least infested or not infested. Jasmine plants in the field were treated with different acaricides at the field recommended doses separately using high volume knapsack sprayer (using spray volume @625 litres/ha). Mites (immature stages for buprofezin and hexythiazox; adult females for other acaricides) were released for laboratory bioassay using field treated jasmine leaves placed on wet cotton wad in polyethylene trays. Starting from one day after treatment/application, treated jasmine leaves were used for bioassay on alternate days and mortality of mites was recorded up to 48 h. The residual toxicity of different synthetic acaricides used in the study ranged from 11.73 days (diafenthiuron) to 17.12 days (spiromesifen). The results from these studies are discussed in the light of available literature in this Chapter. 5.1 Taxonomic identification of crimson spider mite, Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard Based on morphological characters the spider mite species which infested Jasminum spp. and used for biological & toxicological investigations in the present study was identified as Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard. BLAST analysis of DNA sequences (mitochondrial COI and nuclear ITS2) of the mite also confirmed its taxonomic identification as T. lombardinii. Thus, integration of morphological data and molecular data established the identification of the mite species more precisely. 5.2 Occurrence of Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard on Jasminum spp. Anonymous (2016) considered T. lombardinii as a potential mite pest of Jasminum spp. under Bangalore conditions. Except this report, no further information on its biological characteristics, seasonality etc. is either available or documented in the country, more particularly on cultivated species of Jasminum. Outside India, Meyer and Rodriguez (1966) recorded T. lombardinii on a wild host, Jasminum nudiflorum in South Africa. Probably in anticipation of its emerging nature, Coates in 1974 carried out biological studies with T. lombardinii on cultivated host plants like papaya and banana. Meyer (1981) reported severe incidence of T. lombardinii on banana and papaya crops in South Africa and provided complete details of nature and symptoms of damage by the mite on these crops. Data from roving survey between September 2016 and Feb. 2017 in the present study indicated the occurrence of crimson spider mite, T. lombardinii in 11 major districts of Karnataka on three major cultivated species of Jasmine viz., Jasminum 62 Chidananda Muddaiah Hirematha, M.Sc. (Agri.) 2017 sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum in agricultural fields and in traditional gardening system. The spider mite pest species was found associated with both insect and mite natural enemies, of them, phytoseiid predatory mite, Neoseiulus longispinosus (Evans) was more prevalent. During roving survey in the present study, J. sambac crop in a farmer’s field in Eklaspur village (near Raichur) recorded maximum number of 105 mites/leaf during Nov I week. Byatnal (2002), while surveying for the pests of J. sambac and J. multiflorum in Dharwad and Raichur area also noticed the potential damage by two spotted spider mite Tetranychus urticae almost throughout the year, while the damage by bud borer and blossom midge was more severe at the flowering stage. Coates (1974) attributed severe damage by T. lombardinii on banana and papaya crops in South Africa, to warm and dry conditions especially during late spring and summer seasons. 5.3 Population dynamics of crimson spider mite, Tetranychus lombardinii under Bangalore conditions Crimson spider mite was active throughout the study period i.e., August 2016 to June 2017 on all the three species of Jasminum viz., J. sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum (Fig. 2) under Bangalore conditions i.e., IIHR, Hessaraghatta and GKVK. Comparatively, J. sambac harboured more no. of mites, 12.72 mites/ twig of 6-8 leaves, compared to J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum (10.39 to 10.95 mites). Overall mite activity (& natural enemies) across Jasminum species under Bangalore conditions depicted in Fig. 3 revealed gradual increase in mite population from August onwards leading to a peak of 23.24 mites during Nov. II FN. Further, the mite population recorded low intensity peaks (10-11 mites during Feb. I FN & April II FN). But Rajakumar et al. (2005b), who also studied the seasonality of red spider mite on Jasmine crop in Raichur district of Karnataka observed peak mite activity (8.50 to 9.36 mites/leaf) between last week of April and first week of May. This variation in the peak activity of spider mite in Bangalore and Raichur area might be due to difference in the geographical location as well as the prevailing weather conditions, more particularly the temperature. T. lombardinii causes damage by sucking the sap from the leaves of Jasmine plant. Jasminum plant, being a perennial shrub put forth ample foliage almost throughout the year (unless pruned/trained during summer months) and serves as a continuous food source for the crimson spider mite. However, significant influence of rainfall on mite activity at IIHR, Hessaraghatta requires mite population data generated over a longer period of time, for any valid explanation. 5.4 Crimson spider mite, T. lombardinii as an emerging pest In India, so far T. lombardinii has been reported on only one cultivated plant species, Indigofera tinctoria (Indigo) in Assam (Gupta, 1985; Gupta and Gupta, 1994). It is evident from the present study that only T. lombardinii infests and damage Jasminum species. Also, T. lombardinii could not be cultured successfully in the laboratory in the present study on host plants reported by Bolland et al. (1998) like, bean, papaya, datura, amaranthus and cucumber. Rearing of T. lombardinii was also not successful on mulberry (Morus indica), a commonly used laboratory host for rearing different species of Tetranychus in the Acarology laboratory at Bangalore. Tetranychus urticae, a well-known cosmopolitan and polyphagous mite species (with >200 cultivated host plants) could not be reared/cultured on Jasmine leaves in the laboratory and hence, T. urticae may not be considered as a potential pest of Jasminum species. Thus, it is inferred that only T. lombardinii may be an emerging pest of J. sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum. However, its potential damage in economic terms like crop loss etc. needs to be ascertained by more systematic studies. 64 Chidananda Muddaiah Hirematha, M.Sc. Bionomics and control of red spider mite, Tetranychus lombardinii ….. infesting Jasminum spp. 71 VI SUMMARY Investigations on developmental biology & demography of Tetranychus lombardinii infesting Jasminum spp. and toxicity of selected acaricides to this mite pest were carried out during 2016-17 in the Acarology unit of Department of Agricultural Entomology, University of Agricultural Sciences, Bangalore. The outcome of these investigations is summarized below: Integrative approach of using conventional morphological data and molecular data (mitochondrial COI and nuclear ITS2 sequences) established the taxonomic identification of the spider mite species infesting cultivated Jasminum spp. in the present study as Tetranychus lombardinii Baker and Pritchard. This is the first report (after Zeity, 2015) of T. lombardinii infesting/ damaging jasmine crop on economical scale in India and the world. Data from roving survey in 11 districts of Karnataka namely, Bangalore (IIHR, GKVK- UAS & UHS), Bilagi (Bagalkot dist.), Belagavi, Muddebihal (Bijapur dist.), Melur (Chikkaballapur dist.), Dharwad (UAS Campus), Haveri, Balagere (Kolar dist.), Agalkera (Koppal dist.), Malavalli (Mandya dist.) and Eklaspur (Raichur dist.) between September 2016 and Feb. 2017 revealed the occurrence of crimson spider mite, T. lombardinii on three major cultivated species of Jasmine, J. sambac, J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum. In Raichur district (Eklaspur), maximum number of 105 mites/leaf was recorded during Nov. I week on Jasminum sambac crop in a farmer’s field. Under Bangalore conditions i.e., IIHR (Hessaraghatta) and GKVK, crimson spider mite was active throughout the study period i.e., August 2016 to June 2017 on all the three species of Jasminum, J. sambac, J. multiflorum, and J. grandiflorum. Comparatively, J. sambac harboured more mean no. of mites, 12.72 mites/ twig of 6-8 leaves compared to J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum (10.39 to 10.95 mites). Overall mite activity on jasmine crop (Jasminum spp.) around Bangalore showed gradual increase in mite population from August onwards leading to a peak of 23.24 mites during Nov. Crimson spider mite completed its development as female (from egg to adult) on leaf disks of Jasminum spp. in 23.86 to 24.85, 10.81 to 14.46, 10.5 to 11.56 and 8.74 to 9.21 days at constant temperature and humidity conditions of 20℃ & 83-88% RH, 25.3℃ &71-74% RH, 30℃ & 73-77% RH and 35℃ & 74-79% RH, respectively. For male mite the corresponding durations of development were, 22.37 to 24.26, 10.18 to 13.86, 9.57 to 10.44 and 7.62 to 9.10 days. Development of T. lombardinii was faster (shorter) (24.85 to 8.74 days for female; from 24.26 to 7.37 days for male) as the rearing temperature increased from 20℃ to 35℃. Life cycle of the mite was shortest (7.37 days for male and 8.74 days for female) at the maximum rearing temperature of 35℃ and 74 to 79% RH. In terms of preferential development of T. lombardinii across Jasminum species of host plants, the total life cycle of the mite (male & female) was shortest (7.62 to 22.37 and 9.04 to 23.86 days, respectively) on J. sambac followed by J. multiflorum and J. grandiflorum at all the four rearing temperature (20℃- 35℃) & relative humidity (71- 88%) conditions. Reproduction attributes of T. lombardinii mated females such as longevity, oviposition period, fecundity and sex ratio (male:female) showed a declining trend (22.61 to 7.96 days, 18.68 to 4.27 days, 49.24 to 16.12 eggs/female and 1:13.6 to 1:4.3, respectively) as the rearing temperature increased from 20℃ to 35℃. At higher rearing temperature (20℃ to 35℃) comparatively female lived shorter, laid less number of eggs over a short oviposition period and produced a progeny with a lower male to female sex ratio in the progeny. T. lombardinii preferred J. sambac for its reproduction as its mated females lived longer with relatively longer oviposition period and higher fecundity on J. sambac leaf disks vis-a-vis J. multiflorum or J. grandiflorum. Life table data was generated for T. lombardinii at four different temperature and humidity conditions on three different species of Jasminum. Mean Generation Time (T) of the mite ranged from 32.76 to 35.01, 19.78 to 21.79, 18.55 to19.95 and 11.42 to 14.03 days at 20℃, 25.3℃, 30℃ and 35℃ rearing temperature, respectively. The most important demographic trait, rm (the number of female offsprings/ female/day) was relatively low at lower temperature of 20℃ (0.092 to 0.107) and relatively high at higher temperature of 35℃ (0.151 to 0.213), while it was more consistent between 25℃ and 30℃ (0.153 to 0.191 at 25℃ & 0.165 to 0.189 at 30℃). Comparative demography of T. lombardinii on Jasminum spp. indicated that its rearing on J. sambac leaf disks (at 25℃ to 30℃) was more advantageous in terms of shorter Mean Generation Time (18.55 to 19.78 days), shorter Doubling Time (3.63 to 3.66 days), higher Gross Reproductive & Net Reproductive Rates (42.37 to 49.85; 33.47 to 43.52) and higher rm values (0.189 to 0.191). Laboratory bioassay data showed that hexythiazox was more toxic to immature stages of crimson spider mite, T. lombardinii with the lowest LC50 value of 0.11 ppm followed by buprofezin with the LC50 value of 0.83 ppm. Comparatively, newer generation acaricides, fenpyroximate, fenazaquin, fenpropathrin and spiromesifen were more toxic to adult females (LC50 of 0.14 to 0.95 ppm). Based on the combined toxicity data (to immature stages & adults), the descending order of toxicity of acaricides to T. lombardinii was: Hexythiazox (0.11 ppm) > Fenpyroximate (0.14 ppm) > Fenazaquin (0.42 ppm) > Fenpropathrin (0.56 ppm)> Buprofezin (0.83 ppm) > Spiromesifen (0.95 ppm) > Dicofol (1.49 ppm) > Propargite (4.49 ppm) > Diafenthurion (8.80 ppm). Foliar application of acaricides on jasmine plant in the field was recorded to be potentially toxic for 11 to 17 days and gradual reduction in their toxicity to mites over time was evident. The residual toxicity data of acaricides computed by Probit analysis 74 Chidananda Muddaiah Hirematha, M.Sc. (Agri.) 2017 (LT50 value) and PT method (persistent × time) were comparable. Descending order of residual toxicity based on LT50 values was, Spiromesifen (17.12 days) > Fenazaquin (14.54 days) > Fenpyroximate (14.08 days) > Propargite (13.98 days) > Dicofol (13.63 days) > Hexythiazox (12.92 days) > Buprofezin (12.52 days) > Fenpropathrin (12.43 days) > Diafenthiuron (11.73 days). From overall findings of the present study it is evident that crimson spider mite, T. lombardinii would be a more potential emerging pest on jasmine crop. Susceptibility of Jasminum sambac to the mite damage is more apparent as it is more preferred by the mite for its development, reproduction and population performance (high rm). Use of newer acaricides may be advocated in view of their inherent toxicity, more particularly their good residual toxicity against the mite.
