STUDIES ON FLORAL MORPHOLOGY AND BIOLOGY IN JASMINUM SPP. ABSTRACT An investigation was carried out to assess the morphology and biology of flowers in 38 genotypes of Jasminum spp. at the Division of Floriculture and Medicinal Crops, ICAR-IIHR, Bengaluru. The studies made on morphology and biological characters revealed high level of variation among the genotypes. J. grandiflorum var. CO.1 Pitchi recorded the longest flower bud length (4.81 cm) and corolla tube length (2.92 cm). J. nitidum recorded longest corolla length (4.93 cm) and biggest flower size (2.15 cm). Number of forks per cyme and number of petals were recorded maximum in J. auriculatum var. CO.1 Mullai (40.13) and J. sambac - IIHR JS - 1(30.95). Calyx number was highest in Gundumallige (8.79) whereas, longest calyx lobe was in Soojimalli (1.49 cm). Flower bearing habits observed were 3-5 forked cyme, many flowered cyme and clustered cyme. Shapes of flower buds were pointed and long, round and short, pointed and short. Colour of the flower bud varied from green white (157 B), white (155 B, 155 C, 155 D) and pink (186 B). Flower types observed were single, double and multi-whorled (3-6). All genotypes recorded solitary style and had 2.00 to 3.00 stamens. CO.1 Pitchi recorded the longest stamen (2.13 cm) and style length (2.32 cm). The peak time of anthesis was recorded between 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. and anther dehiscence between 4:00 to 7:00 p.m. The stigma was receptive 12 h before and 24 h after anthesis and the maximum receptivity was observed between the anthesis to 12 h after anthesis. Shapes of pollen were observed viz., spherical, triangle and tricolpate. Bigger size of pollen was recorded in IIHR JS - 4 (61.50 µm). Pin and thrum type of flowers were observed. The above information generated is useful for the breeders to take up systematic crop improvement in Jasminum spp. Kalaiyarasi, A. Dr. Dhananjaya, M. V. INTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the most important ornamental flowering plants that belong to the family Oleaceae. The term jasmine is derived from the Arabic word „Jessamine‟ (Bhattacharjee, 1980) and also on old Persian name „Yesmyn‟ meaning fragrance. It is a native of Indo-Malayan region (Anonymous, 1959). The genus Jasminum is comprised of diploid (Jasminum sambac, 2n=2x=26), triploid (Jasminum primulinum, 2n=3x=39), tetraploid (Jasminum angustifolium, 2n=4x=52) with basic chromosome number of n=x=13 (Taylor, 1945; Krishnaswamy and Raman, 1948). Different species of jasmine are grown in garden as shrubs and climbers. Several species and varieties are grown on a large scale in different states for loose flower purpose. It is also grown for garden decoration, landscaping, for making garland, hair decoration and for extraction of essential oil. The essential oil content among the different species of jasmine ranges from 0.14 to 0.34 per cent. The basic compounds reported in jasmine oil are Indole, quinoline, 2- methyl quinoline, methyl anthranilate, methyl N-methyl anthranilate, methyl N-acetyl anthranilate, alkylated pyridines and alkylated nicotinates (Diwakar and Bhupal Rao, 1980). The reports on jasmine, suggested that the total number of species in this genus is about 200 (Rendle, 1925; Bailey, 1958). A critical analysis revealed the number of true species is only 89 (Veluswamy et al., 1973) in which 40 species originated from Indian sub-continent and comprises of commercially cultivated species like Jasminum grandiflorum, Jasminum sambac and Jasminum auriculatum. The main beauty and uniqueness of jasmine is its fragrance, which cannot be imitated by any known synthetic aromatic chemical. It is widely cultivated in the Southern and Eastern parts of India and esteemed for their attractive and fragrant flowers. In the South, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have grown this crop on a commercial scale. Mysore Mallige, Udupi Mallige, Ramanathapuram Gundumalli and Madurai Malli are world famous. The countries which grow jasmine on commercial scale are France, India, Italy, Moracco, Sicily, Spain and Egypt. In India, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar growing jasmine on commercial scale (Bhattacharjee, 1980). However, the largest area under jasmine flower production is in Karnataka followed by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu (NHB Database 2014-2015). The annual production of jasmine is 56.57 metric tonnes (NHB Database 2014-2015). Jasmine oil is said to blend with every ﬂoral scent and hence extensively used as an important perfumery item throughout the world. The main beauty and uniqueness of jasmine is its fragrance, which cannot be imitated by any known synthetic aromatic chemical. It is widely cultivated in the Southern and Eastern parts of India and esteemed for their attractive and fragrant flowers. In the South, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu have grown this crop on a commercial scale. Mysore Mallige, Udupi Mallige, Ramanathapuram Gundumalli and Madurai Malli are world famous. The countries which grow jasmine on commercial scale are France, India, Italy, Moracco, Sicily, Spain and Egypt. In India, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar growing jasmine on commercial scale (Bhattacharjee, 1980). However, the largest area under jasmine flower production is in Karnataka followed by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu (NHB Database 2014-2015). The annual production of jasmine is 56.57 metric tonnes (NHB Database 2014-2015). Jasmine oil is said to blend with every ﬂoral scent and hence extensively used as an important perfumery item throughout the world. It is in good demand in the world market and used widely in cosmetic and perfumery industries and has a great export potential. The most unique type of fragrance is derived from Jasminum grandiflorum which is highly appreciated all over the world. The oils are used in the manufacture of high grade perfumes, cosmetics, soaps, confectionery, perfumes, perfumed tobacco, syrups, aerated water, ointments and disinfectants, detergents, in medicinal and pharmaceutical beverages. Morphological traits like size and shape of leaf, internodal length (Raman, 1955), shape of flower bud, petal shape and number of whorls (Bhatnagar, 1956), length of style and stigma (Khan et al., 1970, Indiresh et al., 1989) have been documented in some species. Variations in concrete recovery, benzyl acetate per cent have also been reported by Singh and More (1982) among different varieties even within a species. Different seedling characters, plant characters and floral characters have been correlated with economic traits such as yield of flowers, essential oil content and recovery. Studies on cytological variations have helped in knowing the ploidy levels. These efforts have helped in grouping the plants based on morphological traits. The knowledge of floral morphology and biology are essential pre- requisite for initiating any breeding programme. Introduction, clonal selection, half-sib evaluation, hybridization, mutagenesis and ploidy breeding have been attempted for identifying superior forms in respect of flower bud characters, yield, quality of fresh flower and essential oil content only in the commercial jasmines not in wild and non-cultivated species. Many of the wild species have been found to have tolerance to biotic stresses as well as different notes of fragrance. These traits when identified and documented can help in the jasmine improvement programmes. Considering this, the present study has been conducted to identify the valuable floral character present in different wild and non-cultivated species. During the course of the study, the jasmine genotypes were characterized for various floral morphological and biological traits. The information compiled in this study would be useful to researcher, students and other stake holders involved in the ﬂoriculture sector. Keeping this in view the study entitled “Studies on floral morphology and biology in Jasminum spp.” has been conducted with following objectives: 1. To study floral morphology among different Jasminum spp. 2. To study floral biology of Jasminum spp. II. REVIEW OF LITERATURE In spite of high export demand in jasmine, its use in perfumery and cosmetic industry, there have been limited efforts to improve this crop and hence the availability of literature is also very scanty. An attempt has been made to review the available literature related to jasmine improvement. In this chapter, the literature pertaining to the various aspects of the present investigation is reviewed. They also found that weight of flower buds, length of internodes and number of days taken for flowering is directly related with corolla tube length. Thangaraj (1977) studied variability and genetic improvement in J. auriculatum and found that the maximum genetic potentiality was available in flower bud length, flower bud diameter and flower yield from seedling originated plants. According to Dickey (1970), Jasminum is a genus of more than 200 species. Many of these species are, however, synonyms and about 90 species are considered to be true in existence (Muthukrishnan and Pappiah, 1980). Some of the important species are described below.  J. auriculatum produced white flower, sweet scented, borne in pubescent compound many flowered flax cymes; corolla lobes elliptic, carpels solitary and globose. Fruits black. Flowers used for production of perfumes.  J. calophyllum and J. flexile are profuse flowering species, generally grown in home gardens. Flowers are scented, white and produced practically round the year and free from pest and disease attack.  J. grandiflorum syn. J. officinale var. grandiflorum produce large size flowers, white, reddish beneath, delightfully fragrant and are borne in lax, axillary or terminal cymes.  J. multiflorum syn. J. pubescence is commonly called as furry jasmine, downy jasmine, star jasmine, pinwheel jasmine. Flowers are sessile, large, fragrant, white and borne in terminal umbels; petals six to nine, lanceolate.  J. nitidum produce flowers with fragrance and produced in few to many flowered clusters. Buds are tinted pink on the outside but flowers are white when open and about 4.0 cm across.  J. officinale syn. J. affine otherwise called as Poet's jasmine or White jasmine produces flowers are white with fragrance and are borne at branch terminals in loose clusters.  J. sambac produces white flowers, fragrant, usually in small, three forked cymes. Em (±) 0.83 C. D. (p=0.05) 2.34 V. DISCUSSION Jasmine is an important crop with wide diversity in terms of vegetative and floral characteristics. In India, it is used mainly as loose flower and for extraction of essential oil which has commercial value. Initial efforts have helped in evolving varieties with high yield and/or essential oil content. However, such studies are limited. Due to lack of identification of economic traits for utilization in breeding programme, importance has to be given for understanding the floral morphology and biology. The present investigation was undertaken using 38 genotypes of jasmine to study the variability in floral morphology and biology. The evaluation was done in randomized block design with three replications. The findings of the present investigation are discussed under the following headings: 5.1 Floral morphology traits among different Jasminum spp./genotypes 5.2 Floral biology traits in different Jasminum spp./genotypes 5.1 Floral morphology traits among different Jasminum spp./genotypes In this study, floral morphological variations were observed to a greater extent among 38 different jasmine genotypes. There are significant floral morphological variations found among genotypes. Evaluation of genotypes will help the breeder to select genotypes with desired genetic background for understanding crop improvement activities aimed at evolving superior cultivars. Studying the extent of variability for economically important traits and floral morphological and floral biology characters could facilitate the breeder in making prudent choice on superior background amenable for hybridization. Therefore, 38 genotypes were evaluated for different floral morphology traits. 5.1.1 Quantitative characters The economic importance of any jasmine species depends on flower characters in terms of number of petals, flower bud length, corolla and corolla tube length as they are commercially important for loose flower trade and essential oil extraction. These four traits were prominent in most of the commercial and non-cultivated genotypes. These characters influence ornamental value of tied flower strings and garlands. Longest flower bud length and corolla tube length is a preferred trait which was recorded in J. grandiflorum var. CO.1 Pitchi (4.81 cm and 2.92 cm) and Arka Surabhi (4.59 cm and 2.78 cm) while, shortest was recorded in J. sambac - IIHR JS - 1 (2.12 cm and 1.11 cm). Corolla length was longest in J. nitidum (2.15 cm) and Arka Aradhana (2.11 cm) while, shortest was recorded in J. auriculatum - IIHR JA - 2 (0.66 cm). Similar findings in jasmine for flower bud length were reported by Champa, B.V. (2012). Jasminum grandiflorum genotypes usually bear long conical buds with high fragrance recorded longest flower stalk length (1.54 cm). These genotypes are being generally used for essential oil extraction. Moreover, longest stalk length is a desirable trait for easy picking. Thangaraj et al. (1982) have reported high variability for flower bud weight, corolla tube length and flower bud diameter. The economic traits of flower trade such as length and diameter of bud, flower diameter and stalk length of flower were studied in 15 accessions of Jasminum sambac by Khan et al. (1970).They had revealed that the variations in these characters could be due to spontaneous mutation, natural crossing and simple auto polyploidy. Similar conclusions were made by Khan and Muthuswamy (1969) while studying various characters viz., flower diameter, weight of the flower bud, corolla tube length and style length. They opined that occurrence of such variants could be either through bud sports or chance hybrids which offered scope for improvement of cultivated types through hybridization and mutation. Maximum number of forks per cyme was recorded in J. auriculatum var. CO.1 Mullai (40.13) followed by J. auriculatum var. CO.2 Mullai (33.73). The number and length of calyx plays an important role in commercial varieties in terms of easy harvesting. Maximum number of calyx was found in J. sambac var. Gundumallige (8.79) followed by J. sambac var. Single mogra (8.48) and longest calyx lobe length was recorded in J. sambac var. Soojimalli (1.49 cm) followed by J. nitidum (1.28 cm). Similar reports pertaining to important floral characters have also been reported Raman et al. (1969) in jasmine. Maximum flower size was recorded in J. nitidum (4.93 cm) followed by J. grandiflorum var. CO.1 Pitchi (4.89 cm) and minimum was recorded in J. auriculatum - IIHR JA - 2 (1.74 cm). Similar findings were also reported by Khan et al. (1969). The size of open flowers in J. nitidum was larger than J. auriculatum and cultivars Iruvatchi and Gundumalli of J. sambac. Maximum number of petals was noticed in J. sambac - IIHR JS - 1 (30.95) followed by J. sambac - IIHR JS - 6 (28.52) and minimum was noticed in J. grandiflorum var. CO.1 Pitchi (4.97). 5.1.1 Qualitative characters In respect of flower bearing habit and flower bearing position, all genotypes of J. sambac produced 3-5 forked cymes both in terminal and axillary except J. sambac var. Iruvatchi and IIHR JS - 5 which produced cluster cyme in terminal. All genotypes of J. auriculatum and J. grandiflorum produced many flowered cyme both in terminal and axillary. J. multiflorum, J. rigidum, J. nitidum, J. calophyllum, J. flexile, J. malabaricum and J. officinale produced many flowered cluster cyme in terminal. These findings was confirmed with Arumugam et al. (2002) J. sambac produced three forked cymes, J. nitidum, J. multiflorum produced many flowered cluster flowers in terminal, J. officinale has loose cluster in terminal, J. grandiflorum produced terminal or axillary cyme, J. auriculatum produced pubescent compound many flowered flax cymes. Variation was observed in flower bud shape in all the genotypes, it was grouped in to three category i.e., pointed and short, pointed and long, round and short. The pointed and long shaped flower buds were recorded in 24 genotypes viz., J. sambac var. Soojimalli, Ramabanam, Sankarapuram Mallige - 1, Arka Aradhana, IIHR JS - 2, IIHR JS - 4, IIHR JS - 7, IIHR JS - 9, IIHR JS - 10 and J. auriculatum var. CO.1 Mullai, CO.2 Mullai, Parimullai, IIHR JA - 1, IIHR JA - 3 and J. multiflorum - IIHR JM - 1, IIHR JM - 2 and J. grandiflorum var. The term jasmine is derived from the Arabic word 'Jessamine' (Bailey, 1947) and also from Persian name 'Yesmyn' meaning fragrance. Jasminum belongs to the family 'Oleaceae'. The genus Jasmhmm comprises of about 300 species which are dispersed through warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Pacific region. About 43 species are found in the Indian sub- continent, but only the following four species are important commercially: Jasminum Sambac Ait., Jasminum auriculatum vahl., Jasminum grandiflorum linn., and Jasminum multiflorum Roth. It is cultivated throughout the country over an area of about 8,000 hectares, both in plains and on hiUs (up to 3,030 m MSL) contributing substantially to the national economy. Different parts of the plant like leaves, stem, bark, root, fruit and seed are also used for medicinal purposes. REVIEW OF LITERATURE Jasmines are one of the important groups of traditional flowers of south India grown extensively in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka States. Jasmine flowers are used in our day to day life and on almost all occasions. Although they have such a vast usage, under normal conditions, in the market, flowers do not remain for more than a day and show signs of browning or rotting on the second day. So, their shorter post-harvest life is the main constraint of growers, vendors and end-users. Out of several ways of extending the shelf life of horticultural commodities, packaging and use of chemicals are in practice now. Since, very meagre information is available on the above mentioned two practices in case of loose flowers, an attempt is made to present the literature available on packaging and use of chemicals in the post-harvest behaviour of flowers as well as vegetables and the same is presented under the following headings. 2.1 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.2 Effects of sucrose on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.3 Effects of silver salts and other salts on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.4 Effects of potassium permanganate on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.5 Effects of packaging and chemicals on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.6 Economics of packaging and usage of chemicals in post-harvest life of flowers and vegetables 2.1 Effects of packaging on post harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables Since the rate of evaporation from any given commodity is directly proportional to the water vapor pressure deficit (W.V.P.D) of its immediate surroundings and the amount of evaporation can occur is limited by the amount of water which air can hold, a reduction in water loss can be achieved either by limiting the amount by reducing the volume of air in the immediate environment. The only way to achieve this is by packaging commodity in perforated plastic bags (Robinson et al., 1975). Post-harvest loss reduction is an indirect way of increasing the availability of horticultural commodities. Packaging and storage play a vital role in post-harvest practices of these commodities. Packaging apart from providing convenient unit for marketing and distribution, it also protects delicate and highly perishable horticultural commodities from undue damage during post-harvest life. Storage, on the other hand, aims at sensible marketing, by way of extending the period of their availability beyond the season of harvest (Roy, 1990). Use of sealed package films will also result in development of high humidity. Since polymorphic films have a low water vapour transmission rate, the moisture will tend to condense within the package. Fluctuation in temperature will also cause the depositions of moisture. Hence, the produce can wilt and decay. This will also result in microbial attack. The condensation of water with in the film bays can be controlled by providing sufficient perforations to the bags Piercing of film to reduce fogging and provide sufficient ventilation is now an established method. The number, location and radii of holes are calculated to obtain maximum results (Sahoo, 1992). 2.1.1 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of flowers 2.1.1.1 Jasmine The flowers of Jasminum sambac packaged in unventilated polyethylene bags were always fresher than those packaged in ventilated bags. Shelf life of jasmine flowers increased by 3 33 days when packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of size 18 cm x 23 cm as compared to 100 and 300 gauges. Whereas, increase in percentage of ventilation decreased the shelf life (Nirmala and Venkatesh Reddy, 1992). 2.1.1.2 Tuberose Madaiah (1991) found that packaging tuberose flowers in 300 gauge polyethylene bags of size 21.6 cm x 20.9 cm with no ventilation and stored in cool chamber was most effective in extending the shelf life (5 days) and improving marketable quality. 2.1.2 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of vegetables 2.1.2.1 Tomato Seal packaging of individual tomatoes with 10|im high density polyethylene film doubled the storage life as compared to control with out packaging (Ben-Yehoshna, 1978). Packaged tomatoes showed greater fruits acceptability than unpacked fruits. Among various packs, corrugated fibreboard cartons and polypropylene bags increased the shelf life by 8 days over control (Bhatnagar et al., 1990). Naik et al. (1993) in their studies revealed that the shelf-life of tomatoes can be increased almost four times (42 days), compared to control (unpackaged) by packaging the breaker stage tomato fruits in 300 gauge polyethylene bags of size 10.5" x 7.5". Fruit decay was significantly higher in tomato fruits harvested at pink and red maturity stages and packaged in non-perforated sealed polyethylene bags of size 30 cm x 25 cm than in the other treatments (Klnge et al, 1996). 2.1.2.2. Brinjal Majeed Mohammed and Lennox sealy (1986) sealed the fruits of 'Lapastora' and 'Long purple' cultivars of melongenes individually in films of low density polyethylene, high density polyethylene, shrink wrap and wrapped in paper bags and examined for their marketable quality after 10 days and 17 days of refrigeration. There was significant increase in the fresh weight loss of melongenes in the un- sealed control for both varieties compared with other packages. The quality of melongene in high-density package was superior to those in other packages over longer storage period. Eight varieties of brinjal pre-packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of size 20 cm x 23 cm were tested for their weight loss by Sambhi and Bal (1997). The lowest weight loss was recorded in Punjab Modi, 5.6 per cent closely followed by Pant Rituraj, Jamunigola, Punjab Neelam, BH 1 and BH 2. 2.1.2.3 Okra Pre-packaging of pods of okra cultivars 'Pusa Sawani' in 400 gauge polyethylene bags of size 30 cm x 20 cm under room conditions had a shelf life of 9 days as against 2-3 days in control (without package) as reported by Singh et al. (1980). Saimbhi and Randhawa (1983) found that ventilated polyethylene bags of 200 gauge or 400 gauge were better than un-ventilated bags for pre-packaging of okra pods for improving the shelf life. Kariyanna and Khan (1998) reported that more than 97 per cent of the produce was marketable when packaged in polyethylene bags (18 cm X 23 cm) of 200 gauge with no ventilation and this extended the shelf life of okra from 3 to 6 days. 2.1.2.4 Other vegetables Ventilated polyethylene package gave best results in extending the shelf life of vegetables like dolichos, coriander, long melon, amaranth, pointed gourd and bitter gourd, both in refrigerated and non- refrigerated storage (Basak, 1980). Vegetables like broccoli and cucumber when stored in perforated polyethylene films maintained their freshness and firmness three to four times more than that of conventional methods (Elkashif et al., 1983). (1989) obtained optimum storage life (7.08 days) in case of lettuce heads packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of 30 cm X 25 cm size with-out ventilation. Placing pepper fruits in perforated low density polyethylene packages (17.5 cm x 20 cm x 0.044 cm) reduced water loss rates by 20 times or more. Packaging also eliminated flaccidity and reduced colour development of cultivar at 14°C and 20°c temperature of storage (Lownds et al, 1994). Among pre-packaging treatments, polyethylene bags (22 cm x 26 cm) of 300 gauge with 0.5 per cent and 200 gauge with 0.5 per cent ventilation recorded highest shelf-life of 35.08 and 22.25 days in Kharif and Rabi, respectively (Lingaiah and Reddy, 1997). 8 Packaging of cabbage in 150 gauge polyethylene bags of size 18 cm X 23 cm with 0.25 per cent ventilation resulted in reduced physiological loss in weight even after 2 weeks of storage and also no browning and very less spoilage were observed after one week of storage (Kariyanna et al., 1998). Venkatesh et al. (1998) studied the shelf-life of packaged coccinia and found that coccinia packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags (33 cm x 23 cm) with 1.0 per cent ventilation exhibited least spoilage and extended shelf-life up to 10 days. 2.2 Effects of sucrose on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.2.1 Flowers Sugars, usually used in the form of sucrose, play their role in opening and maintenance of flowers by serving either as an energy source in respiration or as an active substance helping in maintaining the turgidity of the expanding carolla. 2.2.1.1 Jasmine Soaking loose flowers of Jasminum sambac in different concentrations of sucrose (1%, 2% and 4%) promoted the longevity of flowers. The flowers are fragrant having a pubescent pedicel of about 0.3 cm in length. The corolla is single whorled with 6 to 8 lobes. The petals are white and elliptic to acute. DISCUSSION Among the traditional flowers of India, Jasmines occupy a pride place especially in the southern states. Jasmines are highly scented and produce pleasant fragrance. There are a few scentless species, too However, it is quite interesting to note that scentless {Jasminum multiflorum) and scented species are equally priced in Karnataka As flowers are highly perishable commodities, they do not live longer i.e., for not more than a day, generally. They start showing signs of browning or rotting on the next day. If they could be preserved for some more time, by any means, it would really be rewarding to those who are involved in growing and business of jasmines. Hence, keeping in view the above-mentioned problem experiments were conducted to explore the possibility of extending the shelf life of flowers. The results obtained by the experiments conducted are thoroughly discussed as under. Among the different parameters that were considered for studying effects of packaging and preservative chemicals on the post-harvest behaviour of jasmine flowers, parameters such as physiological loss in weight (%), flower opening index (%), fresh flower percentage, retention of colour and shelf life (days) fell under the category of non- destructive parameters, whereas moisture content (%), fragrance, total phenols (^ig/g) and electrolytic leakage (|i mhos) fell under the category of destructive parameters. And, economics worked-out would serve as an index for consumer based on his/her preference. 5.1 Effects of packaging flowers of jasmine in polyethylene bags of different gauges and at different levels of ventilation. 5.1.1 Physiological loss in weight (%) The flower buds of both the species of jasmine packaged separately in polyethylene bags of 100 gauge with no ventilation 72 recorded significantly lower cumulative physiological loss in weight. Similar observations were made by Anandaswamy and lyenger (1961) is okra, Hardenburg (1991) in tomato, Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasmimim sambac and Lingaiah and Reddy (1997) in carrot when the commodities were packaged in polyethylene bags. Provision for more exchange of gases in 100 gauge polyethylene packaging and maintenance of high relative humidity under no ventilated conditions might have resulted in lower cumulative physiological loss in weight of jasmine flowers. 5.1.2 Flower opening index (%) In general, packaging of flowers of Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum separately and without ventilation, maintained significantly higher percentage of unopened flowers compaed to untreated and unpackaged control. These results are in accordance with the findings of Mukhopadhyay et al. (1980) in flowers of Jasminum sambac packaged in polyethylene bags. As the gauge of polyethylene package increases, higher retention of humidity inside the bags is maintained under no ventilation condition. This might have helped in keeping higher percentage of unopened flowers in both Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum. The relative humidity maintained inside the polyethylene bag might have absorbed the field heat with in the polyethylene bag itself 5.1.3 Fresh flower percentage Percentage of fresh flowers decreased at a faster rate in both the species of jasmine day by day after packaging. 73 Significantly higher percentage of fresh flowers was recorded in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with no ventilation, while non-treated non- packaged flowers showed lower percentage of fresh flowers in both the species of jasmine. Similar results were recorded by Nagaraja (1998) who packaged tuberose in 200 gauge polyethylene bag with no ventilation. Similarly, 100 gauge polyethylene bag without ventilation, which provides greater exchange of gases between inside and outside coupled with high relative humidity might' have resulted in getting higher percentage of fresh flowers. 5.1.4 Retention of colour A dip in the retention of colour was observed day by day after packaged in both the species of jasmine. In both the species of jasmine, Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum flower buds packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags without ventilation retained the colour and delayed the development of brown colour compared to untreated and unpackaged control. The present results are in line with those of Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac and Nagaraja (1998) in tuberose when flowers were packaged is polyethylene bags without ventilation. The delay in brown colour development or the retention of characteristic white colour in packaged flowers could be attributed to the increased carbon dioxide concentration and decreased oxygen concentration inside the package which is semipermiable to gases such as CO2 and hydrogen and also low cumulative physiological loss in weight and higher percentage of fresh flowers recorded. 74 5.1.5 Moisture content (%) A gradual decrease in moisture content of flower was observed day by day after packaging. Polyethylene package, in general, and 100 gauge without ventilation, in particular, registered higher moisture content (%) in both the species of jasmine compared to control (No packaging i.e., kept under open conditions). Anandaswamy et al. (1963) obtained similar results in okra packaged with no ventilation. Non-ventilated polyethylene package does not allow the relative humidity accumulated inside the package to escape due to evapotranspiration that had occurred during storage life. This might have resulted in the maintenance of higher moisture content (%) of flower as supported by lower cumulative physiological loss in weight obtained. 5.1.6 Fragrance Fragrance was maintained at constant level up to one day after packaging and then a decreasing trend was observed in both the species of jasmine. Significantly higher fragrance was recorded polyethylene bags in general, in 100 gauge without ventilation, in perticular compared to non-packaged flowers in both the species of jasmine. These results are in conformity with those of Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac when flowers were packaged in unventilated polyethylene bags. Semipermeable nature of polyethylene bags especially that of lower gauge (100 gauges) might have effectively retained fragrance of flowers although, it allows the gases to some extent. 75 5.1.7 Total phenols (jig/g) Total phenols content of flowers of both the species of jasmine increased at a faster rate day after day during storage. However, packaging of jasmine flowers with-out ventilation resulted in lower total phenols content particularly in the flowers packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with-out ventilation. Similar trend was observed by Nirmala (1991) in Jasminum sambac and Nagaraja et al. (1999) in tuberose who obtained lower total phenols content after analysing the flowers packaged in un ventilated polyethylene bags. Polyethylene package in the form of a bag provides semipermebility to the exchange of gases particulary O2 and CO2 Due to this nature, controlled respiration might have delayed senescence of flowers packaged, otherwise would have resulted in the production of more phenolics. 5.1.8 Electrolytic leakage (|i mhos) Electrolytic leakage gradually increased day after day during storage. Lower electrolytic leakage was recorded in packaged jasmine flowers compared to non packaged control. The integrity of the cell membrane which was lost during storage might have led to higher ion leakage in control and the same was prevented by packaging. 5.1.9 Shelf life (days) Higher shelf life (2 to 2.5 days) was experienced in both the species of jasmine flower buds packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with-out ventilation. The present findings are in consonance with the findings of Ben-Yehoshna (1978) in tomato, Singh et al. (1980) in okra, Karla et al. (1989) in Lettuce, Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and 76 Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac, Naik et al. (1993) in tomato, Kariyanna and Khan (1998) in okra and Nagaraja (1998) in tuberose who obtained shelf life prolonged by packaging flowers in polyethylene bags Consequence to the maintenance of lower cumulative physiological loss in weight, higher percentage of unopened flowers and higher fresh flowers at different days after packaging, greater retention of colour, higher fragrance and higher moisture content at different days after packaging and lower total phenols content and electrolytic leakage tested, in polyethylene package, in general, and 100 gauge polyethylene package with-out ventilation, in perticular, could have resulted in better shelf life of packaged jasmine flowers of both the species. Improved shelf life could be attributed to the advantages proviled by the 100 gauge non-ventilated polyethylene bags. 5.2 Effects of sucrose, STS, KMn04 and their combinations with packaging of jasmine flowers {Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum) 5.2.1 Physiological loss in weight (%) Flowers of both the species of jasmine maintained significantly lower cumulative physiological loss in weight when packaged in polyethylene bags and treated with or without chemical preservatives like sucrose (2% or 4%), STS (0.5 mM) and KMn04 (0.2%). And, polyethylene bag as known is semipermeable to gases and non-permeable to water vapour. 78 5.2.4 Retention of colour. Treating flowers of Jasminum auriculatum with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and packaged resulted in significantly higher retention of colour, whereas in Jasminum grandiflorum, sucrose (2% or 4%), STS (0.5 mM) and KMn04 (0.2%) in combination produced •the same effect. Nagaraja et al. (1999) in tuberose recorded observation in a similar pattern when STS and others were used for treating flowers. Sucrose, which is known to maintain mitochondrial structure, and STS and KMn04 as ethylene action inhibitor and ethylene absorbent, respectively, might have helped in retaining colour of flower. 5.2.5 Moisture content (%) There was a gradual decrease in moisture content of flowers day by day after packaging. These results are in accordance with the findings of Nirmala (1991) in Jasminum sambac and Nagaraja et al. (1999) in tuberose who used sucrose and STS and others for treating flowers. Maintenance of turgid condition of flowers could be attributed to obstruction by polyethylene bag for moisture to escape thereby increasing the relative humidity inside the bags and the role played by both sucrose and STS. 79 5.2.6 Fragrance Similarly, here too, there was a gradual decrease in fragrance from 2 days after packaging, however, with the maintenance of constant fragrance up to 1 day after packaging in both the species of jasmine. Significantly longer shelf life was obtained in flowers treated with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and packaged. Shelf life is the ultimate criterion in deciding the salability of flowers. Notwithstanding lower total cost to shelf life ratios obtained in other treatments, shelf life was considered as basis in adjudicating the economics. Owing to longer shelf life (2.94 - 3.5 days) obtained in both the species of jasmine when treated with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and packaged, although slightly higher total cost to shelf life ratios were obtained, the latter (2% sucrose + package) would serve as a means of extending the shelf life of packaged flowers of both the species of jasmine due to their lower shelf life to total cost ratios when compared between themselves. The results obtained from the investigations carried out revealed that treating flowers with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and then packaging in 100 gauge polyethylene bags produced longer shelf life in both Jasminum auriculatum (3.5 days) and Jasminum grandiflorum (2.94-3 days). Based on the economics worked out and lower cumulative physiological loss in weight, higher percentage of fresh flowers, higher retention of colour, higher moisture content (%) and higher fragrance associated with sucrose (2%) treated flowers as compared to distilled water treated flowers, sucrose (2%) + polyethylene package (100 gauge) emerged an a better treatment in extending the shelf life of flowers of both the species of jasmine. The preservative chemicals used were sucrose (2% and 4%), STS (0.25 mM and 0.5 mM) and KMn04 (0.1% and 0,2%) Observations were recorded on shelf life and its dependent parameters. EVTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the most important traditional commercial flowers of tropical India, particularly the eastern and southern states. The term jasmine is derived from the Arabic word 'Jessamine' (Bailey, 1947) and also from Persian name 'Yesmyn' meaning fragrance. Jasmimim belongs to the family 'Oleaceae'. The genus Jasmimim comprises of about 300 species which are dispersed through warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Afrtca and Pacific region. About 43 species are found in the Indian sub continent, but only the following four species are important commercially: Jasmumm Sambac Ait., Jasmimim auriculatum vahl., Jasmitmm grandiflorum linn and Jasmimim multiflorum Roth. (Bhattachaijee, 1980). In India, jasmine mainly is grown in the states of Tamil Nadu, Kamataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. It is cultivated throughout the country over an area of about 8,000 hectares, both in plains and on hiUs (up to 3,030 m MSL) contributing substantially to the national economy. In Kamataka, jasmine is cultivated in about 3,720 hectares with an annual production of 9,300 tonnes of flowers (Anon, 2000). The annual flower production is worth over Rs. 8 to 10 crores (Sumangala, 1997). With characteristics of elegant star like flowers, rich fragrance (with an exception of Jasmimim multiflorum) and hardy growth habit, they are regarded as highly valued ornamental flowering plants for home gardens and commercial cultivation as well. They are widely used as floral ornamentals and also for decorating hairs. Essential oil extracted from jasmine flowers is widely used in cosmetics throughout the world and attempts are being made to improve the production of flowers and essential oil content of these flowers to meet both domestic and international demands. Different parts of the plant like leaves, stem, bark, root, fruit and seed are also used for medicinal purposes. India has a sizable base for jasmine concretes and ottos which have earned the coimtry a place in the world trade. India has a natural advantage for large scale production of jasmine concrete because of favourable climatic conditions and cheap labour availability during most part of the year. Fresh flowers are used in the country and are also exported to neighbouring countries like Sri Lanka, Singapore and even to the Middle East. REVIEW OF LITERATURE Jasmines are one of the important groups of traditional flowers of south India grown extensively in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka States. Jasmine flowers are used in our day to day life and on almost all occasions. Although they have such a vast usage, under normal conditions, in the market, flowers do not remain for more than a day and show signs of browning or rotting on the second day. So, their shorter post-harvest life is the main constraint of growers, vendors and end-users. Out of several ways of extending the shelf life of horticultural commodities, packaging and use of chemicals are in practice now. Since, very meagre information is available on the above mentioned two practices in case of loose flowers, an attempt is made to present the literature available on packaging and use of chemicals in the post-harvest behaviour of flowers as well as vegetables and the same is presented under the following headings. 2.1 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.2 Effects of sucrose on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.3 Effects of silver salts and other salts on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.4 Effects of potassium permanganate on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.5 Effects of packaging and chemicals on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.6 Economics of packaging and usage of chemicals in post-harvest life of flowers and vegetables 2.1 Effects of packaging on post harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables Since the rate of evaporation from any given commodity is directly proportional to the water vapor pressure deficit (W.V.P.D) of its immediate surroundings and the amount of evaporation can occur is limited by the amount of water which air can hold, a reduction in water loss can be achieved either by limiting the amount by reducing the volume of air in the immediate environment. The only way to achieve this is by packaging commodity in perforated plastic bags (Robinson et al., 1975). Post-harvest loss reduction is an indirect way of increasing the availability of horticultural commodities. Packaging and storage play a vital role in post-harvest practices of these commodities. Packaging apart from providing convenient unit for marketing and distribution, it also protects delicate and highly perjshable horticultural commodities from undue damage during post-harvest life. Storage, on the other hand, aims at sensible marketing, by way of extending the period of their availability beyond the season of harvest (Roy, 1990). Use of sealed package films will also result in development of high humidity. Since polymorphic films have a low water vapour transmission rate, the moisture will tend to condense within the package. Fluctuation in temperature will also cause the depositions of moisture. Hence, the produce can wilt and decay. This will also result in microbial attack. The condensation of water with in the film bays can be controlled by providing sufficient perforations to the bags. Piercing of film to reduce fogging and provide sufficient ventilation is now an established method. The number, location and radii of holes are calculated to obtain maximum results (Sahoo, 1992). 2.1.1 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of flowers 2.1.1.1 Jasmine The flowers of Jasminum sambac packaged in unventilated polyethylene bags were always fresher than those packaged- in ventilated bags. Shelf life of jasmine flowers increased by 3.33 days when packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of size 18 cm x 23 cm as compared to 100 and 300 gauges. Whereas, increase in percentage of ventilation decreased the shelf life (Nirmala and Venkatesh Reddy, 1992). 2.1.1.2 Tuberose Madaiah (1991) found that packaging tuberose flowers in 300 gauge polyethylene bags of size 21.6 cm x 20.9 cm with no ventilation and stored in cool chamber was most effective in extending the shelf life (5 days) and improving marketable quality. 2.1.2 Effects of packaging on post-harvest behaviour of vegetables 2.1.2.1 Tomato Seal packaging of individual tomatoes with lOpm high density polyethylene film doubled the storage life as compared to control with out packaging (Ben-Yehoshna, 1978). Packaged tomatoes showed greater fruits acceptability than unpacked fruits. Among various packs, corrugated fibreboard cartons and polypropylene bags increased the shelf life by 8 days over control (Bhatnagar e/a/., 1990). Naik et al. (1993) in their studies revealed that the shelf-life of tomatoes can be increased almost four times (42 days), compared to control (unpackaged) by packaging the breaker stage tomato fruits in 300 gauge polyethylene bags of size 10.5" x 7.5". Fruit decay was significantly higher in tomato fruits harvested at pink and red maturity stages and packaged in non-perforated sealed polyethylene bags of size 30 cm x 25 cm than in the other treatments (Klnge et al., 1996). 2.1.2.2. Brinjal Majeed Mohammed and Lennox sealy (1986) sealed the fruits of 'Lapastora' and 'Long purple' cultivars of melongenes individually in films of low density polyethylene, high density polyethylene, shrink wrap and wrapped in paper bags and examined for their marketable quality after 10 days and 17 days of refrigeration. There was significant increase in the fresh weight loss of melongenes in the un sealed control for both varieties compared with other packages. The quality of melongene in high-density package was superior to those in other packages over longer storage period. / Eight varieties of brinjal pre-packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of size 20 cm x 23 cm were tested for their weight loss by Sambhi and Bal (1997). The lowest weight loss was recorded in Punjab Modi, 5.6 per cent closely followed by Pant Rituraj, Jamunigola, Punjab Neelam, BH 1 and BH 2. 2.1.2.3 Okra Pre-packaging of pods of okra cultivars 'Pusa Sawani' in 400 gauge polyethylene bags of size 30 cm x 20 cm under room conditions had a shelf life of 9 days as against 2-3 days in control (without package) as reported by Singh et al. (1980). Saimbhi and Randhawa (1983) found that ventilated polyethylene bags of 200 gauge or 400 gauge were better than un-ventilated bags for pre-packaging of okra pods for improving the shelf life. Kariyanna and Khan (1998) reported that more than 97 per cent of the produce was marketable when packaged in polyethylene bags (18 cm X 23 cm) of 200 gauge with no ventilation and this extended the shelf life of okra from 3 to 6 days. 2.1.2.4 Other vegetables Ventilated polyethylene package gave best results in extending the shelf life of vegetables like dolichos, coriander, long melon, amaranth, pointed gourd and bitter gourd, both in refrigerated and non- refrigerated storage (Basak, 1980). Vegetables like broccoli and cucumber when stored in perforated polyethylene films maintained their freshness and firmness three to four times more than that of conventional methods (Elkashif et al., 1983). Shelf -life of cauliflower in perforated polyethylene bags could be doubled than those stored without polyethylene bags (Ceausesue et al., 1988). Karla et al. (1989) obtained optimum storage life (7.08 days) in case of lettuce heads packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags of 30 cm X 25 cm size with-out ventilation. Placing pepper fruits in perforated low density polyethylene packages (17.5 cm x 20 cm x 0.044 cm) reduced water loss rates by 20 times or more. Packaging also eliminated flaccidity and reduced colour development of cultivar at 14°C and 20°c temperature of storage (Lownds et al., 1994). Among pre-packaging treatments, polyethylene bags (22 cm x 26 cm) of 300 gauge with 0.5 per cent and 200 gauge with 0.5 per cent ventilation recorded highest shelf-life of 35.08 and 22.25 days in Kharif and Rabi, respectively (Lingaiah and Reddy, 1997). Packaging of cabbage in 150 gauge polyethylene bags of size 18 cm X 23 cm with 0.25 per cent ventilation resulted in reduced physiological loss in weight even after 2 weeks of storage and also no browning and very less spoilage were observed after one week of storage (Kariyanna et al., 1998), Venkatesh et al. (1998) studied the shelf-life of packaged coccinia and found that coccinia packaged in 200 gauge polyethylene bags (33 cm x 23 cm) with 1.0 per cent ventilation exhibited least spoilage and extended shelf -life up to 10 days. 2.2 Effects of sucrose on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables 2.2.1 Flowers Sugars, usually used in the form of sucrose, play their role in opening and maintenance of flowers by serving either as an energy source in respiration or as an active substance helping in maintaining the turgidity of the expanding carolla. 2.2.1.1 Jasmine Soaking loose flowers of Jasminum sambac in different concentrations of sucrose (1%, 2% and 4%) promoted the longevity of flowers. All the buds opened within 96 hours. Only 10 to 30 per cent flowers remained fresh up to 96 hours (Mukhopadhyay et al, 1980). 2.2.1.2 Chrysanthemum The cut flowers of chrysanthemum cv. Co - 2 pulsed with 2 per cent sucrose recorded vase life of 5 days compared to control (Rajagopalan and Khader, 1993). Glucose, fructose and sucrose contents in florets and leaves of irradiated chrysanthemum decreased more rapidly than those of unirradiated ones when the cut flowers were held in a vase solution without sucrose. The sugar contents of florets and leaves and the respiratory rate of irradiated chrysanthemums held with sucrose were higher than those of untreated ones. It was suggested that sucrose (2%) in a vase solution is used as a respiratory substrate and facilitated the repair of radiation (750 GY) induced damage, resulting in extended vase life of irradiated chrysanthemum cv. Seishu (Nakahara, 1998). 2.2.1.3 Rose Kaltaler and Steponkus (1976) opined that applied sugar has its effect in extending longevity of cut roses by maintaining mitochondrial structure and function of flower. Complete flower bud opening is characterized by an increase in the petal area, and by enhancing dry and fresh weight of petals. The import of dry matter in the petal is used for osmotic, biosynthetic and respiratory demands. However, flowers of 'Medelen' cut roses frequently fail to open completely under post-harvest conditions. An aqueous solution containing 45 mM sucrose induced proper flower bud opening, even when the cut roses had been exposed initially to a sucrose-free solution for 48 h. This points to a requirement for a supply of organic matter from source to the flower as main sink. This conclusion is confirmed by the observation that complete flower bud opening can also be achieved without any addition of sucrose by reducing the number of participating petals (Kuiper et al., 995). White sim were opened using bud-opening solutions after storage. Acceptable vase life period was achieved by treating the flowers with 10 per cent sucrose at 25°C than at 18°C. Effects of potassium permanganate on post-harvest behaviour of flowers and vegetables Reduction of ethylene level may be accomplished by the use of ethylene scrubbers which act either by absorbing the gas or by a combination of absorption and reaction. The removal of ethylene from the storage atmosphere is known to have extended the shelf life of flowers (South wick and Smock, 1943). All treated flowers maintained freshness for 48 hours compared to control in which 60 per cent of flowers wilted (Mukhopadhyay et al, 1980). Treating the loose flowers of Jasminum sambac with sucrose (2% and 4%), 0.25 mM concentration of SIS and packaged, distilled water and packaged in 18 cm x 23 cm size 200 gauge polyethylene bags recorded maximum shelf life of 4 days each compared to one day in control (Nirmala, 1991). 2.5.1.2 Chrysanthemum Pulsing cut chrysanthemum with silver nitrate (50 ppm) + sugar (5%) for 16 hours before 4 days of simulated shipment significantly increased the longevity of the flowers (Kofronck and Halevy, 1989). Su et al. (1991) by treating cut chrysanthemum blooms with 5 per cent sucrose + 150 ppm citric acid for 16 hours and stored at 0°C for 5 weeks recorded increased soluble sugar content during first 2 weeks especially with STS treatment which pronounced greater effect. Chandrama flowers were cut when the first 2 whorls of petals had just opened and were placed in a solution of 0.2 per cent aluminium sulphate + 3 per cent sucrose. The treatment recorded the longest vase life (12.33 days) compared to control (7.33 days) (Barman et al., 1992). The cut flowers of chrysanthemum cv. Polaris were held in water or one of 5 preservative solutions in the laboratory (25°C and 66% RH) or under refrigeration (7-8°C and 100% RH). MATERIAL AND METHODS The present investigations on "Packaging of chemically treated jasmine flowers (Jasminutn auficulcituin vahl. and Jasminurn grandiflorum linn.) for extending shelf life" were carried-out during 1999-2000 at the Division of Horticulture, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra, University of Agricultural Sciences, Bangalore. The details of the location, the material used and the techniques adapted during the period of experimentation are presented below. 3.1 Location The experiments were conducted at the Division of Horticulture, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra, University of Agricultural Sciences, Bangalore under normal room conditions. 3.2 Species of jasmine The flower buds of the two important species of Jasmine viz., Jasminurn auriculatum and Jasminurn grandiflorum were used for the studies. 3.2.1 Characteristics of Jasminurn auriculatum flowers The inflorescence is a compound cyme and many flowered. The flowers are fragrant having a pubescent pedicel of about 0.3 cm in length. The corolla is single whorled with 6 to 8 lobes. The petals are white and elliptic to acute. The calyx has 5 to 6 teeth, is 0.2 cm long and pubescent. The stamens are two; the anthers are yellowish green to brown. The ovary is bicarpellary, with two ovules in each. The stigma is bifid, 0.38 cm long (Bhattacharjee, 1980). m 3.2.2 Characteristics of Jasminum grandiflorum flowers The inflorescence is an axillary or a terminal corymbose with few flowered cymes. The flowers are delightly fragrant. The corolla tube is 2.4 to 2.6 cm long. The corolla is a single whorl of five lobes, rarely 4. The petals are white, often tinged with purple or pink on the outside, obviate to elliptic. The stamens are two, rarely three. The anther is light green to yellow. The ovary is bicarpellary, with two ovules in each. The stigma is bifid and 0.42 cm long (Bhattacharjee, 1980). 3.3 Source for jasmine flower buds The loose-flowers of Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum used for the studies were brought from Krishna Rajendra market. DISCUSSION V. DISCUSSION Among the traditional flowers of India, Jasmines occupy a pride place especially in the southern states. Jasmines are highly scented and produce pleasant fragrance. There are a few scentless species, too. However, it is quite interesting to note that scentless {Jasminum multiflorum) and scented species are equally priced in Karnataka. As flowers are highly perishable commodities, they do not live longer i.e., for not more than a day, generally. They start showing signs of browning or rotting on the next day. If they could be preserved for som.e more time, by any means, it would really be rewarding to those who are involved in growing and business of jasmines. Hence, keeping in view the above-mentioned problem experiments were conducted to explore the possibility of extending the shelf life of flowers. The results obtained by the experiments conducted are thoroughly discussed as under. Among the different parameters that were considered for studying effects of packaging and preservative chemicals on the post-harvest behaviour of jasmine flowers, parameters such as physiological loss in weight (%), flower opening index (%), fresh flower percentage, retention of colour and shelf life (days) fell under the category of non destructive parameters, whereas moisture content (%), fragrance, total phenols (^ig/g) and electrolytic leakage (|a mhos) fell under the category of destructive parameters. And, economics worked-out would serve as an index for consumer based on his/her preference. 5.1 Effects of packaging flowers of jasmine in polyethylene bags of different gauges and at different levels of ventilation. 5.1.1 Physiological loss in weight (%) The newer buds of both the species of jasmitte packaged separately in polyethylene bags of 100 gauge with no ventilation recorded significantly lower cumulative physiological loss in weight. Similar observations were made by Anandaswamy and lyenger (1961) is okra, Hardenburg (1991) in tomato, Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and Reddy (1992) \'n Jasminttm sambac and Lingaiah and Reddy (1997) in carrot when the commodities were packaged in polyethylene bags. Provision for more exchange of gases in 100 gauge polyethylene packaging and maintenance of high relative humidity under no ventilated conditions might have resulted in lower cumulative physiological loss in weight of jasmine flowers. 5.1.2 Flower opening index (%) In general, packaging of flowers of Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum separately and without ventilation, maintained -significantly higher percentage of unopened flowers compaed to untreated and unpackaged control. These results are in accordance with the findings of Mukhopadhyay et al. (1980) in flowers of Jasminum sambac packaged in polyethylene bags. As the gauge of polyethylene package increases, higher retention of humidity inside the bags is maintained under no ventilation condition. This might have helped in keeping higher percentage of unopened flowers in both Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum. The relative humidity maintained inside the polyethylene bag might have absorbed the field heat with in the polyethylene bag itself. 5.1.3 Fresh flower percentage Percentage of fresh flowers decreased at a faster rate in both the species of jasmine day by day after packaging. Significantly higher percentage of fresh flowers was recorded in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with no ventilation, while non-treated non- packaged flowers showed lower percentage of fresh flowers in both the species of jasmine. Similar results were recorded by Nagaraja (1998) who packaged tuberose in 200 gauge polyethylene bag with no ventilation. Similarly, 100 gauge polyethylene bag without ventilation, which provides greater exchange of gases between inside and outside coupled with high relative humidity might have resulted in getting higher percentage of fresh flowers. 5.1.4 Retention of colour A dip in the retention of colour was observed day by day after packaged in both the species of jasmine. In both the species of jasmine, Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum flower buds packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags without ventilation retained the colour and delayed the development of brown colour compared to untreated and unpackaged control. The present results are in line with those of Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac and Nagaraja (1998) in tuberose when flowers were packaged is polyethylene bags without ventilation. The delay in brown colour development or the retention of characteristic white colour in packaged flowers could be attributed to the increased carbon dioxide concentration and decreased oxygen concentration inside the package which is semipermiable to gases such as CO2 and hydrogen and also low cumulative physiological loss in weight and higher percentage of fresh flowers recorded. 5.1.5 Moisture content (%) A gradual decrease in moisture content of flower was observed day by day after packaging. Polyethylene package, in general, and 100 gauge without ventilation, in particular, registered higher moisture content (%) in both the species of jasmine compared to control (No packaging i.e., kept under open conditions). Anandaswamy et al. (1963) obtained similar results in okra packaged with no ventilation. Non-ventilated polyethylene package does not allow the relative humidity accumulated inside the package to escape due to evapotranspiration that had occurred during storage life. This might have resulted in the maintenance of higher moisture content (%) of flower as supported by lower cumulative physiological loss in weight obtained. 5.1.6 Fragrance Fragrance was maintained at constant level up to one day after packaging and then a decreasing trend was observed in both the species of jasmine. Significantly higher fragrance was recorded polyethylene bags in general, in 100 gauge without ventilation, in perticular compared to non-packaged flowers in both the species of jasmine. These results are in conformity with those of Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac when flowers were packaged in unventilated polyethylene bags. Semipermeable nature of polyethylene bags especially that of lower gauge (100 gauges) might have effectively retained fragrance of flowers although, it allows the gases to some extent. 5.1.7 Total phenols (pg/g) Total phenols content of flowers of both the species of jasmine increased at a faster rate day after day during storage. However, packaging of jasmine flowers with-out ventilation resulted in lower total phenols content particularly in the flowers packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with-out ventilation. Similar trend was observed by Nirmala (1991) in Jasminum sambac and Nagaraja et al. (1999) in tuberose who obtained lower total phenols content after analysing the flowers packaged in un ventilated polyethylene bags. Polyethylene package in the form of a bag provides semipermebility to the exchange of gases particulary O2 and CO2. Due to this nature, controlled respiration might have delayed senescence of flowers packaged, otherwise would have resulted in the production of more phenolics. 5.1.8 Electrolytic leakage (p mhos) Electrolytic leakage gradually increased day after day during storage. Lower electrolytic leakage was recorded in packaged jasmine flowers compared to non packaged control. The integrity of the cell membrane which was lost during storage might have led to higher ion leakage in control and the same was prevented by packaging. 5.1.9 Shelf life (days) Higher shelf life (2 to 2.5 days) was experienced in both the species of jasmine flower buds packaged in 100 gauge polyethylene bags with-out ventilation. The present findings are in consonance with the findings of Ben-Yehoshna (1978) in tomato, Singh et al. (1980) in okra, Karla et al. (1989) in Lettuce, Madaiah (1991) in tuberose, Nirmala and Reddy (1992) in Jasminum sambac, Naik et al. (1993) in tomato, Kariyanna and Khan (1998) in okra and Nagaraja (1998) in tuberose who obtained shelf life prolonged by packaging flowers in polyethylene bags. Consequence to the maintenance of lower cumulative physiological loss in weight, higher percentage of unopened flowers and higher fresh flowers at different days after packaging, greater retention of colour, higher fragrance and higher moisture content at different days after packaging and lower total phenols content and electrolytic leakage tested, in polyethylene package, in general, and 100 gauge polyethylene package with-out ventilation, in perticular, could have resulted in better shelf life of packaged jasmine flowers of both the species. Significantly longer shelf life was obtained in flowers treated with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and packaged. Shelf life is the ultimate criterion in deciding the salability of flowers. The results obtained from the investigations carried out revealed that treating flowers with either distilled water or sucrose (2%) and then packaging in 100 gauge polyethylene bags produced longer shelf life in both Jasminum auriculatum (3.5 days) and Jasminum grandiflorum (2.94-3 days). SUMMARY Studies were undertaken on two species of jasmine (Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum) to know the effects of packaging the flowers treated with preservative chemicals in polyethylene bags (100, 200 and 300 gauges) without or with ventilation (0%, 2.5% and 0.5%) under room conditions, at the Division of Horticulture, University of Agricultural Science, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra, Bangalore. The preservative chemicals used were sucrose (2% and 4%), SIS (0.25 mM and 0.5 mM) and KMn04 (0.1% and 0.2%). Observations were recorded on shelf life and its dependent parameters. Benefit: cost ratio was worked out to know the efficacy of polyethylene packaging coupled with chemicals in extending the shelf life. STUDIES ON POLLEN VIABILITY AND COMPATIBILITY IN JASMINUM SPP. ABSTRACT The investigations on pollen viability and compatibility in Jasminum spp. was carried out during 2016-17 at ICAR-IIHR, Bengaluru. Six species i.e. Jasminum sambac, J. auriculatum, J. grandiflorum, J. malabaricum, J. multiflorum, and J. flexile were used in this study. The results revealed that anther dehiscence started before anthesis in all the six species. Stigma was receptive 12 hours prior to anthesis and peak was observed at the time of anthesis except J. multiflorum while it was 12 hours after anthesis. J. malabaricum exhibited highest percentage of pollen viability (96.57%) and germination (91.58%) than other species, followed by J. flexile (84.92% and 81.86%) and J. auriculatum (71.32% and 71.08%) under in vitro condition. The species J. sambac recorded the lowest pollen viability (34.27%) and germination (34.09%). J. malabaricum exhibited maximum pollen germination (91.58%) in modified Brewbaker and Kwacks medium (100ppm H3BO3 + 300ppm Ca(No3)2 + 200ppm MgSO4) supplemented with 10% sucrose and 15% Polyethylene glycol. Highest percentages of normal shaped pollen grains were observed in J. auriculatum (96.93%) and J. malabaricum (96.89%). No fruit setting was observed in J. sambac when used as both male and female parent. Highest seed set was observed in open pollination in all the species studied compared to self-pollination and artificial cross pollination. Fruits were aborted in many crosses before entering into matured stage. Compared to other species, seed set and high degree of cross compatibility was observed in the crosses involving J. auriculatum with J. grandiflorum, J. malabaricum and J. malabaricum with J. flexile and also its reciprocal crosses. This information gathered on pollen viability, stigma receptivity, compatibility and seed set in different mode of pollination would help the breeders in further crop improvement in Jasminum species. INTRODUCTION Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) belongs to the family Oleaceae, order Oleales. The genus has a basic chromosome number of n=x=13 (Taylor, 1945; Krishnaswamy and Raman, 1948). Plant habit is climbing, trailing or erect flowering shrub. There are both deciduous and evergreen species in jasmine. Leaves are opposite and alternate, simple, trifoliate or pinnate; leaflets are entire. Flowers are white, yellow or rarely reddish, sometimes solitary, more often in cymose clusters of three to many, usually fragrant, the flower is acrid, bitter with a sharp taste; 2 loculed with 1 to 4 erect ovules (Arumugam, 2002). Fruit is a berry and black in colour, rarely with separate capsules and each having one seed. In India, jasmine is cultivated throughout the country. However, the largest area under jasmine flower production is in Karnataka followed by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu (NHB Database, 2014- 2015). The annual production of jasmine is 56.57 metric tonnes (NHB Database, 2014-2015). The annual production of concrete is more than 15 tonnes in India, the largest producer being Egypt, followed by Morocco, India, Italy, France and China. Jasmine is characterized by its distinct fragrance, which cannot be imitated by any known synthetic aromatic chemical and has a unique status in the perfume world. INTRODUCTION Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) belongs to the family Oleaceae, order Oleales. The genus has a basic chromosome number of n=x=13 (Taylor, 1945; Krishnaswamy and Raman, 1948). Plant habit is climbing, trailing or erect flowering shrub. There are both deciduous and evergreen species in jasmine. Leaves are opposite and alternate, simple, trifoliate or pinnate; leaflets are entire. Flowers are white, yellow or rarely reddish, sometimes solitary, more often in cymose clusters of three to many, usually fragrant, the flower is acrid, bitter with a sharp taste; 2 loculed with 1 to 4 erect ovules (Arumugam, 2002). Fruit is a berry and black in colour, rarely with separate capsules and each having one seed. In India, jasmine is cultivated throughout the country. However, the largest area under jasmine flower production is in Karnataka followed by Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu (NHB Database, 2014- 2015). The annual production of jasmine is 56.57 metric tonnes (NHB Database, 2014-2015). The annual production of concrete is more than 15 tonnes in India, the largest producer being Egypt, followed by Morocco, India, Italy, France and China. Jasmine is characterized by its distinct fragrance, which cannot be imitated by any known synthetic aromatic chemical and has a unique status in the perfume world. The fragrance derived from Jasminum grandiflorum is highly appreciated all over the world. The oils are used in the manufacture of high grade perfumes, cosmetics, soaps, confectionery, perfumed tobacco, syrups, aerated water, ointments, and disinfectants, detergents, in medicinal and pharmaceutical beverages, for curing various ailments and as a source of yellow pigment and fruits are edible in some species. Jasmine plants are of great economic value as a flower crop for the florist, landscaping as well as for medicinal and pharmaceutical industries (Green and Miller, 2009). Jasmine oil blends well with every floral scent imparting smoothness and elegance to the perfume composition. It is useful in treating diseases of the mouth and teeth, especially for toothache (Kirtikar and Basu, 1993). Jasmine essential oil is a popular natural remedy for improving mood, overcoming stress and balancing hormones. Through aromatherapy, the oil have an effect on a number of biological factors - including heart rate, body temperature, stress response, alertness, blood pressure and breathing. Jasmine is one of the most important ornamental flowering shrubs widely cultivated in the Southern and Eastern parts of India and esteemed for their attractive and fragrant flowers. They are grown for garden decoration, landscaping, for making garland, hair decoration and for extraction of essential oil which is a highly lucrative business of late. Jasmine loose flowers are sold every day in big cities viz., Kolkatta, Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai and Bengaluru. Among these species, J. grandiflorum, J. auriculatum and J. sambac are commercially cultivated for oil extraction (Green and Miller, 2009). Although, 40 species have been identified in India and 20 are cultivated in Southern India (Bhattacharjee, 1980). Jasmine can be grown under several climatic conditions and soils. Generally, it prefers mild tropical climate for its economic growth. Mostly, jasmine plants are grown in houses and gardens for ornamental purposes, and are also used for loose flowers to make garlands. Efforts taken for genetic improvement in jasmine are negligible. The most important barrier is non-fruitfulness in most species and cross combinations. Under natural conditions seed set varies with variety in species (Veluswamy, 1981). However, jasmine has almost no seeds. Investigations reported that only 0.17% (ranged from 0.13% to 0.19%) of its plants can set seeds in the fields mainly due to low pollen viability (Lai, 1995; Lai et al. 1997). In breeding programmes for Jasminum species, interspecific hybridisation is one of the methods to create variations, although this may be restricted because of incompatibility. In India, efforts on evolving jasmine varieties/hybrids for cultivation are negligible. Only few selected open pollinated cultivars are used for cultivation. Due to the less compatibility between different species for normal sexual reproduction, presence of variable ploidy level, lack of sufficient and fertile pollen among different species, self - cross incompatibility, and occurrence of zygote formation but inability to grow at mature embryo are the major limitations to breeders for evolution of new hybrids/varieties. Research on genetic improvement in jasmine through sexual hybridization is very limited. The breeder should first know which species are to be crossed. Out of these, one is selected as a male/pollen parent and another as a female/seed parent. The development of desirable varieties with desirable character is possible only through sexual means. Development of hybrids or cultivars in jasmine is associated with many problems such as undescribed genetic variability, self-incompatibility and poor seed setting. Before taking up any systematic breeding programme, a thorough knowledge of floral biology, degree of compatibility, seed setting and seed germination in existing cultivars and newly developed hybrids is a pre-requisite. For hybridization programme, the knowledge of floral biology is mandatory in order to find out parents with desirable characters viz., time and duration of flowering, anthesis, anther dehiscence and stigma receptivity. Keeping this in view, the study entitled “Studies on pollen viability and compatibility in Jasminum spp.” was under taken to assess different species with following objectives.  To identify seed parents and pollen parents through seed setting and pollen viability among different Jasminum spp.  To study compatibility among different Jasminum spp. II. REVIEW OF LITERATURE Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) is one of the important flower crops grown for loose flowers, garlands and essential oil extraction. Banerjee (1969) observed that though pollination, fertilization and the embryonic development in Chattlion rose cultivar followed the normal pattern until 22-24 days after pollination, afterwards the flowers dried up and development was ceased. 2.5.2 INCOMPATIBILITY Pipino et al. (2011) observed that fertility of hybrid tea roses is often reduced due to their interspecific origin but also to intensive inbreeding. New genotypes used as pollen donors represent an economic risk for a breeding programme, as their influence on seed production is unknown. In this study, 11 cut rose genotypes were selected from a company database as high fertile or low fertile male parents, according to the number of seeds per hybridization. Pollen morphology and in vitro germination of the selected genotypes were characterized. Pollen was either small (mean diameter <30 μm), shrunken, and irregular (abnormal), or large (mean diameter >30 μm), elliptical and crossed by furrows (normal). High correlations were found between the number of seeds produced per hybridization and the pollen diameter (r=0.94) or the percentage of normal pollen (r=0.96). Pollination studies on tuberose (Polianthes tuberosa L.) revealed self-incompatibility in single with no fruit set and 63.78 per cent fruit set on cross pollinating with variegated cultivar. This variegated cultivar is a both male and female fertile variety with sufficient pollen production and recorded a seed set of 12.13 and 28.84 per cent when self- and cross-pollinated, respectively. But seeds obtained after cross pollination with the variegated variety as a female parent recorded lower seed viability and rate of seed germination, suggesting lower fertility and seedling vigour (Uma and Gowda, 2000). Boyle et al. (1994) demonstrated the existence of self-incompatibility (SI) in Easter cactus (Rhipsalidopsis) cultivars Britton and Rose. In a full diallel cross among R. gaertneri cv. Crimson Giant and 4 R. x graeseri cultivars, 18 out of 20 outcrosses resulted in 68-100 per cent fruit set, whereas reciprocal crosses between two of the cultivars and all five self-pollinations failed to set fruit. Pollen tube growth was greatly inhibited in styles of selfed pistils, but there was no evidence of pollen tube inhibition in compatibly crossed pistils. Easter cactus exhibited characteristics typically found in sporophytic SI systems (trinucleate pollen, papillate stigmas and scant stigmatic exudate) together with those associated with gametophytic SI systems (stylar inhibition of pollen tube growth and absence of reciprocal differences in outcrosses). Uma (1990) reported breeding behaviour and pollination efficiency of Polianthes tuberosa with two cultivars viz., Single and Variegated. No fruit set was recorded when tuberose cv. “Single” was both selfed and open pollinated, but when cross-pollinated with cv. “Variegated” as male parent gave 63.78 per cent fruit set. The highest fruit set of 12.13 per cent and 28.84 per cent were obtained when cv. “Variegated” was self-pollinated and cross pollinated with Single, respectively. Aswath (1985) studied three climbers‟ viz., Pyrostegia venusta, Tecoma jasminoides and Arrabaedia magnifica and observed that degradation of ovules occurred at different stages of development commencing from degeneration of archesporium and megaspore mother cell. Eleven garden chrysanthemum siblings obtained through two generations of single-plant self- pollination were selfed and crossed in a complete diallel. Outcrosses to unrelated individuals were performed to test for male and female fertility. Since eleven crossing patterns were found in the diallel, at least three genes must be assumed. The data suggest independent gene action with intragenic dominance. One inbred, 77-AM3-3, expressed a high level of pseudo-self-compatibility (PSC) by giving some very low cross seed set along with high self seed set. This inbred also exhibited variable PSC from season to season (Zagorski et al.1983). Veluswamy (1981) reported successful fruit set in the combinations involving J. auriculatum with J. flexile and J. grandiflorum; J. grandiflorum with J. auriculatum, J. calophyllum and J. flexile; J. sambac with J. grandiflorum. But in all these cases, the seeds failed to germinate showing a strong barrier for crossability and hybrid inviability existing among the different species and also the possibility of endosperm antagonism in operation.
