These findings may indicate that the poor pollen tube growth in interspecific crosses is not a result of inhibition but results from the lack of an accelerative factor in the style (Asano, 1980). The localization of incompatibility barrier in the ovary and demonstrated that it was neither in the stigma nor in the style of Lilium longiflorum (Fett et al. 1976; Ascher, 1978) whereas, Hiratsuka et al. (1983) opined that the self-incompatibility in Lilium longiflorum occurred in all portions of the inner surface of the stylar canal and was not restricted to any portion. In the genus Gasteria, Brandham and Owens (1978) showed that self-incompatibility reaction was controlled at least by two genes and confirmed that site of pollen tube inhibition was the ovule. Kawase and Tsukamoto (1977) determined percentage of self-fertility following self-pollination in chrysanthemum. The plants were generally self-compatible, but this varied from year to year and even between individual flowers on the plant. In self-pollinated progenies, the degree of self-incompatibility was generally similar to that of parents but progeny of cv. Katanazakura (KB line) displayed a comparatively high degree of compatibility. With nine progenies of KB line, self-fertility was higher in tubular than ray florets. Anther dehiscence in G. superba starts from 8:30 to 9:00 a.m. and stigmas become receptive next day by about 9:00 a.m. to 10:30 a.m. and remain so for 27-32 hrs. Pollen fertility in the elemental species is higher but seed setting varies greatly. G. superba, G. lutea, G. carsonii, G. virescens and G. rothschildiana were found setting seed abundantly while G. richmondensis did not produce seeds either by selfing or cross pollinations (Prakash, 1976). Arisumi (1975) observed the effect of pollination on seed yield of crosses in Daylily. The seed set in 7 out of 12 Daylily crosses was temperature sensitive when seed parents were exposed for 6 hrs at 23.9°C, 29.4°C, or 35°C. In six crosses at 35°C and two crosses at 29.4°C, seed set was lower than those at 23.9°C and in four crosses, was lower at 35°C than 29.4°C. The six cultivars studied were self- incompatible. Differences in seed set observed in reciprocal crosses were probably caused by differential fertility and temperature sensitivity between pollen and seed parent of the same cultivar. “Frosted Pink” “Blonde Princess” and “Kanapaha” were temperature sensitive as seed parents: “Caballero” and “Crimson Glory” as pollen parents, and “Vulcan” as both seed and pollen parent. The phenomena underlying crossing barriers are incompatibility and incongruity. Incompatibility operates in intraspecific crosses and is the result of the activity of S-alleles. Incongruity occurs in interspecific crosses as a result of a lack of genetic information in one partner to complete pre- and post- pollination processes in the other (Hogenboom, 1973). In Chrysanthemum morifolium, during genetic studies of self-incompatibility, Drewlow (1973) reported that homozygosity of alleles is resulted from the dominance of S-alleles in the sporophytic systems. He observed reciprocal differences in cross-compatibility indicating that dominance among S- alleles was present and more than one locus is operating for self-incompatibility. Drewlow (1971) showed that 24 to 48-hour heat treatment in the range of 35°C to 40°C occasionally resulted self-seed yield in some garden chrysanthemum clones. Shivanna and Rangaswamy (1969) reported that to overcome self-incompatibility, bud pollination proved to be more successful in Petunia axillaris. The self-incompatibility could be overcome to a greater degree in young buds than old buds. Seed set consequent to bud pollination was invariably lower than that of bud cross pollination and bud pollinated two days prior to anthesis proved more successful in Petunia axillaris. Ovary as the site of inhibition for the occurrence of gametophytic self-incompatibility was reported in narcissus, hemerocallis, lilium, gasteria and annona (Arasu, 1968) and Freesia (Pandey, 1970). The time of anthesis (opening of flowers) was recorded when the tagged flowers open. 3.6.1.2 Anther dehiscence For determining the time of anther dehiscence, the flower buds marked at 15 minutes‟ intervals from 2 p.m. were examined with the help of a hand magnifying lens. The observations were made during February to June, 2017. 3.6.1.3 Stigma receptivity The stigma receptivity was recorded by treating the hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) on the stigma. To determine the stigma receptivity, 10 flowers in each replication for individual species were examined. Experiment was conducted with hydrogen peroxide; a drop was added on the stigmatic surface of flower. Receptive stigmas were characterized by high enzymatic activity. The occurrence of bubbling action on the stigmatic surface as an indicator of Peroxidase activity was determined by H2O2. Observations were recorded when stigma showed pure foam producing bubbles as a receptive stigma. The time, period of effervescence was calculated at different time intervals to study the duration of stigma receptivity. The stigma receptivity was evaluated based on the density of bubbles produced. Results were recorded as follows: -, none; +, less; ++, moderate; and +++, high. 3.6.1.4 Corolla tube length and style length Corolla tube and style length is one of the criteria for post pollination failure. It was measured and expressed in centimeter. 3.6.2 Pollen viability test Pollen viability was evaluated by different methods: (1) staining techniques; (2) pollen shape and size; (3) in vitro pollen germination test; or (4) analyzing final seed set. 3.6.2.1 Staining technique The pollen viability (%) of six species was estimated by using Alexander staining solution. Freshly dehisced pollen grains were taken on a slide with one to two drops of Alexander stain on which cover slip was placed and was kept for two to three minutes for proper and uniform staining (Alexander, 1969). The pollen grains which were round and deep purplish pink color stained were recorded as viable. The shriveled and green pollen grains recorded as sterile / non-viable. The average viable pollen grains were estimated and expressed in percentage. Pollen viability % = Number of stained pollens × 100 Total number of pollens 3.6.2.2 Pollen shape and size Round shape pollen grains were recorded as normal shaped pollen grains in all the species included non-viable pollen grains. Ten randomly selected pollen grains were used to measure the pollen diameter in each replication. The images were obtained with a photomicroscope and the cell sens standard software attached to the microscope (Olympus-BX43, Tokyo, Japan). Normal shaped pollen grains (%) = No. of round shaped pollens × 100 Total number of pollens 3.6.2.3 Pollen germination test Pollen germination statuses of six Jasminum species were estimated by using hanging drop technique in vitro (Stanley and Linskens, 1974). Pollen germination % = No. of germinated pollens × 100 Total number of pollens Media composition for pollen germination test Pollen germination was estimated by using Modified Brewbaker and Kwack‟s (1963) medium which was prepared by using following protocol. The base medium constituted of sucrose (10%) supplemented with 100 ppm boric acid, Calcium Nitrate 300 ppm and Magnesium Sulphate 200 ppm. Concentrations were altered based on the response of pollen germination percentage (%). Procedure for hanging drop technique Hanging drop technique (Stanley and Linskens, 1974), wherein small drop of medium was placed on cover glass and dusted with pollen. Cover glass was slowly and gently tilted to correctly fix it on to the cavity of slide. Cavity slides were taken and then kept in Petri dishes lined with moist filter paper and examined under an Olympus - BX43 microscope at low magnification (10X) at one, two, three, four and twenty-four hours‟ time intervals to know the germination percentage and pollen tube length. The pollen grain was considered as germinated when its pollen tube length becomes equal to or larger than the pollen diameter (Chagas et al. 2010). The pollen tube growth was observed and images were captured with a photomicroscope (Olympus-BX43). 3.6.3 Seed set studies All the six species were utilized for their seed setting behavior by open pollination, cross pollination and natural self-pollination under natural conditions. 3.6.3.1 Open pollination All the six species were utilized to study the seed setting behavior by open-pollination. Fully developed flower buds in each female parent were tagged and left for open-pollination. Fruit set and seed set data were recorded and that was expressed in percentage. 3.6.3.2 Controlled self-pollination All the fully developed flower buds in the single inflorescence were bagged to ensure self- pollination. 3.6.3.3 Artificial cross pollination The six-species selected as female and male parents to study the cross-compatibility behavior. All possible cross combinations were tried among the selected species used for the present investigation. Fully developed flower buds of female parents were emasculated 1-2 hours prior to anther dehiscence by removing anthers. Simultaneously, sufficient numbers of matured flower buds from the selected male parents were collected for pollen purpose. The fresh pollen from collected flowers was dusted on the stigmatic surface on the same day evening at the time of anthesis (5:00 to 7:00 p.m.) and also in next day morning of anthesis (6:00 to 7:00 a.m.) to study the effective stage of stigma receptivity. After pollination, flowers were covered with butter paper covers and labeled. Needles were used for pollination and they were regularly sterilized with ethanol to ensure that they are free from contamination of foreign pollen. Fruit set was observed at 25-30 days after pollination. Fruit set and seed set were estimated, and expressed in percentage (%). 3.6.3.4 Number of days taken for fruit and seed set The period required for fruit set was recorded from the day of pollination to the day of fruit appearance. For seed set the day of fruit appearance to the day of harvesting of the berries. 3.6.3.5 Number of seeds per berry Number of seeds per berry was counted from open pollinated, self-pollinated, and cross pollinated fruits and average number of seeds per berry was calculated. 3.6.4 Statistical Analysis The data generated from present investigation were subjected to the statistical analysis in accordance with the procedure outlined by Gomez and Gomez (1984). The significance of differences among treatment means were tested by F-test. Completely Randomized Design was used in statistical analysis of pollen viability and Randomized Complete Block Design (RCBD) was used in statistical analysis of fruit and seed set studies. DISCUSSION Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) is one of the most important economical loose flowers that are being commercially cultivated in different parts of India. Hybridization for crop improvement requires a sound knowledge of floral biology. Precise information is not available with regard to the time of anthesis, anther dehiscence and stigma receptivity in Jasminum species and also seed setting behavior of species. However, the success of this approach necessitate judicious choice of parents for their use as a male or pollen parent and another as female or seed parent. Seed setting studies in interspecific crosses is a prerequisite for development of new genotypes. Screening of desirable parents, study of floral biology, assessment of pollen viability and germination, and knowledge of seed setting behavior are essential pre- requisites for the selection and execution of appropriate breeding strategies. The present investigation was undertaken using six species of Jasmine viz. Jasminum sambac cv. Ramanathapuram Gundumalli, Jasminum auriculatum cv. Parimullai, Jasminum grandiflorum cv. Co.1 (Pitchi), Jasminum malabaricum, Jasminum multiflorum and Jasminum flexile for the study of floral biology, pollen viability and germination, and compatibility behavior of different species. The evaluation was done in Complete Randomized Design and Randomized Complete Block Design with four replications. The findings of different experiments are discussed under the following headings: 5.1 Floral biology traits - Anthesis, Anther dehiscence, stigma receptivity, corolla tube and style length. 5.2 Identification of pollen parent through pollen viability and pollen germination among Jasminum species. 5.3 Identification of seed parent through fruit and seed set studies under open, controlled self and artificial cross pollination among Jasminum species. 5.1 Floral biology traits - Anthesis, Anther dehiscence, stigma receptivity, corolla tube and style length Time of anthesis There are significant variations for floral biology traits among species. From the pollination point of view, time of anthesis and anther dehiscence is very important observations for hybridization. In all cases, the flower opening was preceded by anther dehiscence and the time lag in between the two (time of anthesis and anther dehiscence) ranged from 1 to 3 hours. The flower opening was late in the month of February occurring between 6:30 p.m. and 9:45 p.m. while it was earlier during the subsequent months. In May, the flower buds opened earlier than the other months. The cool days and nights during the former month might be reason for promote later flower opening. Time of anther dehiscence The time of anther dehiscence was more or less constant during the five months period ranging from 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. except in Jasminum multiflorum and it was started from 6:00 p.m. onwards only. But a trend towards slightly early anther dehiscence, particularly in April and May was also noticed which was about 3:30 p.m. and 3:00 p.m. This indicates that the increasing of day and night temperatures in April and May is related with the earlier anther dehiscence. Veluswamy et al. (1980) reported Jasminum species had differential influences of season on flower opening of different species. Stigma receptivity Stigma receptivity is an important factor for successful completion of the post-pollination events. Stigma receptivity refers to the ability of the stigma to support pollen germination and tube growth of viable, compatible pollen grain. Stigma receptivity is a critical stage in maturation of the flower that may greatly influence the success of pollination at different stages in the flower (Barrett, 2002). Peak time of stigma receptivity was recorded at the time of anthesis except in Jasminum multiflorum in which species stigma receptivity was peak in next day morning of anthesis. So, the best time for pollination in Jasminum multiflorum was found at 12 hrs after anthesis. Sivaram et al. (2015) observed peak time of receptivity was at the time of anthesis in Pterospermum reticulatum. Generally, receptivity is maximum soon after anthesis; it varies among species and depends upon temperature and humidity (Shivanna and Johri, 1985). Joshirao and Saoji (1989) also stated that the period of receptivity may vary from species to species. Maximum duration of stigma receptivity was recorded in Jasminum flexile, Jasminum malabaricum and Jasminum grandiflorum. The flowers were suitable for pollination at the time of anthesis. Peroxidase activity was observed less in Jasminum sambac, In Jasminum flexile, stigma receptivity was continued up to 24 hrs after anthesis it started from 12 hrs before anthesis. Corolla tube length and style length There are significant variations for corolla tube and style length. A particularly interesting in examining the causes, effects of different pollination in seed setting rate is important to know the compatibility between the different species. Corolla tube and style length is one of the criteria for post pollination failure. The maximum corolla tube and style length was recorded in Jasminum grandiflorum which might be a reason for poor fruit set. The minimum corolla tube length and style was measured in Jasminum sambac in which species there was no seed set found in different kind of pollination. Because of this reason, corolla tube and style length may not be associated with the seed setting in Jasminum sambac. 5.2 Identification of pollen parent through pollen viability and pollen germination among Jasminum species Pollen viability can be evaluated by different methods: (1) staining techniques; (2) pollen shape and size; (3) in vitro pollen germination test; or (4) analyzing final seed set. The choice of method depends on the crop or species. Pollen viability through pollen staining technique Identification of pollen parents based on the viability decides the extent of success in fruit and seed set. Study on pollen viability through pollen staining and shape gives an assessment of viability of pollen grains of a particular species. The results indicated that, Jasminum malabaricum recorded highest percentage of pollen viability followed by Jasminum flexile. The lowest percentage of pollen viability was recorded in Jasminum sambac, Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum multiflorum which had a viability percentage less than 50 per cent. For example, Koshy and Jee (2001) showed that low pollen viability is one of main factors responsible for failure of seed set in Bambusa vulgaris. The species Jasminum malabaricum, Jasminum flexile and Jasminum auriculatum were found to be better pollen parent through pollen viability compared to other Jasminum species used in this study. Quantity of pollen grains obtained from Jasminum sambac was also very less. This might be one of the reasons for zero fruit set in artificial cross pollination when Jasminum sambac used as a pollen parent. Dadlani and More (1988) studied pollen viability in Jasminum and reported that lack of seed setting was due to the absence of anthers and/or pollen, or pollen sterility, non-viability or failure to germinate depending upon the genotype involved. Pollen shape and size In almost all species, pollen grains were spherical shape except Jasminum multiflorum which has a mix of spherical and triangular shape of pollen grains. Raman et al. (1970) observed the shape of the pollen grains was spheroidal in J. grandiflorum and spheroidal or slightly square shaped in J. auriculatum. More than 90 percentage of normal shape pollen grains were recorded in Jasminum auriculatum, Jasminum malabaricum, Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum flexile. Non-viable pollen grains were also having normal shape of pollen grains but with less diameter. Viable pollen diameter measured ranged from 40 to 50 µm, while non-viable pollen diameter was ranged from 20 to 35 µm. Diameter of viable pollen was reduced with loss in pollen viability as those got shrunk. In vitro pollen germination in jasmine Pollen germination was conducted to ascertain the viability of pollen grains while selecting pollen parents. Pollen germination was conducted at in-vitro condition with using modified Brewbaker and Kwack‟s media. From the results on pollen germination using modified Brewbaker and Kwack‟s media with 15 per cent sucrose and 15 per cent PEG4000 was recorded with highest percentage pollen germination in Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum multiflorum. In Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum flexile, good pollen germination was found in 10 per cent sucrose and 20 per cent PEG-4000 media with highest pollen germination percentage. Pollen germination in Jasminum malabaricum was found with 10 per cent sucrose with 15 per cent PEG-4000 concentration media. In case of Jasminum sambac pollen germination test 15 per cent sucrose, 10 per cent PEG- 4000 and 100 ppm KNO3 was found good media. Raman et al. (1970) reported pollen germination in sucrose solution of different concentrations was generally poor in all the Jasminum species and varieties studied. The maximum pollen grains germinated only when flowers were collected at the time of anthesis. But, Yan-ming et al. (2014) reported that pollen for highest viability should be collected at 8.00 a.m. - 9.00 a.m. in Jasminum sambac Aiton. Pollen germination increased with the increase time of incubation. Minimum in-vitro germination per cent was recorded 1 hour after incubation. Maximum percentage of pollen germination was recorded 24 hrs after anthesis. The reason for higher pollen germination with the increase in duration for which the pollen grains were exposed to the pollen germination media could be attributed to adequate amount of nutrient absorption for a longer period. The pollen grain was considered as germinated when its pollen tube length becomes equal to or larger than the pollen diameter. From in-vitro pollen germination study, maximum percentage of pollen germination was recorded in Jasminum malabaricum which was about more than 90 per cent followed by Jasminum flexile and Jasminum auriculatum. Minimum percentage of pollen germination was recorded in Jasminum sambac followed by Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum multiflorum. Hui-chao et al. (2011) reported the highest percentage of pollen germination in Jasminum nudiflorum with 91.04. Pollen tube length Increase in length of the pollen tube was recorded with increase in duration for which the pollen grains were incubated. The pollen tube length was minimum at 1 hour after incubation. It increased with the increase in incubation time up to 24 hrs after incubation. The reason for increased pollen tube length with the increase in duration for which the pollen grains were exposed to the germination media was due to adequate amount of nutrient absorption for a longer period. Pollen tubes revealed abnormalities like bulging and coiling of tips was observed in Jasminum sambac and Jasminum grandiflorum (Fig. 3b and 3c). This might be one of the reasons for no fruit set when Jasminum sambac used as pollen parent and less fruit set observed in Jasminum grandiflorum (♂ parent). Sun et al. (2010) were observed no seed set in the interspecific cross between Dendranthema grandiflorum and D. nankingense, in that only very few pollen grains germinated on stigmas after pollination and most of them germinated abnormally. From the experiments on pollen staining and germination, clearly observed that the species Jasminum malabaricum was found highly superior as a pollen parent followed by Jasminum flexile and Jasminum auriculatum compared to other species taken for study. 5.3 Identification of seed parent through fruit and seed set studies under open, controlled self and artificial cross pollination among Jasminum species Open pollination Significant variations were found in the observations of natural cross pollination. On open pollination, fruit set was observed in five species namely Jasminum auriculatum, Jasminum grandiflorum, Jasminum malabaricum, Jasminum multiflorum and Jasminum flexile. However, the species Jasminum malabaricum recorded highest percentage of fruit setting which was about 70 per cent. In Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum flexile species were found more than 50 per cent of fruit setting under open pollination. The probable reasons for higher fruit set might be due to more number of genotypes availability in the germplasm. Similar results of higher fruit set under open pollination were also reported in tuberose (Uma, 1990) and (Hemanta, 2015) also in fruit crops like pomegranate (Josan et al. 1979b) and almond (Sharma and Dhaliwal, 1991). No fruit set was recorded in Jasminum sambac. In Jasminum sambac, flowers pedicel senescence very soon after anthesis. So, holding of pollinated flower on a plant after anthesis was difficult. Pollinated flowers were dried with pedicel. Among six species observed, highest number of seeds were recorded in Jasminum malabaricum (19.50) followed by Jasminum auriculatum (12.75). If more cytological and embryological studies are carried out, it would be useful. This may help to know the problems associated with chromosomal level if any. VI. SUMMARY The present investigation entitled “Studies on pollen viability and compatibility in Jasminum spp.” was conducted at the ICAR - Indian Institute of Horticultural Research, Bengaluru during 2016 - 17. Six species were studied to know the floral biology i.e. the time of anthesis, time of anther dehiscence, stigma receptivity, pollen viability, pollen diameter, in vitro pollen germination and pollination studies by open pollination, controlled self-pollination, artificial cross pollination and seed setting behavior in different pollination methods. The salient findings of the experiment are summarized below: 6.1 Floral biology traits - Anthesis, Anther dehiscence, stigma receptivity, corolla tube and style length. 6.2 Identification of pollen parent through pollen viability and pollen germination among Jasminum species. 6.3 Identification of seed parent through fruit and seed set studies under open, controlled self and artificial cross pollination among Jasminum species. 6.1 Floral biology traits - Anthesis, Anther dehiscence, stigma receptivity, corolla tube and style length  Anthesis started from 5:00 p.m. and continued till 9:00 p.m. during the observation and completed on the same day. The peak time of anthesis was from 6:00 to 7:00 p.m. In the month of February, all the species were taken long time for anthesis compared to following months.  Time of anthesis in Jasminum sambac was ranged from 6:15 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. and J. auriculatum (4:30 to 6:30 p.m.), J. grandiflorum (5:30 to 6:30 p.m.), J. malabaricum (6:15 to 7:30 p.m.), J. multiflorum (7:15 to 9:45 p.m.), J. flexile (7:05 to 7:20 p.m.) for all months.  Time of anther dehiscence in Jasminum sambac was ranged from 5:45 p.m. to 6:40 p.m. and J. auriculatum (3:00 to 5:30 p.m.), J. grandiflorum (4:45 to 5:30 p.m.), J. malabaricum (5:10 to 6:30 p.m.), J. multiflorum (6:00 to 8:45 p.m.) and J. flexile (4:30 to 6:45 p.m.) for all months.  The stigma receptivity started from 12 hrs before anthesis and the peak time of receptivity was observed at the time of anthesis except in J. multiflorum. Tricolpate shape of pollen grains was observed in J. malabaricum.  Highest percentage of normal shaped pollen grains were observed in J. auriculatum (96.92 %) and J. malabaricum (96.89 %) followed by J. grandiflorum (93.63 %) and J. flexile (91.70 %), while lowest percentage of normal shaped pollen grains were observed in J. sambac (70.63 %).  The maximum percentage of pollen viability was observed in J. malabaricum (96.57 %) followed by J. flexile (84.92 %) and J. auriculatum (71.32 %), while the minimum percentage of pollen viability was observed in J. sambac (34.27 %).  Highest percentage of pollen germination was recorded in J. auriculatum and J. multiflorum with 15 per cent sucrose and 15 per cent PEG 4000 of modified Brewbaker and Kwack's media. It occupies a pride of place in home gardens and is important commercially since flowers of some Jasminum species are valued as cut flowers, while a few yield essential oil used in the perfumery industry. The flowers and buds are used for making garlands and bouquets, and used by ladies for hair adornment and for religious offerings. The jasmine oil that is extracted from the flowers is regarded as unique as it blends well with other floral extracts and is highly valued through- out the world for producing high grade perfumes, perfumed hair oils, attars and is also used in soap and cosmetic industries. Flowers of some species are used for fla- vouring food and drinks and also find use in medicines. The genus Jasminum belongs to the family Oleaceae and the name Jasminum is derived from the Per- sian word 'Yasmyn' meaning fragrance (Bhattacharjee, 1980). It consists of about ninety species distributed over Asia, Africa, Australia and Southern Europe. About forty species are reported to occur in India (Muthuswami and Abdul Khader, 1986). Jasmines are grown on a commercial scale in France, India, Italy, Morocco, Algeria, North Africa, Spain and Egypt. In India, they are cultivated throughout the country and the important states growing jasmines are Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. Although the correct statis- tics of the area and production in India are not avail- able, it is estimated that it occupies an area of about 8,000 hectares with an annual production of flowers worth Rs.80-100 million (Muthuswami and Abdul Khader, 1986). In Karnataka, jasmines are grown in an area of 2,319 hectares with an annual production of 11,571 tonnes (Anon., 1991). The most commonly cultivated species in India are J.grandiflorum, J.sambac, J.auriculatum and J.multiflo- rum. Species such as J.calophyllum, J.flexile, J.humile and J.pubescens are grown in home gardens for their scented flowers. Propagation of jasmines by seeds is followed only in crop improvement programme and is not commercially followed owing to poor germination of the seeds. Layer- ing, a traditional method of vegetative propagation in jasmine, is seldom followed now, since it is time consum- ing and the number of plants propagated from a bush is o limited. Propagation by cuttings has been attempted by some workers in many species of Jasminum. In the propagation of plants by stem cuttings, the process of regeneration is largely controlled by internal and exter- nal factors. External factors such as the rooting medi- um, environmental conditions like light, humidity etc., largely determine the success in rooting of cuttings. Under ordinary propagation conditions, the per- centage of success in rooting of jasmine cuttings is less, but it is reported that under intermittent mist, a higher percentage of rooting can be obtained. However, many practical problems such as irregular supply of electricity and high costs involved in installing a mist system, limit the use of mist chambers by jasmine growers and propagators. Easy multiplication of various horticultural plants by planting cuttings in rooting medium within closed polyethylene frames is possible (Hartmann and Kester, 1986). The use of closed medium polyethylene sachets (CMS) has facilitated the quick propagation of various horticultural plants through cuttings. The polybags provide an inexpensive and protective cover, and maintain high humidity for rooting of cuttings (Sweet, 1952; Lipp, 1953; Floor, 1954; Hurov, 1961). Although this method has been attempted to propagate J.qrandiflo- rum by shoot tip cuttings (Srivastava, 1989), there are no reports on the propagation of the commercially impor- tant Jasminum species by the closed medium sachet method using semi-hard wood cuttings. Hence, the present inves- tigation was planned to study the suitability of the closed medium sachet method to propagate the commercially important Jasminum species by semi- hard wood cuttings with the following objectives: 1. To study the percentage of success in rooting of semi-hard wood cuttings of four species of Jasminum in closed medium sachets. 2. To study the effect of different concentra- tions of indolebutyric acid (IBA) on the rooting and survival of cuttings and to standardise the optimum concentration of IBA for rooting in each species of Jasminum. 3. To compare the seasonal effect on the success in rooting of cuttings. 4. To assess the biochemical composition of cuttings associated with rooting. 5. To study the ontogeny and histochemistry of adventitious roots in semi-hard wood cuttings of the four Jasminum species to know the causes for their differential rooting behaviour. REVIEW OF LITERATURE II REVIEW OF LITERATURE Cuttage is the most important means of propagating ornamental shrubs and several other plants of horticultural importance. By cuttage many new plants can be obtained in a limited space from a fev/ stock plants and the technique is simple^ inexpensive and rapid. Greater uniformity is obtained and the parent plant is usually reproduced true to type with no genetic change when propagated by cuttings. Many horticultural plants when propagated by cuttings show a wide variability in their ability to root. Certain species root easily under ordinary condi- tions of propagation while a few others root only when optimum conditions for rooting are provided. Jasmines are usually propagated by cuttings. Layering is seldom followed now on a commercial scale since it is time consuming and cumbersome. Seed propaga- tion though uncommon is followed for crop improvement through planned hybridization. Propagation through cuttage under intermittent mist has been attempted in certain species of Jasminum grown on a commercial scale. There are, however, several factors such as type of cutting, rooting media, treatment with growth regulators, < environmental conditions, etc., which influence root formation in cuttings. The studies done on jasmines and other horticultural crops with respect to their propagation by cuttings and the factors influencing rooting of cuttings and on the anatomical basis of root- ing are reviewed in this chapter. 2.1 GROWTH REGULATORS IN ROOTING OF CUTTINGS The purpose of treating cuttings with auxin/type growth regulators (hormones) is to increase the percent- age of cuttings that form roots, to hasten root initiation to increase the number and quality of roots produced per cutting, and to increase uniformity of rooting. The synthetic root-promoting chemicals that have been found most reliable in stimulating adventitious root production in cuttings are indolebutyric acid (IBA) and napthaleneacetic acid (NAA) although lAA can also be used to a lesser extent either alone or in combinations with other auxins. 2.1.1 Rooting of cuttings of jasmines with the aid of growth regulators El-Hakim (1954) observed better rooting in cut- tings of Arabian jasmine (Jasminum sambac) when treated with 25 ppm lAA for 24 hours. Singh and Bhatnagar (1955) Studied the effect of lAA and NAA on rooting of soft and hard wood cuttings of J.grandiflorum. The highest root- ing of 90 per cent was recorded in soft wood cuttings treated with 1000 ppm lAA and in hard wood cuttings treated with 500 ppm NAA. Bose and Mondal (1972) ob- served 100 per cent rooting in cuttings of J.pubescens var. rubescens treated with 3000 ppm IBA. Cuttings of J.auriculatum and J.grandiflorum which showed a low percentage of rooting under ordinary propagation facilities, were found to have developed roots under intermittent mist and further increase in the percentage of rooting and number of roots was observed with IBA and NAA treatment (Bo'se et aJ,. , 1973). Callus is an irregular mass of parenchymatous cells in various stages of lignification. Frequently, the first roots appear through the callus, leading to the belief that callus formation is essential for rooting. In several kinds of plants, the formation of callus and the forma- tion of roots are independent of each other; that they often occur simultaneously is due to their dependence upon similar internal and environmental conditions. In some species, however, callus formation apparently is a precursor of adventitious root formation. Callus growth proliferates from young cells at the base of the cutting from different regions of the stem. "5 n Chadv/ick and Rash (1961) reported that callus developed from the cambium tissue in the stem cuttings of Ilex opaca in the treated (wounding or NAA or NAD or wounding+NAA) and in untreated ones. Callus proliferation resulted from the activities of both cambium and the phellogen, occuring inside the sclerenchyma which surrounded the phloem. Profuse callusing was also observed beneath the lenticels and arose from the lenticel phellogen in the stem cuttings of Actinidia chinensis (Messina jind Testolin, 1984). MATERIAL AND METHODS Ill MATERIAL AND METHODS The investigation on "Closed Medium Sachet (CMS) method of propagation of commercially important Jasminum species" was carried out during the year 1990-91 in two seasons viz., December, 1990 and June, 1991 at the Horti- cultural Research Station, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra, University of Agricultural Sciences, Bangalore, situated at an elevation of 930 M above mean sea level, 12 58' North latitude and 77°35' East longitude. The meteoro- logical data indicating the average rainfall received, temperature and relative humidity during the period of investigation and the data on temperature and relative humidity within the closed polyethylene sachets are presented in Appendix la and lb. The present investiga'jion was undertaken to study the effect of different concentrations of indolebutyric acid (IBA) on the root and shoot growth in semi-hard wood cuttings of four species of Jasminum in closed medium sachets. 3.1 SOURCE AND PREPARATION OF THE CUTTINGS Shoots of past season's growth were selected from the plants of the four Jasminum species. Semi-hard wood 37 cuttings of length 15-20 cm were made by giving a slant cut just below a node at the base of the cuttings and a horizontal cut at the top and retaining 2-4 leaves in each cutting. 3.2 PREPARATION OF THE ROOTING MEDIUM AND POLYETHYLENE SACHETS Clean river bed sand was used as the rooting medium after treating it with captan (0.2%). Polyethyl- ene sachets of size 40 cm x 15 cm and of thickness 250 gauge were filled upto a height of 15 cm with clean and dry sand. The rooting medium was then watered to field capacity. I 3.3 DESIGN AND LAYOUT The experimental design adopted was Factorial CRD with semi-hard wood cuttings of four species of Jasminum treated with five different concentrations of indolebu- tyric acid. In total, there were twenty treatment combi- nations. Each treatment was replicated thrice and con- sisted of forty five cuttings with fifteen cuttings per replication. Twelve well rooted cuttings from each treatment were transplanted into pots containing leaf mould and garden soil in the ratio of 50:50 and watered at frequent intervals. Thirty days after transplanting, the percent- age of survival of the transplanted cuttings was recorded for each treatment. 3.8 BIOCHEMICAL ANALYSIS At the time of planting, in both the seasons composite samples of plant material consisting of semi- hard wood cuttings of the four species of Jasminum were collected and oven-dried for the purpose of analysis for total sugars, starch, total carbohydrate, total nitrogen, and total phenols. The methods followed for estimating the different plant constituents are as follows: 3.8.1 Total sugars The total sugar content in the plant samples were estimated by following the colorimetric method (Nelson, 1944) and the results expressed as percentage on dry weight basis. 41 3.8.2 Starch The plant samples were analysed for their starch content by direct acid hydrolysis method (Anon., 1960) and the results expressed a? percentage on dry weight basis. 3.8.3 Total carbohydrate The total carbohydrate content in the plant samples was calculated by adding together the total sugar and starch contents for each sample and expressed as percentage on dry weight basis. 3.8.4 Total nitrogen The total nitrogen content was determined by following the micro-kjeldhal method (Anon., 1970) and expressed as percentage. 3.8.5 Carbohydrate/Nitrogen (C/N) ratio The carbohydrate/nitrogen ratio was obtained by dividing the value of total carbohydrate by the value of total nitrogen for each sample. 3.8.6 Total phenols Total phenols in the samples were determined by following the Folin-Denis method (Swain and Hillis, 1959) (., and compared with a standard curve prepared by using a standard solution of tannic acid. The results were expressed as ug per gram on dry weight basis. 3.8.7 Root promoting co-factors At the time of planting, 100 grams each of fresh samples of plant material consisting of semi-hard wood cuttings of the four species of Jasminum were collected and assayed for the root promoting co-factors following the mung bean (Phaseolus aureus Roxb.) bioassay technique and the root promoting co-factors were identified as per the Rf values (Hess, 1961a). 3.9 ONTOGENY AND HISTOCHEMISTRY OF ADVENTITIOUS ROOTS IN SEMI- HARD WOOD STEM CUTTINGS OF FOUR Jasmintim SPECIES An anatomical study was carried out to know the ontogeny and histochemistry of adventitious roots in semi hard wood stem cuttings of four Jasminum species. 3.9.1 Procedure Stem portions of 1.0-1.5 cm length were excised from the basal end of the cuttings of the four Jasminum species periodically and each sample was split longitudi- nally into two equal halves. The prepared materials were fixed in Carney's B solution (Alcohol:Chloroform:Acetic I O acid in the ratio of 6:3:1) for three hours and dehydrat- ed using ethanol-n'butanol grades followed by infiltra- tion and embedding in paraffin wax. Transverse serial sections of 12 urn thickness were taken using an ERMA rotary microtome and affixed on slides using gelatin (0.3%). Subsequently, the sections were subjected to deparaffinisation followed by histo- chemical staining for localisation of different cytoplas- mic components as given in Table 1. After histochemical staining, the sections were dehydrated and mounted in DPX medium. Standard controls were followed for different methods (Jensen, 1962). 3.9.2 Histochemical observations Assessment of the different cellular chemical compounds was done based on the intensity of staining for the specific stain used. Epidermis consisted of a single layer of closely arranged oval or rectangular, tangentially flattened cells, and covering the epidermal layer externally was a clear layer of cuticle and a few multicellular hairs. The epidermal cells were intense in proteins, cytoplasmic RNA and total insoluble polysaccharides. Cortex was interior to the epidermal layer. Below this zone were ten to twelve layers of thin-walled circular or oval, compactly ar- ranged parenchymatous cells. Both the collenchymatous and parenchymatous cells were rich to low in proteins, cytoplasmic RNA and total insoluble polysaccharides. Starch grains were deposited in the inner cortex. The outer pericycle represented by the sclerenchymatous zone consisted of two to three rows of polygonal cells which formed a more or less continuous ring of varying thickness around the stele. These cells were circular to oval in cross section, smaller than the cortical parenchyma cells and rich in cytoplas- mic RNA, and proteins and low in polysaccharides. Vascular bundles in the stem of Jasminum were collateral and open; made up of phloem and xylem with cambium in between. The thick- ness of this layer varied with the species (Table 14a and 14b). In between the phloem and xylem was the cambium made up of a few layers (two to four) of thin-walled, flattened, roughly rectangular meristematic cells. The xylem ring was relatively narrower in J.grandiflorum as com- pared to that in the other three species (Plate 10). DISCUSSION V DISCUSSION The study entitled "Closed Medium Sachet (CMS) method of propagation of commercially important Jasminum species" was taken up to evaluate the effect of species and indolebutyric acid on the success in rooting of cuttings. Further, studies on the effect of season, biochemical composition of the cuttings, and ontogeny and histochemistry of adventitious roots to know the causes of differential rooting behaviour in the four species of Jasminum were undertaken. The significance of the results obtained have been discussed in this chapter in the light of reports by the earlier workers. 5.1 ROOT PARAMETERS 5.1.1 Percentage of rooting The results on the percentage of rooting in the four Jasminum species presented in Table 2 indicate that there were significant differences among the species with respect to the percentage of rooting of cuttings. The percentage of rooting was higher in J.grandiflorum and J.sambac (78.67-92.89) in both the seasons, whereas, it was lower in J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum (0.00-8.44%) 9 ..,> at the end of forty five days in both the seasons. These differences in rooting of cuttings among the four species may be attributed to the differences in the innate root- ing ability of the cuttings taken from them irrespective of whether they are treated with IBA or not. Such dif- ferences in rooting ability have been reported in some species of Ixora, Jasminum and a few varieties of hibis- cus (Bose et al.. , 1973) and in different Jasminum species (Bhattacharjee and Balakrishna, 1983b). The cuttings treated with IBA (1000-4000 ppm) showed better rooting (41.67% to 46.67% in December, 1990 and 47.22% to 52.78% in June, 1991) compared to the un- treated cuttings which had 32.78 and 37.22 per cent rooting in the first and second season respectively. This increase in the percentage of rooting in the auxin treated cuttings compared to the control may be due to the stimulative effect of exogenous IBA in combination with endogenous growth substances on adventitious root formation. Similar results on the percentage of rooting as induced by auxin treatment have been reported in many ornamental plant species (El Hakim, 1954; Singh and Bhatnagar, 1955; Bose and Mondal, 1972; Bose et al., 1973; Pal Singh, 1979; Philip and Gopalakrishna, 1982; Bhattacharjee and Balakrishna, 1983a). 37 The highest percentage of rooting was obtained from cuttings treated with IBA at 4000 ppm compared to other concentrations, both in the first and second season (46.67 and 52.78 respectively). IBA 4000 ppm must have been more effective in inducing adventitious roots to a greater extent than the other concentration. In differ- ent trials Singh (1976 and 1979a) obtained maximum root- ing percentage in cuttings of J.sambac treated with IBA 4000 ppm. Srivastava (1989) obtained a higher percentage of rooting (91.00) in cuttings treated with 4000 ppm IBA and planted in June than in those planted in December (63.00). From the Table 3 it is evident that the interac- tion effect between species and indole-3-butyric acid on percentage of rooting was non-significant in both the seasons. 5.1.2 Number of roots per cutting The number of roots per cutting varied significantly with the species in both the seasons. In J.qrandiflorum tthe highest percentage of survival was obtained from cutting treated with 4000 ppm lAA (83.33 in December, 1990 and 91.67 in June, 1991). In J.sambac the highest percentage of survival (100) was obtained in cuttings treated with IBA 2000 ppm to 4000 ppm in the first season and in cuttings treated with IBA 1000 ppm to 4000 ppm in the second season. The better survival of the cuttings tre'ited with IBA than the con- trol might be due to the production of more number of roots per cutting and longer roots in IBA treated cut- tings than in the control. 'Flore-pleno' and by Widiastoety and Socbijanto (1988) in Hibiscus rosa-sinensis. 5.4 BIOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION OF STEM CUTTINGS The success in rooting of stem cuttings with or without the aid of auxins reflects partly on the biochem- ical composition or the physiological condition of the n cuttings at the time when they are taken from the stock plant and planted in the rooting medium. Internal fac- tors, such as auxin levels, rooting co-factors, carbohy- drates, nitrogen and phenols can, of course, influence root initiation in cuttings. Hence, in the present investigation, these biochemical constituents have been assessed. 5.4.1 Total sugars The total sugar content was high in the easy-to- root J.grandiflorum (2.569% and 1.915% in the first and second seasons respectively) and J.sambac (2.652% and 1.986% in the first and second seasons respectively), but compartively less in the difficult-to-root J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum in both the seasons. This high and low contents of total sugars in the easy and difficult-to- root species might have influenced the differential rooting behaviour in them. These results agree with the results obtained in other plant species with respect to the levels of soluble sugars /Sen and Bose, 1967; Stoltz, 1967; Ghosh and Ghosh, 1971; Nanda et al., 1971; Mokashi, 1978; Foong and Barnes, 1981; Kumar et al.. , 1985). 5.4.2 Starch The starch content v/as higher in J. grandiflorum and J.calophyllum than in J.sambac and J.auriculatum. 1 n" The higher level of starch in J.grandiflorum and moderate level in J.sambac in combination with other factors must have contributed to enhanced rooting in them. However, J.calophyllum cuttings inspite of having high starch content did not show good rooting. This may be because of the inability of the cuttings to make use of the available starch or due to non-availability of starch for root initiation. 5.4.3 Total carbohydrate The total carbohydrate content was higher in the easy-to-root. Hence, to study the effect of season on rooting of cuttings of the four Jasminum spe- cies, this investigation was carried out in two seasons viz., December, 1990 and June, 1991. In the present study, the experiment on rooting of cuttings of four Jasminum species carried out in the second season (June, 1991) showed better results with respect to the percentage of rooting, length of longest primary root, number of sprouts and length of longest Ill sprouts and the percentage survival of rooted cuttings compared to the first season (December, 1990) in which only the number of roots per cutting was higher. The effect of season on rooting might be related to growth and development of the source plant. During June, the plants showed active vegetative growth, and during December the plants attained reproductive phase. Differences in rooting of cuttings taken in June, 1991 and December, 1990 might be related to the growth phase of the stock plant during thoie periods. The results of the present study as regards the season, that was found best for rooting agree with the work done by Spethmann (1982) who found early June to be the best time for planting juvenile cuttings of oak, beech and birch and obtained better rooting than in other months. Similarly, Dzhananloekova (1983) reported the best rooting (85-97%) in soft wood cuttings of rose cultivars struck in May- June. Standardi (1988) found June to be the best month for planting cuttings of different culttivars of azalea. Srivastava (1989) obtained 91 per cent rooting in cut- tings taken in June. Wang (1989) observed best rooting in cuttings of Japanese box wood taken in April, June and October. Reports by Spellerkerg (1985), Balakrishna- murthy (1988) and Kamel and Nada (1986) are contradictory 112 to the results of this study, since they found other seasons/months of the year favourable for rooting of cuttings than June. 5.6 EFFECT OF POLYETHYLENE ON ROOTING OF CUTTINGS In the present study, the cuttings were planted in rooting medium (sand) enclosed by polyethylene sa- chets. Irrespective of whether the cuttings were treated with IBA or not, the cuttings performed well with respect to rooting. It could be observed that the cuttings that were not treated with IBA showed more than 60 per cent rooting in both the seasons in J. grandif loruin and J.sambac. This shows that, the micro-environment for rooting must have been favourable inside the polyethylene sachets since the success in propagation of plants by cutting is largely controlled by factors such as the planting material, planting environment and treatment with growth substances. The microclimate within the polyethylene sachets might have been congenial, maintain- ing low temperature and high relative humidity, thus sub- stituting for a mist chamber. Hence, the study of anatomy of stem in relation to rhizogenesis has relevance in plant species in which adventitious roots arise endopenously from within the stem cutting. The anatomy of stem cuttings of the four Jasminum species was generally similar, with few differences, relating to the thickness of selerenchyma band, width of vascular bundles and the size of the pith. Adventitious roots developed from the wounded tissue only after the stem cuttings were made. Such wound-induced root formation was observed by Carlson (1933) in roses; Smith (1936) in Begonia; Mahlstede and Watson (1952) in Vaccinium corym- bosum, Brutsch et al.. (1977) in Pecan and White and Lovell (1984) in Griselinia sp. Roots in the stem cuttings of jasmine stem cut- tings originated mainly in the cambial zone. This may be because of the ability of the cells of the cambium to divide and become meristematic. These actively dividing cells were recognised by their dense cytoplasm and large, more or less centrally located nuclei. Such adventitious roots originating from the cambial zone were observed by Carlson (1933) in 'Dorothy Perkins' and 'American Pillar' roses; Mahlstede and Watson (1952) in Vaccinium corymbo- sum; Kachecheba (1975) in Hibiscus sp. and White and Lovell (1984) in Griselinia sp. The root initiating cells that proliferated from the cambial zone divided repeatedly and organised into a 117 primordium in - situ i.e., quite close to the cambium. Such behaviour is comparable to the one reported in Griselinia sp. (White and Lovell, 1984). In addition to the cambial zone, the callus tissue of cambial and cortical origin, was also found to initiate and form root primordia in J.sambac and J.auriculatum. This may be because of the congenial microenvironment in specific loci of callus which promoted the root primordial initiation. This is similar to the results obtained by Girouard (1967) in Hedera helix; Cameron and Thomson (1969) in Pinus radiata; Wu and Overcash (1971) in red raspberry hybrid and Brutsch et aJL. (1977) in pecan. Root initiation in these two species of Jasminum is not due to preformation but it must have occured within the callus tissue after the cuttings were detached from the stock plant and as a result they were wound-induced roots. Hence, in J.sambac and J.auricula- tum, callus formation must have preceded root initiation. Although roots may originate within the callus, and callus formation and root initiation often occur simulta- neously through reliance on similar internal and external environmental conditions, nevertheless, they seem to be independent of each other (Hartmann and Kester, 1986). 11^ Following root initiation and root primordium formation, further growth and development of the root promordium occured as a consequence of elongation of the cells, thus resulting in the'development of a root with vascular transition tissues connecting to the vascular bundles of the stem. Growth of the root from the root primordium might have been influenced by the vascular transition tissues connecting the primordium to the vascular bundles of the stem ensuring the translocation of nutrients and hor- mones. Similar observations were recorded by authors studying induced root primordia in several plant species (Stangler, 1956; Kawase and Matsui, 1980). During the development of the root in jasmine stem cuttings some cells in its proximity, both internal and external to the sclerenchyma band showed depletion of their cell con- tents. The metabolites from these cells must have been absorbed by the growing roots leading to the dissolution and mechanical separation of the adjacent tissue system. 11^ similar observations were made by Mahlstede and Watson (1952) in Vaccinium corymbosum. Many structural and histochemical changes associ- ated with callusing and rooting were seen in the stem of the four species of Jasminum. These changes might possi- bly be due to the formation of meristematic cells which showed active cell division leading to the increase in the size of certain zones in the stem. In some species such as J.qrandiflorum and J.sambac, the pith size showed reduction with callusing and root formation. This may be due to the depletion of metabolites from the cells, consequently leading to shrinkage of the pith. t The developed root passed radially through the sclerenchyma band and the cortical tissue which were disorganised by the proliferating callus from the cambi- um, phloem parenchyma, pericyclic parenchyma and the cortex. The root finally emerged out of the stem through the epidermal layer which had breakages probably induced by the pressure of the proliferating callus in the corti- cal zone and the pressure exerted by the growing root. These results agree with the reports of Kachecheba (1975) in Hibiscus sp. and White and Lovell (1984) in Griselinia sp. This accumulation of starch must have allowed for supplementing nutritional requirements of the growing primordia which were present in greater frequency than in the other species. Many authors have reported on such starch accumulation near the base of the roots in stem cuttings (Altman and VVareing, 1975; Eliasson, 1980; Rodriguez et a_l. , 1988) and could indicate another possi- ble role for auxin in the mobilization of sugars from the places where they are synthesised to the rhizogenic region (Davies and Wareing, 1965). In the present study, treated (IBA 4000 ppm) and untreated cuttings of the four Jasminum species were used. Although, the sites of origin of callus and adventitious roots were similar in auxin treated and untreated cuttings, they differed in the amount and proportion of callus formed in different tissues number of roots initiated and the time taken to callus and for root formation. The treated cuttings showed more callusing, had more number of roots and formed callus and roots earlier than the untreated cuttings. These differ- ences between treated and untreated cuttings may be due 12 O " to the fact that auxins which are known to promote root initiation in cuttings generally (Hartmann and Kester, 1986), stimulated cambial activity and promoted callus formation and root initiation in the treated cuttings. These results indicate that auxin is important both for the formation of growth centres and for the subsequent development of root primordia. Similar results on the effect of IBA on callus and root formation were reported by Brutsch et al^. (1977) in pecan and Rodriguez et al. (1988) in Corylus avellana. Of the four species studied J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum were found to be slow in rooting when compared to J.qrandiflorum and J.sambac. This delay in rooting can be attributed to a number of factors. 1. It may be due to the overabundance of basal callus in the stem cuttings of the slow rooting species as in Pinus species (Reines and McAlpine, 1959). The overabundance of basal callus might probably be due to the utilization of the available nutrients and other growth factors (auxins) for callus growth rather than for root initiation and root growth. 2. It is probably due to the lack of formation of root initials, possibly affected by anatomical factor (sclerenchyma fibres) which prevents the receipt of the initial stimulus (auxins from the leaves) for cell divi- sion by the target cells. Nonetheless, some chemical constraint could be involved, in that the fibre ring restrict the movement of an inhibitor out of the region of the target cells (cambial cells). 3. It may be due to the lack of power of the cells cut off from the initially activated cambial cells to divide further (to form root primordia) until several days had elapsed. By this time, the cells must have been displaced outwards and it is possible that material from the damaged cells viz., auxin might have provided the further stimulus necessary for division of the target cells and subsequent primordium organisation (Sheldrake and Northcole, 1968). 4. Alternatively, the delay in response time, could possibly be caused by 'dilution' of the initial stimulus. 5. Four callus formation and root initiation different internal conditions must be necessary, as it is commonly agreed that high auxin concentrations favour callus formation, an effect enhanced by either gibberel- lins or cytokinins. Root initiation proceeded under high auxin concentrations, but is inhibited by gibberellins (Murashige, 1965; Leetham, 1966). The differential rooting behaviour of the two difficult-to-root species must have been due to the presence of auxin, gibberellins and cytokinins in concentrations favouring callus forma- tion, but not root initiation. 6. Poor rooting may be due to the absence of the necessary root promoting co-factors. Root development and 'elongation must be regarded as processes distinct from root initiation requiring different conditions, for these are inhibited by high concentrations (Supra optimal) of either auxins or cytok- inins (Burstrom, 1954). The effect of indolebutyric acid (IBA) at differ- ent concentrations viz., 0, 1000, 2000, 3000 and 4000 ppm on the rooting and survival of cuttings of four Jasminum species viz., J.qrandiflorum, J.sarabac, J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum was studied with an objective to standar- dise the optimum concentration of IBA for maximum rooting in each species in closed medium sachets. Observations on percentage of rooting in cuttings, number of roots per cutting, length of longest primary root, number of sprouts per cutting and the length of longest sprout were recorded at forty five days after planting in both the seasons. Biochemical analysis of the cuttings for total sugars, starch, total carbohydrate, total nitrogen, carbohydrate/nitrogen (C/N) ratio, total phenols was carried out. The mung bean bioassay was carried out for the root promoting co-factors' in tthe fresh samples of the stem cuttings. The salient findings of this study are summarised in this chapter. 1. Root forming capacity of the semi-hard wood cutt- ings varied significantly with the species in both the seasons. J.grandiflorum and J.sambac showed very good rooting, whereas, J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum showed poor rooting at forty five days after planting. 2. Significant improvement in rooting (percentage of rooting, number of roots and length of longest primary root) of cuttings by IBA treatment was noticed over the untreated cuttings. IBA at all concentrations (1000-4000 ppm) was found to improve rooting over the control in both the seasons. 3. In J.grandiflorum, the highest percentage of rooting was observed in cuttings treated with 4000 ppm IBA (91.11% in December, 1990 and 95.56% in June, 1991). IBA at all concentrations increased the number of roots, length of longest primary root, number of sprouts and length of longest sprout in both the seasons. 1?3 4. In J.sambac, the highest percentage of rooting (95.55) was observed in cuttings treated with 2000 ppm IBA in December, 1990. But, in the cuttings planted in June, 1991, IBA at concentra- tions ranging from 2000 ppm - 4000 ppm was found to increase the rooting percentage (97.78%- 100.00%). IBA at all concentrations improved the number of roots, length of longest primary root, number of sprouts, and length of longest sprout in both the seasons. 5. The performance of J.auriculatum and J.calophy- llum with respect to rooting was very poor in both the seasons. However, rooting was slightly better in th(^ second season (0.00-4.44% in J.auriculatum and 2.22-15.56% in J.calophy- llum) than in the first season (0.00-2.22%) in J.auriculatum and 0.00% in J.calophyllum). Sprouting in the cuttings of both the species was enhanced by IBA treatment in both the seasons. 6. Percentage survival of rooted cuttings of J. qrandiflorum and J.sambac was enhanced by pre- treatment of the cuttings prior to planting in the rooting media. 1 0>^ J. -. J 7. Significant differences were obtained in the stem cuttings of the four species with respect to their total sugars, starch, total carbohydrate, total nitrogen, C/N ratio and total phenols in both the seasons (except C/N ratio in the second season, which differed non-significantly among the species). 8. J.sambac showed the presence of all the four rooting co-factors (1, 2, 3 and 4) in both the seasons. J.grandiflorum had co-factors (2, 3 and 4) in both the seasons, but did not have the co-factor 1 which had an inhibitory effect. In J.auriculatum, all the four rooting co-factors were absent in the first season, but showed the presence of co-factors 3 and 4 in small amounts in the second season. J.calophyllum showed the presence of co-factor 3 in the first season and co-factors (1, 2 and 3) in the second with the others being absent. 9. Among the two seasons, June, 1991 was better than December, 1990 with respect to rooting of cuttings in all the four species. 10. An anatomical study was carried out to know the ontogeny and histochemistry of adventitious roots in semi-hard wood stem cuttings of four Jasminum species viz., J.qrandiflorum, J.sambac, J.sambac, J.auriculatum and J.calophyllum and to understand the causes for their differential rooting behaviour. i) A few differences in the anatomy of stem re- lating to the thickness of sclerenchyma band, width of vascular bundles and size of pith were observed in the four species. ii) Callus originated from the cortex, pericyclic parenchyma, phloem parenchyma and cambium in all the four species. Basal callus was more in proportion in J.auriculatum and J.calo- phyllum than in J.grandiflorum and J.sambac. iii) Adventitious root?, originated mainly in the cambial zone in the four species.. However, root primordia were also seen in the callus tissue in J.sambac and J.auriculatum. iv) Many structural and histochemical changes in stem cuttings were associated with callusing and rooting. v) Treated (IBA) cuttings had more callus in all the four species and higher frequency of root V'D primordia in J.grandiflorum and J.sambac than the untreated cuttings. vi) Sclerenchyma band was not found to be a physical barrier to root initiation, growth and emergence in all the species. vii) Of the four species studied, J.grandiflorum and J.sambac were found to root earlier and easily compared to J.auriculatum and J. calophyllum which showed poor and late rooting. Bengaluru November, 2016 (Roopini GA Reddy) “STUDIES ON SEASONAL INCIDENCE OF PESTS ON Jasminum spp. EMPHASIZING ON BUD BORER COMPLEX AND THEIR MANAGEMENT ON Jasminum multiflorum (BURM. f.) ANDREWS” ROOPINI GA REDDY THESIS ABSTRACT Seasonal incidence of pests on Jasminum spp. emphasizing on bud borer complex and their management were undertaken at College of Horticulture, Bengaluru during 2015-16. Among the pest species observed, eriophyid mite was predominant on J. multiflorum and was significantly and positively influenced by maximum temperature followed by bud and shoot worm. Peak incidence of bud worm was noticed during February with negative significant correlation with morning and evening relative humidity. Shoot web worm and thrips had a significant positive correlation with maximum temperature. An unidentified pupal parasitoid (Hymenoptera: Ichneumonidae) on Elasmopalpus jasminophagus, two Hymenopteran larval parasitoids, Dolichogenidea stantoni (Braconidae) and Tetrastichus sp. (Eulophidae) on both, E. jasminophagus and Hendecasis duplifascialis were documented. Among the four jasmine species observed viz., J. multiflorum, J. sambac, J. auriculatum and J. grandiflorum only J. multiflorum and J. sambac were severely infested by H. duplifascialis and E. jasminophagus whereas, J. grandiflorum was completely free from bud borers. Total life cycle of E. jasminophagus on J. multiflorum lasted for 32 to 41 days under laboratory and 31 to 40 days under field conditions with five larval instars. Average fecundity was 50 eggs per female and laid preferably on green bud calices. Among six insecticides and two botanicals evaluated against bud borers of J. multiflorum, chlorantriniliprole 18.5 SC @ 0.2 ml/l, profenophos 50 EC @ 2 ml/l, quinolphos 25 EC @ 2 ml/l, spinosad 45 SC @ 0.2 ml/l and NSKE (5%) recorded lower larval population with higher yield and cost benefit ratio. INTRODUCTION Jasmine is a highly valued commercial flower crop and ornamental plant for home gardens. It belongs to the family Oleaceae of the order Oleales and genus Jasminum, which comprises of about 300 species distributed in the warmer parts of Asia, Africa, Europe and Pacific region. More than 40 species have been identified in India and about 20 species are identified in South India and 10 to 12 species are under cultivation (Bhattacharjee, 1980). Flowers and buds are used for making garlands and for religious offerings, while ‘veni’ is used as hair adornment. The flowers are also used for the production of essential oils and attars. Jasmine essential oil has a sweet and floral aroma. It is regarded as unique, as it blends well with other floral extracts and is highly valued throughout the world for its high grade perfumes. The perfumes are used in soap and cosmetic industries and in flavoring mouth wash liquids. Flowers should preferably be picked at late evening for extraction of essential oil. Jasmine fragrance is said to give a feeling of optimism, confidence and it is helpful against depression, nervous exhaustion and stress related conditions. Different parts of jasmine like leaf, stem, bark, root and seed are also used for curing medical problems. India is the largest exporter of jasmine oil in the world accounting for over 40 per cent of total world export. India earned US $ 329 million through export of essential oil in the year 2008-09. Jasmine oil (US $ 527 per 500 g) stands next only to rose oil (US $ 3432 per 500 g) which commands highest price in the international essential oil market. The leading export markets for Indian jasmine oil are France, accounting for over 36 per cent of total jasmine oil exports from India, followed by UAE, USA, Germany and UK (Anon., 2010). Among the jasmine species, Jasminum grandiflorum (Pichi) is cultivated in more than 60 per cent of the area followed by Jasminum auriculatum (Mullai). Tamil Nadu is the leading producer of jasmine in the country with an annual production of 77,247 tonnes from a cultivated area of 9,360 hectare. Karnataka is the second highest producer of jasmine flowers. During the year 2004, Karnataka has produced 20,244 tonnes of jasmine flower from 3,451 hectare earning 8,265 lakh rupees. The Tigala community in and around Devanahalli and Chickkaballapur are extremely good at growing jasmine flowers. Jasmine species Bailey (1947) and Muthukrishnan and Pappiah (1980) reported that about 90 species of jasmine occur in India. Out of these, only 20 species are under cultivation in South India. Some important species of jasmine are J. auriculatum, J. beesianum (Rosy Jasmine), J. calophyllum, J. dichotomum (Gold Coast Jasmine), J. dispermum, J. faveri, J. caudatum, J. humile, J. bignoniaceum (Yellow jasmine or Italian jasmine), J. multiflorum, J. nitidum, J. officinale, J. parkeri, J. polyanthum, J. primulinum, J. pubigerum, J. revolutum, J. rex (Kings Jasmine), J. sambac, J. grandiflorum, J. smilacifolium, J. stephanense, J. trinerve, J. volubile or J. gracile (Australian or Wax Jasmine) and J. wallichianum of all these four species are commercially cultivated. Jasminum auriculatum Vahl is a shrub with shiny leaves and auricles. Flowers are white, sweet scented, borne in pubescent, compound, many flowered flax cymes. Corolla lobes are elliptical and fruit is black. Flowers are used for production of perfumes. Jasminum grandiflorum L. is commonly called as Spanish Jasmine. It is a woody bush with pinnate leaves bearing three to five leaflets of equal size. It bears large, white flowers with delightful fragrance, borne in lax axillary or terminal cyme. It is extensively used for preparation of garland and decorative bunches. Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton is popularly known as Arabian or Tuscan Jasmine. It is an evergreen twiner having simple cordate to oblong dark green leaves. Flowers are white, fragrant and small with three forked cymes. Essential oil is extracted for perfumery industry. The flowers are used for making garland, bouquet etc. Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews is commonly called as Fussy or Downy or Star Pinwheel Jasmine. It is a strong woody vine bearing simple, opposite leaves. Flowers are sessile, fragrant, large, white and borne in terminal umbels, having six to nine petals. During the production of any crop there will be constraints which may influence the yield. Among the abiotic factors temperature is very important. Jasminum sambac prefers a night temperature above 15°C and day temperature lower than 20°C. In India, jasmine is grown in open field conditions. Hence, for successful cultivation mild winter, warm summer, moderate rainfall and sunny situations are ideal. Among biotic factors pests and diseases are threats for economical returns. Under normal situation, a crop is attacked by number of insects, mites, birds, mammals, nematodes which together form a complicate interacting pest complex. Besides, diseases which are reported to pose threat are leaf blight (Cercospora jasminicola and Alternaria jasmini), rust (Uromyces hobsoni) and wilt (Fusarium solani and Sclerotium rolfsii). More than 20 insect and mite pests are reported to attack jasmine crop and cause considerable damage. Among them bud worm, Hendecasis duplifascialis (Hampson); bud and shoot worm, Elasmopalpus jasminophagus (Hampson) cause heavy damage to flowers which is the economic product (Reddy et al., 1978). Apart from floral parts, foliage is also affected by several pests, among them leaf web-worm, Nausinoe geometralis (Guenee), shoot web worm, Margaronia unionalis, red spider mite, Tetranychus cucurbitae Rahman, jasmine eriophyid mite, Eryophes spp. are major pests. Tingid bug, Corythauma ayyari (Drake), whitefly, Dialeurodes kirkaldyi (Kotinsky), jasmine bug, Antestia cruciata Fabricius, flower thrips, Isoneurothrips orientalis (Bagn.), green plant hopper, Flata ocellata Fabricius, brown plant hopper, Ricania fenestrata Fabricius and blossom midge, Contarinia maculipennis Fabricius are minor pests (David, 1958). Among the different insect pests recorded on jasmine, bud borers are known to pose a serious threat for flower production. Larvae are found inside the bud or in flower cluster feeding on buds. The larvae makes tunnels of silk and excreta within an affected flower cluster, thus affecting the flower opening and flower buds may drop off (David, 1958). Even though bud borers are important pests of jasmine causing considerable economic loss, they are one of the least studied groups. Yield loss due to bud borers was reported as 30 to 70 per cent (Dhandapani et al., 1989) and around 32 per cent (Chandramohan and Manoharan, 1990). There has been no further work to evaluate the injury to the crop by other insect pests or mites. Much of the work on jasmine pests, extent of damage, life cycle and management are confined only to J. sambac and its cultivars. David (1958) did comprehensive work on pests occurring on jasmine in Madras state. Few workers have reported pests occurring on jasmine and their control. However, information is scanty about pests damaging jasmine from eastern dry zone of Karnataka. Above all, there is gradual increase in the area under other jasmine species which are bound to be damaged by different insect pests. In view of the above, the present investigation was undertaken during 2015-16 to study the seasonal incidence of jasmine pests, bud borer complex on jasmine species, biology and management of bud borers with the following objectives: 1) Seasonal incidence of different pests on Jasminum spp. and recording their natural enemies, 2) Studies on bud borer complex of jasmine under eastern dry zone, 3) Studies on biology of major jasmine bud borer in laboratory and field conditions 4) Management of bud borers in Jasminum multiflorum II. An attempt has been made to review the available literature related to jasmine pests. In this chapter, the literature regarding jasmine pests, their seasonal incidence, biology and management is reviewed.
