A new shoot borer, Sycophila sp. its nature of damage, intensity of damage on J. grandiflorum was reported by Eswaramoorthy et al. (1980). Hymenia fascialis Butler damaged leaves of J. pubescens and J. sambac (Yadav and Pareek, 1985). Infestation of bud worm, blossom midge, leaf web worm and mite ranged between 1.50 to 23.20 per cent, 3.60 to 25.20 per cent, 0.00 to 9.80 per cent and 0.00 to 8.90 per cent, respectively in 98 farms in Madurai taluk of Tamil Nadu (Gunasekaran, 1989). Incidence and the extent of damage by bud borers in J. multiforum varied from 9.20 to 43.60 per cent, whereas, it was 7.60 to 15.20 per cent in J. sambac around Bengaluru (Shobitha, 2001). For the first time in Iberian Peninsula, Corythauma ayyari (Heteroptera: Tingidae) was found damaging ornamental plants causing necrosis on the leaves, among which jasmine was most common. Four specimens were collected in Puigmolto (Santpere de ribes, Baracelona, Spain) 45 km southwest of Barcelona city (Marcos and Marta, 2014). Grubs of Holotrichia sp. was first time recorded on jasmine and nerium plants in Agricultural college and Research Institute, Coimbatore. Grubs were noticed 10 to 25 cm deep in soil (Perumal et al., 1971). Tetranychus neocaledonicus Andre reported on jasmine in Chennai caused mottling of leaves leading to yield reduction (David and Kumarswamy, 1975). Gall mites, Calacarus jasmini and Phyllocopters sulnaliae produced galls on leaves of jasmine (Chakrabarti and Mondal, 1979). Dialeurodes kirkaldyi was recorded and collected for first time in USA on Morinda citrifolia. A survey for this species was made by Plant Pest Control Division, US Department of Agriculture by which it was also found on Jasminum spp. (Russel, 1964) Thrips, Isothrips orientalis appear in colonies on jasmine and flowers are often badly damaged giving them a decayed look (Ananthakrishnan, 1969). The pseudococcid, Downey snow line mealy bug, Rastrococcus iceryoides was observed in September 1984 in Bangalore, Karnataka, India, infesting leaves of Jasminum rigidum. Maximum populations of nymphs were found on tertiary branches on third pair leaves from top (Vasundhara et al., 1990). 2.2 Seasonal incidence of jasmine pests 2.2.1 Hendecasis duplifascialis In a survey, bud borer damage of 0.01 to 32.92 per cent was recorded from North Arcot district of Tamil Nadu on jasmine (Chandramohan and Manoharan, 1990). Maximum incidence (11.10%) of H. duplifascialis occurred on J. sambac during June, while it was 0.00 to 1.90 per cent on J. auriculatum and J. grandiflorum. Maximum incidence of H. duplifascialis (37%) occurred in Madurai, south taluk, while in all other taluks, the incidence ranged from 1.50 to 23.20 per cent. Infestation at Valayapatti ranged from zero in February to a maximum of 7.80 per cent during May. A maximum of 111 adults were caught in light traps during April month and in remaining months it ranged from 12 to 96 adults in entire Madurai district and for every one degree increase in minimum temperature, bud borer damage increased by 2.30 per cent but there was no significant correlation between weather factors and monthly mean bud borer incidence (Gunasekaran, 1989). In Raichur taluks maximum flower damage recorded was 19.73 per cent during May (Eklaspur), 17.67 per cent during June (Hosur), 21.60 per cent during May (Katlatkur), 18.54 per cent in May (Yapaldinni) and 15.26 per cent in May (Kadagamadoddi). In Huvinahadagali taluk maximum of 13.48 per cent was recorded in July ranging from 5.60 to 15.70 per cent on J. sambac (Sudhir, 2002). 2.2.2 Margaronia unionalis In Raichur and Huvinahadagali taluks shoot web worm was found to be highest during October. In Raichur taluks maximum number of 12.68 per cent affected shoots per bush was recorded (Eklaspur), 11.90 per cent in Hosur, 8.42 per cent in Katlatkur and 7.28 per cent in Yapaldinni. In Huvinahadagali taluk maximum of 8.46 per cent was recorded during November. Incidence of Margaronia unionalis was recorded higher during September and October months, i,e., monsoon and post monsoon period (Sudhir, 2002). 2.2.3 Elasmopalpus jasminophagus Infestation of bud and shoot worm around IIHR, Hesaragatta, Bengaluru was maximum during January (1.47 larvae per cluster) and minimum during April first fortnight (0.23 larvae per cluster) (Shobitha, 2001). Highest flower cluster infestation (14.21%) was recorded during October in Kadagamadoddi, Raichur. Whereas in Huvinahadagali taluk of Bellary district it ranged from 5.96 to 21.64 per cent with a maximum of 16.67 per cent flower infestation (Sudhir, 2002). 2.2.4 Nausinoe geometrails Caterpillars of Nausinoe geometrails in Agricultural College and Research Institute, Coimbatore attacked mostly lower bushy and shaded portions of plant. Density of population during 1957-58 increased from May onwards and reached peak in July and continued to be heavy up to December and diminished thereafter till it reached the lowest level in April (David and Venugopal, 1962). Maximum incidence of leaf web worm was during November (12.70%) and it remained below ten per cent in other months in Madras south taluk (Gunasekaran, 1989). In Raichur taluk, maximum number of 4.68 webs per bush was recorded during October (Eklaspur), 4.52 during October (Hosur), 6.48 during September (Katlatkur), 5.40 in October (Yapaldinni) and 15.26 per cent in May (Kadagamadoddi). In Huvinahadagali taluk maximum of 1.95 was recorded in September on J. sambac. Very less incidence of Nausinoe geometrails was noticed during May which gradually increased to reach peak level during November and zero during December to April months (Sudhir, 2002). 2.2.5 Contarinia maculipennis Maximum blossom midge incidence observed was 29 per cent with higher incidence (13.80%) during October compared to other months. Incidence was persisting throughout the year in Madurai (Gunasekaran 1989). Blossom midge infestation was found only on J. sambac during April and July, 2002. Maximum of 7.89 per cent incidence was recorded during July and it ranged from 1.63 to 12.18 per cent discoloured flowers in Raichur and Huvinahadagali taluks (Sudhir, 2002). 2.2.6 Tetranychus cinnabarinus Maximum incidence (10.50%) of T. cinnabarinus was observed during December on J. grandiflorum followed by J. sambac and J. auriculatum in Madurai taluk (Gunasekaran, 1989). Hole and Salunkhe (1997) observed mite, T. urticae population in both winter and summer season of 1991-92, which increased gradually from February and reached peak in March (69.65 mites per plant) and declined thereafter. The population fluctuations were found to be positively and significantly correlated with maximum temperature and relative humidity. Red spider mite population was recorded across taluks of Raichur and Huvinahadagali in Raichur and Bellary districts, respectively. Maximum mite population of 13.67 mites per leaf was recorded during June (Eklaspur), 14.53 mites per leaf during August (Hosur), 12.66 mites per leaf during May (Katlatkur), 15.28 mites per leaf during June (Kadagamadoddi) and 12.97 mites per leaf during May (Yapaldinni). In Huvinahadagali taluk it ranged from 8.19 to 16.86 during April. Population of mite appeared during seventh standard week and increased as summer progressed and reached peak during June and July due to absence of rain during 2001-02 in Raichur taluk. Population of mite was less on J. multiflorum compared to other jasmine species (Sudhir, 2002). In a study conducted in Eklaspur village near Agricultural College and Regional Agricultural Research Station, Raichur on J. sambac, maximum incidence was seen in first week of May (9.36 mites/leaf), due to dry weather during May 2002 to April 2003. No population was seen during third week of November, 2002 to last week of January, 2003 as these weeks registered rainfall. Maximum and minimum temperature recorded positive and significant relationship with mite population whereas rainfall showed significant negative relationship (Rajakumar et al., 2005). 2.2.7 Aceria jasmini Presence of eriophyid mite (Aceria jasmini) infesting jasmine was recorded throughout the year in Annigeri (Dharwad). Untreated crop was severely affected during July to August (Mallapur and Kubsad, 2000). Maximum of 75 per cent leaves were affected by A. jasmini from April to October in Madras taluk of Tamil Nadu on jasmine (Letchoumanane and Subramanian, 1981). Eriophyid mite was not recorded on J. sambac, while it affected J. auriculatum (87.25% infestation) seriously compared to J. rigidum (20.08% infestation). Leaves were free from erenial growth during December on both the species (Sudhir, 2002). 2.3 Natural enemies on Insect and Mite pests of Jasmine A braconid parasitoid, Phanerotoma hendecasiella Cam was recorded in India on Hendecasis duplifascialis larvae (Kalsoven, 1950). Phanerotoma sp. caused zero to 8.8 per cent parasitization on Hendecasis duplifascialis larvae in field condition (Chandramohan and Manoharan, 1990). Cantheconidea furcellata (Wolff) a Pentatomid predator was observed in Delhi preying on the larvae of Hendecasis duplifascialis (Prasad et al., 1983). Apanteles sp. was believed to attack the leaf web worm in larval stage. Characteristic feeding and webbings were found arrested and then reduction in the larval population due to predatory activity of spiders and mantids (David and Venugopal, 1962). Goniozus rugosus, a larval parasitoid of Nausinoe geometrails was reported by Samad (1974). A larval parasitoid, Elasmus brevicornis Gahan (Hymenoptera: Elasmidae), a predator Chlaenius hemifer (Coleoptera: Carabidae) and also seven spider spices are also reported (Shukla and Sandhu, 1983). Third and second instar grub of predator preferred first instar larvae by consuming 8.5 larvae per two predators and six larvae per two predators, respectively. Predatory potential was observed maximum to an extent of six numbers when third instar grub was released on seven first instar larvae (Rajabaskar, 2006). 2.4 Bud borer complex on Jasminum spp. The caterpillar of H. duplifascialis feeds on inner most petal of the closed bud of jasmine in initial instars and emerges through a circular hole made usually on the tubular portions of corolla to bore into the nearby bud (Reddy et al., 1978). Purple discolouration of flower buds in J. sambac was due to blossom midge and buds finally dry up and fall prematurely (David, 1958). Bud worm, H. duplifascialis larvae caused the greatest injury to immature buds of J. sambac. Two species of bud borers E. jasminophagus and H. duplifascialis were involved in bud damage on J. multiflorum and J. sambac. E. jasminophagus was most dominant species than H. duplifascialis which was found to occur in very low population levels (Ayyar, 1963). Elasmopalpus jasminophagus, another borer attacking buds and shoot where the larvae lived outside the bud in tunnels of silk and excreta and in rare cases it was found inside the buds in early instars. Larvae grew to an inch in length and developed laterodorsal brown streaks and later turned into completely brown colour before pupation. Pupation occurred in tunnels in leaf folds (David, 1958). Bud borer, H. duplifascialis incidence was maximum on J. sambac followed by J. auriculatum and J. multiflorum in Raichur and Bellary districts from May 2001 to April 2002 while the bud and shoot worm, E. jasminophagus occurred only on J. multiflorum from October to February (Sudhir, 2002). Among the five jasmine species considered, only Jasminum multiflorum and Jasminum sambac were infested by the bud borers. Variation in flower bud and cluster characteristics were observed among different jasmine species. The mean number of buds per cluster and inter cluster distance was high in Jasminum multiflorum compared to other species. Whereas inter bud distance was lower in case of Jasminum multiflorum and Jasminum rigidium. Bud length and weight was higher in Jasminum multiflorum while the bud diameter was greater in Jasminum sambac. There was high positive correlation between bud damage and the number of buds present in a cluster and bud weight hence, Jasminum multiflorum was more prone to damage by bud borers. Larvae of bud borers, E. jasminophagus and H. duplifascialis damaged green buds, white buds and open flowers of Jasminum multiflorum. There was a high positive correlation between the total bud availability and the extent of damage. Early larval instars preferred green buds, while later larval instars preferred white buds and open flowers (Shobitha et al., 2001). 2.5 Biology of Bud and shoot worm Elasmopalpus jasminophagus biology done both in laboratory and field conditions, revealed that during oviposition period of three to four days females laid over 90 eggs. Each of which took three to four days to hatch. Larval duration was 15 to 20 days, prepupal and pupal stages lasted for two to three and six to seven days, respectively. The total life cycle from egg to adult lasted for 26-38 days (Shobitha, 2001). 2.6 Management of Bud borers Among the insecticides evaluated against bud worm, H. duplifascialis and blossom midge, Contarinia maculipennis, quinolphos (0.054%) and monocrotophos (0.05% and 0.1%) gave effective control (Reddy et al., 1978). Soil application of carbofuran 3G at 40 g per bush and foliar application of cypermethrin @ 25 g ai/ha at fortnightly intervals, fenitrothion 0.1 per cent and monocrotophos 0.08 per cent effectively reduced purple discoloration and drying of flower buds in J. sambac caused by blossom midge (David and Natarajan, 1988). Among the insecticides evaluated against bud worm, H. duplifascialis in two field trials at Thimmanapalyam, Pudhur and Kalapatti villages of Coimbatore district, Tamil Nadu, deltamethrin 2.5 EC at 25 g ai per ha gave maximum reduction in damage upto 90.21 per cent followed by cypermethrin 10 EC 150 g ai per ha which reduced damage upto 90.11 per cent and monocrotophos 36 EC 360 g ai per ha reduced damage by 78.28 per cent and it was suggested that alteration of monocrotophos 36 EC 360 g ai per ha with pyrethroids like cypermethrin 10 EC 150 g ai per ha or deltamethrin 2.5 EC at 25 g ai per ha avoids sucking pest resurgence (Dhandapani et al., 1989). Field trials in a J. sambac orchard in North Arcot district, Tamil Nadu, India, showed that endosulfan (0.07%) alone or alternated with fenvalerate (0.015%) was the most cost effective treatment against H. duplifascialis which also had the lowest impact on its parasitoid, Phanerotoma spp. (Chandramohan and Manoharan, 1990). Significantly higher mortality was obtained with NSKE (5%) and Neem cake extract (5%) followed by Neem oil (1%) (Nelson et al., 1993). At Madurai, HCH 2.5 kg ai per ha and phosalone 440 g ai per ha were most effective at seven and 14 days after treatment against H. duplifascialis, respectively. Besides these methyl parathion 320 g ai per ha, endosulfan 440 g ai per ha and dichlorvos 950 g ai per ha were effective at 14 days after treatment, at seven days after treatment nochi leaf extract (5%) and monocrotophos 360 g ai per ha were superior to all other treatments which gave better control of H. duplifascialis (Gunasekaran, 1989). Six homeo products (plant extract) and one neem oil formulation tested for its efficacy on first instar larva of E. jasminophagus in laboratory revealed that after 12 hours of treatment neem oil (1 ml per litre of water) caused 6.60 per cent larval mortality and all other treatment had no effect. At 24 and 36 hours after treatment neem oil (1ml per liter of water) caused maximum of 46.70 and 33.33 per cent larval mortality, respectively (Gunasekaran, 1989). Among eight insecticides evaluated for field control of bud borers, chlorpyriphos (0.005%), endosulfan (0.07%) and methyl parathion (0.05%) recorded lower larval population. Spray of chloropyriphos thrice at an interval of 15 days provided control upto one month and the farmers need to repeat spray schedules at 44 days after third spray (Shobitha, 2001). Efficacy of insecticides against bud borer damage indicated that, indoxacarb 14.5 SC (0.0073 per cent) and spinosad 45 SC (0.023 per cent) gave good protection at 2, 7 and 14 days after spray by reducing damage over control by 71.58 per cent and 69.92 per cent, respectively (Sudhir, 2002). Population of thrips in J. sambac (Mysore mallige) ranged from 2.00 to 5.00 thrips per flower. MATERIAL AND METHODS The present study entitled “Studies on seasonal incidence of pests on Jasminum spp. emphasizing on bud borer complex and their management strategies on J. multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews” was carried out both in field and laboratory conditions at Department of Entomology, College of Horticulture, Bengaluru, Karnataka during the year 2015-16. Details of the materials used and procedures followed during the course of the investigations are presented in this chapter. The weather conditions recorded at the experimental site were obtained from meteorological observatory of AICRP on agro- meteorology, UAS, GKVK, Bengaluru (Appendix I). 3.1 Experimental location Field experiments were carried out on three year old jasmine plots of Floriculture Section, Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre, College of Horticulture campus, GKVK, Bengaluru (Plate 1), which comes under Eastern dry zone of Karnataka. Geographical location of the experimental plot is 13° 05' N latitude and 77° 354' E longitude at an altitude of 924 m above mean sea level. 3.2 Seasonal incidence of different pests on Jasminum multiflorum and recording their natural enemies To study the seasonal incidence of insect pests of jasmine, ten plants of J. multiflorum were selected randomly and tagged. From such tagged plants fortnightly observations were taken from August 2015 to March 2016. The methodology followed to record the incidence of different pests on J. multiflorum is given below: a. Bud worm, Hendecasis duplifascialis and bud and shoot worm, Elasmopalpus jasminophagus Four shoots in four directions and one central shoot were selected in each bush and five flower clusters per branch was considered for observation. Totally 25 flower clusters per plant were taken for recording observations. In every flower cluster, number of larvae present, total buds and damaged buds were recorded (Plate 2). The extent of damage was expressed in percentage. b. Shoot web worm, Margaronia unionalis The number of shoots damaged per plant was counted among the tagged plants by randomly selecting five shoots each in ten tagged plants (Plate 2). c. Eriophyid mite, Aceria jasmini Eriophyid mite infested leaves show felt like growth on leaves known as erenium. A total of five shoots per plant were selected in which total number of leaves in top ten centimeters of shoot and leaves showing erenial growth (Plate 2) were counted and expressed in percentage. d. Flower thrips, Isoneurothrips orientalis Five flower clusters per plant were selected in each plant randomly and number of thrips was counted. Flower cluster selected was tapped on a white paper so that the thrips drop on to the paper. Using magnifying lens the thrips were counted (Plate 2). 3.2.1 Natural enemies Larval stages of insect pests were collected and brought to laboratory while studying seasonal incidence at fortnightly intervals and kept in a cage by providing the food. Emerged parasitoids were collected, mounted and were identified by Dr. Ankitha Gupta, Scientist, National Bureau of Agriculturally Important Insect Resources, Bengaluru. 3.3 Bud borer complex on Jasminum spp. This study was carried out to know the incidence of different bud borers infesting different species of jasmine in Bengaluru under unsprayed field conditions. Five plants each of four species of jasmine viz., J. multiflorum, J. sambac, J. auriculatum and J. grandiflorum were selected randomly and tagged from which five branches were considered for observations. Five flower clusters were observed for bud borer incidence. Stages of pests available at fortnightly intervals viz., adults, eggs, larvae or pupae was collected from the field and reared to adulthood. The adults were mounted and were identified by Dr. C. A. Viraktamath, Principal Investigator, Network project on Insect Biosystematics, Department of Entomology, GKVK, Bengaluru. 3.3.1 Species of jasmine Four species of jasmine selected for observation of bud borer complex were Kakada (Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews), Gundu mallige (Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton), Malle mallige/Bellary mallige (Jasminum auriculatum Vahl) and Jaaji mallige (Jasminum grandiflorum L.) (Plate 3) which were planted during 2012 kharif. 3.3.2 Bud borers The damage of two species of bud borers, Hendecasis duplifascialis (Hampson) and Elasmopalpus jasminophagus (Hampson) was observed. The characteristic damage of each species was identified and their damage extent was recorded separately. 3.3.3 Nature of damage Nature of damage caused by two bud borers, location of feeding within bud, presence or absence of webbing and damage to different parts of the bud were the characteristic observations documented to differentiate the borer species. Observations were made from August 2015 to March 2016. 3.4 Biology of jasmine bud and shoot worm Study on the biology of E. jasminophagus was carried out both in the field and laboratory conditions from October 2015 to January 2016. 3.4.1 Biology studies under laboratory condition Under laboratory conditions 140 larvae were collected from field and were reared till they pupated. From these pupae, hundred healthy pupae were selected in which male and female pupae were separated (Plate 4) and kept in different containers for adult emergence. Freshly emerged adults were allowed into insect cages of dimension 0.30 m × 0.30 m × 0.30 m in 1:1 ratio for mating and oviposition provided with fresh shoots of J. multiflorum. Cut ends of the shoots were enveloped with cotton and were pierced into wet foam. The old shoots were replaced with fresh shoots when they showed wilting symptom. Cotton soaked with 10 percent honey solution was kept in insect cages to serve as adult food (Plate 5). Eggs laid were transferred to petriplates lined with wet blotting paper at the bottom for recording incubation period. The hatched larvae were kept in the mesh box with fresh flower clusters as food and observed for the duration of different instars and variations exhibited during each instar (Plate 6). Durations of pre-pupa and pupa were recorded. After adult emergence, the durations of mating, pre-oviposition, oviposition and post oviposition periods and the adult longevity with and without food (10% honey solution) were observed. 3.4.2 Biology under field condition Under field conditions, five plants were randomly selected and on each plant healthy shoots were selected which were covered with nylon mesh sleeves (Plate 11). Pair of freshly emerged adults was allowed into each mesh sleeves. Experiment was laid out in randomized block design (Plate 7) with six insecticides and two botanicals (Table 2) replicated three times and with one untreated control. Each replication contained eight plants in each treatment and among these, five plants were selected for observation. Three sprays were given at an interval of fifteen days using gutter sprayer and solid cone nozzle. Initial larval count was recorded one day before spraying. First spray was initiated on 15th December, 2015 and following two sprays at fifteen days interval till 15th January, 2016. Larval population count was taken on 5th, 10th and 14th day after each spray in five randomly selected flower clusters in five plants. Flowers were harvested from three selected plants from each replication thrice after every spray. Preparation of botanical solutions Neem seed kernel extract was prepared using 500 g of neem seed kernels which were gently pounded and powdered well followed by overnight soaking in water. In the morning the solution was stirred using wooden plank till it appeared milky white. It was filtered through double layer of muslin cloth, mixed with detergent (0.02%) and the volume was made up to 10 liter for spraying. Vitex negundo leaf extract was done by collecting 500g of Vitex negundo fresh leaves from field. Leaves were crushed and made into paste along with water using mixer grinder and kept overnight. In the morning the paste was stirred well and filtered using single layer of muslin cloth and volume was made up to 10 liter for spraying. 3.6 Cost benefit analysis of management of bud borers in J. multiflorum Cost benefit ratio of various chemicals and botanicals imposed for the management of jasmine bud borers was worked out based on the cost of insecticides used, labour cost and yield obtained (Appendix III). 3.7 Statistical analysis Results obtained from the studies on seasonal incidence of insect and mite pests of jasmine were correlated and regressed with various weather parameters. Weather conditions recorded at the experimental site were obtained from meteorological observatory of AICRP on agro- meteorology, UAS, GKVK, Bengaluru (Appendix I). Statistical analysis of the results obtained from management trails was done using analysis of variance (ANOVA) using Web Agri Stat Package (WASP). Data were transformed with square root method (√x+0.5) before subjecting to ANOVA. IV. It was only 0.48 and 0.13 larvae per 25 clusters per plant on J. sambac (Plate 9) and J. auriculatum, (Plate 9), respectively and E. jasminophagus could not be recorded infesting J. grandiflorum. In J. multiflorum the maximum number of 17.60 larvae of E. jasminophagus per 25 clusters per plant was observed during the month of second fortnight of January, 2016 and minimum of 5.60 and 5.80 larvae per 25 clusters per plant, respectively during first and second fortnight of August and first fortnight of December, respectively (Table 10). In J. sambac, it ranged between a maximum of 1.20 larvae per 25 clusters per plant during second fortnight of August (Table 10). Whenever the pest was recorded on J. auriculatum, a maximum of 0.2 larvae per 25 clusters per plant was observed and it was nil during September, November and January months (Table 10). Elasmopalpus jasminophagus infestation was not recorded on J. grandiflorum throughout the study period (Table 10). 4.2.2 Hendecasis duplifascialis Hendecasis duplifascialis relatively preferred J. sambac (2.28 larvae per 25 clusters per plant) (Plate 10) followed by J. multiflorum (1.18 larvae per 25 clusters per plant) (Plate 10) and J. auriculatum (0.15 larvae per 25 clusters per plant) (Plate 10), while no infestation was seen on J. grandiflorum. In J. multiflorum, the maximum number of 5.00 larvae per 25 clusters per plant was observed during second fortnight of February, 2016. It was nil during August, October and January months (Table 10). First and second instar larvae of E. jasminophagus preferred green buds. It made a pin hole at the base of bud stalk or on the bud through which it entered in and fed on the inner content of the bud. Second, third and fourth instar larvae mostly preferred white bud followed by open flowers and fed on the inner petals. Last instar larvae damaged the whole cluster by silken webbing, making a thick gallery of excreta. Fecal pellets were dry and relatively larger in size. Flower cluster adjacent to the infested cluster were also webbed as a consequence, the cluster turned brown and dried up completely. Larvae of H. duplifascialis preferred buds same as that of E. jasminophagus but, the larvae remained inside the bud feeding on the inner content of buds. It webbed individual flower with fecal pellets and relatively less dense silken webbings than of E. jasminophagus. The fecal pellets of H. duplifascialis were smaller in size and wet in the webbings. 4.3 Biology of E. jasminophagus Studies on biology of the major bud borer species, E. jasminophagus on Jasminum multiflorum under both ambient laboratory and field conditions at COH, Bengaluru are presented here under. 4.3.1 Biology under laboratory condition Female moth laid eggs on calyx of buds, near the base of green bud stalk and on bud. Freshly laid eggs were creamish white coloured, round which gradually turned yellow with age (Plate 13). Incubation period ranged between three to four days with a mean of 3.50 days (Table 11). There were five larval instars with a total duration of 17.40 days (Table.11). Neonate larva was pale green with a light brown head (Plate 13) and the duration of the first instar larvae ranged between 2.60 to 3.60 days with a mean of 3.10 days. Second instar larvae were light green with dark brown head having two black spots on prothoracic segment (Plate 13) and the duration ranged between 1.80 to 3.00 days with a mean of 2.40 days. Third instar larvae were dark green with a dark brown head. Prothoracic segment was black in colour (Plate 13). Duration of the third instar larvae ranged between 3.40 to 4.40 days with a mean of 3.90 days. Fourth instar larvae were dark green with a dark brown head. At this stage brown bands were seen on dorsolateral side of the body, running from thorax to last abdominal segment (Plate 13). Duration of fourth instar larvae ranged from 3.20 to 4.20 days with a mean of 3.70 days. Fifth instar larvae were dark green with distinct brown dorsolateral bands. At the end of the larval instar, larvae turned reddish brown (Plate 13). Duration of fifth instar larvae ranged from 3.80 to 4.80 days with a mean of 4.30 days. The first and second instar larvae bored into buds and fed inside bud by leaving excretory pellets. Third, fourth and fifth instars webbed the buds in a cluster and fed on them and the larvae remained inside the excretory galleries. Before pupation, larvae stopped feeding and encased themselves in a silken cocoon and moulted inside the pupal case (Plate 13). Duration of pre-pupa ranged between 2.3 to 3.3 days with a mean of 2.83 days (Table 11). Pupae were obtect type and pupation took place in flower cluster in between buds and with leaves adjacent to flower clusters (Plate 12). Initially pupae were dark green and later turned brown. Duration ranged between 6.83 to 8.33 days with a mean of 7.58 days (Table 11). Adult moths were grey in colour with grey forewing having black wavy lines and pale hind wings (Plate 13). Adult longevity when supplemented with food (10% honey solution) ranged from 5.16 to 6.83 days with a mean of 6.00 days in female and 4.00 to 4.83 days with a mean of 4.41 days in male (Table 11). Adult longevity without food ranged from 3.60 to 4.50 days with a mean of 4.05 days in female and 2.50 to 3.00 days with a mean of 2.75 days in male. Pre-ovipositional period ranged from 2.20 to 3.00 days with a mean of 2.60 days. Ovipositional duration lasted for 2.03 to 2.36 hours with a mean of 2.19 hours. Post-ovipositional period ranged from 2.60 to 3.40 days with a mean of 3.00 days. Female laid eggs singly or in groups of two to three on calyx of flower bud, at the base of the bud stalk and on the bud. On an average, a female laid 51 eggs during her life time. 4.3.2 Biology under field condition Larval characters remained same as that observed in laboratory studies except slight variations in durations. Incubation period ranged between three to four days with a mean of 3.50 days. Duration of I instar larvae ranged from 2.30 to 3.00 days with a mean of 2.65 days, II instar ranged from 2.00 to 3.60 days with a mean of 2.80 days, III instar ranged from 3.00 to 3.90 days with a mean of 3.45 days, IV instar from 3.00 to 4.00 days with mean of 3.50 days and duration of V instar ranged from 4.40 to 5.40 days with a mean of 4.90 days (Table 12). Noticeably population was high during winter periods i.e., maximum of 42.90 and 41.90 larvae per 25 clusters per plant during first and second fortnights of January 2016. It was observed that the bud damage and incidence of E. jasminophagus was dependant on the bud availability. Similar studies were done by Shobitha (2001) from IIHR, Bengaluru and Gunasekaran (1989) from Coimbatore that, occurrence of E. jasminophagus was seen throughout the year and mostly preferred J. multiflorum over other species of jasmine. Correlation and regression analysis with weather factors prevailing a fortnight prior to pest record revealed that, all the weather parameters showed non-significant relationship with the bud and shoot borer incidence. Similar observations were made by Gunasekaran (1989) that there was no significant correlation between weather factors and monthly mean pest incidence in Coimbatore. There was a negative correlation between the incidence of H. duplifascialis and E. jasminophagus on J. multiflorum (Fig. 3) which was also reported by Shobitha (2001) from IIHR. Extent of bud damage by these bud borers ranged from minimum of 16.96 per cent during second fortnights of February and August and maximum of 41.38 per cent during second fortnight of November. Whereas, the highest number of bud borers was recorded during first and second fortnight of January. Reason for this non synchronization of highest pest incidence and maximum bud damage might be that the number of larvae would be more when the resource is still available and the damage is yet to be done and at maximum bud damage the adult moth prefer not to lay eggs due to less availability of food for larvae. Another reason might be that at higher number of larvae per flower cluster, the larvae present are of initial instars and hence the damage done is less. More damage is done by fourth and fifth instar larvae. At this point the number of larvae per cluster will be less as later instars need more food and space and so they prefer to disperse among the flower cluster in the plant. 5.1.3 Shoot web worm Shoot web worm causes damage to growing shoots and feed on individual leaf by rolling it with silken threads by remaining inside the leaf web. Data obtained from present investigation revealed that maximum incidence of M. unionalis (7.20 mean terminal webbings per plant) was seen first fortnight of October (Fig. 5). A survey by Sudhir (2002) in Raichur and Bellary districts and report of Janarthanan and Abu Bucker (1968) from Coimbatore relate to the present findings that a large number of larvae and pupae were available in the field during September and October months than in other months but these findings were done on J. sambac. Correlation studies clearly indicated a fairly strong and positive association of M. unionalis with rainfall (Fig. 10). The negative non-significant association observed with maximum temperature is in conformity with Sudhir (2002) in Raichur and Bellary districts during 2001-02. 5.1.4 Eriophyid mite Eriophyid mite, A. jasmini was recorded throughout the study period and the most dominant pest species infesting J. multiflorum at COH, Bengaluru during 2015-16 with a mean damage of 25.48 per cent (Fig. 6) with maximum damage during first fortnight of March 2016 and minimum during first fortnight of December 2015. Damage extent was highest during March and was found minimum during winter months. Among weather parameters, positive significant relationship was seen with maximum temperature and negative significant with morning relative humidity. Rainfall showed non- significant negative relationship (Fig. 11). The above results are in close agreement with the reports of Mallapur and Kubsad (2000) from Dharwad, Letchoumanane and Subramanian (1981) from Tamil Nadu and Sudhir (2002) from Raichur and Bellary district that the infestation was low during winter months and was seen increasing towards summer months. Whereas, David (1958) reported eriophyid mite infestation on J. sambac. 5.1.5 Flower thrips Incidence of thrips was almost similar in August, September and October months with maximum of 8.30 thrips per five flowers cluster per plant during second fortnight of February. Population reduced during winter months. Maximum temperature was found significant and positively related with pest incidence and evening relative humidity was negative and significantly related (Fig. 12). Studies on jasmine thrips is limited to mere documentation of pest record and the current study documents the seasonal incidence pattern on J. multiflorum. 5.1.6 Natural enemies Parasitoids belonging to families Ichneumonidae, Braconidae and Eulophidae were recorded during the study. Unidentified Ichneumonid parasitized pupae of E. jasminophagus, which was also documented by Sudhir (2002) from Raichur and Bellary districts and Shobitha (2001) from IIHR, Bengaluru. Dolichogenidea stantoni forms a new record of parasitoid in jasmine ecosystem on first and second instar larvae of both H. duplifascialis and E. jasminophagus in the present study. Record of Tetrastichus sp. parasitizing larvae of both E. jasminophagus and H. duplifascialis is a new record even though it is not new to jasmine ecosystem. It was reported to parasitize the larvae of blossom midge in Raichur and Bellary districts of Karnataka (Sudhir, 2002) and in Tamil Nadu (David et al., 1990). 5.2 Bud borer complex among jasmine species Studies on bud borer complex of jasmine species revealed that two species viz., E. jasminophagus and H. duplifascialis were the major species of bud borers infesting J. multiflorum and J. sambac at College of Horticulture, Bengaluru during August 2015 to March 2016. These two species of bud borers were also reported as the major jasmine bud worms in Coimbatore by David (1958) and Gunasekaran (1989). These two species can be easily identified in field based on size and colouration of larvae. David (1958) has given a brief record of larval characteristics for easy identification in field. Though, these two species of bud borers were found infesting, simultaneously, E. jasminophagus was the most dominant species at College of Horticulture, Bengaluru during 2015-16 (Table 10). Observations made in laboratory indicated that adult females are much active than males with maximum survival period of six days in females and four days in males which is common to insects in general and Lepidoptera in specific. During their life span a female laid 51 eggs on an average, with incubation period of three to four days. Larval period lasted for 15 days to 20 days (Fig.17), whereas prepupal and pupal period was about two to three days and six to eight days, respectively. Total life cycle of the E. jasminophagus from egg to adult lasted for 32 to 41 days (Fig.18). Availability of green buds lasts for a longer time than compared to white buds and open flowers and this might be the reason for more damage on green buds. There may be a strategy by female E. jasminophagus for egg laying and resource allocation for neonate larvae to overcome the discomfort/toxicity by essential oils which can develop by feeding on green buds which contain lesser amount of essential oils and remain on same bud till they moult in next instar. This also provides an opportunity to explore the essential oils of jasmine in developing insecticides. 5.4 Management strategies against bud borers in J. multiflorum Out of the eight insecticides evaluated for control of bud borers in field, chlorantriniliprole 18.5 SC @ 0.2 ml/l, profenophos 50 EC @ 2 ml/l, quinolphos 25 EC @ 2 ml/l, spinosad 45 SC @ 0.2 ml/l and NSKE @ 5 per cent spraying thrice at an interval of fifteen days recorded lower larval population of bud borers in J. multiflorum. Recovery of larval population after fifteen to thirty days indicated that chemical control does not provide complete control of the pest owing to new growth (Table 13). Chandromohan and Manoharan (1990) reported that endosulfan at 0.07 per cent alone or alternated with fenvalerate at 0.015 per cent was the most cost effective treatment against Hendecasis duplifascialis. Reddy et al. (1978) reported quinolphos at 0.054 per cent and monocrotophos at 0.05 and 0.1 per cent was effective and Gunasekaran (1989) recorded better control when monocrotophos and fenvalerate were used. Shobitha (2001) reported that chlorpyriphos at 0.05 per cent, endosulfan at 0.07 per cent and methyl parathion at 0.05 per cent recorded lower population when sprayed three times at fifteen days interval. Sudhir (2002) reported that effective control of bud borers was obtained by spraying indoxacarb 14.5 SC at 0.0073 per cent and spinosad 45 SC at 0.023 per cent. Next best chemicals were lambda cyhalothrin 2.5 EC at 0.0013 per cent and profenophos 50 EC at 0.05 per cent. Economics of borer complex management varied from 1:0.7 to 1:5.3 (Table 14) which is dependent on the cost of plant protection chemical and yield. In the present study, there was an increase in yield, ranging from 3.34 t (Malathion 50 EC @ 3 ml) to 6.947 tonnes (chlorantriniliprole 18.5 SC @ 0.2 ml). Though, chlorantriniliprole was found effective in increasing the yield, the C: B ratio was only 1:1.2 as cost of the chemical was very high (Appendix III/Table 14). Under non chemical greener options NSKE emerged as a best option for the management of jasmine bud borers which had recorded higher yields as well as an appreciable cost benefit ratio. The negative C: B ratio in V. negundo might be due to increased damage by larvae under the influence of repellent or anti-feedant activity. It might be also due to reduced natural enemies which need to be overlooked. Efforts are needed to explore the natural and augmentative biocontrol in jasmine ecosystem besides the large scale evaluation of neem seed kernel extract and other plant origin insecticides and plant oils. As the pesticide effects are not disappearing after a fortnight’s interval, efforts are needed to evolve a suitable schedule for jasmine which can offer the best protection against bud borer complex as well as other pests of jasmine. Future line of work: 1. Exploring the diversity of natural enemies in jasmine ecosystem and their utilization through conservation and augmentation. 2. Identification and characterization of pesticidal properties of essential oils from Jasminum spp. 3. Development of ecofriendly and economical pest management schedule with botanicals and safer insecticides. VI. SUMMARY Investigation on various aspects viz., Seasonal incidence of different pests on Jasminum spp. and documentation of their natural enemies, bud borer complex of Jasmine under eastern dry zone (Bengaluru), biology of major jasmine bud borer in laboratory and field conditions and eco-friendly management of bud borers in Jasminum multiflorum undertaken at Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre and Department of Entomology, College of Horticulture, Bengaluru, Karnataka during the year 2015-16 and the results of the investigation are summarized here. INTRODUCTION Jasmine is one of the oldest of fragrant flowers and is specially appreciated in India, where most people have a love for the fragrant flowers. The word Jasmine has been derived from Persian word. ‘Yasmyn’ meaning fragrance since time immemorial, it is considered as a spiritual flower of India. The scent emitted by jasmine is so well liked that the word jasmine has become a synonym for fragrance and we have climber such as Solanum jasminoides, Trachelospermum jasminoides and Pandorea jasminoides (Tecoma jasminoides), which are totally unrelated to jasmine, except for their sweet fragrance. For the past many centuries jasmines have adorned the gardens of Central Asia, Afghanistan, Iran, Nepal and many other tropical and sub-tropical countries and many of the jasmine species are native of India and have their origin in the Southern Foothills of the Himalayas. The jasmine belongs to family ‘Oleaceae’ and the Genus Jasminum comprises of about 300 species, which are dispersed in the warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific region (Bhattacharjee, 1980). More than 40 species have been identified in India and in South India about 20 species are in cultivation (Watt, 1890, Krishnamurthy and Raman, 1948). In India, jasmines are commercially cultivated in the states of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and West Bengal. Although, correct statistics of the area and production are not available, it is estimated that in India, jasmines occupy an area of 8000 ha with an annual production of flower worth Rs. 80 to 100 million. In India, Tamil Nadu has the largest area under jasmine cultivation followed by Karnataka, which together account for 98 per cent of the total cultivated area. In Karnataka, they occupy an area of more than 3978 ha with an estimated production of nearly 26253 tonnes of fresh flowers, and ranks first among the commercial flowers crops of the state followed by chrysanthemum and marigold (Anon., 2004). A market survey of the commercial flowers sold in the big cities around Malaprabha and Ghataprabha irrigation project areas, namely Hubli, Dharwad, Gadag, Bijapur and Jamakhandi was done in 1975 by the Department of Horticulture, Agriculture College, Dharwad and noted that jasmine ranks first among the commercial flowers sold. With 43.4 tonnes of fresh jasmine flowers sold annually in these cities. It is also reported that this area is suitable for commercial cultivation of Jasmine (Anon., 1975). Of the different species and varieties the commercially important ones are J. sambac Ait. (Gundumallige), J. grandiflorum L. (Jajimallige), J. auriculatum Vabl. (Sooji mallige) and J. multiflorum Andr. (Kakada). In Karnataka, J. auriculatum are extensively grow for fresh flower production and are very popular due to their pleasant fragrance and superior quality. In India, the fresh flowers of jasmine are highly valued and are used for making garlands, bouquets, venis for decorating hair of woman and for religious and marriage ceremonies. The flowers of J. auriculatum are also used for production of perfumed hair oils and attars. India exports fresh jasmine flowers to the neighbouring countries like Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia and of late to the Gulf countries. Recently, jasmine cultivation has received a fillip through research findings which indicated the potentiality of South Indian Jasmine. But one of the serious limiting factors which affects both jasmine flower growers and the consumers and which is likely to affect commercial production, is that the flowering of all the Jasminum species is seasonal. There are peak and lean productive seasons with consequent gluts and scarcity which affect the price trends greatly. Developments after the discovery of growth regulators and their application in agriculture and more specially in horticulture are significant. Regulation of plant growth and development using natural plant hormones for greater production have received the utmost attention (Leetham et al., 1978). Growth and flowering responses of ornamental plant to these chemical substances have been intensively studied with a view to have compact plants with greater number of flowers and also to hasten or delay flowering according to the needs of the grower (Cathey, 1980). Regulation of flowering in jasmine has immense practical value. Timing of the peak flowering to coincide with the time of greatest demand and generally modifying the flowers sequence to avoid peak production at about the same time would confer great advantage to the grower and consumers. It is in this respect that the possibility of using plant growth regulators for regulation assumes significance. Keeping this in view, the present investigation was therefore taken up with the following objectives. 1. To know the effect of growth promoters (GA3 and NAA) on growth and yield of Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. 2. To know the effects of growth retardents (cycocel and ethrel) on growth and yield of Jasminum auriculatum Val. II. REVIEW OF LITERATURE Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. var. Parimullai is commercially cultivated for its keeping quality, fragrance and also for the preparation of perfume. Retardation of vegetative growth, hastening of flowering and increase in flower yield are important in a crop like jasmine, when apical dominance is playing a role. For the past few years, interest in Soojimallige (J. auriculatum Vahl.) cultivation has received a fillip through research findings which indicated the potentialities of South Indian Jasmine. Plants produce a number of growth hormones which co-ordinate and control various phases of plant growth and development. These hormones are defined as organic compounds, other than nutrients, produced by plants in minute quantities, which in low concentration regulate namely promote, inhibit or otherwise modify different phases of plant growth and development. Besides these endogenous plant hormones, a number of synthetic chemical components are also know to regulate and modify growth in a similar manner. Plant physiologists have recognized five well defined groups of plant growth substances. These are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, inhibitors (ABA) and senescent hormone ethylene. The use of plant growth regulators had led to intensive scientific activity for their commercial exploitation. Since, 1949 many beneficial effects of different plant growth regulators have been reported on different horticultural crops and other field crops. Growth regulators were first identified in the early 1930’s as significant tools in increasing crop production. The growth and flowering of many flower crops and bedding plants were successfully controlled by growth regulators to produce high quality horticultural products. In addition an increase in yields of commercial flower crops and vegetables by growth regulators sprays were reported. Desirable responses including retardation of vegetative growth, hastening of flowering sequence and increase in flower yield of commercial crops. These responses followed the application of these growth regulators as foliar sprays or dips. Such application caused a drastic initial reaction, as opposed to the gradual uptake by the roots. Use of growth regulators in jasmine has received its attention only in the recent past and as such on its information available is very mearge. Hence, such information in respect of other flower crops and ornamental plants have been included in the review. The review is presented under different growth regulators tried on morphological characters, flowering and yield. 2.1 EFFECT OF PLANT GROWTH PROMOTERS ON GROWTH AND YIELD OF J. auriculatum Vahl. 2.1.1 NAA (Alpha-naphthalene acetic acid) NAA is a synthetic auxin most widely used as a practical growth regulator. It is mainly used in rooting of stem cuttings in Horticultural crops, inhibition of flower drop, bud bole shedding, button shedding and inhibit sprouting and development of suckers. 2.1.2 Effect on morphological characters Pal et al. (1980) reported that NAA slightly promoted the shoot length in Jasminum sambac var. Khoya. In J. auriculatum, NAA appreciably reduced the plant growth. As far as branching was concerned in J. sambac the number of branches were increased due to NAA applications. In chrysanthemum, the plant height was not affected by NAA application (Tsukomoto et al., 1968). Bhattacharjee and Mukherjee (1979) reported that NAA inhibited plant growth in tuberose and resulted in marked reduction in the emergence of new shoot. Spraying of PP333 (Paclobutrazol), NAA based on formulation resulted in dwarfing of plants in cultivars of ageratum, Antirrhinum, Begonia, Celosia, Chrysanthemum, Cinerjias, Cloeus, Euphorbia, Fuchsia, Gompherna, Vinca and Zebrina but Lilium longiflorum was not affected (Shanks, 1981). Scott (1982) reported that hydrangea sprayed with PP333 resulted in reduction in shoot length. NAA reduced plant height in china aster (Reddy et al., 1983) and vegetative growths were reduced with increasing concentrations and caused leaf epinasty (Furutani et al., 1985). Number of laterals and number of leaves were increased by the foliar application of CCC (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977). Similar results were reported in J. acriculatu by spraying CCC (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1978) and in J. multiflorum Cycocel greatly increased the lateral shoots (Murali and Narayan Gowda, 1988). In African marigold, the greatest growth retardation was observed in plants treated with Cycocel 500 ppm (Vijayakumar et al., 1976). Reduction in height of the plants with thick stems and closely spaced leaves with dark green colour due to CCC application has been reported by many workers in various ornamental plants like chrysanthemum (Lemper, 1964). Carnation (Semeniuk and Taylor, 1970 and Cathey, 1960), rhododendrons and marigold (Reed et al., 1974 and Kozel et al., 1970). Suppressed plant height with stout stem were noted by Shanmugam and Muthuswamy (1973) in chrysanthemum and in china aster (Narayana Gowda, 1985). Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1974) reported that CCC had only slight growth retarding effect on dahlia. Plant height was decreased in hybrid tea roses, treated with CCC at 2500-10000 ppm (Maharana and Pani, 1982). Aswath et al. (1994) reported that application of CCC at the rate of 1500 ppm resulted in the reduction of plant height, branch length and internodal length, higher number of leaves in china aster. Chakradhar and Khirathkar (2003) reported that application of CCC (900 ppm) reduced minimum plant height and maximum shoot diameter in chrysanthemum. Bhattacharjee (1994) reported that maximum retardation of height was observed with the spray of 1000 ppm of CCC to J. auriculatum, J. arburescebs and J. calophyllum which were 11, 19, 10, 51, 21 and 64 per cent respectively over control. (2003) reported that increased number of secondary shoots per plant (64.45 nos), leaves (30.85 nos) and leaf area per shoot (1680.75 cm2), number of inter nodes per shoot (15.4 nos) were produced with application of CCC @ 500 ppm in Jasminum sambac. Plant height was greatly reduced in oleander, jasmine, hibiscus and bougainvillea plants when treated with CCC (Poole, 1970). In marigold, Parmar and Singh (1983) reported that, spraying of CCC at 750 ppm gave maximum flower yield and at 1000 ppm delayed flowering apart from reduction in plant height. 2.2.2 Effect on flowering and yield Cycocel caused significant increase in the flowering of Zinnia and Helianthus (Sen and Sen, 1968a), early flowering and more number of flowers in ‘Red Rocket’ Snapdragon and ‘Brownie Scot’ marigold (Reed et al., 1974) and in chrysanthemum and china aster delay in flowering (Sen and Maharana, 1972 and Narayan Gowda, 1985a). Gibberellins are the most widely used and proven growth substances in horticulture. These are group of diterpenoid acid, that function as plant growth regulators influencing a range of developmental processing in stem elongation, germination, breaking of dormancy flowering, sex expression, enzyme induction and leaf and fruit senescence. Gibberellin are characterized by gibbane skeleton and based on the substitution of gibbane skeleton more than 100 gibberellins are available at present. The most commonly used one is GA3. Kohl and Kofranek (1957) were among the first to investigate the possible use of GA3 in floriculture crops. Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1978) reported that GA3 at 50 and 75 ppm registered the highest shoot length (67.2 and 85.6 cm) and they also observed the increase in the secondary shoot length and markedly increased in the internodal length in Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. 2.3.1 Effect of GA3 on other species of Jasminum 2.3.1.1 Effect on morphological characters Bhatacharjee (1983a) reported that application of GA3 increased shoot length in Jasminum grandiflorum L. elongation of internodal length and enhancement of shoot growth have been reported in Jasminum multiflorum Andr. (Murali, 1984). Nagegowda (1988) reported that application of GA3 resulted in elongation of internodal length and enhancement of shoot growth in Jasminum sambac Ait. 2.3.2 Effect of GA3 on other flower crops 2.3.2.1 Effect on morphological characters Marth et al. (1956) reported stem elongation in various ornamentals like Salvia, Pionsettia, dahlia, Petunia etc. Application of GA3 promoted the stem elongation and longer internodes having very thin thread like stem but at maturity with greater diameter. Winter annuals treated with GA3 increased in height (Singh, 1966). Mittal (1967) reported that foliar spray of gibberellic acid at 300 ppm twice before flowering significantly increased plant height, secondary and lower branches in dahlia. In China aster, gibberelic acid application of 100 ppm increased plant height, number of branches and plant spread (Reddy, 1978). Jayanthi and Gowda (1990) obtained similar results by sprays of GA3 at 100 to 500 ppm in the same crop. Sayad and Muthuswamy (1974) reported that application of GA3 on crossandra resulted in increased plant height and hyper elongation of stem and internodes in Zinnia and Helianthus (Sen and Sen, 1968a). Masterlerz (1965) observed increased stem length in roses, Laiche and Box (1973) reported reduction of height in lillies by GA3 sprays. GA3 resulted in maximum height and reduced branching in chrysanthemum (Ravindra, 1980). Gibberellic acid (150 ppm) at 6-8 leaf stage increased plant height in (Jana and Biswas, 1982). Jan and Jahangir (1987) studied the effect of gibberellic acid on carnation cv. Improved Marguerite. Gibberllic acid foliar spray at 100 ppm increased plant height (70.50 cm) compared to untreated control (62.33 cm). Similar results were also obtained by Mukhopadhyaya (1990) in the same crop with different variety. Foliar spray of GA3 @ 500 and 1000 ppm increased the plant height, number of shoots per plant and length of shoots in chrysanthemum frutescence (Dahab et al., 1987).

Super star (Narayan Gowda, 1985). Reduction in the number of flowers was noted in lilies (Laiche and Box, 1973). The yield was decreased by GA3 in crossandra (Sayed and Muthuswamy, 1974) and in Jasminum multiflorum (Murali, 1984) and also Jasminum sambac (Nage Gowda, 1988). 2.4 ETHREL (2-chlro ethyl phosphonic acid) Ethrel, an ethylene releasing compound or a mixture of 2-chlroethyl phosphonic acid and related compound is widely used as a practical plant regulator. It has shown activity in dwarfing, inducing abscission stimulating laterals or basal branching and increasing the number of branches formed following the topping. A number of new facts have become available concerning the influence on many ornamental plants. 2.4.1 Effect on morphological characters In Jasminum grandiflorum, ethrel significantly reduced the length of shoots (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977). Application of ethrel in general retarded the shoot length and lower concentrations of the chemical encouraged large number of branches per plant in J. arborescens and J. humile. Shanks (1969) reported that dwarfing of young snapdragon plants as well as petunia and marigold was obtained following the application of ethrel as foliar spray. Dwarfing of plants by ethrel due to the shortening of internodes has been reported in chrysanthemum (Tijia et al., 1969, Lopes and Weiler, 1974), caladium (Piersol, 1973), carnation (Dicks and Rees, 1973, Johnson, 1972). Bhattacharjee (1984b) reported that application of ethrel at 2000 ppm delayed flower bud appearance by 6-15 days in dahlia. Mukhopadhyay (1981) observed that ethrel spray of 500 and 1000 ppm retarded linear stem length but promoted lateral branching in carnation. Manna and Mukerjee (1983) reported that foliar application of ethrel at 250 and 500 ppm to chrysanthemum cultivars like ‘Eva tuner’, Gloria Dea and Templation has significantly reduced plant height in ‘Eva turner’ and templation. But, in Gloria Deo, both the concentrations failed to restrict growth. Tickonor (1969) reported that ethrel significantly reduced the plant height in rhododendron. In roses, ethrel at 1000 ppm retarded the plant height considerably (Carpenter, 1975). Simialr results were also observed in Poinsetia (Zieslin and Halevy, 1976). Murali and Narayana Gowda (1984) observed that ethrel at 200 ppm reduced the shoot length, the number and length of the internodes, leaves, leaf size in Jasminum multiflorum. In Jasminum grandiflorum, ethrel significantly reduced the length of shoots (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977). (1980) observed that ethrel delayed flowering in several ornamental plants. In Jasminum humile and J. arborescens onset of flowering was due to ethrel treatment (Bhattacharjee and Sharma, 1981). Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1977 and 1978) found that ethrel delayed the onset of flowring in Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum auriculatum. In J. auriculatum significantly higher total flower bud length and width of flower bud were observed due to ethrel application. In J. humile and J. arborescens delay onset of flowering. Increase in diameter of the flower and significant rise in yield of flower were reported by Bhattacharjee and Divakar (1984). In J. humile resulted in drastic reduction in the flower number. Eldabad et al. (1978) reported that ethrel at 1000 ppm delayed flowering in tulip. Murali and Narayana Gowda (1984) reported delayed flowering due to foliar application of ethrel at 150 and 200 ppm in Jasminum multiflorum. Munsi et al. (1980) observed that ethrel delayed flowering in several ornamental plants. In Jasminum humile and J. arborescens onset of flowering was due to ethrel treatment (Bhattacharjee and Sharma, 1981). Shanks (1969) found that ethrel delayed flower formation in chrysanthemum, hydrageas and azaleas. A slight delay in flower bud formation was also noted in Poinsettias (Cohpanakakol et al., 1974). Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1974) reported production of more flower in dahlia by ethrel treatment. Ethrel at 500 ppm reduced the yield, caused bud abortion or malformation and shoot die back of carnations (Butters, 1974). Carpenter (1975) observed that foam sprays of ethrel at 1000 and 2000 ppm increased the total number of flower per plant in roses. The number of flower increased with the increased level of ethrel from 10 to 30 ppm in roses, particularly during winter months (Hassan et al., 1976). Bhattacharjee and Divakar (1984) reported that when one year old plants of Jasminum auriculatum, J. calophyllum, J. flexile and J. grandiflorum sprayed with ethrel. It appreciably increased flower yield in all the species. Murali and Narayana Gowda (1984) reported the mean increase in flower yield by weight and number owing to ethrel spray at 150 and 200 ppm in Jasminum multiflorum over 53.61 and 65.79 per cent by weight and 48.38 and 57361 per cent, respectively by number over untreated (control) plants. Ma et al. (1985) found that when rose cultivar ‘Kushi’ was sprayed with ethrpon, increased the flower yield by 46.2 per cent. Bhattacharjee (1983a) reported that ethrel spray at 500, 1000 and 2000 ppm concentrations improved the flower quality and yield in Jasminum grandiflorum. Bhattacharjee (1984b) reported that application of ethrel at 2000 ppm delayed flower bud appearance by 6 to 15 days in dahlia and delayed flowering in Jasminum spp. Roychoudhuri et al. (1985) reported that ethrel at 100 ppm increased flower size and length of flower stalk in gladiolus. III. MATERIAL AND METHODS The present investigations were carried out in Floriculture Unit of the Department of Horticulture, College of Agriculture, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad during 2005- 06. The materials used and techniques adopted during the course of the present investigation are described in this chapter. 3.1 GEOGRAPHICAL LOCATION OF THE EXPERIMENTAL SITE Floriculture Unit of the Department of Horticulture, Dharwad is situated in the Agro- Climatic Zone-8 (northern transitional zone) of Karnataka state. Geographically, Dharwad is located at 150-26' North latitude, 750-07'. East longitude and at an altitude of 678 m above mean sea level (MSL). The meteorological data for the year 2004-05 recorded at meteorological observatory, Agriculture College Farm, Dharwad are given in Appendix I. 3.1.1 Soil characteristics The experimental site had red soil of the sandy clay type. The physical and chemical characteristics of the soil are furnished in Appendix II. 3.2 DESCRIPTION OF THE SPECIES Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. Jasminum auriculatum, a scandent shrub having shiny leaves with minute lateral leaflets. The plant produce numerous star shaped white sweet scented blooms and are very good as loose flowers. These flowers are borne in pubescent compound many flowered flax cymes. Black fruits are produced in abundance. 3.3 EXPERIMENTAL TECHNIQUES 3.3.1 Details of the experiment The following growth regulators were used in the present study below structural formula of different growth regulators is given in Fig. 1. In the beginning of the experiment in the last week of December. The plants were pruned by normal labour removing dead, diseased and unwanted branches by cutting back all the bushes at a height of 70 cm from the ground level. The plants were supplied with 120 g of nitrogen, 240 g of phosphorus and 240 g of potassium per plant in two equal split doses, once at the time of pruning and second time during June along with 15 kg of farm yard manure (FYM) per plant. The farm yard manure was applied around the plants by mixing well with the soil. The fertilizers were placed in 15 cm deep furrows opened around the plants 20 cm away from the base of the stem. Irrigation was given at 10 to 15 days intervals depending upon the rainfall and moisture content in the soil. Hand weeding was done once in a month, spray of dicofol (0.05%) and rogar (0.05%) at 15 days intervals was given as a preventive measure. 3.5 COLLECTION OF DATA The following observations were recorded to asses the effect of plant growth regulators. 3.5.1 Growth measurement Growth measurement of primary and secondary lateral shoots were recorded as detailed below. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS The results of the investigations carried out on the effects of growth regulators on growth, flowering and yield of Jasmine (Jasminum auriculatum Vahl.) are presented in this chapter. 4.1 GROWTH The effect of plant growth regulators tried on the vegetative growth are presented in Table 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. 4.1.1 Length of primary lateral shoot (cm) Both the concentrations of gibberellic acid (GA) recorded significant increase in the primary lateral shoot length at different intervals (Table 1 and Fig. 2). The highest shoot length was recorded in GA3 25 ppm at different intervals (60 DAP – 88.96 cm, 90 DAP – 124.59 cm, 120 DAP – 143.16 cm), while cycocel, ethrel and alpha-naphthalene acetic acid (NAA) registered the lowest length of shoot. Spraying with NAA 25 ppm (T1) was most effective treatment in reducing shoot length at different intervals 60, 90 and 120 DAP (41.23, 77.44 and 91.43 cm), ethrel at 200 ppm (T8) (44.63, 81.79 and 95.20 cm) also recorded appreciable growth retardation. The reduction of shoot length was not influenced much due to application of cycocel 1000 ppm (T4), ethrel at 100 ppm (T7) and NAA 50 ppm (T2) was not much. Cycocel at 500 ppm (T3) recorded shoot length at different intervals of 60, 90, 120 DAP (54.56, 85.51, 102.63 cm) which were on par with untreated control (59.70, 89.40 and 107.06 cm). 4.1.2 Length of secondary shoots (dm) Significant differences were observed in the secondary shoot length in all the plant growth regulators tried (Table 2 and Fig. 3). Cycocel at 500 ppm (T3) resulted in earlier flowering (34.00 days) followed by cycocel 1000 ppm (T4) (36.33 days), however all other treatments except ethrel registered early flowering. DISCUSSION Despite its probability and reputation as a commercial flower crop, Jasmines suffer from two important drawbacks. The highly perishable nature of the flowers for which the produce has to be sold field fresh in the urban market. Another detracting feature is the high level of fluctuation in daily and seasonal outputs. Scarcity during certain other months, pushes up price level and peak productivity during other months floods the market with flowers, depresses the prices and reduce the returns. Price fluctuation ranges from five rupees to thirty rupees per kilogram of the flowers is common. Expansion of area magnifies these problems since greater production would only accentuate the wide dispurities in price level. In other annual field crops or perennial crops, production in confined to certain foreseeable season lending itself to certain measures of control in organizing the marketing and sales ends. Jasmines on the other hand flowers almost throughout the year, in South India but flowering properties between the species, place of cultivation and month are highly variable (Raman et al., 1969). Also the demand is mostly confined to certain sections of the people and is often so unpredictable that no regulatory measure over price control is possible unless the flowering itself can be regulated by some means. An economically viable cultivation practice will, therefore, demand the highest level of productivity from the smallest possible unit area which requires the support of know-how and the most profitable and economic cultivation practices designed to produce the most at the least cost. These developments, therefore merit a reorientation in the traditional cultural practices with more attention to be paid towards regulating growth and flowering of these plants in such a manner that the productivity will not only be increased but will also be distributed over the whole productive season without creating conjection and attendant problems in any part of the year. The role of nutrition and horticultural practices like pruning and use of growth regulators in this respect, has already been emphasized (Kumargurupar, 1974; Muthuswamy and Pappaiah, 1980; Murali, 1984 and Narayana Gowda et al., 1986), plant growth regulators yet another means for such crop regulation practices. 5.1 EFFECT OF ALPHA-NAPHTHALENE ACETIC ACID (NAA) Alpha-naphthalene acetic acid appreciably reduced the plant growth and increased the productive shoots. NAA at 25 and 50 ppm recorded 81.66 productive shoots and number of internodes were 32.33 per shoot. These results in accordance with those reports in Jasminum sambac (Pal et al., 1980), chrysanthemum (Ravindra, 1980), china aster (Reddy and Suladamath, 1983) and many other ornamental plants (Shanks, 1981). The leaf area of NAA treated plants reduced in case of Jasminum multiflorum (Murali, 1984). The appreciable feature of practical importance of this auxin compound is the significant improvement in the yield of flowers compared to control. NAA increased the yield (408.15 g/bush) while untreated plants recorded only 285.83 g per bush. Increase in yield was 42.79 per cent and 16.64 per cent more over control in 25 and 50 ppm of NAA, respectively. The improvement in flowering was partly due to more number of productive shoots developed on the treated plants. The results are in confirmity with the reports on Jasminum sambac and J. auriculatum (Pal et al., 1980). Though, there was increase in yield of flowers, the detracting feature of this chemical was the delayed flowering of treated plants and reduced the duration of flowering. Delayed flowering by the application of NAA has been reported by many workers in chrysanthemum (Tsukomoto and Harda, 1957; Tsukomoto et al., 1968; Ono, 1961 and Ravindra, 1980). 5.2 EFFECT OF CYCOCEL The retarded growth of primary and secondary lateral shoots and internodal length by cycocel particularly at 1000 ppm resulted into known effect of this chemical on Jasminum auriculatum, J. grandiflorum and J. multiflorum (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 and 1978; and Murali and Nage Gowda, 1988). The results are in consonance with the effects of this chemical reported by several other workers also (Reed et al., 1974 and Maharana and Pani, 1982). The most conspicuous effect of this growth retardant was the greatly increased number of laterals and the markedly early flowering which were noted in other species of jasmines also. The yield was also increased appreciably by cycocel. The two features viz., the reduction in number of days for flowering by as much as 10 days and nearly double the yield by cycocel treatments are of special significance. It has been already shown that cycocel induced early flowering and increased the yield in Jasminum grandiflorum, J. auriculatum and J. multiflorum (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 and 1978). Many other workers reported the same results in several other ornamental plants (Hore and Bose, 1972 in hibiscus; Will, 1972 and Jansen, 1974 in pelargonium and Fossard, 1973 in Chenapodium rubrum). The reduced yield by GA3 was however accompanied by decreased length of the flower bud. Similar results were reported in J. auriculatum (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 and 1978; J. multiflorum by Murali, 1984 and J. sambac by Nage Gowda, 1988). 5.4 EFFECT OF ETHREL Ethrel at 200 ppm concentration arrested the growth of primary and secondary lateral shoot and reduced the number of internodes, leaves, leaf size and leaf area. This inhibited vegetative growth could be a desirable feature in maintenance of shape and size of Jasmine bushes helping in easy harvest of flowers. These results are in consonance with the reports of Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1977 and 1978) in Jasminum auriculatum and J. grandiflorum and Murali and Nage Gowda (1984 and 1988) in Jasminum multiflorum and J. sambac. But the delayed flowering and only a slight increase in yield have detracted its usefulness. Ethrel might have increased the endogenous growth promoting substances particularly auxins, which might account for delay in flowering in the present studies. Similar results were reported by Tijia et al. (1969) in Chrysanthemum morifolium and Bhattacharjee (1984) in Dahalia variabilis. The increased yield by ethrel spray is only minimum and does not merit the additional expenditure that the sprays of ethrel would entail, in comparison to cycocel where the increase in yield is remarkable. The extreme dwarfing was not accompanied by an stimulation of productive shoot growth in the present study. In roses, Halvey (1970) reported more button breaks but in the present studies productive shoots number was more in the present studies productive shoots number was more in cycocel sprayed plants than ethrel sprayed plants. The reduction of leaf size (length and width) due to ethrel treatments observed by many workers (Tijia et al., 1969; Piersol, 1973 and Dicks and Rees, 1973). An overall appreciation of the results would show that cycocel besides arresting growth to a moderate degree and induced remarkably early flowering and the yield was also considerably increased by cycocel. Ethrel also retarded the growth and induced remarkably early flowering and yield was also considerably increased by this ethrel and it ranked next to cycocel. Evidently the cycocel sprays gave several advantages like early flowering, higher yield, better flower size and longer duration of flowering. Cycocel is a true-anti-gibberellin biosynthesis. The fact that cycocel sprays induced early flowering suggests that a reduction in level of endogenous gibberellin may be a pre-requisite for floral induction. While the growth retardation was greater under higher concentration of cycocel, the time taken for flowering did not show clear trend, but the yield of flowers declined with the increase in the concentration of cycocel. In other words, the higher concentration of 1000 ppm cycocel while reduced the shoot length and reduced the yield level. It seems that, safer to employ 500 ppm cycocel for deriving maximum advantages mentioned above. Ethrel at 100 ppm can also be employed for obtaining higher yield. The early flowering induced cycocel and the higher quantum of yield in the flowering season promoted by the chemical are of practical importance in crop regulation in cultivated jasmines. Judicious combination of cultural practices like pruning and fertilizer application as well as growth regulator sprays, it is possible that flowering can be manipulated atleast to a reasonable extent to avoid the heavy glut due to peak flowering in a particular part of the year, which is very common in commercial species of Jasmines. FUTURE LINE OF WORK Based on the present investigation the following suggestions are made for future line of work in Jasmine with respect to plant growth regulators.  Some of these growth regulators can be tried during August to December of vegetative growth phase to know the effect on quantity and quality of main season crop.  Other growth regulators (Ethephon, Jasmonic acid and Brassinolide) can be tried at different concentrations to enhance the growth and yield in Jasmine.  To study the effect of plant growth regulators in different seasons on Jasmine. VI. SUMMARY A study on the effects of four growth regulators viz., alpha-naphthalene acetic acid (NAA), cycocel, gibberellic acid and ethrel each at two concentrations was carried out on Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. in the Floriculture unit of the Department of Horticulture, College of Agriculture, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad during 2004-05. The main objective was to evaluate their effects on growth, flowering and yield of Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. The salient findings of the study are summarized below; 1. Gibberellic acid (GA3) at both the concentrations significantly increased primary and secondary shoot length. NAA, ethrel and cycocel significantly reduced the shoot length. 2. Cycocel and ethrel were equally effective in increasing the number of productive shoots closely followed by NAA. Reduced number of productive shoots was observed under higher concentration of GA3. 3. Gibberellic acid (GA3) recorded more number of internodes and the lowest was in cycocel. GA3 had an enhancing effect on the internodal length, whereas ethrel has reduced the internodal length. 4. Gibberellic acid (GA3) increased the length and width of the leaves with an associated increase in the total leaf area and slightly reduced number of leaves, whereas cycocel at lower concentration (500 ppm) increased number of leaves. NAA at 50 ppm reduced the number and length of the leaves whereas cycocel at 500 ppm reduced the width of the leaf and total leaf area. 5. Cycocel at both the concentrations induced early flowering. Maximum delay in flowering was noted in NAA, GA3 and ethrel treated plants. Cycocel at 500 ppm induced earliest flowering and registered longer duration of flowering. 6. Cycocel at 500 ppm recorded the highest yield in terms of both weight and number of flowers, whereas both the concentrations of GA3 registered lowest values. 7. Cycocel at 500 ppm recorded highest length of flower bud, followed by cycocel at 1000 ppm, whereas both the concentrations of GA3 (25 and 50 ppm) registered lowest length of flower bud. GA3 at 50 ppm reduced the weight of hundred flower buds and cycocel at both the concentrations increased the weight of hundred flower buds. 8. Cycocel at 500 ppm increased chlorophyll ‘a’ content whereas ethrel at 100 ppm increased chlorophyll ‘b’ content. The total chlorophyll content was maximum cycocel at 500 ppm. However, GA3 at 50 ppm registered lowest total chlorophyll content. Based on these studies, it can be recommended that flower yield can be increased by spraying of cycocel at 500 ppm in Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. under Dharwad conditions. Ethrel at 100 ppm was next to cycocel in increasing flower yield. Cycocel induced early flowering and longer flowering duration, whereas delay in flowering was observed with NAA treatments.
