ANGADI Major Advisor ABSTRACT Jasmine is one of the important commercial flower crop, grown for its white fragrant flowers, largely used for garland and floral decoration. The jasmine belongs to family ‘Oleaceae’. A study on the effects of four growth regulators viz., NAA, cycocel, gibberellic acid and ethrel each at two concentrations was carried out on Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. in the Floriculture Unit of the Department of Horticulture, College of Agriculture, University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad during 2005-06. The main objective was to evaluate their effects on growth, flowering and yield of Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. GA3 at both the concentrations significantly increased primary and secondary lateral shoot length, GA3 gave more number of internodes and the enhancing the internodal length. GA3 increased the length and width of the leaves with an associated increase in the total leaf area and slightly reduced number of leaves. Cycocel and ethrel were equally effective in increasing the number of productive shoots closely followed by NAA. Reduced number of productive shoots was observed under high concentration of gibberellic acid. Cycocel at 500 ppm induced early flowering and registered longer duration of flowering. Cycocel at 500 ppm recorded highest yield in terms of both weight and number of flowers, whereas both the concentrations of GA3 registered lowest values. Cycocel at 500 ppm recorded highest length of flower bud and increased the weight of hundred flower buds, whereas both the concentrations of GA3 recorded lowest length of flower bud and reduced the weight of hundred flower buds. Cycocel at 500 ppm increased chlorophyll ‘a’ content whereas ethrel at 100 ppm increased chlorophyll ‘b’ content. The total chlorophyll content was maximum with cycocel at 500 ppm.

CHAPTER - I miTlBCDlDJOrcSIKKDFI I . iisrrRODUcmoisr Jasmine is an important commercial flower grown mainly for fresh flowers and for concrete extraction. Fresh flowers are used for garland making, in places of worship and for hair adornments. The flowers are also used commercially for extracting essential oil. "Jasmine concrete' extracted from the flowers of Jaji mallige (Jasminum grandiflorum), is in great demand in the International market and it is used in the manufacture of high grade perfume. The term "Jasmine' is derived from an Arabic word "Jesseonine' (Bailey, 1947) and also an old Persian name "Yasmyn' meaning fragrance. It is native of India haviiig its origin in southern foot hills of Himalaya (Bailey, 1947). It has secondary origin in Burma and China. The genus Jasminum belongs to family oleaceae and includes over 200 species distributed in the tropical and sub- tropical regions around the world (Mahammad and Rania, 1969). It is said that jasmine has spread to Mediterranean countries from the place of its origin. Some of the countries growing jasmine on commercial scale are France, India, Italy, Moracco, Algeria, North Africa, Spain and Egypt. Important states which grow jasmine in India on commercial scale are Tamilnadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar. In Karnataka, jasmine is cultivated in about 1300 hectares with an approximate annual production of about 66,000 tonnes of flowers (Annon, 1959). It is reported that 15 tonnes of flowers are sold daily in four major cities of India, viz., Madras, Bangalore, Delhi and Calcutta. Bailey (1947) reported that about 90 species of jasmine are grown in India. Similar report was also given by Muthuswamy and Pappiah (1980). Out of these, only about 20 species are under cultivation in South India (Georgewatt 1980). Of the several species reported, only three are commercially exploited in India (Anon, 1959) and these are : Jasminwn grand! florum L. " Ja j imal 1 ige ' J. auricuiatiun Vahl. "Soo j imal 1 ige ' J. sambac Ait. "Gundumal1ige' In addition, one more species that has been exploited commercially for cut flower production is J. multiflorum Andr. "Kakada". A cheaper, less cumbersome and efficient method with minimum usage of plant material would be raising plants through cuttings. The details of materials used and the methods adopted for the experiment are given below. 3.1 Location The experiment was carried out at the New Orchard of the University of Agricultural sciences, Dharwad which is situated in the transitional tract of Karnataka at 15°-26' North latitude and 75°-07' East longitude and at an altitude of 678 m above the mean sea level. 3.2 Climate The average annual rainfall is about 835 mm with fairly even distibution from April to October. The average maximum temperature reaches 37°C in the month of April and the minimum goes upto 12'*C in the month of December. The relative humidity fluctuates between 50.00 and 87.00 per cent. The meteorological data for the year 1991 and the average data for preceeding 40 years (1951-1991) as recorded at the Meteorological Observatory of the Main Research Station, Dharwad are presented in the appendix-I. 23 3.3 Experimental details The present study was undertaken to evaluate the effect of types of cuttings and pre-treatment with Beta-indole- 3-butyric acid (IBA) and Alpha-napthalene acetic acid (NAA) at different concentrations on rooting of selected JaBOiinum species by cuttings. 3.3.1 Source and preparation of the cuttings The matured one year old shoots of past season were selected from about five to six years old bushes of different species of jasmine. All the lateral braches and leaves from the base to middle portion of the shoots were removed by leaving only a few leaves at the terminal portion. The shoot was divided into three parts, i.e., hardwood, semi-hardwood and softwood. Cuttings of length 10 to 15 cm from the basal portion of matured stem were used as hardwood cuttings. A slant cut was given at the base of the cuttings and each cutting had about five to six buds. The middle portion of the branch was used for semi-hardwood cutting. The terminal portion of the stem was used for softwood cuttings. A few leaves were left both in semi-hard wood and soft wood cuttings. Similar procedure was adopted in the preparation of both semi-hardwood and softwood cuttings. 24 3.3.2 Preparation of the rooting medium River bed sand was used as the rooting medium. This was thoroughly washed in running water to remove salt and organic matter. The washed sand was filled up in pots. Before planting, the rooting medium was treated with captan to prevent rotting of cuttings. 3.4 Design and layout Split plot design was adopted for- laying out the experiment with nine main tareatments and six sub-treatments with three replications. Each treatment consisted of 20 cuttings planted in the sand pot. The treatments were randomized. 3.5 Treatments Main treatments: Nine combinations of three species and three types of cuttings. Species: (1) Jasminum grandif1 orurn L. (2) Jasminum auricula turn vahl. (3) Jasminum sambac Ait. Types of cutting: (1) Hardwood cutting (2) Semi-hardwood cutting (3) Softwood cutting 25 Sub-treatmentG Six concentrations of growth regulators. ( 1) 0 ppiu (control ) (2) IBA 2000 ppm (3) IBA 4000 ppm (4) IBA 6000 ppm (5) NAA 2000 ppm (6) NAA 4000 ppm 3.6 Preparation of different concentrations of IBA auid NAA Different concentrations of both the growth regulators viz., Indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) and a-napthalene acetic acid (NAA) were prepared as follows. The required amount of growth regulators were dissolved in few ml of 80 per cent ethanol. The volumes were made upto sufficient level by adding distilled water. 3.7 Treatment of cuttings with IBA and NAA solutionB and planting The basal portion of the cuttings were dipped in IBA and NAA solutions for 10 seconds. The cuttings used for control were dipped in 50 per cent alcohol solutions. For planting the treated cuttings, holes were made in sand medium with the help of a dibbler and the cuttings were planted in such a way that one or two nodes of the cutting were inside the medium. The cuttings were pressed around the base and watered. 26 3.8 After Care To prevent the attack of fungal infection spray of Dithane M-45 was given at fortnightly intervals. 3.9 Observations recorded After 70 days of planting the rooting percentage and other root and shoot characters were recorded. The cuttings were carefully removed from the pot and dipped in water to remove all the sand adhering to the roots. The following observations were recorded. 1. Number of Primary roots per cutting. 2. Number of Secondary roots per cutting. 3. Length of longest primary and secondary root. 4. Number of sprouts per cuttings and length of longest sprout, 5. Number of leaves per rooted cutting. 6. Dry weight of the roots per rooted cutting. 7. Survival percentage of rooted cuttings in the field. 3.10 Field establishment of rooted cuttings Five well rooted cuttings from each treatment were planted in polythene bags containing equal parts of sand, soil and compost. One rooted cutting per bag was transplanted and the potted cuttings were kept under shade and watered daily for hardening. After a week, the plants were removed from the shade and kept in open field and survival percentage was 27 recorded 60 days after transplantation of the rooted cuttings. 3.11 Biochemical analysis At the time of preparation of the cuttings for planting a composite sample of lOOg of plant material from each of the three species was collected and oven dried for the purpose of analysis for sugars, starch, nitrogen and phenolic compounds. The methods used for the estimation of different chemical constituents are give below. 3.11.1 Total sugars For estimation of total sugars, 500 mg of oven dried finely ground sample was extracted successively thrice using 80 per cent ethanol. A known volume of this extract was taken in a test tube and the alcohol was evaporated. Distilled water was added and the volume made upto a known level. The total sugar content in the alcohol free extract was determined after hydrolysing a known volume of this extract with IN H2SO4 on a hot water bath for 30 minutes at 49"'C and after neutralising it with IN NaOH by following the procedure of Nelson (1944). 3.11.2 Reducing sugars Reducing sugars in the extract was determined by using Nelson's modified Somogy's method {Nelson, 1944). 28 3.11.3 Non-reducing sugars Non reducing sugars are computed by deducting the value of reducing sugars from the amount of total sugars. 3.11.4 Estimation of starch The residues obtained after alcohol extraction of the sample was dried and known amount of it was hydrolysed for three hours with one ml of concentrated HCl adding distilled water in 1:10 (v/v) proportion. This carbohydrate fraction was made soluble by hydrolysis and was estimated as reducing sugars. The amount of starch was computed by multiplying the value of this fraction by 0.9 (steele, 1949). 3.11.5 Nitrogen The total nitrogen was determined by following Mlcro- kjeldhal method and the results were expressed in percentage (A.O.A.C, 1970). 3.11.6 Estimation of total carbohydrates The values obtained for total sugars and starch were arithmetically summed up to get the content of total available carbohydrates. 3.11.7 C/N ratio The values of total carbohydrate divided by the value of total nitrogen gives carbohydrate/nitrogen ratio. 29 3.11.8 Estimation of total phenols The amount of total phenols was estimated by Folinciacalteu reagent (FCR) method (Mahadevan, 1975). 3.12 Statistical analysis The data pertaining to root and shoot characters were tabulated treatment and replication wise and statistically analysed. The data relating to the number of primary roots, length of longest primary root, number of secondary roots, length of longest secondary root, dry weight of roots per rooted cutting, number of sprouts, length of longest sprout and number of leaves were transformed using square root values and the data relating to the percentage of rooting and percentage of survivability of rooted cuttings were transformed into angular values and analysed statistically (Leclerg et al., 1962). After the statistical analysis of the data, Fisher and Yate's tables (1957) were consulted for knowing the tabulated 'F' values at 5 per cent level of significance for corresponding degrees of freedom. Inferences were drawn as revealed by the analysis of Tables. D I S C U S S I O N The advantage of the practice of vegetative propagation in producing uniform clonal planting material have long been recognised. At present, jasmine is propagated by ground layering, which is a time consuming process and the percentage of success in very less, although some efforts on the use of growth regulators for rooting made in the past have indicated poor response on the rooting of cuttings in jasmine. The present investigation on the effect of growth regulators and type of cuttings on rooting of different species of jasmine was therefore undertaken to evaluate the effect of Indole-3- butyric acid (IBA) and Napthalene acetic a d d (NAA) and different types of cuttings on rooting. Further, studies on the survival of rooted cuttings as well as biochemical compost ion of the three Jasminum species were also made. The significance of the results are discussed in the following pages under different headings as indicated below. 5.1 Root parameters 5.1.1 Percentage of cuttings rooted 5.1.2 Number of primary roots per cutting 5.1.3 Length of the longest primary root 5.1.4 Number of secondary roots per cutting 5.1.5 Length of the longest secondary root 5.1.6 Dry weight of roots per rooted cutting 56 5.2 Shoot parameters 5.2.1 Number of sprouts per cutting 5.2.2 Length of the longest sprout per cutting 5.2.3 Number of leaves per cutting. 5.3 Biochemical studies 5.3.1 Total sugars 5.3.2 Starch 5.3.3 Ni trogen 5.3.4 Carbohydrate/Nitrogen ration 5.3.5 Total phenols 5.4 Survival of transplanted rooted cuttings 5.1 Root parameters 5.1.1 Percentage of cuttings rooted The results presented in Table-1 indicate that J.Sambac semi-hardwood cuttings resulted in highest percentage (69.08) of rooting. The J. grandiflorum hardwood cuttings resulted in 68.33 per cent of rooting, whereas, in J.auriculatum softwood cuttings, 62.29 per cent of rooting was observed. The differences in rooting may be attributed to the inherent species differences. From the present study, it is clear that both IBA and NAA treatments increased the percentage of rooting in stem s V 57 cuttings of Jasminum species. A similar increase in percentage of rooting in Jasminum species was observed with growth regulators (IBA, NAA and lAA) by many workers (Muthuswamy and Pappiah, 1976 ; Singh, 1979 ; Jayapal, et al., 1980 ; Singh and Motial, 1981 ; Bhattacharjee and Balakrishna,1983). The Indole butyric acid treatment at 4000 ppm resulted in the highest percentage of rooting (79.90) whereas, among NAA treatements, 4000 ppm resulted in 70.50 per cent rooting. Similar results with 4000 ppm IBA and NAA on jasmine were recorded by Singh (1979) in J. sambac cv 'Motia', Singh (1979) in i7. sambac cvs 'Madanban', Mogra, Singh and Motial (1981) in J. sambac cv 'Madanban' and Bhattacharjee and Balakrishnan (1983) in J. auriculatum, J. grandiflorum, J.sambac and J. multiflorum. It is interesting to note that at higher concentration of IBA, the percentage of rooting decreased. This might be due to toxic effect. Similar observations were made by Vijayakumar (1973) in guava cuttings treated with IBA and Mokashi (1976) in 'Thompson seedless' grape cuttings treated with IBA. It is evident from the Table-1 that, the hardwood cuttings of J. grandiflorum treated with 4000 ppm of IBA gave the highest percentage of rooting (90.00). In J. auriculatum soft-wood cuttings treated with 4000 ppm (78.42) of IBA, the 58 highest percentage of rooting was noticed. The semi-hardwood cuttings of J. sambac treated with 4000 ppm of IBA resulted in 90.00 per cent of rootings. Similar result was observed by Singh (1979), Jaypal et al. (1980) and Singh and Motial (1981). 5.1.2 Number of primary roots per cutting A maximum number of primary roots per cutting was observed in case of J. grandiflorum hard-wood cuttings (5.43). In J. auriculatum, primary roots were found in higher number in semi-hardwood cuttings (4.84). Similarly, in J. sambac softwood cuttings had higher number (4.94) of primary roots as compared to other types of cuttings. The use of growth regulators significantly increased the production of a higher number of primary roots. The maximum number of primary roots was observed in IBA 4000 ppm (Table 2). Increased number of primary roots recorded in the present study is comparable to the findings in different crops by various other workers (Hitchcock and Zimmerman, 1944; Bid and Mukherjee, 1969) who also reported the production of more number of roots by the use of growth substances. As observed in the case of percentage of rooting, the maximum number (5.54) of primary roots was found with IBA 4000 ppm resulted in the production of a higher number (4.90) of primary roots. The maximum length (5.56 cm) of the longest primary root was obtained in J. grand!florum hardwood cuttings. In J. auriculatum the greater length of primary root was found in softwood cuttings, (4.81 cm) but in J.Sawbac the highest length of primary root was found in the semi-hardwood and soft wood cuttings (4.49 cm). The use of growth regulators has been found to increase the average length of roots. This was reported by several researchers such as Purkayastha and Kumar (1975), Vijayakumar (1973) and Bhujbal and Kale (1975). In the present study, both IBA and NAA treatments could significantly increase the length of the longest primary root over the control. The Indole butyric acid at 4000 ppm concentration brought about the maximum length of primary root (5.22 cm). This finding is in agreement with that of Singh and Motial (1981), who also obtained the longest roots with IBA treatment at 4000 ppm in J. sambac cv ""Madanban' . Here the increase in the length of roots over the control may be due to the enhanced hydrolysis of carbohydrates caused by the 60 treatment with auxins. The Napthalene acetic acid at 4000 ppm resulted in the production of longest primary root (4.68 cm). These results were in line with findings of Singh and Motiai (1981) while experimenting on J. sambac cv. ^Madanban', 5.1.4 Number of secondary roots per cutting There was a large variation regarding the number of secondary roots per cutting of different species of jasmine. The maximum number of secondary roots was found in J. grandiflorum hardwood cuttings (12.42). In J. auriculatum the higher number of secondary roots was found in soft-wood cuttings (10.11); but in J. sambac, the semi-hardwood and soft- wood cuttings registered a higher number of secondary roots (11.25) and (11.09) respectively. This can be attributed to the presence of more number of primary roots which in turn increase the number of secondary roots. All the concentrations of growth regulators significantly increased the number of secondary roots when compared to the control. The Indole butyric acid at 4000 ppm resulted in the maximum number of secondary roots (12.66). The Napthalene acetic acid at 4000 ppm, resulted in an increased number of roots (11.26). It was observed in the study that, with an increase in concentrations of both the growth regulators (IBA and NAA) there was a corresponding increase in the number of secondary roots. 61 The interaction effects regarding the number of secondary roots per cutting were found to be non-significant. 5.1.5 Length of the longest secondary root The maximum length of secondary root was obtained in J.grand!flor urn hardwood cuttings (2.11 cm) which was significantly superior over all other species. In J.auriculatum the higher length of secondary root was associated with the hardwood cuttings (1.42 cm), whereas, in J.sambac the softwood cuttings registered a higher length of secondary roots (1.56 cm). All the concentrations of growth regulators used, significantly increased the length of the longest secondary root over the control. A maximum length of secondary root was obtained at 4000 ppm of IBA. This finding is in line with the findings of Singh and Motial (1981) while experimenting on J.sambac cv. 'Madanban' with IBA at 4000 ppm. Here the increase in length of roots over the control may be due to the enhanced hydrolysis of carbohydrates caused by the treatment with auxins. Among the various concentrations of NAA used, 2000 and 4000 ppm resulted in a similar enhancement. And it is well known that auxins naturally occuring or exogenously applied is a requirement for initiation of adventitious roots on stems. The division of the fast root initial cells is dependent on either applied or endogenous auxins. 62 5.1.6 Dry weight of roots per rooted cutting A maximum dry weight of roots per cutting was observed in case of J. grandiflorum hard wood cuttings (0.69 g). In J. auriculatum dry weight of roots was found in maximum in hard-wood cuttings. Similarly, in J. sambac semi-hardwood cuttings had higher dry weight (0.57 g) of roots as compared to other types of cuttings. The use of growth regulators significantly increased the maximum dry weight of roots. The maximum dry weight of roots was observed in IBA 4000 ppm. The Napthalene acetic acid at 4000 ppm resulted in an increased dry weight of roots. The dry weight of roots in all the types of cuttings seems to be related with the number of primary and secondary roots and length of longest primary and secondary root. Similar views were held by earlier workers (Ghosh and Basu, 1973 and Singh, 1977 and 197 9 in Justicia, Ixora and Jasminum respectively). It is obvious that the auxin treatment induced higher number of primary and secondary roots which might have resulted in elongation of these roots through cell division accounting for higher dry weight of roots. The interaction effects regarding the dry weight of roots per cutting were found to be non-significant. 63 5.2 Shoot parameters 5.2.1 Number of sprouts per cutting Here, the effects among the different species of jasmine were found to be non-significant. However, all the concentrations of growth regulators increased the average number of sprouts per cuttings. The maximum number of sprouts (1.63) was observed per cutting at 4000 ppm, as against 1.23 in the control. The reduction in the average number of sprouts per cutting at the higher concentration (6000 ppm) of IBA could be linked to its inhibitory or toxic effect. Similar inhibitory effects of IBA at higher concentrations were also reported by Shekharappa (1982) in pomegranate. The Napthalene acetic acid at 4000 resulted in the production of a higher number (1.45) of sprouts per cuttings., than the other concentrations. Interaction effects regarding the number of sprouts per cuttings were found to be non-significant. 5.2.2 Length of longest sprout per cutting The hardwood cuttings of J. grand!florurn recorded a maximum length of sprouts (4.84 cm) and this was significantly superior to other main treatments. In J. auriculatum semi- hardwood cuttings registered a higher length of the longest sprouts (3.99 cm). In J. sambac, semi-hardwood cuttings (4.30 cm) recorded the maximum length. This may be due to auxins treatment and favourable weather conditions like temperature 64 and relative humidity which are congenial for bud sprout and its growth. The Indole-3-butyric acid at 4000 ppm resulted in the maximum length (5.03 cm) which is significantly superior to all other sub-treatments. These results are in line with findings of Nagaraja (1984) while experimenting on Jasmine. The highest concentrations of both IBA and NAA reduced the length of longest sprout. This may be due to the Inhibitory or toxic effects at the higher levels. The interaction effects between the main and sub- treatments on length of the longest sprout were found to be non-significant. 5.2.3 Number of leaves per cutting As observed in number of sprouts per cutting, the maximum number of leaves (5,08) was found in J. grandiflorum hardwood cuttings, which was significantly superior to other main treatments. The semi-hardwood cuttings of both J.auriculatum and J. sawbac produced a higher number of leaves compared to other types of cuttings taken from them. All the concentrations of growth regulators increased the number of leaves. The Indole-butyric acid at 4000 ppm resulted in the highest number of leaves (5.42). The Napthalene acetic acid at 6000 ppm resulted in producing highest number of leaves (4.99). But NAA at 4000 ppm resulted in significant reduction in the number of leaves (4.13). 65 Among the interaction effects, J. grandiflorum hardwood cuttings treated with IDA (4000 ppm) exhibited a significantly higher number of leaves (6.18). This may be due to greater stability and low mobility of IBA which induces all the growth responses. Semi-hardwood cuttings treated with IBA at 4000 ppm, a higher number of leaves (5.33) was observed. But, in J. auriculatum the percentage of starch was higher in semi-hardwood cuttings (5,98 %) as compared to the hardwood (5.80 %) and softwood (4.60 %) cuttings. In J, sambac a higher percentage of starch was found in the hardwood cuttings (7.01 %) as compared to 6.93 and 6.51 per cent in the semi-hard wood and soft-wood cuttings, respectively. 66 The higher levels of starch noticed in all the types of cuttings in all the species (except the hardwood cuttings of J, grandiflorum) might have brought about the favourable conditions for root initiation. 5.3.2 Total sugars The data on the biochemical constituents revealed a considerable difference in the quantity of total sugars among different types of cuttings in the same species. It was observed that hardwood cuttings of J. grandiflorum showed a higher percentage of total sugars (8.11) as compared to semi- hardwood (6.60 %) and softwood (7.12 %) cuttings. But, in J.auriculatum the softwood cuttings were found to contain a higher percentage of sugar (7.59) as compared to semi-hardwood (7.32 %) and hardwood cuttings (5.90 % ) . Similarly, in J.sambac, a higher percentage of sugars was found in the softwood cuttings (7.50) as compared to semi-hardwood (6.79 %) and hardwood (6.70 %) cuttings. The relatively higher sugar content found in all the types of cuttings in all the species of jasmine (except of hardwood cuttings of J. auriculatum) was perhaps favourable for rooting. In J, sambac a higher percentage of starch was found in the hardwood cuttings (7.01 %) as compared to 6.93 and 6.51 per cent in the semi-hard wood and soft-wood cuttings, respectively. 66 The higher levels of starch noticed in all the types of cuttings in all the species (except the hardwood cuttings of J, grandiflorum) might have brought about the favourable conditions for root initiation. 5.3.2 Total sugars The data on the biochemical constituents revealed a considerable difference in the quantity of total sugars among different types of cuttings in the same species. It was observed that hardwood cuttings of J. grandiflorum showed a higher percentage of total sugars (8.11) as compared to semi- hardwood (6.60 %) and softwood (7.12 %) cuttings. But, in J.auriculatum the softwood cuttings were found to contain a higher percentage of sugar (7.59) as compared to semi-hardwood (7.32 %) and hardwood cuttings (5.90 % ) . Similarly, in J.sambac, a higher percentage of sugars was found in the softwood cuttings (7.50) as compared to semi-hardwood (6.79 %) and hardwood (6.70 %) cuttings. The relatively higher sugar content found in all the types of cuttings in all the species of jasmine (except of hardwood cuttings of J. auriculatum) was perhaps favourable for rooting. Thus, it can be reasoned that the poor rooting of hardwood cuttings of J. auriculatum was probably related to their possession of low quantity of sugars in them. This observation agrees with those made by previous workers (Sen and Bose, 1967 ; • Ghosh and Ghosh, 67 1971; Nanda et al. 1971; Reuveni and Adato, 1974) who also opined that a high regeneration capacity of cuttings was associated with the higher levels of soluble sugars. 5.3.3 Total nitrogen It may be seen from the Table 10 that J. grand!florum softwood cuttings contained a higher percentage (1.52) of nitrogen as compared to semi-hard wood (1.22 %) and hardwood (0.82 %) cuttings. J. auricula turn hardwood cuttings contained the highest percentage of total nitrogen (2.40 %) followed by 1.99 and 1.61 per cent in softwood and semi-hardwood cuttings, respectively. J. sambac softwood cuttings contained a higher percentage of nitrogen (0.95) as compared to 0.92 and 0.79 per cent in semi-hardwood and hardwood cuttings, respectively. Thus, the relatively lower level of nitrogen present in all the types of cuttings of all the species, except the hardwood cuttings of J. auriculatum, might have helped better rooting. The report of Haun and Cornell (1951); All and Westwood (1966); Basu and Ghosh (1974) and Uthaiah (1975) reveal that low nitrogen has increased the rooting 'cofactors' activity and thus resulted in better rooting. The present study also confirms the findings of the above workers indicating that low nitrogen brings about better rooting. Another justification that could be given for low nitrogen causing better rooting is that, the C/N ratio is increased by 68 low n i t r o g e n p e r c e n t a g e , which i s conducive for b e t t e r r o o t i n g (Vi jnyfikuinar, 1973; tJthaiali, 1975; Mokafihi, 1976). 5.3.4 Carbohydrate to nitrogen (C/N) ratio Hardwood cuttings of J. grandiflorum showed a higher C/N ratio (15.00) when compared to semi-hardwood (10.40) and softwood (9,00) cuttings. But, in J. auriculatum the hardwood cuttings showed the lowest C/N ratio (5.25) followed by softwood (5.93) and the semi-hardwood (8.71) cuttings. Thus it can be summarized that the higher C/N ratio favors better rooting in cuttings. Ghosh and Basu (1973) and Basu and Ghosh (1974) observed that higher carbohydrate to nitrogen ratio was found to increase rooting 'cofactors'. activity and better rooting in Justicia cuttings. In the light of this, the lowest C/N ratio observed in hardwood cuttings of J. auriculatum might be one of the reasons responsible for the poor rooting. 5.3.5 Total Phenols It is seen from Table 10 that the J. grand!florum softwood cuttings contained higher amount of total phenols (425.20 ug/g.d.wt) as compared to either semi-hardwood or hardwood cuttings. In J. auriculatum, semi-hardwood cuttings contained a higher amount of total phenols (309.32 ug/g.d.wt) whereas, the 69 hardwood cuttings contained the lowest amount of total phenols (225.22 ug/g.d.wt). But in J. sambac, softwood cuttings contained a higher amount of total phenols (396.72 ug/g d.wt) as compared to semi-hcirdwood and hardwood cuttings. These results indicate that the relatively higher contents of total phenols present in both i7. grandiflorum and J". sambac cuttings might have favored the better rooting. Jackson and Harney (1970), after studying the reaction with chromogenic reagents, attributed the initiation of roots in mung bean cuttings to the presence of chemical substances tentatively identified as phenolic compounds. Similarly, several workers (Bose et al., 1970 : Basu et ai., 1975 ; Roy et al., 1973) are of the opinion that the phenolic compounds act as synergists to the auxin action in root formation. In the present study too, the greater rooting observed in J. grandiflorum and J. sambac cuttings can be attributed to the presence of the higher amounts of phenolic compounds than that found in J. auriculatum cuttings, where comparatively a poor rooting was observed. 5.4 Survivability of transplanted rooted cuttings. As observed in case of the rooting of cuttings the maximum survivability of rooted cuttings (67.67) was obtained in J. grandiflorum, a higher percentage of survivability of cuttings was found in hardwood (65.28) cuttings as compared to 70 other types of cuttings. The softwood cuttings of J.auriculatum resulted is a higher percentage of survival (77.67) when compared to other types of cuttings. The Indole-3-butyric acid at 4000 ppro resulted in the highest percentage of survival of rooted cuttings (82.07) whereas in the control, it was only 39.41 per cent. Among different NAA concentrations, 4000 ppm resulted in a higher mean survival (64.19) percentage. At the highest concentration (6000 ppm) IBA showed a decrease in the survival percentage. These results are in conformity with the findings of Singh (1979), Singh and Motial (1981) Bhattacharjee and Balakrishnan (1983). From the interaction effects, it is observed that the J. sambac semi-hardwood cuttings treated with 4000 ppm of IBA, resulted in the maximum survival percentage (91.00). The hardwood as well as the softwood cuttings, treated with 4000 ppm of IBA exhibited in the survivability percentage of 87.67. In J. grand!florwn. hardwood cuttings treated with 4000 ppm of IBA resulted in a higher percentage (86.67) of survivability. In J. auriculatum, softwood cuttings treated with 4000 ppm of IBA and NAA showed 67.67 per cent survivability. The higher percentage of success after transplantation in the field can be attributed mainly to the possession of more number of primary and secondary roots as well as higher number of sprouts and leaves. CHAPTER-VI VI .SUMMARY The investigations were carried on the propagation aspects of some Jasminuin species at the University of Agricultural Sciences, Dharwad, during 1991-92, The effect of IBA at 0, 2000, 4000 and 6000 ppm and NAA at 0, 2000 and 4000 ppm concentrations on different types of cuttings {Hardwood, semi-hardwood and softwood) in J. grandiflorum, J. auriculatum and J. sambac cuttings were studied with an aim to find out the optimum combination of the above two factors. Observations on rooting factors, morphological parameters and biochemical characters viz., starch, total sugars, total nitrogen, carbohydrate to nitrogen ratio and the total phenols were studied. The salient findings of the investigation are suinmarised below. 1. In J. grandiflorum hardwood cuttings with IBA 4000 ppm gave the highest percentage (90.0) of rooting, more number of primary roots and secondary roots, longest root length and more dry weight of roots. The same treatment exhibited better shoot parameters. Soft wood and semi- hardwood cuttings were next in their performance. 2. In i7. grandi f lorum and J .auriculatum, the softwood cuttings when treated with IBA 4000 ppm gave higher percentage of rooting (78.42). However, a poor root formation was IZ noticed in its hardwood cuttings. 3. In J. sambac, semi-hardwood cuttings with IBA 4000 ppm exhibited highest percentage of rooting (90.0) as well as in other root and shoot parameters. 4. The cuttings of both J. grandiflorum and J. sambac contained the higher amount of total sugars, reducing and non-reducing sugars, higher C/N ratio and lower nitrogen than in the cuttings of J. auriculatum. 5. The phenolic compounds, were found in higher amounts in both J. grandiflorum and J. sambac as compared to J. auriculatum. 6. The rooted cuttings of all the three species of jasmine treated with IBA at 4000 ppm survived better and established well as compared to the other treatments. On the basis of these investigations, it may be concluded that J. grandiflorum, J. auriculatum and J. sambac can be propagated by hardwood , softwood and semi-hardwood cuttings, respectively, by treating the cuttings in a solution of IBA 4000 ppm concentration for 10 seconds by employing quick dip method and subsequently planting them in the field under partial shade. 73 Future line of work 1. INTRODUCTION No page of human history antedates the use of essential oil in perfumes and cosmetics. Their story would seem to be as old as the story of man on the earth. Fragrance has from the begining of world been appreciated by man. Jasmines are one of the most important flowering plants widely cultivated for their attractive fragrant flowers and concrete extraction. The flowers of jasmine are used for making garlands, adorning hair by women, religious and cererr,.jnial functions, for production of essential oil and perfumery. There is an increasing demand for jasmine concrete in the international market for its use in perfumery and cosmetic industry. Jasmine belongs to the family oleaceae and the name is derived from Arabic word of "Yasmin" meaning fragrance. The genus Jasminmncomprisina of 20 genera and more than 200 species is dispersed throughout the warm parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and Pacific region with only one representitative in North America (Bhattacharjee, 1980). However a large number of species are centred round the area comprising the Himalyas, China and Malaysia, About 40 species are recorded in India (Anon, 1959), The countries which grow jasmine on conmiercial scale are France, India, Italy, Moracco, Sicily, Spain and Egypt, In India Jasmine is cultivated throughout the country over an area of about 8000 ha, India produces flowers worth rupees 8-10 crores annualy (Muthuswamy and Shanraugavelu, 1982), In India, Tamil Nadu, K*rnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and Bihar are the states which grow jasmine on commercial scale (Bhattacharjee, 1980), In Kamataka, jasmine is cultivated in about 1522,9 ha with an approximate annual flower production of 7614,5 tonnes (Anon., 1985), Among the jasminum species with fragrant flowers, four species viz, Jasminum grandiflorum L,, J, auriculatum Vahl, ,J, samba c Ait,, and jj, flexile Vahl are commercially important as a source of fresh flowers or for the extraction of perfume. The essential oil content among the different species of jasmine ranges from 0,14 to 0,34 per cent. The basic compounds reported in jasmine oil are Indole, ; quinoline, 2_methyl . qtxinoline, methyl anthranilate, methyl N-methyl anthranilate, methyl N-acetyl anthranilate, alkylated pyridines and alkylated nicotinates (Diwakar and Bhupal Rao, 1980), Jasmine flowers occupy important position in the commercial floriculture of the country. But this crop has received little attention in the field of genetic improvemento In nature, a large variation in floral characters exists among the different species of jasmineo The study of quantitative traits and their association with yield and other characters is of paramount importance in any selection programme. Correlation studies of phenotypic traits and environmental factors are useful tools in making selections in plant breeding. The sign and magnitude of correlation based or. yenotypic traits will help the breeder in enhancing the rate of selection response. In plant breeding several methods may be used to increase the genetic variability within a crop followed by selection procedures to identify useful genotypes. One of the main method attempted to achieve this is cross breeding, where plant breeder tries to combine beneficial characters from different sources into one genotype. Mutation breeding on the other hand makes use of the possibility of altering genes by exposing seeds or other plant parts to chemical or physical mutagens. Today mutation breeding, notably that of vegetatively propagated plants is one of the accepted methods available to the breeder to improve the crop. For various reasons vegetatively propagated crops are highly suitable for application of mutation breeding methods. The generally high degree of heterozygosity which causes a complex inheritance of genetic factors as well as freequent polyploidy - both serious handicaps in convent- ional breeding, are advantageous in mutation breeding as large variations can often be observed in the irradiated planto Mutation breeding is the only method available to create large variability in plants which are exclusively vegetatively propagated and where seeds are hard to set^ As seed setting is very difficult in most of the jasmine species, the only alternative left to improve the crop is through mutation breedings In any mutation breeding programme, IDcr) ^^ ^^ important parameter as doses close to LDc^ ^^s effective in inducing mutation. With this background in view experiments were conducted with the following objectives: 1. to study the variation in flower characters among the different species of jasmine^ 2, to correlate various quantitative traits with the flower weight so as to enhance the rate of selection response^ 3. to find out the LDc^-, dosage of gamma radiation for different species of jasmine cuttings and 4, to study the rooting response of jasmine cuttings irradiated with different doses of gamma radiation. To meet this demand there is a need to improve the yield and essential oil content by the way of breeding, As a result of extensive research some promising clones with high yields of flowers and concrete have been released. But the improvement of a crop is a never ending process and there is still lot of scope to improve the flower yield and recovery of essential oil by the way of evaluation of germplasm, selection, crossing and mutation. Thus in the present study an attempt has been made to study the variability so that the genotypes with desirable characters may be used for further improvement programme by the way of selection or hybridization resulting in development of new genotype with the required desirable characters. Besides an attempt has been made in this study to know the nature and magnitude of association of different characters with yield which will help to simplify selection process. Besides crossing, mutation breeding is another method available for plant breeder to increase the genetic variability in the crop. The ability of mutation breeding in creating variability in a plant is undisputed (Broertjes and Vanhartan, 1978), It is also a known fact that the 59 doses close to ID^^. are most effective in inducing mutation< Thus an attempt to know the LDj.^ dose for different species of jasmine has been made in the present study. In this chapter the results for the different aspects obtained during the course of the experiment have been discussed under seperate sub-headings, 5,1 Variability for floral characters among genotypes The presence of variability for different characters among the genotypes gives ample scope for crop improvement. The mean values of different characters of different genotypes have been computed (Table 1 and Fig 1 to 3) and also represented through metroglyph graph (Fig 4), In the present study, analysis of variance revealed highly significant variation among the genotypes for all the characters studied, viz, corolla tube length, number of petals per flower, diameter of the flower, width of petal, length of petal, length of style, length of anther, length of flower bud, width of bud, weight of hundred flower buds and weight of hundred flowers. However, all the genotypes had the same number of anthers. Similar variations for different characters in jasmine have been reported by Khan and Muthuswamy (1969), Khan _et al, (1970) Muthuswamy et al. (1972), Thangaraj (1977), 60 Thangaraj et aj..(l981) and Thangaraj et a^.(1982). This clearly indicates that there is lot of scope for improvement of this crop by selection or through cross breeding. Though variations were observed for different characters, it should be remembered that environment also plays a important role in influencing the eaqsression of the characters, Allard (1960) has reported phenotypic expression to be the sum of a general population mean, a genotypic effect, an environmental effect and an interaction effect. Thus any predictions based on phenotypic measure may not give an idea about the actual breeding nature of these characters. Accurate estimates of components of variation will provide a basis for critically evaluating breeding and testing procedures. Thus it was necessary to partition the phenotypic variability in to genetic variability and environ- mental variability, Weber (1952) seperated genetic variance from total variance by the use •: environmental variance. Now it is a widely accepted fact that all bicxnetrical studies help in arriving at precise conclusions about the true breeding value of genotype. Thus the phenotypic estimates of different characters of different genotypes obtained in this experiment was divided into phenotypic and genotypic coefficients of variability and the heritability and predicted 61 genetic advance of yield and other characters were computed from the phenotypic estimates (Table 4 and Figo5), Phenotypic coefficient of variation (PCV) was more than genotypic coefficient of variation (GCV) for all the characters studiedo This indicates the influence of environment on the characters, Doijoide and Sulladmath(l986) observed in pumpkin PCV to be high than GCV for all the characters studied. However with the exception of length of flower bud, a difference of very low magnitude was observed between phenotypic and genotypic variances indicating a low interaction of characters with the environment. But for the length of flower bud the difference between phenotypic and genotypic coefficients of variation was high, indicating high influence of environment on the expression of this character. Maximum GCV was exhibited by length of style followed by width of petal, length of antiher, weight of hundred flowers, weight of hundred flower buds and length of petals. The GCV was moderate for the diameter of flower, length of corolla tube and number of petals per flower. These clearly indicate that the variations are genetically controlled with less environmental influence on the expressability of the character and hence are more stable. 62 The lowest level of GCV was shown by width of bud and length of flower bud indicating that these characters were less stable, Thangaraj (1982) reported wide variability for flower bud yield and low variability for flower bud weight, corolla tube length, and flower bud diameter in case of open pollinated seedlings of J, auriculatum. In Portulaca grandlflora Katsuyoshi and Harding (1969) observed much greater plant to plant variation for petal number than for petal length and width, 5,2 Heritability and genetic advance The effectiveness of any breeding programme depends not only on the extent of variability present for different characters between the genotypes and within the genotypes but also on the extent to which these variabilities are inherited by the progeny frcro the parent, i.e, variability should be genetically fixable and this is called "heritability", Thus estimating heritability will give an idea about the relative genetic strength and extent of transmitability of the character based on which predictions may be made. So heritability estimates for different characters were ccxnputed in the present study (Table 4 and Fig, 6), 63 Herltability estimates for all the characters studied was very high except in case of length of flower bud. The heritabil y estimates of corolla tube length number of petals per flower, diameter of flower, width of petal, length of petal, length of style, anther length, width of flower bud, weight of hundred flower buds and weight of hundred flowers were high indicating transmita- bility of these characters from parent to progeny. Because of large amount of genetic variance and high heritabilities considerable progress in modifying a character could be expected during the breeding programme (Legg and Lippert, 1966), The herltability estimate of length of flower bud though high, was ccxnparatively lower to that of other characters. The GCV for this character was also low indicating that this trait is influenced by environment and the expression is to some extent controlled by environment along with genes. Katsuyoshi and Harding (1969) observed high herltability for petal number, intermediate herltability for petal width and low herltability for petal length in _P. grandif lora. Herltability indicates the effectiveness with which selection of genotypes can be based on phenotypic performance. If genotypic variance is equal to the phenotypic variance (i.e herltability =100 per c^nt) then phenotypic performance 64 would be a perfect indication of genetic value. But even in such a hypthetical situation the heritability value in itself provides no indication of the amount of genetic progress that would result. The genetic progress would increase with an increase in variance. Therefore, the utility of estimates of heritability is increased when they are used in conjunction with genetic advance (Johnson et _al., 1955a). In the present study high genetic advance as per cent mean was recorded for length of style, width of petal, length of anthers, weight of hundred flowers, weight of hundred flower buds, length of petals and diameter of flower. These characters also had high heritability indicating that these characters were controlled by additive gene action. Hence there is ample scope for improvement of these characters. Corolla tube length, number of petals per flower and length of flower bud had a moderate genetic advance as per cent mean. Genetic advance was low for width of bud. Though width of bud had high heritability„ there seems to be not much promise in the improvement of this character due to its low genetic advance. The present findings are in agreement with the findings of Thangaraj et al. (1982), 65 5.3 Correlation analysis Every aspect of phenotype of a plant is the result of Interaction of a large number of factors. Plant characters are often correlated with each other either due to plelotrophy or due to genetic linkage» A knowledge of association between yield and other traits is therefore of pararooiint importance in selecting a plant type with better yield. In general high genotypic correlation coefficients were observed than the phenotypic correlation coefficients Indicating that there was a strong inherent association between the characters studied which was reflected in the phenotypic expression. Johnson et _al, (1955b) have also reported higher values of genetic correlation coefficients than phenotypic values between character pairs in soybean. The correlation studies indicated the weight of 100 flowers to be positively and significantly correlated with flower diameter, petal width, petal length, anther length, flower bud length, width of bud and 100 flower buds weight both at genotypic and phenotypic level. All these characters also had a high heritability. This explains that there is a strong correlation of these characters at phenotypic level and hence selection for these characters at phenotypic level 66 may result in a promising genotype with high yield. In other words, the genetic and environmental causes of correlation combine to give the phenotypic correlation. If both characters have low heritabilities, the phenotypic correlation is determined chiefly by the environmental correlation. If they have high heritabilities then genotypic correlation is more important one (Falconer, 1980), Thus while selecting for yield, the genotype showing maximum expression for these characters will be a high yielder. INTRODUCTION India, one of the oldest civilizations of the world, is the center of origin for several commercially important crops. Many crops have been cultivated from time immemorial, for which the country owes a lot to the farmers, who have preserved these crops over the years. One such crop is Jasmine. Jasmine (Jasminum species) belonging to the family Oleaceae, is one of the oldest traditional crops cultivated for its flowers in India. For the past many centuries, they adorned the gardens of Central Asia, Afghanistan, Iran, Nepal and many other tropical and subtropical countries. India exports jasmine flowers to the Asian countries like SriLanka, Singapore, Malaysia, Japan, U.K., USA, Scandinavian and Eastern European countries (Muthuswamy and Shanmugavelu, 1982), and of late to the Gulf countries. With the characteristic dark green foliage, elegant star like flowers with rich fragrance and hardy growth habit, they are highly valued ornamental plants for home gardens and commercial cultivation as well. Flowers and buds are used for making garlands, bouquets, vent, used as hair adornments and for religious offerings. They are also used for the production of perfumed hair oils and 'attars'. Jasmine oil is extracted from the flowers of the Spanish jasmine {Jasminum grandiflorum). Jasmine oil is regarded as unique as it blends well with other floral extracts, hence, highly valued throughout the world for producing high-grade perfumes, used in soap and cosmetic industries, and in flavouring mouth washes. The flowers are also used for decorating lampshades, buildings during religious ceremonies and for scenting food, wine and drinks. The odour of jasmine flowers cannot be imitated by any known synthetic aromatic chemical or natural isolates, thus giving it a unique status in the perfume world (Seemanthini et al., 1995). Much of the early work in jasmine has been on basic genetic studies, propagation, commercial cultivation, extraction of oil and crop improvement, which has resulted in the release of improved and high yielding varieties through selection and hybridization. Besides, there are many ecotypes under commercial cultivation, which remain enigmatic with respect to their origin and classification. Since, this crop is under cultivation from antiquity, lot of confusion exists in the identification of plants. Use of morphological traits viz., size and shape of leaf and intemodal length (Raman, 1955), flower bud shape, number of whorls (Bhatnagar, 1956), length of style and stigma (Mohammad et al, 1970; Indiresh et al, 1989) have also been documented in some species. Variations in economic characters have been reported by Singh and More (1982) among different varieties even within a species. These morphological characters currently available for evaluations are extremely useful but, most often, the desired phenotypic characters are phylogenetically inherited and highly influenced by environmental conditions. Hence, the data obtained by such evaluations are not easily understood at geneic level, often, resulting in maintenance of duplicate accessions. Moreover, the maintenance and evaluation of germplasm, which requires the plants to be grown to a suitable developmental stage for screening, demands higher cost and enormous efforts in a perennial crop like jasmine. One approach to reduce the cost is to develop a 'core collection' (Frankel and Brown, 1984), which represents the genetic diversity of a crop species and its relatives with minimum repetitions. The main purpose of the core fraction is to provide efficient access to the whole collection that should represent the diversity at hand. The immediate priority is to catalogue the available germplasm and identify the duplicates at various centers. In this regard, the recently developed DNA - based markers like Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP), Randomly Amplified Polymorphic DNA (RAPD), Amplified Fragment Length Polymrophism (AFLP) etc. provide excellent tools to study the genetic diversity, eliminate duplicates in germplasm, study genetic relationships, gene tagging, genome mapping, PVR (Plant Varietal Rights) purposes etc. These markers measure diversity at DNA level and are seldom influenced by environmental conditions. With this background information, an investigation entitled "Characterisation of important cultivars of Jasminum species using molecular markers" was carried out at the Plant Molecular Biology Laboratory, Division of Horticulture, UAS, GKVK, Bangalore with the following objectives. a. Standardizing the protocols for extraction of high quality DNA and RAPD protocols for amplification of DNA from Jasminum species. b. Estimating the genetic diversity and genetic relatedness of important cultivars of Jasminum species viz., Jasminum sambac Ait, Jasminum auriculatum Vahl., Jasminum grandiflorum Linn, and Jasminum multijlorum (Burm.f) Andr. The word 'Jasmine' is said to have been derived from old Persian name of 'Yasmyn' meaning fragrance (Bhattacharjee, 1980). The genus was originally reported to comprise about 200 species (Rendle, 1925; Bailey, 1958). But a critical analysis of species position revealed the number of true species to be only 89 (Veluswamy, et al., 1975), which lends credence to the reports of Cooke (1905). The distribution pattern of as many as 72 species in India, Malaysia and China provides a strong base to claim that India is one of the principal centers of origin of Jasminum species. Among these, about 40 species are reported to occur in India. Large number of species are however, centered on the area comprising the Himalayas, China and Malaysia (Veluswamy et al., 1975). Other countries where jasmine is cultivated are France, Italy, Morocco, Algeria, North Africa, Spain and Egypt. The cultivated jasmines fall into four species viz., Jasminum sambac, Jasminum auriculatum, Jasminum grandijlorum, and Jasminum multijiorum (Kakada), which have been reviewed in detail. In India, the three species Jasminum sambac, Jasminum auriculatum, and Jasminum grandiflorum have been mentioned in the ancient Tamil literature (500 B.C to 200 A.D) and India could have been an important center of origin for many of the Jasminum species (Veluswamy et al., 1975). Kamataka, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and West Bengal are the main states growing jasmine. In Karnataka, it occupies a prime position and is cultivated in 3720 hectares of land with a production of 9300 MT (Ramamurthy and Ramakrishnappa, 2000). 2.3 Taxonomy 2.3.1 Classification and Descriptive studies in Jasminum species Walpers (1852) classified Jasminum into two sections based on leaf lets and further classified the sections into sub sections based on calyx characteristics. Section I - Unifoliata. la. calyx: lobes subulate and elongate lb. calyx: subtruncate. Section II - Trifoliata Ila. Calyx: shortly dentate lib. Calyx: lacinate One of the earliest accounts of descriptive studies in 43 jasmine species was accomplished by Hooker (1882), who divided Jasminujti into two main groups as below. Groups (i) with simple leaves, calyx pubescent or glabrous, subulate or short. (ii) with compound leaves either trifoliate or imparipinnate Engler and Prantl (1897) cited about 160 species of jasmine in the tropical and subtropical regions of Asia, Africa, Australia and over 40 in India. They considered that the simple leaf was only the transformed terminal leaflet of the imparipinnately compound leaf. They grouped jasmine into four series: Section I - Unifoliata Section II - Trifoliata Section II - Trifoliata Section III - Alternifolia Section IV - Pinnatifolia In India, Gamble (1936) published description of 20 species occurring in Presidency of Madras and classified them based on Hooker's classification, of which the simple leaved species viz., Jasminum sambac and Jasmimm pubescens were categorized under the group - calyx pubescent, subulate and long. Compound leaved species like Jasminum auriculatum was grouped under- Leaves trifoliate, lower leaflets wanting and calyx lobes small; and Jasminum grandiflorum was categorized under- Leaves imparipinnate and opposite. Taxonomic descriptions of six species were made by Bor and Raizada (1946) and four species viz., Jasminum sambac, and Jasminum grandiflorum were considered for this study. Bailey (1947) gave the taxonomic description of 23 species of jasmine as well as the key for identification. Brief description of eight South Indian species of jasmine, has been given by Padmanabha Raja (1953). Anon., (1959) gave the description, medicinal uses and cultivation aspects of 13 species of jasmine. Apart from these species, distribution, flowering period, flower colour and odour and ornamental value of 18 other species were also listed. Wight (1963) gave the taxonomic description of 21 species along with good illustrations of Jasminum sambac, Jasminum grandiflorum and Jasminum auriculatum. 2.3.2 Chromosome number and mode of speciation in Jasmine Taylor (1945) in his work on the Cytotaxonomy and Phylogeny determined the basic chromosome number of this genus as X=13. Krishnaswamy and Raman (1948) recorded diploids, triploids and tetraploids in this genus. They reported that Truvantige' and 'Yellusuthu-mallige' were diploids (2n=26) and 'Dundumallige' was a triploid (2n=39). Two other species viz., Jasminum auriculatum and Jasminum grandiflorum as diploids (26). Raman (1955) reported that both allopolyploidy and autopolyploidy appear to have played a role in evolution of jasmine. Sharma and Sharma (1958) reported the chromosome number of J. granciijloviwi as 2n=26 and J. pubcsccns as 2n 39. Veluswamy (1981) listed the chromosome numbers of seven clones ('Long Round' i.e. 'Co-r, 'Long Point', 'Parimullai', 'Short Round', 'Short Point', SR-24 and SP- 15) in J. auriculatum and six clones of J. grandiflorum ('Bangalore', 'Coimbatore', 'Lucknow', 'Tenkasi White', 'Thimmapuram' and 'Triploid'). All of them had 26 chromosomes except for the triploid clone of J. grandiflorum, with 39 chromosomes. Raman (1955) also gave a schematic representation of the lines of differentiation in corollas of four varieties in J. sambac and from his studies on cytology, evolved a scheme for the possible course of evolution of different varieties and species of Jasmine and discussed the relationship between simple and compound leaves, and the origin in respect of leaves, calyx and corolla lobes. Sharma and Sharma (1958) stated that speciation in this genus has been principally affected by the structural alteration of chromosomes and continuous accumulation of these structural changes has been the main reason for the origin of new species, although polyploidy too has assisted to some extent initially, in the speciation of this genus. Rajendra Gupta and Sharma (1972) reported that polyploidy and gene mutation played a major role in the origin of various species in jasmine and that there is great scope for evolving new and still more attractive and fragrant jasmine bloom, continuing to bloom for a larger part of the year, and per)iaps containing more perfume in it. 2.4 Morphological studies of different species and varieties 2.4.1 Jasminum auriculatum. Vahl. Raman (1955) recorded differences in morphological characters (size in leaf and corolla lobes) in wild and cultivated forms as follows. Wild (cm) Cultivated (cm) Terminal leaf 3.0x2.0 7.0x3.5 3.0x2.0 Lateral leaf Corolla leaf 1.0x0.5 0.9 X 0.2 2.0 X 1.0 1.3x0.4 The percentage of fruit set was quite high in J. auriculatum (Bhatnagar, 1960). The loss in weight while opening was less in varieties of J. auriculatum as compared to the varieties oiJ.sambac. The per cent loss in weight ranged from 4 to 9 in the five varieties of J. auriculatum. Flowering was observed in this species from February to December with a peak blooming period from April to August (Raman et al, 1969). Five morphological variants were spotted in this species differing in important floral characters like diameter of open flower, weight of flower bud, corolla tube length, fruit set and style length. The occurrence of such variants has been reported to be either tlirough bud sports or chance hybridization and, this offered scope for improvement of cultivated types through hybridization and mutation (Mohammad AliKhan and Muthuswamy, 1969). 2.4.2 Jasminum gramiiflorum. Linn. Mohammad Ali Khaii et al., (1969) made a comparative account of morphological characteristics of triploid and diploid forms of J. grandijlorum. The triploid was found to be more vigorous with larger leaves and petals, longer peduncles and corolla tube. Fruit set was noticed only in the diploid. The observations recorded on the per cent loss in weight by Raman et al, (1969) showed no major difference between the diploid and triploid forms, though the size of the buds in triploid was more than double compared to diploid clone. They also found that this species flowered in all the twelve months of the year with peak flowering between July and January. A study was conducted (Veluswamy et al, 1973) with six types (five pink and one white), of which one (pink) was triploid and the rest were diploids. Considerable variations were noted in floral characters. Two promising clones were isolated. Fruit set was noticed in all the clones including the triploid in contrast with the findings of Mohammad AliKhan et al, (1969) who noticed fruit set only in diploids. However, these characters may change with enviromnental conditions. Furthermore, the actual identity of some cultivars is still in question, because similar cultivars grown in different areas often have various names (Lakshminarayana, 1980). The prime advantages of the morphological markers are simplicity, inexpensive assays, even from herbarium specimens and other dead tissues. Having effective means, by which cultivars could be identified and verified, is therefore, important. In this regard use of reliable gene markers is of great value. 2.6 Molecular markers 2.6.1 Protein markers Enzyme polymorphisms have been used successfully to identify cultivars in various fruit crops, where analysis is carried out based on the proteins extracted. From past three decades, enzyme polymorphisms have been successfully used to identify cultivars in various fruit species, including avocado (Goldring et ai, 1985), apple (Weeden and Lamb, 1985), loquat (Degani and Blumenfled, 1986), cherimoya (Ellstrand and Lee, 1987) and pineapple (De Wald et al, 1988). Enzyme polymorphism have also been used to distinguish hybrids from selfs (Degani and Gazit, 1984; Goldring et al, 1987; Degani et al, 1989) and zygotic from nucellar seedlings in citrus (Torres et al, 1982; Roose and Traught, 1988). Isozymes, as genetic markers, have been proven to be reliable, consistent and essentially unaffected by environmental conditions (Torres and Bergh, 1980; Bailey, 1983). Mango leaf isozymes of esterases, aspartate aminotransferase, acid phosphatases, and alkaline phosphatases were used to detect possible genetic variation among individuals of so- called clones (Gan et al, 1981). However, enzyme polymorphism in mango has not been examined systematically. Gan et al, (1981) and more recently by Degani et al, (1990) and Schnell and Knight (1992) have demonstrated the feasibility of using isozymes as biochemical markers in mango. Isozyme variation among mango trees of the same putative cultivar was described by Gan et al, (1981), thereby indicating that somatic mutation may occur frequently in certain mango clones. Enzyme polymorphisms were used by Degani et al, (1990) to differentiate among mango cultivars and to identify parentage of certain modem mango cultivars. Schnell and Knight (1992) have been able to differentiate zygotic from nucellar seedlings on the basis of enzyme polymorphisms. Although isozyme markers provide the basis for relatively simple tool for genetic analysis and linkage studies, it is unlikely that sufficient number of isozymes will be found to saturate the genome completely and uniformly (Tanksley, 1983). The enzymes extracted and subjected to electrophoresis are a tiny and probably non- representative sample of the total array of proteins present in them. Further, isozymes are influenced by stages of development and tissue used for extraction (Feret and Bergmann, 1976). 2.6.2 DNA based markers Among several of the recently developed DNA-based markers, Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism (RFLP), Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism (AFLP) and Randomly Amplified Polymorphic DNA (RAPD) markers provides excellent tools to study the genetic diversity, eliminate duplicates in germplasm, study genetic relationships, gene tagging, genome mapping, PVR (Plant Varietal Rights) purposes etc. These markers measure diversity at DNA level and are seldom influenced by environmental conditions. The most exciting feature of DNA based markers is the extent of detectable polymorphisms. The DNA content in higher plants is highly variable. Armuganathan and Earle (1991) estimated the DNA content in over 100 important crop species. DNA content varied from 0.30 picogram (pg) per 2C nuclei or 145 million base pairs (mbp) in Arabidopsis to over 50 pg or 24,255 mbp in leek. However, the DNA content of most of the intensively mapped diploid species (tomato, rice, arabidopsis) is in the range of 0.30 to 1.0 pg. Fraxinus americana L. (diploid), which belongs to the same family of Jasmine ('Oleaceae'), has a DNA content of 3.2 pg per cell (Bennett et al., 1982). Most higher plants have a considerable portion of DNA as repetitive non- coding DNA that is not transcribed. Species with large genomes have more repeated DNA and higher proportion of repeated DNA to single copy DNA (Tanksley and Pichersky, 1988). Thus, only small fraction of the total genetic variation at a DNA nucleotide sequence level reveals itself as a distinct trait, showing Mendelian inheritance. The degeneracy of the genetic code ensures that one in three nucleotide changes will not affect the amino acid sequence of protein produced. Thus, the great bulk of genetic variation at the nucleotide level may not have any detectable expression at phenotypic level. It is this genetic variation that is expressed as DNA- based polymorphism. Restriction Fragment Length Polymorphism This method involves digestion the DNA of the subjected genome with cleaving restriction endonucleases (Grodzicker et al., 1974), fractionating the fragments electrophoretically, and then preferentially visualizing fragments containing particular homologous sequences by hybridizing them to specific DNA probe. RFLP analysis has been used in construction of linkage maps for many important crops such as lettuce (Landry et al, 1985), maize (Helentjaris et al, 1986), Arabidopsis (Chang et al., 1988), pepper (Tanksley et al, 1988), rice (McCouch et al, 1988), tomato (Paterson et al, 1988; Tanksley et al, 1988), potato (Gebhardt et al, 1989), lentil (Havey and Muehlbauer, 1989), Brassica sp. (Slocum et al, 1990; Landry and Hubert, 1991; Song et al, 1991), barley (Huen et al, 1991) and sorghum (Whitkus et al, 1992). However, RFLP analysis is relatively labour-intensive, expensive and involves use of radioactive chemicals, which are harmful to the users. Amplified Fragment Length Polymorphism (AFLP) The technique involves restriction of the DNA and ligation of oligonucleotide adapters, selective amplification of sets of restriction fragments and gel analysis of the amplified fragments. AFLP technique is a very effective tool to reveal restriction fragment polymorphisms, generate fingerprints of any DNA regardless of the origin or complexity and construct genetic marker maps (Vos et al, 1995). This technique has been successfully followed in lettuce (Hill et al, 1996), tea (Paul et al, 1997), neem (Singh et al, 1999) and eucalyptus (Marques et al, 1999). However, AFLP as a technology is intensive and involves use of radioactive probes. Randomly amplified polymorphic DNA (RAPD) markers This method of DNA polymorphism analysis was developed independently by two different groups (Welsh and McClelland, 1990; Williams et aL, 1990). This procedure detects nucleotide sequence polymorphisms in a DNA amplification-based assay using only a single primer of arbitrary sequence using Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR). In this reaction, a single species of primer binds to the genomic DNA at two different sites on opposite strands of the DNA template. If these sites are within amplifiable distance a fragment is amplified. The presence of each amplification product identifies complete or partial nucleotide sequence homology, between the genomic DNA and the oligonucleotide primer at each end of the amplified product On an average, each primer will direct the amplification of several discrete loci in the genome, making the assay an efficient way to screen for nucleotide sequence polymorphism between individuals. The major advantage of this assay over RFLP method is that there is no prior requirement for DNA sequence information of the genome. The protocol is also relatively quick and easy to perform and uses fluorescence in lieu of radioactivity (Williams et al.^ 1992). Because the RAPD technique is amplification-based assay, only nanogram quantities of DNA are required and automation is feasible. These RAPD protocol is simple and fast. The procedure involves extraction of DNA from different accessions, by any of the standard protocol and amplifying the DNA by PCR using random primers. The profiles of accessions are scored for presence or absence of bands directly by running agarose gel, stained with ethidium bromide. Since RAPD approach is being adopted in the present study much of the literature reviewed pertains to use of this techmque. 15 RAPDs for discriminating cultivars in ornamentals Matsumoto and Fukui (1996) reported that, RAPD markers were successfully tested for the identification of nine rose cultivars and three clonal plants. All the cultivars were identified by using only three primers. Moreover, unique RAPD marker bands also distinguished individual cultivars.
