Seventeen olive cultivars, including oil and table olive cultivars originating from throughout the Mediterranean area, were screened using RAPD markers. The results indicated a high degree of polymorphism in the germplasm examined. Forty random decamer primers were screened. Seventeen of these produced 47 reproducible amplification fragments useful as polymorphic markers. Each of the' 17 cultivars was discriminated with a few primers. Results were analysed for similarity among the cultivars and a cluster analysis was performed. These analyses revealed two main groups, one comprising primarily small-fruited cultivars grown mainly for oil production and the other characterized by having large fruit. There was no apparent clustering of olive cultivars according to their geographic origins. Another attempt on molecular characterization of olive varieties using RAPD markers was carried out by Wiesman et al. (1998). Primers were identified and used in combination to discriminate between different varieties. Significant biodiversity was demonstrated among 'Nabali' olive trees, suggesting that the grouping known as 'Nabali' is actually a mixture of genetically distinct variants. On the other hand, RAPD profiles of selected variants of 'Souri', revealed a high degree of similarity, indicating that these variants represent environmental phenotypes of the same genome. Molecular differences were demonstrated between the 'Nabali' group variants and 'Souri'. Other more recently developed or introduced varieties showed individually distinct RAPD profiles. Iqbal et al., (1995) showed that RAPD markers have the potential to reveal genetic similarity among plants. Profiles of thirteen rhododendron hybrids, species and cultivars were analyzed to study their genetic relationships. The cluster analysis grouped together varieties and/or hybrids in accordance with their known genetic relationship. For instance, two varieties of Rhododendron yakushimanum, var. 'Mist Maiden' and var. 'Ken Janeck', clustered together while R. yakushimanum var. 'Pink Parasol' clustered with a hybrid of 'Pink Parasol' x Rhododendron smirnowii. These three varieties and the hybrid then clustered with R. smirnowii. Similarly, the other hybrids with common parents showed a closer genetic relatedness with each other than with other rhododendrons. The genetic relationship revealed from cluster analysis on the basis of RAPD profiles was similar to their known genetic makeup. Nucleic acid extracts from 23 alstroemeria cultivars were amplified with 8 random decamers by PCR. The distinctive RAPD patterns generated from these cultivars could be used as genomic fingerprints to establish the identity of a given genotype. The 'Orchid' and 'Butterfly' types were clearly separated in distinct subclusters in a phyllogram obtained by unweighted pair group method analysis (UPGMA) of the genetic distances. The 'Hybrid' types were distributed in two major subclusters, reflecting the diversity of the parental species used to generate the population. This phyllogram conformed to expectations based on the available pedigree data (Joseph et al., 1997). Fingerprinting of thirty four Pelargonium genotypes was carried out on the basis of their amplification profiles. Multiple band profiles were generated using twenty three selected primers, leading to ninety six markers (76 % of them polymorphic). The results clearly indicate that RAPD markers are suitable for Pelargonium varietal identification (Renou ei al:, 1997). Whereas, in Heliconia species, which are polymorphic in nature with a large number of cultivars, the identification, has been primarily based on morphological differences. The percentage similarity among Heliconia species, cultivars and hybrids were determined. Data from 11 primers indicated that RAPD technology is useful in distinguishing species and cultivars of Heliconia, Using a single 10-mer primer distinct RAPD profiles for 16 cultivars of H. psUtacorum could be generated. The triploid cultivars of H. psUtacorum showed identical RAPD profiles with 10 different primers, suggesting that they are of same genotype (Prakash et al., 1998). 18 RAPD markers were successfully used to generate a RFLP marker, which could discriminate with 100 % accuracy, between semi-double and double-flower phenotype in carnations of both Mediterranean and American groups. RAPD marker co-segregating as homozygous for recessive allele was cloned and used as RFLP probe for further use in discrimination (Scovel et al., 1998). Lim et a/., (1999) reported on the genetic closeness of various species of Vanda using RAPD markers. Strap leaved Vanda species (including Vanda sanderiana) and Aseocentura miniatum were more closely related to each other than to the terete-leaved Vauda species studied. RAPD analysis supported the suggestions that terete-leaved Vanda terete and Vanda hookeriana be classified in the separate genus Papilionathe and that Vanda sanhoriana should remain in the genus Vanda. Like wise, Starman et al., (1999) investigated the DNA amplification fingerprinting to evaluate the genetic relationship among 11 cultivars of poinsettia. Thirty one per cent of the bands were polymorphic and distinguished among cultivars. Use of RAPD markers in related horticultural crops Twenty-five accessions of apple, representing eight cultivars ('Golden Delicious\ 'Delicious\ 'Gala', 'Jonagold', 'Jonathan', 'Fiorina', 'Fior di Cassia', and 'Imperatore Dallago') have been characterized with RAPDs. The reliability of the method was tested by analyzing separate scions of the same clone and also by comparing different accessions of the same cultivar. Using two separate ten base primers, it was possible to obtain a distinctive fingerprint for each of the cultivars. The method is simple, rapid and should provide a useful system for documenting the identity of clonal material (Mulcaliy et at., 1992). Identification of apple cultivars was also done by using RAPD markers by Roller et al (1993). Eleven apple cultivars were differentiated using RAPD markers obtained by the PGR. Cheng et al., (1996) identified co-dominant RAPD markers tightly linked to fruit skin colour in apple. A simple genetic basis for the red/yellow skin-colour polymorphism in apple was verified using DNA markers. Bulked segregant analysis identified one 10-mer base oligomer that generated different fragments in each of the bulks. After testing the primer in four populations, two fragments were associated with red skin colour and another two fragments associated with yellow skin colour. In the cross 'Rome Beauty' X 'White Angel' population, two fragments were associated with red skin colour: one fragment designated as Al (1160bp) was from 'Rome Beauty' and another fragment A2 (llSObp) was from 'White Angel'. Progeny possessing both fragments, or one of them, had red fruits. Both parents displayed an alternate fragment, al (1230 bp), associated with yellow-skinned fruit. In three other crosses tested, only fragment Al co-segregated with red skin colour and two fragments, Al and A2 (1230 and 1320 bp, respectively), were associated with yellow skin colour. Identification of avocado cultivars with three RAPD primers (Lewis, 1992) homologous to regions of the chromosomal DNA was carried out. Variety 'Fuerte' and 'Edranol' were found to be closely related compared to 'Haas'. Similarly, identification of raspberry cultivars by RAPD analysis was carried out by Parent et al. (1993). A fast and simple test to accurately characterize the various cultivars of raspberry of the Quebec certification programme was developed based on RAPD analysis using minute quantities of plant DNA. raspberry cultivars amplified with 19 different primers. A combination of three primers was chosen for its ability to differentiate all the cultivars. Novy et al. (1994) identified varietal misclassification and regional divergence in cranberry {Vaccinium macrocarpon (Ait.) Pursh), using RAPD technology to characterize 22 cranberry varieties. Twenty-two decamer primers amplified 162 scorable DNA fragments, of which 66 (41%) were polymorphic. On the basis of these 66 silver-stained RAPD (ssRAPDs), 17 unique profiles were identified rather than the expected 22. Fourteen varieties had unique ssRAPD profiles, while the remaining eight were represented by three ssRAPD profiles. Permutational analyses of the data suggested that the observed ssRAPD profile duplications were examples of varietal misclassification. Further analyses identified two ssRAPD markers that were found only in Eastern varieties (from Massachusetts and New Jersey) and not in Wisconsin varieties. The varieties differing on an average by 22 bands, ssRAPDs were shown to be useful in varietal identification and the assessment of genetic diversity in cranberry. Pooler and Scorza (1995) reported that the genetic analysis of polymorphic RAPD markers could be complicated by the sensitivity of the RAPD-PCR procedure and the dominant nature of the markers. Using a unique system of six doubled haploid peach parents and their seven resulting F1 hybrid populations, they found that 18 % of the 50 scorable bands from 25 primers did not follow expected inheritance patterns. Bands present in parents were not transmitted to the progeny, or non-parental bands appeared in the progeny. Differences in RAPD patterns were also observed between haploids and spontaneous diploid bud sports on the same tree. Because peach is a long-lived clonally propagated crop, it is possible that somatic rearrangements occur which would lead to this unexpected inheritance of RAPD markers. Such anomalous patterns indicate that RAPD markers should be used cautiously in peach mapping and genetic diversity studies. Identification of cultivars and validation of genetic relationships in Mangifera indica L. was carried out using RAPD markers (Schnell et al., 1995). Twenty-five accessions of mango were examined for genetic markers with 80 decamer random primers. Of the 80 primers screened, 28 gave reproducible, polymorphic DNA amplification patterns. Eleven primers were selected from the 28, for the study. The number of bands generated were primer and genotype dependent, and ranged from one to ten. No primer gave unique banding patterns for each of the 25 accession; however, ten different combinations of two primer-banding patterns produced unique fingerprints for each accession. A maternal half-sib (MRS) family was included among the 25 accessions to see if genetic relationships could be detected. RAPD data were used to generate simple matching coefficients, which were analysed phonetically and by means of principal coordinate analysis (PCA), while the randomly selected accessions were scattered with no apparent pattern. RAPD markers have been used to characterise cocoa clones representing the three main cultivated subpopulations: Criollo, Forestero and Trinitario. The use of thirteen different primers of arbitrary sequence proved to be effective to analyse the extent and nature of the polymorphism. Nei's similarity matrix was used to highlight the distinction between the wild cocoa species and cultivars (Wilde et al., 1992). Rong et al, (1995) studied the effectiveness of RAPD analysis for cultivar identification of persimmons {Diospyros kaki) by using 10 base primers. A protocol of reproducible RAPD analysis for persimmon was established by determining suitable buffer and optimum concentrations of DNA polymerase, MgCb, primer and dNTP. Among these elements, the type of buffer and concentration of DNA polymerase and MgCh were found important for reproducibility of RAPD. By this reproducible protocol, two primers (OPA-6 and OPA-8) were selected from among 20 primers as being most effective for cultivar identification. The fifteen cultivars tested were completely distinguishable from each other by RAPDs, using OPA-6 or OPA-8. Furthermore, two bud mutants of cv. 'Hiratenenashi', i.e.' Tonewase' and 'Sugitawase', showed different DNA patterns with a few additional minor bands with OPA-6 primer. It may be possible to identify persimmon mutants by this method. In addition, polymorphisms among 11 Diospyros species were observed by RAPD, using OPA-10 primer. The same method revealed little polymorphism among intraspecific levels of D: kaki or D. lotus. Damasco et al, (1996) detected dwarf off-types in micropropagated Cavendish {Musa spp. AAA) bananas using RAPD markers. A RAPD marker specific to the dwarf off-type from micropropagation of Cavendish group cultivars 'New Guinea Cavendish' and 'Williams' was identified following an analysis of 57 normal and 59 dwarf plants generated from several micropropagation events. Of 66 random decamer primers used in the initial screen, 28.8 per cent revealed polymorphisms between normal and dwarf plants. Primer OPJ - 4 (5'-CCGAACACGG-3') amplified a 1.5 kb band which was consistently present in normal but absent in all dwarf plants of both cultivars. Reliable detection of dwarf plants was achieved using the marker, providing a suitable means of in vitro detection. Other micropropagation-induced RAPD polymorphisms were not associated with the dwarf trait. Levi and Rowland (1997) identified blueberry cultivars and evaluated their genetic relationships using RAPD technology. Fifteen high bush (or high bush hybrid) blueberry cultivars (Vaccinium corymbosum), two rabbiteye blueberry cultivars (K ashei) and one southern low bush (K darrowi) selection from the wild were examined using seventeen 10-base RAPD primers in polymerase chain reactions. Fifteen RAPD markers resulting from these reactions were chosen to construct a DNA fingerprinting table to distinguish among the genotypes included m this study. Similarity values were calculated based on 132 RAPD bands, and a dendrogram was constructed based on the similarity matrix. The V. ashei cultivars and the V. darrowi selection grouped out separately from the V. corymbosum cultivars as expected. However, estimates of relative genetic similarity between genotypes within the V. corymbosum group did not agree well with known pedigree data and, thus indicated that RAPD data did not accurately assess the genetic relationships of cultivars within this species. Ye et al, (1998) reported on DNA fingerprinting utilizing RAPD polymorphisms to investigate the relationship among 16 grapevine cultivars and sports thought to have arisen from these cultivars. From 53 primers, a total of 464 bands were generated, of which 29 % were common to all genotypes tested. Cluster analysis classified all tested cultivars into two main groups {Vitis vinifera L. and Vitis x labrusca Bailey) as expected. No polymorphism was detected among known clones of 'Chardonnay' or 'Pinot Noir'. Genetic chaiacterisation and relatedness among California Almond cultivars and breeding lines were detected by RAPD analysis by Bartolozzi et al. (1998). The genetic relatedness among 17 almond genotypes and one peach genotype was estimated using 37 RAPD markers. Genetic diversity within almond was found to be limited despite its need for obligate outcrossing. Three groupings of cultivar origins could be distinguished by RAPD analysis. A similarity index based on the proportion of shared fragments showed relatively high levels of similarity (0.75 or greater) within the almond germplasm. The level of similarity between almond and the peach was 0.424, supporting the value of peach germplasm to future almond genetic improvement. Genetic chatacterisation of gooseberry germplasm was carried out by Lanham and Brennan (1999) using RAPD, ISSR and AFLP markers. These markers were used to fingerprint and to examined genetic diversity among twelve genotypes of the gooseberry (Ribes grossularia subgenus Grossularia). AFLP generated unique profiles for each genotype. ISSR could not distinguish three of the genotypes, 'Whinham's Industry' and 'Whitesmith' and 'Leveler', whereas RAPD could not distinguish 'Whinham's Industry' and 'Leveler'. Similarity matrices and dendrograms illustrated the genetic similarities between the different genotypes but some clustering varied, depending on which marker type was being used. The results imply that the European cultivated gooseberry has a narrow genetic base and that further improvement to this crop species may require the introduction of additional germplasm into breeding programmes. Rojas et al. (1994) reported RAPD markers and genetic polymorphism in tomato. Five tomato varieties were analysed using the polymerase chain reaction technique with arbitrary primers. The two primers used showed differences in the patterns obtained by means of genome amplification of the varieties. The 'Reverso' primer with 16 bases showed greater intravarietal polymorphism than the 'Universal' primer with 17 bases. Boiano et al., (1995) characterized tomato lines using RAPD- PGR and flow cytometry. Fifteen Fi hybrid lines and their parents were characterized. The RAPD-PCR analysis, based on amplification of markers generated by random arbitrary 21-mer primers, allowed all but two of the lines to be distinguished. Flow cytometry detected individual differences in the DNA content of the majority of the lines. The two techniques were complementary. A study was conducted to know randomly amplified polymorphic DNA in bulb onion and its use to assess inbred integrity by Bradeen and Havey, (1995). They reported the polymorphism (RAPD) between two inbred onion lines ('Alisa Craig' and 'Bright Yellow Globe'), demonstrated their Mendelian inheritance and, discriminatory abilities among the released inbred onion lines. Poor agreement was observed between data sets based on genetically characterized and uncharacterized RAPD markers. The analyses based on genetically characterized RAPD markers revealed that contamination, in addition to drift and/or selection, likely contributed to differences among inbreds. However, RAPD markers did not distinguish confidently among four related inbreds. Maass and Klaas (1995) determined intraspecific differentiation in garlic (Allium sativum L.) using isozyme and RAPD markers. About 48 accessions were selected for a RAPD analysis and data were used to construct dendrograms. Based on the dendrograms and in conjunction with some morphological features, an infraspecific classification of garlic with four major groups was proposed. In agreement with the results of other workers, A. longicuspis lies within the range of the species A. sativum. Numerous forms with varying degrees of domestication were part of the longicuspis group, from which presumably the more derived cultivar groups have originated. A diagnostic test to confirm interspecific Allium hybrids using RAPD from crude leaf DNA extracts was carried out (Dubouzet et al., 1996). Six random decamer primers (OPD 5, 7,14,15,18 and 19) generated characteristic RAPD profiles from leaf DNA of Allium tuberosum cv. 'Tender Pole'. DNA amplification with four random decamers (OPD 14,15,18 and 19) by polymerase chain reaction produced a total of 186 bands; of these, 54 were common bands found in both parents and the putative hybrid, 49 bands were found in the putative hybrid and the male parent only (M bands), 58 bands were found in the female parent and the hybrid plants, and 25 were unique bands found only in the hybrids. One of the seven putative hybrids had no M bands, indicating that it had no relationship to its putative male parent and that it may have been the product of an unwanted pollination. Tivang et al, (1996) detected variation among and within artichoke (Cynara scolymus L.) cultivars and breeding populations using RAPD markers. Variation among individual heads (capitula) from three artichoke cultivars and two breeding populations were evaluated using RAPD markers. One vegetatively propagated cultivar ('Green Globe'), two seed-propagated cultivars ('Imperial Star' and 'Big Heart') and two breeding populations were examined. Two to thirteen polymorphic bands were observed for twenty RAPD primers, which resulted in 178 scored bands. Variation was found within and among all cultivars and breeding populations, indicating that all five groups represent heterogeneous population with respect to RAPD markers. The RAPD heterogeneity observed within clonally propagated 'Green Globe' is consistent with phenotypic variability observed for this cultivar. Khandka et al, (1996) detected polymorphism and identified DNA markers for asparagus cultivars by using RAPD technique. DNA polymorphism among five asparagus {Asparagus officinalis) cultivars ('Imperial , Snow , Steline , UC-157 and 'Larac') was detected via RAPD analysis. Thirty-one. decamer primers were tested, and twenty-six of them yielded amplification products. Fourteen primers gave products with at least one polymorphic DNA fragment. Among a total of 119 amplified fragments, 33 were polymorphic, these RAPD markers enabled the identification of asparagus cultivars. Unique markers for cultivars were identified. The pairwise marker difference between cultivars ranged from 0.08 to 0.17. A phenogram of the genetic relationship based on RAPD fits with the known origin of the cultivars. 2.8 Determining Genetic Purity Walker and Werner (1997) attempted to analyze the 'Cherokee' rose for its putative hybrids 'Silver Moon' and 'Anemone'. RAPD analysis carried out with sixteen primers revealed forty reproducible polymorphisms. Khandka et al, (1996) detected polymorphism and identified DNA markers for asparagus cultivars by using RAPD technique. DNA polymorphism among five asparagus {Asparagus officinalis) cultivars ('Imperial , Snow , Steline , UC-157 and 'Larac') was detected via RAPD analysis. Thirty-one. decamer primers were tested, and twenty-six of them yielded amplification products. Fourteen primers gave products with at least one polymorphic DNA fragment. Among a total of 119 amplified fragments, 33 were polymorphic, these RAPD markers enabled the identification of asparagus cultivars. Unique markers for cultivars were identified. The pairwise marker difference between cultivars ranged from 0.08 to 0.17. A phenogram of the genetic relationship based on RAPD fits with the known origin of the cultivars. 2.8 Determining Genetic Purity Walker and Werner (1997) attempted to analyze the 'Cherokee' rose for its putative hybrids 'Silver Moon' and 'Anemone'. RAPD analysis carried out with sixteen primers revealed forty reproducible polymorphisms. Based on the number of RAPD bands resolved in 'Anemone' (98) and 'Silver Moon' (90), their respective similarities to 'Cherokee' rose were 69.4 % and 22 %, suggesting a 'Cherokee' rose parentage for 'Anemone' but arguing against one for 'Silver Moon'. RAPD markers were used to assess the relationship among species, cultivars and hybrids of lilac. Thirteen random primers were used to examine 87-130 bands per cultivar or hybrid. The percentage band sharing among Syringa x chinensis cultivars 'Alba', 'Saugaena' and 'Red Rothomagensis', and S. x persica was surprisingly high. It was felt that RAPD markers were very useful for assessing the origin of cultivars and hybrids of many plant species (Marsolais et al, 1993). Padgett et al, (1998) investigated the plants intermediate in appearance between Nuphar microphylla and N. variegata (Nymphaeaceae) that have long been assumed to be the result of hybridization. They employed multivariate analyses of morphology, pollen fertility studies, and RAPD markers to test the hypothesis that Nuphar x N. rubrodisca represents a natural interspecific hybrid between N. microphylla and N. variegata. Examination of 15 morphological characters demonstrated the intermediacy of N. x rubrodisca between N. microphylla and N. variegata, and the pollen data revealed a markedly lower mean pollen viability in N. X rubrodisca (23%) compared to the other two species (91 and 86%, respectively). One of the primers, RAPD-12-12 (5'-ACCACCTGGCTC- 3'), generated a product specific to the F1 and male parent (HB), and enabled the female (HA) to be discriminated from the hybrid. In tomato, 12 primers were screened to discriminate two inbred lines, Morioka 20 (M) and Ottawa 48 (O), and four showed polymorphism. One out of four enabled the female line (M) to be distinguished from the F1 (MXO). Thirty primers were screened to segregate another pair of parents, 0 and Veeking (V), and five generated polymorphism. One of them enabled the F1 to be discriminated from O. Four to seven percent of the total PGR products showed polymorphism suggesting that there were close relationships among the parental lines. Rom et al. (1995) also used RAPD technology to test purity control of F1 hybrid tomato. Polymorphism between the parents generated paternal- specific RAPDs, enabling a clear distinction to be made between hybrids and their maternal parents. Most of the variation found by polymorphism (19 out of 24 bands) was between subspecies (Wolff and Richards, 1998). The genetic relationships of Viola species in the subsection Patellares were analysed using RAPD method. Viola species from the series Chinensis and Pinnatae, and five hybrid lines formed a cluster, which divided into three subgroups. Viola species in the series Variegatae and a hybrid line were clustered into a second group. The clustered subgroups from RAPD analysis are in agreement with the conventional taxonomy based on morphological characters. Therefore, RAPD analysis was effective providing an alternative classification system to identify genotypes and morphological characters (Ko e/a/., 1998). RAPD markers were used in cashew to assess the diversity among the varieties and hybrids released in India by Murali (1999). Of the one hundred and twenty random primers screened, ten were chosen to score for 157 bands. The results indicated that the diversity among cashew cultivars and hybrids was moderate. In an attempt to study genetic diversity among fifty mango varieties (Hemanth, 1999), eighty primers were screened, ten of which gave 139 bands. UPGMA analysis based on Jaccard's coefficient revealed a moderate to high degree of genetic diversity among mango cultivars. Molecular classification of Mains involving 20 wild species and 27 cultivars was done using RAPD markers (Dunemann et al., 1994). DNA fingerprinting generated with preselected random primers were analysed for polymorphic amplification fragments, and coefficients estimating genetic similarity were calculated on the basis of about 50 polymorphic RAPD loci in each set of genotypes. Closely related species from section 1 (Mains) was clearly distinguishable from those of sections 111 (Eriobolus) and IV (Chloromeles). A high degree of genetic diversity was found at the molecular level among both different apple cultivars and wild species of the genus Mains. The results gave additional evidence for the hypothesis that M. pnmila and M. sylvestris were involved in the origin of the cultivated apples. In another study, Yae et al., (1995a) classified Mains domestica cultivars using random amplified polymorphic DNA markers. Forty apple (M. pnmila) cultivars were compared By RAPD analysis using 16 random primers. Of the 139 clear and reproducible bands, 106 were polymorphic. From these polymorphisms, the cultivars were divided into 6 groups by cluster analysis. Group 1 contained 'Rail's Janet', 'Fuji' and the bud mutations of 'Fuji'; group 11 contained 'Sikaiichi', 'EarliBlaze', 'Delicious' and its strains formed group IV; 'Jonathan', 'Jonared ', 'Kogetsu' and 'Mollies Delicious' formed group V; and group VI contained only 'Spur Golden Delicious'. Xiang et al., (1996) analysed peach rootstock cultivars using RAPD markers. Eighteen peach rootstock cultivars, most of Prunus persica, were screened for diagnostic RAPD markers using synthetic decamer oligonucleoide primers. Based on combined banding patterns, all 18 rootstocks using 40 RAPD markers produced a dendrogram of genetic relatedness in good agreement with their putative pedigrees. The first major bifurcation in the dendrogram divided these rootstock cultivars into two groups according to their resistance or susceptibility to root-knot nematodes {Meloidigyne incognita and M.javanica). Graham and McNicol (1995) carried out an examination of the ability of RAPD markers to determine the relationships within and between Rubus species. RAPD markers were generated from 13 different Rubus species in order to assess the degree of similarity between species from the important subgenera Idaebats, Eubats and Anoplbats. All ten primers revealed scorable polymorphisms within both the closely related and the genetically diverse individuals. Some 372 markers were generated and scored from the material analysed. Estimates of similarity, dendrograms and principle coordinate analysis were calculated, with the results generally being in agreement with previous classifications of the species studied, confirming the validity and usefulness of the RAPD method. However, amongst the species studied, R. madlaei (subgenera Idaebats) proved more diverse and grouped in with both the subgenera Idaebats and Eubats at only 26 per cent similarity. Machado et al. (1996) detected genetic relationships among 39 Mediterranean mandarins {Citrus deliciosa Tenora) genotypes using RAPD markers. Some 111 amplification products were identified using 21 random primers. Genotype-specific RAPD markers were also found, mainly in known hybrids. UPGMA cluster analysis revealed a low level of genetic variation between accessions of Mediterranean mandarins, whereas their hybrids with other Citrus species showed greater genetic dissimilarity. Twenty accessions yielded similar patterns, suggesting either they could be a single clone, or that the technique was not able to detect genomic variation. However, for the other specimens, genetic polymorphism was easily detected by RAPD, although the genetic variation between accessions was quite low. The large number of hybrids and the low level of polymorphism between accessions support the hypothesis that Mediterranean mandarins are all true hybrids of common mandarins (Citrus reticulata). PCR-based RAPD markers were used to study the extent of redundancy (duplication of genetic materials) within a germplasm collection of butterhead lettuce. PGR amplification using 13 oligonucleotide primers generated 93 polymorphic bands. The variation obtained from these data was compared with variation detected at the DNA level and each was positively correlated. Results demonstrated that RAPD analyses might serve as a major source of information for separation of closely related accessions, especially when integrated with phenotypic measures. Overall, the insanum accessions were more diverse than those of S. melongena. The RAPD results were similar to electrophoretic isozyme survey performed on the same accessions. Yang et al., (1995) characterized celery genome using DNA-based genetic markers. To characterize the celery (2n=2x=22) genome, 126 cDNA clones and 340 random 10-mer primers were used to generate RFLP and RAPD markers between two cultivated types. Of the RAPD markers tested, 28 per cent were single and low-copy, and 26 per cent were high-copy sequences. Eighty-two (23%) of the 340 primers tested yielded useful RAPD markers, but only 3.8 per cent of the amplified products were polymorphic. Nei-Li similarities were computed and used in UPGMA cluster analysis. Accessions and subspecies were clustered into groups corresponding to the three species, but some accessions of some subspecies were most closely related to accessions belonging to other sub species. Value for Nei-Li similarities suggested that Chinese cabbage is more likely to have been produced by hybridization of turnip and pakchoi than as a selection from either turnip or pakchoi alone. A total of 162 bands were generated across all 39 genotypes. Among them 100 (62%) were polymorphic and the remaining 62 (38%) were monomorphic. The 100 polymorphic fragments of the total 162 bands were proved to be very reliable and useful as polymorphic markers. Eight RAPD markers were utilized in variety discrimination of eight watermelon genotypes. Using DNA polymorphisms, the two major clusters were resolved and one of these was subdivided into three clusters. Each sub-group was characterized using morphological and genetic characteristics of the respective genotype. Of the 15 primers tested, all except one (primer 275) directed the amplification of polymorphic products. A total of 162 amplification products were generated across all 39 genotypes. Among the 162 fragments, 35 (21%) appeared to be reliable polymorphic markers. From the dendrograms constructed by UPGMA based on the comparison of RAPD markers, four clusters were resolved. Samec and Nasinec (1996) reported the use of RAPD technique for the identification and classification of Pisum salivum L. genotypes. Amplification with eight decamer primers generated 149 polymorphic products. Genetic similarities of RAPD profiles were estimated using Jaccard's coefficient and the data processed by cluster analysis (UPGMA). Each genotype was clearly identified and separated from the others. These results show that RAPD technology is a rapid, precise and sensitive technique for identification of pea genotypes. Restriction fragment-RAPD (RF-RAPD) analysis, which used DNA predlgestcd with restriction enzymes, increases the detection of polymorphisms compared to normal RAPD analysis. Whilst RAPD analysis detects polymorphism at the primer-binding site, RF-RAPD detects polymorphism of restriction enzyme recognition sites in addition to primer binding sites. Nine additional polymorphic bands were detected between Capsicum annuum cv. HAD 210 and C. annuum var. fasciculatum cv. Yatsufusa using RF-RAPD techniques employing five restriction enzymes in combination with six primers. Different primer-restriction enzymes combinations produced different RF-RAPD bands. Inheritance of RF-RAPD markers agreed well with segregation data based on Mendelian genetics. A total of 59 polymorphic fragments were generated by 35 primers and among them, 13 RAPD markers were uniformly present or absent in all the accessions belonging to C. annuum. C. annuum, C. chinense and C. pubescens were more closely related to one another than to C. baccatum. Cluster analysis separated most genotypes of C. annuum into two main groups. Except for Namjin , Hatvani' and '3-25-27', which were each grouped separately. Assessment of genetic relationships among sexual and asexual forms of Allium cepa were done using morphological traits and RAPD markers (Thieny et al., 1997). A major joint analysis using RAPD and morphological characters was undertaken for the assessment of genetic diversity and crop classification among Allium cepa genotypes. A morphological study describing growth and development was carried out on nested sampling (34 accessions) from two geographical origins (European or tropical) and of different plant status (improved varieties or local ecotypes). Four primers generated 24 scorable DNA bands, which gave individual fingerprinting for representative accessions of both onions and shallots. The results indicated that, the seed propagated shallot is more closely related to onion than to vegetatively propagated shallots and, moreover, reveal geographical structure of genetic diversity. 2.10 Crop improvement Warburton et al. (1996) utilized RAPD markers in identifying genetic linkages to genes of economic interest in peach. The identification of molecular markers linked to economically important traits for use in crop improvement is very important m long-lived perennial species. Genetic distances among 136 cultivars of peach were estimated using 94 markers. These markers were used to form a dendrogram, which yielded twelve clusters. The domestic cultivars were grouped into three clusters, while the exotic cultivars in nine clusters. The results obtained using RAPD method implies that to expand the variability, additional germplasm should be obtained from exotic locations. 2.11 Phylogenetic relationship Application of RAPD markers proved effective for the study of phylogenetic relationships in Digitalis. A total of ninety-one highly reproducible bands amplified with four arbitrarily chosen decamer primers were obtained. Different statistical approaches for RAPD generated data, such as distance and parsimony methods, family clustering and analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA), indicated that these molecular markers were taxonomicaiiy informative (Nebauer et al., 2000). RAPD generated clusters did not always agree with the taxonomic classification based on phenotypic traits. When the two sub-sections of the genus (sub- genera Mangifera and Limns) were analysed separately, the classification more closely agreed with traditional taxonomic relationships. The study was carried out to investigate several factors affecting RAPD band patterns in apple and to establish the optimum RAPD conditions. The optimum composition of PGR reaction solution for RAPD assay of Mains domestica [M. pumila] was 10 ng template DNA, two units Taq polymerase, 10 ng primer, 50-100pM dNTPs, 2.5 pi lOX reaction buffer. Fifty cycles of amplification produced best RAPD band patterns Staub et al (1996) reported the sources of potential errors in the application of RAPD's in cucumber. The influence of tissue age, pathogen infestation, intrapopulation contamination and PGR conditions were assessed as sources of error in RAPD analysis. DNA from young, uninfected tissue from cucumber (lines 0421 and H-19) leaves provided the most consistent results. Gucumber plants infected with Sphaerotheca fnliginea showed variation in RAPD banding patterns compared with those of uninfected plants. Differences in banding patterns were detectable when DNA from the lines was mixed at dilution ratios of 20:1 but not 50:1. Differing lots of commercially available lOX reaction buffer, MgGh stock solutions and Taq DNA polymerase affected RAPD banding patterns and overall yield. MATERIALS AND METHODS An investigation on "Characterisation of important cultivars of Jasminum species using molecular markers" was carried out at Plant Molecular Biology laboratory, Department of Horticulture, University of Agricultural Sciences, GKVK, Bangalore, with the objectives a) Standardizing the protocols for extraction of high quality DNA and RAPD protocols for amplification of DNA from Jasminum species. b) Estimating the genetic diversity and genetic relatedness of important cultivars of Jasminum species viz., Jasminum sambac Ait, Jasminum auriculatum Vahl., Jasminum grandiflorum Linn, and Jasminum multiflorum (Burm.f) Andr. The leaf materials were collected from TNAU, Coimbatore, IIHR, Bangalore, HC&RI, Periakulam, AC&Rl, Madurai and farmers fields in Nilakkottai, TamilNadu, and Hoovinaliadagalli, Mysore in Karnataka. The leaves collected were sealed in brown paper covers and later oven dried in the laboratory and once again sealed in polythene bags. Recently matured young leaves were collected for isolation of DNA. 3.2.2 DNA Isolation Sample preparation The leaf sample for DNA extraction was prepared by following Tai and Tanksley (1990) method with some modifications. Recently matured leaves from jasmine plants were collected and dried at 30 -35° C for 20 hours. The dried leaves were powdered by using a 'Remi' mixer for 45 to 60 seconds. The dried leaves can be stored in sealed polythene bags for over two months. 45 3.2.3 Extraction protocol The powdered leaf sample was sieved using a 60-mesh sieve to obtain fine powder. Porebski et al.^ (1997) method was followed with modifications. The protocol standardized for DNA extraction from jasmine leaves is given below. a) 500 mg of the leaf powder with 20 ml extraction buffer [20 mM EDTA (pH . 8.0), 100 mM Tris-Base (pH 8.0), 1.4 M NaCl, 3 % CTAB and 200 mg Poly Vinly Pyrollidone with I % p-mercaptoethanol] was incubated on a water bath at 65-70° C for 30 minutes with gentle shaking. b) The mixture was then placed in ice bath and 10 ml of cold chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (24:1 v/v) was added and the contents were gently mixed and spun at 6000 rpm for 20 minutes. c) The supernatant was carefully removed and 10 ml of chloroform: isoamyl alcohol (24:1 v/v) was added and the contents were mixed and spun at 6000 rpm for 15 minutes. The supernatant was carefully pipetted out. This step was repeated for three times d) To the aqueous phase, half the volume of 5 M NaCl was added and gently mixed, followed by addition of 0.8 times the volume of cold propanol to precipitate the DNA. The solution was kept at 4° C over night to accentuate the precipitation of DNA. e) The mixture was spun at 8000 rpm for 20 minutes to pellet the DNA. The pellet was washed with 70% aqueous ethanol and dried in a vacuum drier for one hour. f) The pellet was dissolved in 300 pi of TE buffer (10 mM Tris HCl and ImM EDTA pH 8.0) and incubated with RNase 3 pi (10 pi /ml) on a water bath at 37° C for over night. g) The proteins were removed by extracting the solution with equal volume of phenol, then phenol: chloroform and finally chloroform. 46 h) To this 0.8 times the volume of cold propanol was added to precipitate DNA. The precipitation improved by keeping at -40° C for 1 hour and then spun at 8000 rpm for 20 minutes to pellet the DNA. i) The precipitate was dissolved in 300 pi of TE buffer and to it l/io"' volume of 3 M Sodium acetate was added and left overnight. The supernatant was collected after 24 hours by spiiming at 8000 rpm. j) The DNA was quantified by using "Hoefer's Dynaquant" and verified by electrophoresis on 1.2 % agarose gel (GIBCO BRL). The above procedure was suitable for extraction of good quality DNA from three Jasmine species namely J. sambac, J. grandiflorum and J. multiflorum. However, J. auriculatum yielded a viscous DNA, at the first precipitation step. The precipitate DNA did not dissolve completely in TE buffer. Hence, the procedure was modified to extract high quality DNA form J. auriculatum as given below In step 'a' lower quantity of leaf powder (250 mg) was used. After step 'e' the sample was dissolved in TE buffer (300 pi) and then put through steps 'a' to 'j', as mentioned above. This resulted in clean high quality DNA as verified by spectrophotometric analysis. 3.3 RAPD protocols 3.3.1 DNA amplification The PGR procedure outlined by Williams et al (1990) was followed with slight modifications. A single decamer of arbitrary sequence was used in each PGR reaction. PGR reaction conditions were optimized to obtain informative and reproducible fingerprint profiles for jasmine. Amplification reaction were carried out in 25 pi reaction mixture containing template DNA (25 ng), primer (5 pmols), MgGb (1.5 mM), one unit of Tag polymerase (Bangalore Genei and GeneTaq) with 10 X buffer (IX 50 mM KGl, 10 mM Tris-HGl, 1.5 mM MgG^ and 0.1 % Triton X-100) and 150 pM dNTPs (10 mM each, Finnzymes and Fertas). RESULTS The results of the study titled "Characterisation of important cultivars of Jasminum species using molecular markers" are presented in this chapter under the following headings. 4.1 Standardization of protocol for extraction of high quality DNA 4.1.1 Sample preparation Leaf samples were collected from different locations. Recently matured leaves (from to h"' node from the apex) were collected in each cultivar. Young leaves were not preferred and mature leaves were also avoided as they contain high phenols and polysaccharides. The leaf samples were collected from the new flushes emerging after pruning and before the onset of reproductive phase, as the flowering phase is associated with high phenolic content. Leaf samples were packed in brown paper covers and brought to the laboratory. They were evenly spread in the hot air oven and dried at a temperature of 35° C for 20 hours. Prolonged drying of samples for more than 24 hours and high temperature of 45° C and above resulted in poor DNA yield. The dried leaves could be stored in polythene bags, while the leaf powder was not. Powdering was done using a 'Remi' mixer. About 300-400 mg/g of fine powder was obtained after passing through 60-niesh sieve. 4.1.2 DNA isolation Isolation of DNA was done by following CTAB method outlined in Materials and methods (3.2.3). Extractions of DNA from different amounts of leaf powder (125 mg, 250 mg and 500 mg), with different volumes of extraction buffer (15 ml and 20 ml) were tried along with different concentrations of PVP (1 %, 2%, 3 % and 4 %). For J. sambac, J. grandijlorum and J. multiflorum^ 500 mg leaf powder using 20 ml extraction buffer, 1 % PVP resulted in good quality, high molecular weight DNA (<30 ha kb) which was confirmed by gel eiectrophoresis. The DNA yield varied from 8 to 84 |ig/500 mg of leaf powder. In the case of J. auriculalum, DNA isolated was highly viscous and sticky. High quality of DNA was obtained by reducing the sample size to 250 mg with 20 ml extraction buffer and 1 % PVP. 4.2 Standardization of RAPD protocols 4;2.1 Amplification conditions For the diversity study, experimental conditions for amplification were optimized based on the protocol outlined by Williams el al. (1990) and Welsh and McClelland (1990) with slight modifications. Amplification conditions: Each cycle of PGR consisted of the following three steps, which were repeated for 45 times. Initial stand separation or hot-start at 95° C for five minutes. i) Denaturation at 94° C for one minute. ii) Annealing at 35° C for two minutes. iii) Extension at 72° C for two minutes. Final extension at 72° C for five minutes. Different concentrations of template DNA (15 ng, 25 ng and 50 ng), MgClz (1.0 mM, 1.5 mM, 2.0 mM and 2.5 mM) and dNTPs (100 pM, 150 pM, 200 pM and 250 pM) were tried with the same amplification conditions. A concentration of 25 ng of template DNA, 1.5 mM of MgCb and 150 pM of dNTPs was found optimum for obtaining intense, clear and repeatable banding pattern. In all the cases Taq DNA polymerase (1 unit/sample) was used. However, large changes in concentration (i.e. in order of magnitude) of template DNA did affect the amplification, with too little DNA causing either reduced or no amplification of small bands and too much DNA producing a smear effect. Therefore, accurate quantification of the DNA was essential for optimal amplification. Fluorometry provided a more accurate measure of DNA concentrations. 51 4.2.2 Primer selection One hundred and forty Operon random ten-base long single stranded primers were screened using the genotype 'Triploid'. Eighty of which gave atleast one band. Thirty-five primers giving atleast 5 bands/primer were selected for further screening. Eight of the thirty-five primers that gave on an average ten strong, repeatable bands per primer were chosen for measuring diversity. From these primers, 134 bands were amplified in a repeatable manner and were scored. The number of polymorphic amplification products revealed by these primers ranged from 13-26 and the size ranged from 0.3 kb to 3 kb. The RAPD gel profiles of 32 jasmine cultivars using eight Operon primers are presented in Fig. 2a to 2h. 4.2.3 Data scoring and analysis Amplified fragment, named by the primer used and molecular weight in base pairs (bp) were scored for their presence or absence (Echt et al,, 1992). Further, a fragment was counted only if it was intense, clear and strong. Diffuse and/or veiy weak fragments were not scored as such fragments have been reported to possess the greatest propensity for poor reproducibility (Heun and Helentjaris, 1993). Fragments were scored by three persons independently and then compared for avoiding errors. 4.3 Estimating genetic diversity and genetic relatedness in jasmine cultivars 4.3.1 Diversity patterns Statistical analysis The scored band data was subjected to statistical analysis using STASTICA. The cluster analysis on cultivars was based on dissimilarity measure, squared Euclidean distances (SED). This gives the geometric distances in the multidimensional space. DISCUSSION The results of the investigation "Characterization of important cultivars of Jasminum species using molecular markers" are discussed under the following headings. 5.1 Standardization of the protocol for the extraction of high quality DNA in jasmine 5.1.1 Sample collection Jasmine is a perennial flower crop and puts forth new flushes round the. year. The plant is pruned once annually. Although the collection of leaf material can be done anytime in a year it is important to get high quality and quantity DNA, relatively pure for restriction digestion, which is adequate for RAPD analysis. Polysaccharides and phenols pose a major problem in plants because they are difficult to separate from DNA. Polysaccharides like contaminants, which are undetectable by most criteria, can cause anomalous reassociation kinetics (Murray and Thompson, 1977). Jasminum leaves collected during flowering phase posed difficulty in isolating pure DNA. The better period to collect the leaf samples was from new emerging flushes after pruning. 5.1.2 Sample preparation No doubt, use of liquid nitrogen (Franklin and Arkesh, 1991; Porebski et al, 1997) yields good quantities of high quality DNA but the use of liquid nitrogen presented some problems. Once exposed to liquid nitrogen, it is imperative that the tissue not be allowed to thaw before extraction. If large populations of plants were to be extracted the tissue would have to be stored frozen or processed and then stored in a freezer (Jennifer and Paul, 1990). Storage of tissue in freezers may lead to problems involving lack of space. The requirement of manual labour to process frozen tissue may be inefficient and inappropriate when dealing with large populations. In addition, plant materials, which are only available from distant sources, must be shipped frozen at high cost. To circumvent these problems with liquid nitrogen, it has become standard practice to lyophilize plant tissue before extraction. In this freeze dried state, it is not necessary to keep the tissue in a freezer. The tissue lends itself to mechanical processing, and shipping of such materials is relatively easy and inexpensive. Unfortunately, lyophilizers are quite expensive and have only a limited capacity. Moreover, lyophilization requires several days to complete and errors in operation may result in degradation of DNA. Drying leaves using hot air oven or food dehydrator (Tai and Tanksley, 1990) is a new alternate method by which plant tissue can be inexpensively dehydrated, efficiently processed and extracted to consistently yield high molecular weight DNA comparable to lyophilized and fresh frozen material. The present attempt to standardize a simple, cheap arid yet efficient method of sample preparation for extraction of DNA from large number of samples yielded favourable results. The DNA extracted from dried leaf material was of high quality (OD 260/280 = 1.6 to 1.8) adequate for PGR amplification and RAFD analysis. Further, the leaf samples once dried (not powdered) can be stored for over three months in sealed polythene bags without degradation in the quality of DNA. This is the first attempt in Jasmine and offers enormous flexibility for scientists in large- scale sample preparation and storage. Prolonged drying of leaves (beyond 30 hours) greatly reduced the DNA yields and quality. This can be attributed to formation of irreversible complexes between polyphenols and DNA as reported by Wilfmger (1999). 5.1.3 Extraction protocol DNA extraction from tissue needs to be simple, inexpensive and effective when many samples are used, such as in population studies. Polysaccharides, polyphenols and tannins pose a major problem in plants because they are difficult to separate from DNA. Many of the initial problems encountered in the extraction of high quality DNA have been attributed to these contaminants (Murray and Thompson, 1980). Jasmine leaves are rich in polysaccharides and polyphenols. We have sampled most recently matured leaves, which is also rich in carbohydrates, and other secondary prpducts. The protocol involved use of 3 % CTAB and high salt concentrations to remove polysaccharides, the use of PVP (1 %), to remove polyphenols, an extended RNase treatment and a phenol-chloroform extraction. Similar protocol was also followed for extraction of high quality DNA in mango (Hemanth, 1999), cashew (Murali, 1999) and grapes (Wang et al., 1999). The above protocol was found to be sufficient for PCR amplification in J. sambac, J. grandiflorum and J. multiflomm. But in the case of J. auriculatum, we were uniformly unsuccessful in attempts to extract high quality DNA. The main obstacle preventing the extraction of high quality DNA from dried green leaves was difficulty in redissolving isopropanol precipitated DNA in TE buffer (therefore accurate quantitation of DNA could not be done). The resulting suspension was very sticky and almost impossible to draw. A brownish yellow coloured substance, presumably one or more of the polyphenols present in J. auriculatum, often copurified with the DNA, even after rigorous purification. This phenomenon has also been observed in other crops such as cocoa (Jennifer and Paul, 1990), bhendi (Kochko and Hamon, 1990) and cotton (Franklin and Arkesh, 1991), where polyphenols were shown to copurify with DNA. A modified Porebski et al. (1997) method was standardized for J. auriculatum. This protocol involved re-extraction of DNA from the TE buffer suspension, with extraction buffer. Repeated washings with chloroform-isoamyl alcohol resulted in clean DNA, consistently amplifiable by PCR. Probably, the higher PVP and repeated washings with chloroform-isoamyl alcohol may have removed the interfering contaminants. In problematic species with high amount of polyphenols use of two to five per cent PVP was also found beneficial in extracting high quality DNA (Wilfinger, 1999). The present protocol developed for sampling of recently matured leaves, drying for 20 hours at 35° C, use of one per cent PVP and three per cent CTAB in the extraction buffer has consistently given adequate high quality DNA suitable for RAPD analysis. However, average yield ranged from 8-84 pg/SOO mg of powdered leaf tissue. The variation in DNA yield is perhaps partly due to the subtle differences in the leaf maturity leaf constituents, despite sampling young leaves. This was comparable with the similar results obtained by Murali (1999), 157 bands from ten primers in cashew, Shin et al (1995), 162 bands from fifteen primers in watermelon. Jasmine belongs to the family 'Oleaceae' with basic chromosome number X=13. Fraxinus americana L., belonging to the same family of Jasmine, with X=23, has a DNA content of 1.6 pg (Bennett el o/., 1982) or about 770 million bp. Assuming that Jasmine genome is half this size, our analysis of diversity based on 134 random markers is expected to saturate the genome at a density of a marker for every 3 million bp in diploids and 4.5 to 6 million bp in triploid and tetraploids, respectively. However, this saturation is adequate to make meaningful statements about diversity/relatedness among Jasmine cultivars. Similar assessment of genetic diversity based on fewer than 134 RAPD markers have been reported on crops with equal or more DNA content like, olive (Fabbri et al., 1995), mango (Hemanth, 1999) and asparagus (Khandka e/o/., 1996). A perusal of the dendrogram with 32 Jasmine cultivars clearly indicates moderate genetic diversity despite including only commercial cultivars under four species viz. Jasmitium sambac, Jasminum auriculatum, Jasminum grandiflorum, and Jasminum multifJorum. As commercialization results in narrowing genetic diversity, (which is moderate in the present study) inclusion of the other native species is expected to greatly enhance the diversity estimates. Jasmine is believed to have originated in India. It is generally propagated through vegetative means, as there is no seed set in J. sambac, negligible in J. grandiflorum and J. mullijlorum. Karmakar and Srivastava (1987a and 1987b) observed meiotic abnormalities such as sticky chromosome and precocious and tubular cytoplasmic connections in J. grandiflorum, as the reason for negligible seed set. Raman (1955) reported that both allopolyploidy and autopolyploidy appear to have played a role in the evolution of jasmines. Mohammad Ali Khan et al. (1970) opined that spontaneous mutation, natural crossing and simple autopolyploidy might be the possible causes for the origin of the variations in J. sambac. In J. auriculatum, the occurrence of variation might have been brought either through bud sports or chance hybridization as reported by Mohammad Ali Khan et al. (1969). The results of the present investigation based on DNA markers, in general, indicate the clustering of diploids and triploids in the same group. This fact lends support to polyploidization as one of the important reasons for moderate diversity observed in the present investigation. Further, the human activity in selection and migration of desirable variants to different parts of the country has also contributed in maintaining diversity. This is evident by the wide distribution of cultivars with in a species in the dendrogram (Fig. 3). Apart from providing a measure of diversity, the RAPD analysis could also provide a genetic profile, characteristic to a cluster in which the individuals share common morphological trait or place of release. In a perennial crop like Jasmine such a broad association between the cluster and morphological traits, however loose are valuable in further crop improvement programmes. Hence, in the ensuing paragraphs an attempt made to establish a relationship between the cultivars based on RAPD analysis and their relationship with respect to morphological characters and location is discussed. Clustering of cultivars based on Ward's coefficient revealed unique grouping of J. sambac and J. grandiflorum. All the North Indian cultivars of J. sambac grouped' together, which are diploids and have strong fragrance compared to the South Indian cultivars. The North Indian cultivars come to flowering late in the year with a peak period during April to August. Also these cultivars have lower shelf life. The dendrogram reveals grouping of these cultivars viz., 'Bale Japani', 'Iruvantige', 'Butt Mohra', 'Mysore Mallige', 'Single Mohra', 'Khoya', and 'Khoya Large' into single entity. The second cluster consists of two subciusters, which include all the four species namely, J. auriculatum, J sambac, J muhiflorum and J. grandiflorum. This group includes diploid and triploids. They also include fragrant and non- fragrant types like the highly fragrant J. atiricit/alum and ./. sawhac, and non- fragrant type like 7. muhiflorum. Among the J. auriculatum cultivars, 'Co-1 Mullai' and 'Periakulam Mullai' are closer, which leads to speculation that they both have a common ancestor. Likewise 'Pari Mullai' and 'Manamadurai Mullai' may have a common ancestor, as 'Manamadurai Mullai' is a local cultivar prevalent in the Southern districts of Tamil Nadu, while 'Pari Mullai' is a clonal selection from the types in these regions. Similar is also the case with 'Short Point' and 'Nilakottai Mullai'. Cultivars 'Long Point' and 'Co-2 Mullai' are placed close together in the dendrogram, which supports the view of Abdul Khader and Kumar (1995), that 'Long Point' is one of the parents for 'Co-2 Mullai'. Among the J. sambac cultivars, 'Khoya', 'Khoya Large', and 'Single Mohra' are placed in proximity. Mohammad Alikhan et al. (1969) observed the cultivars 'Khoya', 'Khoya Large', and 'Single Mohra' resembled each other closely, probably synonyms of single variety. Similarly, 'Mysore Mallige', 'Rameswaram Mallige' and 'Nilakottai Mallige' are close to each other. They all are triploids, have vigorous growth habits and high yielders. The cultivars 'Rameswaram Mallige' and 'Nilakottai Mallige' were collected from the farmer's field in the same district. The morphological characters are similar, which leads to speculation that they are synonyms of the same cultivar, confirmed by the banding patterns. The reason for 'Ramanathapuram Mallige' present along with J. grandiflorum could not be explained. Among the J. grandiflorum cultivars, 'Co-1 Pitchi', 'Nilakottai Pitchi', 'Periakulam Pitchi', 'Arka Surabhi', 'Co-2 Pitchi', 'Bangalore Pitchi' and 'Lucknow Pitchi' are placed together. While 'Co-1 Pitchi' and 'Arka Surabhi' are clonal selections from 'Lucknow Pitchi', 'Co-2 Pitchi, is an induced mutant from 'Co-1 Pitchi'. Their morphological data also confirms this view. Morphologically 'Nilakottai Pitchi', and 'Periakulam Pitchi' resemble 'Co-1 Pitchi', which is prevalent widely in Tamil Nadu. Hence, the local cultivars 'Nilakottai Pitchi', and 'Periakulam Pitchi' may be synonyms of 'Co-t Pitchi" only; Hence, 'Lucknow Pitchi' is the most probable common ancestor for these cultivars. The cultivars 'Coimbatore Pitchi', 'Thimmapuram Pitchi', 'Triploid' and 'Tenkasi White Pitchi' are placed in a separate cluster. These cultivars are in cultivation over a long period in Tamil Nadu. All these cultivars are moderate yielders, and recovery of jasmine oil and concrete is also high (Velusamy et al, 1973). Bhattacharjee (1980) reported the origin of J. grandiflorum as Subtropical Northwest Himalayas, Nilgiris, Pulney and Tinnevelly Hills (Coimbatore is present in Nilgiris region, Tenkasi is in Tinnevelly hills, Lucknow in Northwest Himalayan region). Hence, it may be safely concluded that 'Lucknow Pitchi' 'Coimbatore Pitchi' and 'Tenkasi White Pitchi' are the major lines of evolution in J. grandiflorum. The mode of speciation of different species reveals significant results. J. auriculatum originated in South India (Bhattacharjee, 1980), and the species is in the process of speciation as per our findings. J. sambac also originated in South India and may have been introduced into North India. This is further strengthened by the fact that the diversity among North Indian cultivars is lower than South Indian cultivars, which also include several triploids. But in the case of J. grandiflorum, there might have been atJeast three independent types in India Viz. 'Lucknow Pitchi' 'Tenkasi White Pitchi' and 'Coimbatore Pitchi' cultivars, and their variants, mostly due to natural mutations and rarely by chance hybridizations. The cultivars in this species do set seeds, though rarely. We could find migration of North Indian types towards South India due to introductions, but not the reverse. Since only two cultivars of J. multiflorum are included in the study, which are present along with the other species, strong suggestions could not be made. Further, there is neither literature nor other cultivars are available. It is very evident from these results that there is an underlying similarity between morphological characters and the geographical locations where they are grown with the clusters generated based on RAPD markers. Similar associations between morphological characters, geographical locations and RAPD profiles have been reported in cashew by Murali (1999), in mango by Hemanth (1999), in peach by Warburton et al. (1996), in onion by Thierry el al. (1997) and in strawberry by Graham et al. (1996). This association, however loose, should aid in early identification of suitable types for breeding purpose. At the same time, the robustness of this approach can be questioned, as there are individuals in the same cluster with diverse morphological characters. Perhaps, with higher number of markers and more collections it is possible to overcome this discrepancy. Based on the outcome of the present investigation, we conclude that RAPD as a molecular marker for fingerprinting as well as analysis of genetic diversity and genetic relationships in jasmine as effective, precise and more efficient than morphological markers. The salient features of the investigation are summarized below. 6,1 Standardisation of the protocol for the extraction of DNA from jasmine 6.1.1 Sample preparation Selection of recently matured leaves and its dehydration at 35° C was found suitable for powdering and for further DNA extraction. Leaves once dried can be stored in polythene covers for over three months. Prolonged drying beyond 35° C and 30 hours was detrimental for the quality of DNA. 6.1.2 Extraction protocol Using one per cent PVP and three per cent CTAB in 20 ml extraction buffer for 500 mg of dried powder resulted in high quality DNA in three species viz., J. sambac, J. grandiflorum and J. tmilliflorum. But in the case of J. auriculatum lower amount of leaf powder (250 mg) and re-extraction with extraction buffer resulted in overcoming the problem of sticky DNA. 6.2 Standardization of protocols for RAPD anlysis Amplification of jasmine DNA for RAPD analysis using Operon primers was standardized. A reaction volume of 25 pi with 25 ng of template DNA, 1.5 mM of MgCb, 100 mM Iris, 50 mM KCl, one per cent Triton-X with 150 pM of dNTPs was found suitable for amplification. Consistent banding patterns were obtained by hot- start for five minutes, 45 cycles with each cycle consisting of one minute denaturation, two minutes annealing and two minutes extension time with final extension of five minutes. 70 6.2 Estimation of genetic diversity and genetic rclatedness among jasmine cuitivars Dissimilarily matrix based on SED and dendrogram and Clustering by Ward's coefficient indicated a moderate diversity among the 32 jasmine cultivars.Two major groups were found between the cultivars. Group 1 consisted of diploid cultivars of sambac. Ail these are North Indian cultivars, which are in the process of speciation. These cultivars have similar morphological characters and show much less variation. Group 2 had two subclusters viz., 'Co-2 Pitchi' and 'Nilakottai Mullai' spanning the extremes in one subcluster and 'Co-1 Pitchi' and *Tenkasi White Pitchi in the other. All the four species are present in this group. Cultivars of J. auriculatum show minimum dissimilarity (13 %) as they all belong to South India only. Cultivars of J. sambac show distinct groupings with North Indian and South Indian cultivars placed in different clusters. The cultivars of J. grandiflorum show atleast two types 'Lucknow Pitchi' and 'Tenkasi White Pitchi' originated separately that led to the present day variation among cultivars. This is a basic work on molecular markers attempted scientifically, to strengthen the database ofjasmine cultivars in India. More work could be done to characterize the cultivars and species, which will be helpful in identifying suitable types for various human needs. Our findings prove the fact that RAPD markers can be used effectively for discriminating cultivars, estimating genetic diversity and genetic relationships in jasmine, which are less expensive, fast and reliable. Aiton) Name of the student : Binapani Taria Admission number : 06FLS/12 Name of the advisor and : Dr. J.N. Das Designation Professor Department of Floriculture and landscaping College of Agriculture, Bhubaneswar Degree for which the : Master of Science in Agriculture (Floriculture thesis is Submitted and landscaping) Year of submission : 2014 ABSTRACT A field experiment was carried out in the garden of the department of floriculture & landscaping, college of Agriculture, Orissa University of Agriculture and Technology, Bhubaneswar, to study the “Effect of plant growth regulators on growth & yield of Jasmine (Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton)” during the year 2013-14. The field was laid out in Randomized Block Design with nine treatments & three replications. The soil of the site is sandy loam with 150.0 kg Available Nitrogen, 68.18 kg Available phosphorus & 306.4 kg Available potassium per hectare. The crop was fertilized with 120g Urea, 240g SSP, and 240gm MOP plant/year. All the agronomic & horticultural package of practices were provided as per above said prescription at appropriate intervals. Adequate plant protection measures in term of prophylactic sprays were taken up to keep the plant disease & insects free. Four randomly selected plants from each treatment were ear-marked and timely observation were taken on eight growth characters like plant height, number of productive shoots, length of primary lateral shoots, number of leaves, leaf length, leaf length, leaf width, leaf area and length of internodes as well as quality parameter like total chlorophyll content and yield attributing characters were measured at different effective growing periods of the crop. The data obtained thereof in respect of various characters at different intervals were subjected to statistical analysis for the result. The results of the experiment revealed that, Gibberellic acid (GA3) at 25ppm & 50ppm significantly increased height of the plant and primary lateral shoot length, more length of internodes (6.35cm), but side by side it registered lowest (228.92 & 243.39) numbers of flowers per plant, lowest number of productive shoots & also reduced the weight (3.17 & 3.75) of hundred flowers respectively. NAA, ethrel and MH significantly reduced the shoot length. MH and ethrel were equally effective in increasing the number of productive shoots closely followed by NAA. NAA at 50ppm reduced the number and length of the leaves. Ethrel at (100 & 200ppm) registered early flowering. Whereas Maximum delay in flowering was noted in NAA, GA3 and MH treated plants. MH at 1000ppm registered longer duration of flowering (3.00days). MH at lower concentration (500ppm) increased number of leaves. MH at 1000ppm reduced the width of the leaf (4.45cm) and total leaf area (21.73cm2). MH at 1000ppm increased (63.70) total chlorophyll content. However, ethrel at 200ppm registered lowest (48.36) total chlorophyll content. MH at 1000ppm recorded highest (266.00) number of flowers, followed by (261.29) number of flowers in MH at 500ppm, MH at both the concentrations (1000 & 500ppm) increased (1.83 & 1.67g) the weight of hundred flowers. MH at 1000ppm & 500ppm concentrations recorded the highest yield (104.30 & 67.80kg/ha) in terms of both weight and number of flowers, whereas GA3 at 50ppm & 25ppm registered lowest yield (51.63 & 59.03 kg/ha) respectively. Based on these studies, it can be recommended that flower yield can be increased by spraying of MH at 1000ppm in Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton under Bhubaneswar condition. NAA at 50ppm next to MH increased flower yield. Ethrel induced early flowering and longer flowering duration, whereas delayed in flowering was observed with MH treated plants. Therefore, plant growth regulators will be useful in extending the flowering season and duration of flowering. The extentension of season of flowering and staggered supply of flowers to the market ensure avoidance of glut and better returns to the growers. Jasmine is considered as the "King of Oils" (Rose is the "Queen") especially for its flowers and sweet fragrance. A single jasmine vine can perfume an entire room or garden. The name jasmine is derived from Arabic word “Yasmin” meaning fragrance. Since the time immemorial, it is considered as a spiritual flower of India. India is one of the centers of origin of jasmine. For the past many centuries jasmines have adorned the gardens of Central and South East Asia, Afghanistan, Iran, Nepal and many other tropical and sub-tropical countries and many of the jasmine species are native of India and have their origin in the Southern Foothills of the Himalayas. In India, jasmines are commercially cultivated in the states of Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and West Bengal. Although, correct statistics of the area and production are not available, it is estimated that in India, jasmines occupy an area of 8000 ha with an annual production of flower worth Rs. 80 to 100 million. In India, Tamil Nadu has the largest area under jasmine cultivation followed by Karnataka, which together account for 98 per cent of the total cultivated area. Tamil Nadu is the leading producer of jasmine in the country with an annual production of 77247 t from the cultivated area of 9360 ha. The flowers produced in the state are being exported to the neighbouring countries viz., Sri Lanka, Singapore, Malaysia and Middle East countries. The major jasmine producing districts of Tamil Nadu are Dindigul, Salem, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Virudhunagar, Trichy, etc. Since the crop requires lots of manpower for harvesting and other operations, only small farmers are cultivating the crop. It is an ideal crop for small farmers whose land holdings are less than 1 acre. 2 The jasmine belongs to family ‘Oleaceae’ and the Genus Jasminum comprises of about 300 species, which are distributed in the warmer parts of Europe, Asia, Africa and the Pacific region (Bhattacharjee, 1980). Jasmine plants are grown both as shrub and climber. With the characteristic dark green foliage, leaves opposite, 3-10cm long, variable in shape, usually ovate acute or acuminate or obtuse, entire glabrous. Elegant star like flowers with rich fragrance solitary or usually in 3 flowered terminal cymes and hardy growth habit; they are highly valued ornamental plants for home gardens and commercial cultivation. Flowers and buds are used for making garlands, bouquets and for religious offerings, while ‘veni’ is used as hair adornment. The flowers are also used for the production of perfumed, hair oils and attars. Jasmine oil is regarded as unique, as it blends well with other floral extracts. It is highly valued throughout the world for its high grade perfumes, which is used in soap and cosmetic industries and in flavouring mouth wash liquids. Jasmine essential oil has a sweet and floral aroma. The flowers should preferably be picked at night for essential oil and hence the oil is expensive. Jasmine fragrance is said to give a feeling of optimism, confidence and euphoria, and is helpful against depression, nervous exhaustion and stress related conditions. The Chinese used jasmine in sick rooms to cleane the air. It was also used by Egyptians to relieve nervous disorders, insomnia and headache. In today’s world, aromatherapy using jasmine oil is said to encourage cell growth and increase skin elasticity. Jasmine is also used for catarrh, coughs, laryngitis, labor pains, uterine disorders and many skin problems. The genus Jasminum is reported to comprise of 500 species. A critical analysis of these species, however, has revealed the number of true species to be only 89, of 3 which 40 inhabit the Indian sub-continent. More than 80 jasmine species are found in India, of which only three species are used for commercial cultivation. They are Jasminum sambac (Gundumalli/ MaduraiMalli), J. auriculatum (Mullai)and J. grandiflorum (Jathimalli / Pitchi). The first two species are mainly cultivated for selling as fresh flowers whereas the last one is cultivated for concrete extraction. Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton is an evergreen vine or shrub reaching up to 0.5 to 3 m (1.6 to 9.8 ft) tall. The species is highly variable, possibly a result of spontaneous mutation, natural hybridization, and autopolyploidy. Only a few varieties reproduce by seed in the wild. Cultivated Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton generally do not bear seeds and the plant is reproduced solely by cuttings, layering and other methods of asexual propagation. The leaves are ovate, 4 to 12.5 cm (1.6 to 4.9 in) long and 2 to 7.5 cm (0.79 to 2.95 in) wide. The phyllotaxy is opposite or in whorls of three, simple (not pinnate, like most other jasmines).They are smooth (glabrous) except for a few hairs at the venation on the base of the leaf. Jasminum sambac L. Aiton is a species of jasmine native to South and Southeast Asia. It is widely cultivated for its attractive and sweetly fragrant flowers. The flowers are also used for perfumes and for making tea. It is known as the Arabian jasmine in English. It is the national flower of the Philippines, where it is known as Sampaguita. It is also one of the three national flowers of Indonesia, where it is known as Melati putih. Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton is classified under the genus Jasminum under the tribe Jasmineae. It belongs to the olive family Oleaceae. Despite the English common name of "Arabian jasmine", Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton is not originally native to Arabia. The habits of Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton support a native habitat of humid tropical climates and not the arid climates of the Middle East. Early Chinese records of the plant points to the origin of Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton as eastern South Asia and Southeast Asia. Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton 4 (and nine other species of the genus) were spread into Arabia and Persia by man, where they were cultivated in gardens. From there, they were introduced to Europe where they were grown as ornamentals and were known under the common name "sambac" in the 18th century. Medieval Arabic "zanbaq" means jasmine flower-oil from the flowers of any species of jasmine. This word entered late Medieval Latin as "sambacus" and “zambacca" with the same meaning as the Arabic, and then in post-medieval Latin plant taxonomy the word was adopted as a label for the J. sambac species. In 1789, William Aiton reclassified the plant to the genus Jasminum. He also coined the common English name of "Arabian jasmine" cementing the misconception that it was Arabian in origin. The flowers bloom throughout the year and are produced in clusters of 3 to 12 together at the terminal ends of branches. They are strongly scented, with a white corolla 2 to 3 cm (0.79 to 1.18 in) in diameter with 5 to 9 lobes. The flowers open at night (usually around 6 to 8 in the evening), and close in the morning, a span of 12 to 20 hours. The fruit is a purple to black berry 1 cm (0.39 in) in diameter. In India, the fresh flowers of jasmine are highly valued and are used for making garlands, bouquets, and venis for decorating hair of woman and for religious and marriage ceremonies. Recently, jasmine cultivation has received a fillip through research findings which indicated the potentiality of South Indian Jasmine. There are peak and lean productive seasons with consequent gluts and scarcity which affect the price trends greatly.
