Developments after the discovery of growth regulators and their application in agriculture and more especially in horticulture are significant. Regulations of plant growth and development using natural plant hormones for greater production have received the almost attention. Growth and flowering responses of ornamental plant to these chemical substances have been intensively studied with a view to have compact plants with greater number of flowers and also to hasten or delay flowering according to the needs of the grower. 5 The term “Plant Growth Regulators” was proposed by Tukey et al. (1954) to include natural and artificial compounds. They defined “Plant Growth Regulators” as organic compounds other than nutrients, which in small amounts promote, inhibit or otherwise modify any physiological process in plants. The term PGR is not only restricted to synthetic compounds but also includes the naturally occurring hormones (Nickell, 1982). Plant growth, especially vegetative growth, can be controlled by a number of cultural and environmental management strategies, as well as with chemical plant growth regulators (PGR). PGRs are chemicals that modify the natural hormonal activity that controls plant growth and development. The cultural and environmental factors that influence plant growth and development can also influence how a crop responds to a PGR. The key uses of plant growth regulators in ornamental horticulture and floriculture include regulation of plant height, profusion of branching, propagation of cuttings, control of flowering, enhancing stress tolerance, increasing postharvest longevity during shipping, storing and marketing besides increasing the display of flowers and potted plants. In most cases, reduction in plant height is desirable in bedding, potted and woody ornamentals but in some cases height enhancement is also desirable for cut flower use. Plants produce a number of growth hormones which co-ordinate and control various phases of plant growth and development. These hormones are defined as organic compounds, other than nutrients, produced by plants in minute quantities, which in low concentration regulate namely, promote, inhibit or otherwise modify different phases of plant growth and development. Besides these endogenous plant hormones, a number of synthetic chemical components are also known to regulate and modify growth in a similar manner. Plant physiologists have recognized five well defined groups of plant growth substances. These are auxins, gibberellins, cytokinins, inhibitors (ABA) and senescent hormone ethylene. 6 The use of plant growth regulators had led to intensive scientific activity for their commercial exploitation. Since, 1949 many beneficial effects of different plant growth regulators have been reported on different horticultural crops and other field crops. Growth regulators were first identified in the early 1930’s as significant tools in increasing crop production. The growth and flowering of many flower crops and bedding plants were successfully controlled by growth regulators to produce high quality horticultural products. In addition an increase in yields of commercial flower crops and vegetables by growth regulators sprays were reported. Desirable responses including retardation of vegetative growth, hastening of flowering sequence and increase in flower yield of commercial crops. These responses followed the application of these growth regulators as foliar sprays or dips. Such application caused a drastic initial reaction, as opposed to the gradual uptake by the roots. Regulation of flowering in jasmine has immense practical value. The species is highly variable, possible a result of spontaneous mutation, natural hybridization and autopolypliody, only a few varieties reproducing by seed in the wild. Cultivated Jasminum sambac generally do not bear seeds and the plot is reproduced solely by cuttings, layering and others asexual propagation methods. The leaves are ovate, 4 to 12.5cm long and 2 to 7.5cm wide. The phyllotoxy is opposite or in whorls of three, simple (not pinnate like other Jasmines). They are smooth except for a few hairs at the venation on the base of the leaf. The flower bloom in summer months and are produced in clusters of 3 to 12 together at the ends of branches. They are strongly scented, with a while corolla 2 to 3cm in diameter with 5 to 9 lobes. The flowers open at night, usually around 6 to 9 in the evening and close in the morning 8 to 9 AM, a span of 12 to 20 hours. 25 3.6.3.6 Cultivars There are numerous cultivars of Jasminum sambac which differ from each others by the shape of leaves and the structure of the collar. The cultivars recognized include: Maid of Orleans: Possesses flowers with a single layer of five or more oval shaped petals. It is the variety most commonly referred to as Sampaguits and Pikake. It is also known as “Motiya”, or “Bella”. Bella of India: possesses flowers with a single or double layer of elongated petals. Grand Duke of Tusacany: Possesses flowers with double petals. They resemble small white roses and are less fragnant than the others varieties. It is also known as Rose Jasmine and Butt Mograw. Mysore Mulli: resembles the Bella of India cultivars but has slightly shooter petals. 3.6.3.7 Sources of organic manures and inorganic Fertilizer Vermicompost was obtained by culturing Eisenia foetida earthworm on leaf waste in Horticulture Research Station (HRS) of Orissa University of Agriculture and Technology, Bhubaneswar nursery. The highest length of primary lateral shoots was recorded at different intervals of 30, 60, 90, 120 & 150 DAP (16.04cm, 16.77cm, 21.87cm, 23.38cm & 28.15cm) respectively. Highest lengths of internodes were also registered (6.72cm). Elongation of shoots by GA3 is one of its well known effects (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 & 1978 worked on Jasminum grandiflorum & Jasminum auriculatum) (Murali, 1984 in Jasminum multiflorum) and (Gowada, 1988 in Jasminum sambac). Increase in leaf length, width and leaf area was noted in GA3 sprayed plants. Gibberellic acid at 50ppm gave highest length of leaves (7.72cm) and GA3 at 25ppm gave highest width of leaf (6.62) which was superior to all the treatments experimented. Maximum leaf area of 27.09cm2 was recorded with GA3 50ppm and the finding are in accordance with the results of Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977. These differential effects could be explained only on the basis of correlation inhibition reported by (Phillips, 1971) on Jasminum auriculatum presumably; a correlation inhibition was enhanced by a possible gibberellins induced auxins biosynthesis. The differences in the level of endogenous auxins and gibberellins might explain the absence of any marked correlation in the case of Jasminum multiflorum and Jasminum sambac. The results presented with Jasminum auriculatum by Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1978) contradicted without results. 54 GA3 25 & 50ppm took (9.00 & 9.05) mean number of days to flower bud initiation to flower opening. Whereas untreated plants took only 9.42 days. It not only increased the earliness of the unset of flowering but also slightly reduced the total duration of flowering in the present studies but contrary result was reported in Jasminum grandiflorum & Jasminum auriculatum associated with greater inactivation of the productive shoots in the GA3 (Pappaiah & Muthuswamy 1978). Thus, GA3 enhancing the correlative inhibition in Jasminum auriculatum have in directly contributed to slight reduction in yield compared to control through less production of shoots. The reduced yield by GA3 was however accompanied by decreased number of productive shoots. Similar result was reported in Jasminum auriculatum (Pappaiah & Muthuswamy, 1977 & 1978;J. multiflorum by Murali, 1984 and J. sambac by Nage Gowda, 1988). 5.2 EFFECT OF ALPHA-NAPHTHALENE ACETIC ACID (NAA) Alpha-naphthalene acetic acid appreciably reduced the plant growth and increased the number productive shoots. NAA at 25 and 50ppm recorded 30DAP (3.08 & 3.17), 60DAP (4.00 & 4.08), 90 DAP (4.58 & 4.67), 120DAP (5.44 & 5.52) & 150 DAP (6.92 & 7.00) productive shoots and length of internodes were 5.82 & 5.77cm. These results in accordance with those reports in Jasminum sambac (Pal et al., 1980). The leaf area of NAA treated plants reduced in case of Jasminum multiflorum (Murali, 1984). The appreciable feature of practical importance of this auxins compound is the significant improvement in the yield of flowers compared to control. NAA increased the weight of flowers 25ppm 6.39 & at 50ppm 6.79g/plant, while untreated plants recorded only 4.31g per plant. Increase in yield was 48.25 per cent and 57.54 per cent more over control in 25 and 50ppm of NAA, respectively. The improvement in flowering was partly due to more number of productive shoots developed on the treated plants. The results are in conformity with the reports on Jasminum sambac and J. auriculatum (Pal et al., 1980). Though, there was increase in yield of flowers, the 55 attracting feature of this chemical was the enhancing flowering of treated plants and increased the duration of flowering. 5.3 EFFECT OF MALEIC HYDRAZIDE The retarded growth of height of the plants, primary lateral shoots & intermodal length by MH particularly at 1000ppm resulted into known effect of this growth regulator on Jasminum auriculatum, Jasminum grandiflorum, Jasminum multiflorum & Jasminum sambac (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 and 1978; and Murali and Nage Gowda, 1988). The results are in consonance with the effects of this chemical reported by several other workers also (Reed et al., 1974). The most conspicuous effect of this growth retardant was the greatly increased number of laterals and the markedly early flowering which were noted in other species of jasmines also. The yield was also increased appreciably by Maleic hydrazide. The two features viz., the reduction in number of days for flowering by as much as 10-15 days and nearly double the yield (141.82%) by application of MH are of special significance. It has been already shown that MH induced branching and increased the yield in Jasminum grandiflorum, J. auriculatum and J. multiflorum (Pappaiah and Muthuswamy, 1977 and 1978). Maleic hydrazide (MH) at 1000ppm recorded the maximum (266.00) number of flowers/plant & highest flower yield of 104.30 kg/ha, which is 141.82% increased more over control, because of the more number of branching & sequence of flowering was also distributed at in the months of March which normally recorded low yield of flowers in Bhubaneswar condition. 5.4 EFFECT OF ETHREL Ethrel at 200ppm concentration arrested the growth height of the plant, primary lateral shoots and reduced the length of internodes, total chlorophyll content, leaf size, leaf area & numbers of leaves at different growth stages. This inhibited vegetative growth could be a desirable feature in maintenance of shape and size of 56 Jasmine plant helping in easy harvest of flowers. These results are in consonance with the reports of Pappaiah and Muthuswamy (1977 and 1978) in Jasminum auriculatum and J. grandiflorum and Murali and Nage Gowda (1984 and 1988) in Jasminum multiflorum and J. sambac. But the flowering is slightly increased in yield have detracted its usefulness. The increased yield by ethrel spray is only minimum and does not merit the additional expenditure that the sprays of ethrel would entail, in comparison to MH where the increase in yield over control is remarkable (46.3%). The extreme dwarfing was not accompanied by a stimulation of productive shoot growth in the present study. In the present studies the number of productive shoots was less as compared to MH sprayed plants than ethrel sprayed plants. An overall appreciation of the results would show that MH besides arresting growth to a particularly apical dominance and induced remarkably more branching, flowering and the yield was also increased by MH. Ethrel also retarded the growth and induced remarkably early flowering and yield was also considerably increased by this ethrel and it ranked next to MH. Evidently the MH sprays gave several advantages like more branching, higher yield, better flower size and longer duration of flowering. MH is a true-anti-gibberellins biosynthesis. The fact that MH sprays induced branching & flowering suggests that a reduction in level of endogenous gibberellins may be a pre-requisite for floral induction. While the growth retardation was greater under higher concentration of MH, the time taken for flowering shows clear trend in yield of flowers which is increased with the increase in the concentration of MH. In other words, the higher concentration of 1000ppm MH while reduced the plant height, but increased the yield level. It seems that, safer to employ 500ppm MH for deriving maximum advantages mentioned above. Ethrel at 200ppm can also be employed for obtaining higher yield. 57 The late flowering induced MH and the higher quantum of yield in the flowering season promoted by the chemical are of practical importance in crop regulation in cultivated jasmines. Judicious combination of cultural practices like pruning and fertilizer application as well as growth regulator sprays, it is possible that flowering can be manipulated at least to a reasonable extent to avoid the heavy glut due to peak flowering in a particular part of the year, which is very common in commercial species of Jasmines. 58 SUMMARY AND CONCLUSION The study on “Effect of plant growth regulators on growth and yield of jasmine (Jasminum sambac (L.) CONCLUSION From the present experiment following conclusion can be drawn regarding effect of plant growth regulators on growth and yield of jasmine (Jasminum sambac (L). Aiton): Based on these studies, it can be recommended that flower yield can be increased by spraying of MH at 500ppm & 1000ppm in Jasminum sambac (L.) Aiton. Gibberellic acid (GA3) significantly increased plant height, primary shoot length, length of internodes, and width of the leaves with an associated increase in the total leaf area. NAA, Ethrel and MH significantly reduced the shoot length. MH and Ethrel were equally effective in increasing the number of productive shoots closely followed by NAA. Reduced number of productive shoots was observed under higher concentration of GA3. MH at higher concentration (1000ppm) increased number of leaves. NAA at 50ppm reduced the number and length of the leaves whereas MH at 1000ppm reduced the width of the leaves and total leaf area. NAA was next to MH in increasing flower yield. MH induced late flowering and longer flowering duration, whereas delay in flowering was observed with NAA treatments. Judicious application of these two growth regulators will be useful in extending the flowering season and duration of flowering. The extension of season of flowering and staggered supply of flowers to the market would ensure avoidance of glut and better returns to the growers. 61 FUTURE LINE OF WORK There is a need to improve the production technology, insect pests and diseases management and harvesting practices of J. sambac. Selection of cultivars for high quality flower production should focus on varieties that could produce flowers even during the rainy months. Another option is infrastructure facilities like poly house for jasmine cultivation during the rainy months to prevent pest infestation of blossoms. A planting scheme can be designed to have jasmine production areas distributed all over the country so that floral buds are available the whole year thus stabilizing the market prices. Population density, fertilization and height of pruning are among the most important factors affecting the production of jasmine flowers. New production techniques and crop protection practices, which could address the current issues on irregularity of flower production, these could be done by having effective and efficient tools in harvesting and using environmentally safe chemicals or plant growth regulators to support the defoliation and pruning practices. Similarly, there is a need to determine the optimum maturity index and to improve harvesting practices for the fresh market. Interaction effect of NPK on available soil nutrients INTRODUCTION INTRODUCTION In the present agricultural scenario o f the country, commercial floriculture is gaining more and more importance. Jasmine is one of the most important commercial flower crops cultivated throughout India and is esteemed for its attractive fragrant flowers. One of the most important traditional flower crops of the country, jasmine offers excellent uses in garland making, religious offerings, personal adorning by women etc. In the important flower markets of the five big cities of India, such as Calcutta, Bombay, Delhi, Madras and Bangalore, it is estimated that about 15,000 kg of loose flowers of jasmine are sold every day (Dohare et al., 1978). The essential oil extracted from jasmine flowers is of high value in perfume industry. C urrently India ex p o rts jasm ine flowers to Singapore, Malaysia, Srilanka and West Asian countries. The genus Jasminum belongs to family Oleaceae and about forty species of this genus are found to occur in India (Natarajan, 1977). The three major cultivated species are J. auriculatum , J. grandiflorum and J. sambac. Of these, the cultivation of bush jasm ine (Jasminum sambac Ait.) is an emerging business for small and marginal cultivators, and in hom esteads as a source of income or sm all scale enterprise for housewives. Expanding the area under cultivation of jasmine would also 2 enable us to meet atleast partially the demand for this flower which is now met almost entirely by our neighbouring states. Practically no studies have so far been conducted regarding the nutrient requirements for bush jasmine in Kerala. Majority of farmers who have started cultivation of this crop are now facing difficulties due to lack of sufficient information regarding the management practices for the crop. With these points in view, a study was undertaken with the objective to standardise the requirement of major nutrients (N, P and K) for the growth and flowering of bush jasmine. Nandakumar (1976) reported no increase in essential oil content due to application of 120 g N, 240 g P and 240 g K plant'1 year'1 in Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. Pal et al. (1984) registered high flow er yield of Jasm inum auriculatum and essential oil content with rising N levels, but P had no beneficial effect. Maximum content and yield of essential oil in Menta pipperita was reported by Dellacecca et al. (1997) with application of N at 200 kg h a '1. Eventhough P was found to have no effect on yield, menthol and methyl acetate contents in essential oil were maximum in crops grown with 150 kg P20 5 h a'1. Subina and Masanova (1970) repo/ted that by applying N and P 20 each at 90 kg hectare'1 increased the content of essential oil in flowers of ‘Red Crimea’ roses, whereas K reduced the oil yields. Increased oil content by 35 per cent was noted by application of N and reduction by 37 per cent was noted when K was applied in pot cultured Menta pipperita Linn, plants (Franz, 1979). However, Harnok (1974) did not observe changes in essential oil content due to supply of nutrients in peppermint. 2.6. Effect of fertilizers on chemical composition The studies o f K um araguruparan (1974) on Jasm inum grandiflorum Linn revealed the following: The leaf N content increased during the preflowering, peak flowering and post flowering phases by foliar application of N at 60 g and 120 g plant'1 year'1. The leaf N content was found reduced in foliar applications combining N and K, while there occured an increase at peak flowering and post flowering phases by foliar spray of P at 240 g plant'1 year"1. The foliar P alone did not affect the leaf P content, but in combination with N, there occurred an increase. A linear relation was found between the applied K and content of K in leaves. N also influenced the carbohydrate content when applied either alone or in combination with P and K. 21 Bik (1970) showed that leaf analysis gave a better indication of the flower yield in roses. Optimum leaf contents of N and K appeared to be 3.8 per cent and 2.1 per cent respectively and that the optimum N:K ratio 1:1. DISCUSSION DISCUSSION Cultivation o f bush jasmine is becoming more and more popular among the farmers o f Kerala especially, as a small scale enterprise by marginal farmers and housewives. Practically no studies have so far been conducted regarding the nutrient requirements for bush jasm ine in Kerala. In order to find out the optimum nutritional requirem ent for bush jasmine, an experim ent was conducted at Departm ent o f Horticulture, College of Agriculture, Vellayani. The experiment consisted of three levels of nitrogen (50, 100, 150 N kg ha'1), three levels of phosphorus (50, 100, 150 P20 5 kg ha'1) and three levels of potassium (50, 100, 150 kg K20 ha'1) in Randomised Block Design. Along with total of 27 treatments, two controls - one as absolute control and other with FYM of 10 kg ha'1 - was also included in the trail. The different characters were critically observed and the results obtained are discussed below. Growth characters Growth is a multi dimensional web of many parameters. In the 88 present study, the growth of bush jasm ine as influenced by various treatments has been elucidated through length of mainshoot, number and length of lateral branches and spread of the bush. Length of main stem Nitrogen application significantly influenced length of main stem. Throughout the growth period, highest dose of 150 kg N ha"1 produced maximum shoot length. This increase in plant height may be due to increased cell division and cell elongation brought about by nitrogen application. Nitrogen being the most potential nutrient element for the vegetative growth and development of plants, its supply and availability would have helped to increase the height of the plant. The effect of nitrogen application in increasing length of main shoot was reported by various w orkers in Jasm inum sam bac (B h attarch arjee, 1985), in Jasminum grandiflorum (Natarajan, 1977) and in Jasminum auriculatum (Hugar andNalawadi, 1994). The application of phosphorus produced significant difference from fifth month of planting. Significant difference in plant height was shown at the highest dose of P at 150 kg P 2C>5 ha"1. Phosphorus application might have resulted in better root formation during initial stages of growth and this inturn later resulted in increased plant height. Beneficial effect of P application in increasing plant height was reported by Srinivasan et al. (1989) in Jasminum sambac, Bose and Jana (1978) in bougainvilleas, Young et al. (1973) in rose. 89 The application of K at the highest level (150 kg K20 h a '1) produced significant difference in plant height during the last quarter of the growth period. The increased plant height at later stages may be due to the complementary effect of K with other nutrients on the growth of plants, better utilization of carbohydrates, promotion of enzyme activity and water transport. Beneficial effect of K application in increasing plant height was reported by Deswal et al. (1982) in gladiolus. N x P interaction was significant with 150 kg N and 150 kg P20 5 ha"1 producing taller plants. Among P x K interaction, 150 kg P2Os with 150 kg K20 ha'1 resulted in maximum height of plants. The results revealed that combined application of NPK was necessary for increasing plant height in bush jasmine. Number of primary and secondary branches Application of nitrogen at the highest dose of 150 kg N ha'1 produced maximum number of branches throughout the growth period. This might be because of the activation of lateral buds, due to better N nutrition. Similar effects were reported in Jasminum grandiflorum by Natarajan and Madhava Rao (1980). Application of 150 kg P20 5 ha'1 was found to produce maximum num ber of primary and secondary branches. Since phosphorus is a constituent of cell nucleus, it is closely associated with cell division and 90 meristematic activity (Ferman, 1965). Its application at higher levels might have resulted in higher rates o f availability of this nutrient leading to an increase in number of branches per plant. Sim ilar results were reported by Srinivasan et al. (1989) in Jasminum sambac. With potassium nutrition, maximum num ber o f branches were produced at highest level o f 150 kg K20 h a '1. Potassium plays an important role in conversion of amino acids to proteins and soluble sugars to starch and other polysaccharides (Ferman, 1965). This might have led to higher vegetative growth at highest level of K application. NP and NK interaction were significant at 150 kg N with 150 kg P20 5 ha'1 and 150 kg N with 150 kg K 20 ha'1 giving maximum number of primary and secondary branches. PK interaction did not significantly influence the number of primary and secondary branches except during the second and nineth month after planting. The controls registered significantly lower number of primary and secondary branches compared to treatments. This indicates that the supply of nutrients in adequate quantity was essential for good branch production. i 91 Application of N at the highest level of 150 kg N ha'1 produced maximum length of prim ary a.nd secondary branches. This can be attributed to the role of N in enhancing vegetative growth and conforms to the observations in Jasminum sambac by Srinivasan et al. (1989), Bhattacharjee (1985) and Pal et al. (1985). Significantly higher length for primary and secondary branches were produced when P was applied at 150 kg P205 h a '1. Phosphorus is closely associated with increased meristematic activity (Ferman, 1965), which inturn leads to increased length for primary and secondary branches. This finding was in conformity with reports of Srinivasan et al. (1989) in Jasminum sambac and Bose and Jana (1978) in bougainvilleas. Maximum length of branches was found at 150 kg K20 h a '1. Increased length of branches may be due to complementary effect of K with other nutrients on growth of plant, better utilization of carbohydrates and water transport. Similar effect of K was also reported by Deswal et al. (1982) in gladiolus. Spread of the plant Application of N at highest dose of 150 kg N ha'1 produced maximum spread for the bushes throughout the growth period. The increased plant spread may be due to increase in length and number of branches as a consequence of N application. Length of primary and secondary branches 150 kg ha"1 of P20 5 was found to produce maximum spread for plants. Both length and number o f branches increased as a consequence o f P application. This inturn increased spread o f bush at highest levels of P. Application of K was found to produce maximum East-West spread at 150 kg K20 ha"1. The effect o f K on increasing length of branches may be attributed to maximum spread of bush. NP interaction was significant at 150 kg N with 150 kg P20 5 ha"1 giving maximum North-South spread of bush. NK interaction was significant at 150 kg N and 150 kg K20 ha"1 effecting maximum spread. PK interaction was also significant with 150 kg P20 5 + 50 kg K20 ha"1 showing maximum North-South spread o f bush while 150 kg P20 5 + 150 kg K20 h a '1 produced maximum East-W est spread of bush. So the availability' of all the nutrients in adequate amounts is essential for proper spread of the plant. The controls registered spread inferior to those obtained from various treatments indicating that inadequate amounts of nutrients cannot produce satisfactory spread of bush. Nitrogen encourages the vegetative development of plants and controls to some extent, the efficient utilization of phosphorus and potassium. According to Russel (1973), as the nitrogen supply increases, the extra protein produced allows the plant leaves to grow larger and hence have surface area available for photosynthesis, which inturn results in better nitrogen use efficiency o f plant and enhanced growth. This might have led to increased assim ilation, higher productivity and increased DMP. The increased DMP with higher dose of N may be due to production of more primary and secondary laterals and increased leaf number. The effect of phosphorus on DMP was also significant. At highest dose of P (150 kg P20 5 ha'1) maximum DMP was attained. A significantly lower DMP was shown by the controls compared to all other treatments. This shows that the nutrient had a great influence on growth of plants. Hence the trial may be continued with higher levels of major nutrients. SUMMARY SUMMARY The present investigation “Nutrient requirement of bush jasmine. Jasminum sambac Ait.” was conducted at the Department of Horticulture. College of Agriculture, Vellayani, Thiruvananthapuram during 1996-98 to find out a suitable recommendation of major nutrients (N, P and K) for the optimum growth and flowering of bush jasmine. The effect of major nutrients on growth, yield, essential oil content of flowers and chemical composition were studied in detail and important findings are summarised below. Application of N, P and K significantly influenced length of main shoot. Effect of N was significant throughout the growth period, while that of P was evident from fifth month onwards and that of K during the last quarter of growth period. In all the cases, highest values were obtained with the highest level of the nutrient. The number of primary and secondary branches were significantly affected by the level of N, P and K. Levels n3, p3 and k3 was found superior over the other levels. Length of primary and secondary branches increased with increase in the level of nutrients. N influenced the length of prim ary and 103 secondary branches throughout the growth period. Effect of P was evident from third month onwards for length of primary branches and from eight month onwards for length of secondary branches. K exerted influence from eight month of planting. The effect of N at n3 level was highly significant in producing maximum North-South spread of plants. Applied P has shown maximum significance at p3 level from sixth month onwards. But applied K was not found to have any influence in the North-South spread of bush. Influence of N at n3 level was highly significant in producing maximum East-West spread of bush. The effect of P was found significant with level p3 superior over p2 and p t . Effect of k2 and k3 were comparable in all the months except fifth, nineth, tenth and eleventh month of planting, where effect of k3 was found significant. Applied N, P and K was not found to influence the number of days taken for first flower picking and weight of hundred flower buds. But the time taken for opening of flowers after harvest was found to be influenced by applied P only. Here, maximum time was taken with level p3 followed by p2 and p t respectively. . Yield of flowerbuds was significantly influenced by applied N, P and K. Maximum flower yield was noticed with highest level of respective major nutrients viz., n3, p3 and k3. 104 M onthly yield pattern in jasmine was seen not to be influenced sig n ifican tly by m ajor nutrients. The leaf N content was found significantly influenced by applied N and applied K. Increasing levels of K reduced content of N. L eaf P content was not found to be significantly influenced by any nutrient treatments. The leaf K content was significantly influenced by N application. H igh content o f leaf K was noticed at nj follow ed by n3 and n2 respectively. Applied P was found to influence highly at p2 level while applied K was found to influence highly at k3 level. DMP was found to be influenced significantly by applied N. Maximum DMP was noticed with n3 level followed by still lower levels viz., n2 and nj respectively. Applied P and K was shown to influence DMP highly at their respective higher levels ie., p3 and k3. Influence of applied N was found significant in the content of available soil nitrogen. Maximum available N in soil was noticed at n3 level. Influence of applied P was found significant at level p3. Applied K was also significant with level’ kj highly superior to other levels. Available P was found significantly influenced by N application. N at level n3 was found highly significant over other levels. Applied P i 105 was found significant highly in p3 producing maximum content of available P in soil. With respect to applied K, available phosphorus content was found maximum with kj followed by k3 and k2 respectively. Influence o f applied N was found sig n ifican t in producing maximum content of available soil K with level nj highly significant followed by n3 and n2 respectively. With respect to applied P, p3 proved to be highly superior to other levels. Influence of K at k3 level was highly significant in producing maximum available K in soil. Carbohydrate content of flowering shoot was found significantly influenced by applied N. Level nj was found highly significant over other levels. Influence of applied P was significant highly at p3. Influence of K on carbohydrate content was found superior with level k3 superior over other levels. A pplication o f N is found to have a significant influence on essential oil content highly at n2 level followed by n3 and n r In the case of applied P, significant influence was observed at level p2. Influence of K on essential oil content was found significant with level k3 superior to other levels. The results of the present investigation thus indicated that the characters ie., growth, yield, time taken for opening o f flowers, content 106 of nutrients in leaves, DMP, carbohydrate content, essential oil content and available soil nutrients, were significantly influenced by levels of nutrients. By ASHA RAJ ABSTRACT OF A THESIS SUBMITTED IN PARTIAL FULFILMENT OF THE REQUIREMENT FOR THE DEGREE OF MASTER OF SCIENCE IN HORTICULTURE FACULTY OF AGRICULTURE KERALA AGRICULTURAL UNIVERSITY DEPARTMENT OF HORTICULTURE COLLEGE OF AGRICULTURE VELLAYANI, THIRUVANANTHAPURAM 1999 ABSTRACT The in v estig atio n “N u trien t requirem ent o f bush jasm ine, Jasminum sambac A it.” was conducted at Department of Horticulture, College of Agriculture, Vellayani, Thiruvananthapuram during 1996-’98 inorder to standardise the requirement of major nutrients (N, P and K) for the growth of flowering of bush jasmine. The treatments consisted of factorial combinations of three levels each of nitrogen (50, 100 and 150 kg N h a'1), phosphorus (50, 100 and 150 kg P20 5 h a'1) and potassium (50, 100 and 150 kg K20 h a '1) with two controls. The experiment was laid out as 33 + 2 Factorial Randomised Block Design with three replications. Vegetative characters like the length of main shoot, number of primary and secondary branches, length of primary and secondary branches, North-South and East-West spread of the bush, were significantly higher at the highest level o f major nutrients viz., 150 kg N, 150 kg P20 5 and 150 kg K20 h a'1. At the maximum level o f major nutrients with 150 kg N : 150 kg P20 5 : 150 kg K20 ha'1, yield of flower buds was found significantly higher. Other flowering characters like monthly yield pattern and weight of hundred flower buds were not found to be influenced by nutritive 2 treatments. However, time taken for opening of lower buds after harvest was maximum at 150 kg P20 5 h a '1. Content o f N, P and K in leaves revealed that maximum content of foliar nitrogen noticed at 150 kg N : 50 kg K20 h a'1 while foliar potassium content was maximum at 50 kg N : 100 kg P20 5 : 150 kg K20 h a '1. Foliar phosphorus content was not at all influenced by nutrient application. Uptake o f nutrients was not found to be influenced by applied nutrients where as DMP was maximum at the highest dose of major nutrients (150 kg N : 150 kg P20 5 : 150 kg K20 ha’1). Available soil nutrient status revealed that maximum content of nitrogen and phosphorus in soil was noticed at 150 kg N : 150 kg P20 5 and 150 kg K20 h a '1. But maximum available potassium was noticed with 50 kg N : 150 kg P20 5 and 150 kg K20 h a '1. Maximum essential oil content was obtained with 100 kg N : 100 kg P20 5 and 150 kg K 20 ha'1. Carbohydrate content of flowering shoot was found to be highest with 50 kg N : 150 kg p20 5 : 150 kg K20 h a '1. In general, highest dose of major nutrients, n3 (150 kg N h a '1), p3 (150 kg P20 5 h a '1 and k3 (150 kg K20 h a '1) was found best for cultivation of bush jasmine. However, as maximum response was shown at respective higher levels o f m ajor nutrients, higher levels of these nutrients can be tried to find out optimum nutrient combination for commercial cultivation.

INTRODUCTION In this liberalized world, high-tech horticulture has emerged as a key area for third-world countries to re-orient their commodity exports. In this regard floriculture offers abundant potential for enhancement of exports. Importance of floriculture to earn foreign exchange to improve India's economy has been realized. The latest estimates of the annual global flower trade is worth 2,500 million US dollars and the Indian contribution at present is about 0.3 million US dollars, indicating lucrative environment which has to be properly utilized. (Surendra prasad and Kumar, 1999). India is mainly focussing on export of essential oils, concretes and absolutes from traditional flowers like jasmine and rose, as India is bestowed with favorable climate and cheap labour during most pai*t of year. The jasmine concrete and absolute are said to be having prices of Rs 12,000/kg and Rs 19,000/kg respectively in International market (Ramadas et al., 1999). The jasmine oil is highly preferred in western world for its aromatic property added to its compatibility with many other floral scents. Jasmines are commercially important flowers, cultivated mainly for fresh flowers and concrete extraction. Fresh flowers are used in garland making, for worshiping and for hair adornments. The importance of it can be traced even in ancient history. Flowers can also be used for extraction of essential oil and products like Jasmine oil. Butter, Attar and Jasmine water. In reality there is no synthetic substitute for the aroma of jasmine. The term jasmine is derived from Arabic word 'Jessamine' (Bailey, 1947) and also persian name 'Yesmyn' meaning fragrance. The Jasmine {Jasmirtum spp) belongs to the family 'Oleaceae' which includes about 300 species, dispersed in tropical and subtropical parts of the globe (Bhattacharjee, 1980). About 90 species of Jasmine are grown in Indian sub-continent (Muthuswamy and Pappaiah, 1980). Among those only 20 species are under culti\'ation in South India (Georgewatt, 1980), but commercially only four species are important. 1. Jasminum sambac Alt. 2. Jasminum multiflorum Roth. 3. Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. 4. Jasminum grandiflorum Linn. The best known species among jasmines is Jasminum sambac Ait, and several varieties of this species viz., Arabian or Tuscan Jasmine (Grand duke and Tuscassy), Motia, hJogra, ^Mallige and Kodi mullai (Bhattacharjee, 1980) are commercially cultivated. The species has several synonyms viz., J. fragrans, J. sambac.rorb, .^Jongam sambac.laik., etc. In ICamataka they are known as hJysore mallige, Mangalore mallige, Udupi mallige, Bellary (or) Hadagali mallige depending upon place of cultivation and 'Iruvanthige', 'Gundu' or Dundu mallige, Yelu-suttina mallige etc., depending upon the shape or morphology of these flowers. In India, jasmine is cultivated through out the country over an area of about 8,000 ha, both in plains and on hills upto 3,030 m contributing significantly to the national economy i.e., worth of Rs. 10 crore. Much of the jasmine is grown in Tamilnadu, Kamataka Andhra Pradesh and Maharashtra. In Kamataka, the jasmine is under cultivation in almost all districts with an area of 3,720 ha and with a production of 9,300 tonnes (Anon., 1997). In North Kamataka, it is grown in almost all districts like Belgaum, Bellary, Bidar, Bijapur, Chitradurga, Dharwad, Gulbarga and Raichur are cultivating jasmine of which Bellary leads both in area and production i.e., 415 ha and 1,038 tonnes (Anon., 1997). Such an important commercial flower crop jasmine is subjected to various diseases incited by fungi, bacteria, nematodes, phytoplasmas and viruses, the latter being a very important one causing major losses. Jasmine chlorotic spot virus (JCSV) disease is widely prevalent on jasmine, very little information is available regarding the identity and effective management of the disease. The review of literature indicates that very little information is available on Jasmine chlorotic spot virus disease. Therefore information available on different viruses reported on jasmine, and Carla viruses on different crops has been highlighted here. 2.1 Occurrence The literature about virus infections of Jasminum spp. indicates that at least six viruses have been found in different Jasmine species. Tobacco ring spot virus (TRSV) on J. nudifloriim, J. mesneyi, and J. officinale (Waterworth, 1971; 1975; Morton et al., 1976); Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV) on J. polyanthum (Anon., 1982) and on J. midiflorum and two undescribed viruses called 'Jasmine mild mosaic' and 'Jasmine latent virus 1' on J. multifloriim and J. odoratissimum, respectively, Arabis mosaic virus (AMV) on J. mesneyi and J. officinale (Waterworth, 1971; Cooper and Sweet, 1976). In addition, in India Wilson (1972) reported chlorotic ring spot (CLRS) of jasmine plants (J. samhac Ait.) growing in a horticultural garden at Trivandrum exhibiting mosaic and ring spot symptoms during October, 1968. Later observations revealed that the disease was prevalent in different parts of Kerala. Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975) reported that yellow ring mosaic virus on J. sambac Ait., was prevalent aroimd Coimbatore during 1972-73. It was also noticed in the neighboring taluks of Coimbatore viz., Avinashi, Bhavani, Erode, Pollachi, Anthiyur and Gopichettipalayam. The incidence ranged from 1.5 to 52.9%. All the varieties of J. sambac Ait., except khoya, and J. pubescens L., were affected severely, and J. auriculatum Vahl., J. humile L., J. grandiflorum L., J. paniculatum L., J. angustiflorum Vahl., J. calophyllum Wall., J. flexile Vahl., J. rigidum Zenk., were found to be free from infection. The survey conducted by Chandra et al. (1979) indicated incidence of Jasmine chlorotic spot virus (JCSV) disease on various species of Jasminum viz., J. sambac Ait., J. angiistiflorum Vahl., J. arbaresoens L., J. calophyllum Wall., J. sua\issimum L.,. The incidence in these susceptible species ranged from 10 to 100% in the existing populations depending upon the varieties / species J. auriculatum Vahl., J. humile L., J. grandiflorum L., J. beesianum Forest and Dials., J. officinale L., did not exhibit symptoms indicating that they possess the factors for resistance to this disease. In Philippines, Benigno et al. (1975) reported an elongated vims particle on J. sambac causing sampaguita yellow ring spot mosaic disease. In Italy, Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) reported chlorotic spots and variegation of J. sambac plants cultivated in large pots in a private garden. 2.2 Symptomatology Wilson, (1972) reported chlorotic ring spot of Jasmine (J. sambac Ait.) plants in Trivandmm characterized by yellow chlorotic spots of varying size and shape intermingled with normal green color of the leaves, and some with mosaic pattern, which were not delimited by vems. Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975) recorded yellow ring mosaic of J. sambac Ait., showing stunting, yellow green to chlorotic flecks scattered on leaves, and yellowish streaks forming into a ring with an island of green area against dark green background. These symptoms were more clear on older leaves. Benigno et al. (1975) reported yellow ring spot mosaic on J. sambac Ait., with ring mosaic systems in Philippines. Chandra et al. (1979) observed jasmine yellow ring mosaic vims in and around Bangalore on different species of Jasminum exhibiting chlorotic spots, rings, oak leaf pattern and mosaic symptoms which were conspicuous on older leaves. Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) noticed some J. sambac Ait., plants cultivated in large pots in a private garden in Italy, showing yellow or chlorotic spots and in some cases variegation on the leaves. Over 100 years ago, Scottish gardeners immersed bulbs in hot water before planting, thus being the first known to use heat for therapy of plants. (Zandbergen, 1964). The therapeutic benefit of heat used against a specific disease became widely known with work of Jensen (Kristensen, 1966). Greenaway (1954) reported that the hot water was used earlier than hot air for control of the sugarcane diseases. He stated that rapid circulation of water around the individual pieces of plant tissue is desirable. Baker (1962) suggested that some of the causes of damage of plants or plant parts treated in water at temperatures necessary for therapy are leaching, water-soaking and asphyxiation of host tissues. Hamid and Locke (1964) successfully treated eye-pieces of potato tubers infected with Leaf roll virus at 40-45°C for 2 hours alternating with 22 hours at room temperatures for 8 weeks or 2 weeks, respectively. The thermal death point of potato tuber eye-pieces at a constant temperature of 34, 37 or 40°C was less than that of the virus. 25 Larsen (1966) found that the percentage of tips free of virus was high only when the tips were held at high temperature for atleast 16 hr daily to control Chrysanthemum virus B. Hamid and Locke (1964) with intermittent exposure inactivated potato leaf roll in 4 days at 40°C, whereas with continuous exposure for 12 days at the same temperature. Galzy (1966) used special technique in heat therapy where in heat treated explants of grape growing on agar at 35°C, which freed the plants from grape fan leaf disease. Rich (1968) removed eyes, both before and after heat treatments, from potato tubers infected with PVX, and implanted them in tubers of a variety immune to PVX. In both cases he obtained plants free of virus. Combining heat treatment with meristem culture or tip removal increased the efficiency of therapy. (Belkengren and Miller, 1962; Campbell, 1962; Ellenberger, 1960; Hakkaart and Quak, 1964; Os, 1969 and Cjuak, 1961). Deogratias et al. (1989) eradicated Prune dwarf virus in sweet cherries by a combination of chemotherapy, thermotherapy and in invitro culture. Kassanis, (1952) suggested that heat treatment may be useful in grouping viruses when more is known about the mechanism of action. Humphrey et al. (1973) studied the growth of heat treated jasmine. Jasminum magnificum plants with chlorotic mottle caused by a virus infection were grown at a constant 1 OO^F heat under continuous light. After 19 weeks plants produced symptomless shoots and also cuttings taken from these shoot tips yielded new plants which grew far better and formed much larger leaves than the non treated plants. 2.7.2 Antiviral principles (AVPs) The application of antiviral principles extracted from the leaves of sorghum and coconut were found to be equally effective in reducing the disease incidence when compared to the insecticides (Narayanasamy, 1983). Studies on the characterization of AVP from sorghum leaves indicated it to be a proteinaceous compound and the translocation mechanism might afford protection against virus infection. Sorghum AVP was found to inhibit lesion development effectively for a period of 10 days after application (Narayanasamy and Ramaiah, 1983). In two field trials the AVP from sorghum and coconut leaves were equally effective in reducing the incidence of tomato spotted wilt virus on groundnut. The pod yield of groundnut was also significantly increased due to the application of AVP from coconut or sorghum alone or in combination with monochrotophos (Narayanasamy and Ganapathy 1986). Field application of AVPs from Basella alba showed that the leaf extract was effective in checking the incidence of Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) and tobacco. Appreciable leaf yield increase was also realized (Narayanasamy, 1984). Murthy and Nagarajan (1986) observed that the leaf extract of Peltophorum ferrugineum and twig extract of Pithecellobium dulce Roxb. reduced the infection of TMV on tobacco both in the nursery and in the main field, when they were sprayed thrice in the nursery and in the main field. The leaf yield and quality were also found to be better as compared to control. The mode of action of antiviral principle has been studied in detail and it is reported that AVP may inhibit poly peptide synthesis, (Owens et al., 1973) may produce virus inhibitory substances in the host which compete for virus infection sites (Vankammen et al., 1961) and may induce resistance in susceptible cultivars (Narayanasamy and Ganapathy, 1986; Rao et al., 1985; Mukherjee et al., 1982; Narayanasamy and Ramaiah, 1983). The AVPs were found to be more effective as preinoculation treatments than as post inoculation treatments (Aiyanathan and Narayanasamy, 1988; Saigopal et al., 1986: Straub et al., 1986). Kulkami (1996) reported that leaf extracts of sorghum and coconut followed by Neem kernel extracts and Mirabilis jalapa L., were effective in inhibiting Groundnut bud necrosis virus when applied as a preinoculation treatment. DISCUSSION Jasmine (Jasminum Spp.) is one of the commercially important flower crop cultivated in Kamataka. Though the crop is known to suffer from the infection by different pathogens, but Jasmine chlorotic spot virus disease (JCSV) incidence is on increasing trend and hence may pose serious threat to cultivation of jasmine. This disease though widely prevalent, has been studied least with respect to identification of its causal agent and management. The results of the present study carried out on the JCSV disease of Jasmine in Kamataka with respect to Survey, Symptomatology, Electron microscopy. Enzyme Linked Immunosorbent Assay, Immunosorbent Electron Microscopy, Ultrathin microtomy. Transmission, Host range and Management have been discussed in detail here under. The JCSV disease of J. Sambac Ait., was characterized by production of chlorotic spots of varying size and shape with green centre and dark green background. These rings were not limited by veins. The leaves developed malformations like crinkling and narrowing when they were young. Hence, the disease under the study has been named as Jasmine chlorotic spot virus disease (JCSVD) and the virus associated as Jasmine chlorotic spot virus (JCSV). Similarly Wilson (1972); Benigno et al. (1975); Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975); Chandra et al. (1979) and Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991)have reported similar type of symptoms. Whereas the symptoms on J. multiflorum Roth., is slightly different from that produced on J. sambac Ait., which were characterized by prominent chlorosis spreading along the veins. Sometimes these symptoms appeared on leaves with more or less circular shapes with white centre and yellow border on green background. Though Waterworth (1971) reported Jasmine latent Virus —1 on J. multiflorum Roth., it never expressed any symptoms. On the other hand Chandra et <3/.(1979) have reported infection of J. multiflorum Roth.,with JYRMV. This indicates that the same vims JCSV might be showing different symptoms on two different species of Jasmine or may be infected by different viruses causing such symptoms. The studies on the incidence of JCSV in Kamataka indicated that its incidence ranged from 3.00 to 95.0 per cent in various parts of North Kamataka. It was observed that JCSV disease was present in all J. sambac Ait., growing fields visited in thirteen villages of six districts. The highest incidence of 95.0 per cent was recorded at New orchard, U.A.S., Dharwad (Dharwad district) and the lowest of 3.0 per cent at Huvinahadagali (Bellary district)(Table:4). The chlorotic ring spots, malformations of leaves and over all chlorosis of plant were the symptoms recorded in both years. Severe leaf malformations were seen when the leaves were young and fleshy due to virus infection. These results are in accordance with reports of Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975) and Chandra et al. (1979) who reported 1.5 to 52.00 per cent incidence in Coimbatore and 10 to 100 per cent incidence in Bangalore, respectively. The symptoms of JCSV infection on J. multiflorum Roth., were recorded only at Floriculture orchard, Arabhavi with 30 per cent incidence. This is in agreement with Chandra et al. (1979) who reported JYRMV infection on J. multiflorum Roth. The survey results clearly showed the presence of JCSV in all the fields ofJ. samhac Ait., surveyed. This might be because of the use of infected propagative material by the farmers. The results also revealed that JCSV was never obseived on J. auriculatum Vahl., and J. grandiflorum Lmn. This variation of the incidence of the disease in different varieties might be because of the different genotj-pic makeup. This also indicates that J. auriculatum Vahl., and J. grandiflorum Linn, possess resistance to the disease which can be used in breeding programmes. Initially in the studies to identify the virus, DAC-ELISA and triple antibody ELISA were carried out using infected leaf extracts of J. samhac Ait., and J. multiflorum Roth., with polyclonal antibodies of CMV, PVY and monoclonal antibodies of TSWV 2B6, TSWV-4E2, INSV-5E11. This was carried out at Indian Institute of Horticultural Research, Bangalore. These antisera were used suspecting the virus based on the symptoms. But, none of the antisera showed positive result, indicating the virus under the study is not belonging to either CMV, PVY or TSWV groups (Table:6 ).While characterizing Jasmine virus disease, Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) reported association of a Carla virus. On the contrary Benigno et al. (1978) suspected it to be Poty virus. When ELISA studies failed to establish the exact identity of the associated virus, electron microscopic studies were carried out at IIHR, Bangalore and lARI, New Delhi. Among the several attempts made following leaf dip method few attempts revealed presence of abundant elongated flexuous virus particles of approximately 630 nm in infected J.samhac leaf samples. The virus morphology and size indicated that JCSV may be a probable member of Carla virus group. Similarly, Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) also observed virus particles of 620-660 nm size in electron microscopic studies with J. samhac Ait., showing chlorotic spots and variegation. This result is also in agreement with the general size of Carla viruses i.e., 620 to 700 nm (Koenig 1982). But on the contrary Benigno et al. (1978) observed virus particles of 700-750 nm size from J. samhac Ait., showing yellow ring spot mosaic symptoms. In the light of the above observations, Immunosorbent electron microscopy (ISEM), studies were carried out at LARI, New Delhi to further identify the virus under study. A total of twelve different antisera produced against members of Poty, Potex, Carla and Clostero virus groups were used (Table:5).But the elongated flexuous virus particles associated with JCSVD of J. sambac Ait., did not react with any of antisera used. This is in contrast to the report of Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991), who reported that elongated particles observed in infected leaf samples of J. sambac Ait., reacted with Shallot latent and Narcissus latent virus, members of Carla virus group. Though the virus imder study did not react with any of the antisera of elongated viruses including member of Carla virus group(Shallot latent virus), based on morphology' and size it was inferred that virus associated with JCSVD in Kamataka may be belonging to Carla virus group, but might be a new virus of the group or a strain of Carla virus. Ultrathin microtomy studies revealed the presence of virus inclusions in the form of laminated rings of only from infected leaves of J. multiflorum Roth. But the attempts to see such virus inclusions in infected samples of J. sambac Ait., were negative. Therefore these studies further failed to provide sufficient evidence regarding exact identity of the virus. But, Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) reported bimdles of paracrystalline plates of virus particles in infected J.sambac samples as a characteristic feature of Carla virus. Where as Benigno et al. (1978) observed pin wheel inclusions in J.sambac samples a characteristic feature of Poty viruses. Hence, for the proper identification of the present virus under study some more experimental evidences are needed. (1994). The non-sap transmissibility of chlorotic spots and variegation of J. sambac Ait., is thought to be due to the presence of aromatic substances / essences in them (Bellardi and Bertaccini, 1991) or their flower extracts may contain anti-viral principles (AVPs) (Rao et al., 1985). The studies of graft transmission indicated that JCSV of J. sambac Ait., could be successfully transmitted by approach grafting. JCSV took 35 days for expression of symptoms on the grafted J. sambac Ait., healthy plants(Table:7). The results are in agreement with the findings of Wilson (1972), Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975), Chandra et al. (1979) and Mali (1980) and Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991). The studies involving the already infected propagative cuttings resulted in good transmission of virus under study to all the vegetative clones (Table:8). These rooted cuttings expressed symptoms in 50-75 days after planting. Mariappan and Ramanujam (1975) and Chandra et al. (1979) also observed similar transmission through the planting material of J. sambac. It can be inferred that use of healthy propagative material helps in containing the disease spread. Soil transmission studies under taken by growing healthy cuttings of J. sambac in soil collected from root zone of infected plants were negative (Table:9 ). These results ruled out the soil transmission of JCSV and involvement of nematode or soil borne fungi in the spread of the vu-us even though both nematodes (Rajaram and Rajendra, 1979) 73 and soil borae iungi (Ramadas et al., 1999) have been reported infecting J. sambac Ait. In the present study, various insects reported to be vectors of Jasmine viruses were tried for their ability to transmit the virus under study (Table: 10). All the insects viz., aphids {Aphis gossypii Glover.); Whiteflies {Bemisia tabaci Germ.) and thrips {Thrips orientalis L.) failed to transmit JCSV from J. sambac Ait. to J. sambac or N. tabacum. Whereas several workers have successfully transmitted jasmine viruses by whiteflies (Wilson, 1972; Benigno et al., 1975; Mariappan and Ramanujan, 1975; Chandra et al. 1978; and Mali, 1980) as well as aphids (Bellardi and Bertaccini, 1991). And even the present findings are not in agreement with general aphid transmission nature of Carla viruses (Koenig, 1982). Host range studies involving twenty different species belonging to seven families by mechanical inoculation of herbaceous hosts and by grafting on the Jasminum species were tried. The virus was transmitted only to J. sambac Ait., by approach grafting and all other Jasminum spp. did not develop any symptoms indicating their resistance. Like wise, none of the herbaceous hosts inoculated mechanically developed symptoms (Table: 11). These results further confirmed the non-transmission of the virus by sap inoculation. These results are in agreement with Bellardi and Bertaccini (1991) and also with Allen (1972) and Bellardi et al. (1994). Management studies involving hot water treatment (HWT) of infected vegetative cuttings was carried out to inhibit JCSV of J. sambac Ait. Though vegetative cuttings were treated at different temperatures and time intervals (Table: 12), the results of these trials were not promising, as the cuttings lost the ability to establish at and above 45°C and 60 min. The results were similar even by keeping treated cuttings in mist chamber where in establishment was good in general. This result is in agreement with the reports of Baker (1962) who explained the causes of damage of plants / plant parts treated in water at temperatures necessary for therapy, such as leaching, water soaking and asphyxiation of the host tissues. Hence, the hot water treatment (HWT) though applicable to control viruses of woody plants is not effective in case ofJ. sambac Ait., to contain the JCSV. The efficacy of antiviral principles (AVPs) to inhibit the JCSV was tested by dipping vegetative cuttings in 5 per cent leaf extracts for 2 hours. The results showed that leaf extracts of coconut followed by mirabilis and maize have some promising results to inhibit JCSV infecting J. sambac Ait., and mirabilis followed by coconut and maize against JCSV infecting J. multiflorum Roth.(Table: 13). These results are in agreement with reports of efficacy of various leaf extracts inhibiting virus infections. (Narayanasamy and Ganapathy, 1986; Narayanasamy, 1986; and Kulkami, 1996). VI. SUMMARY The present investigation on chlorotic spot virus of Jasminum spp. in Kamataka included survey, identification and characterization of causal virus, transmission studies of virus, nature of survival and host range of the virus and management of the disease. Different experiments were conducted at Agricultural College, Dharwad and K.R.C. college of Horticulture, Arabhavi during the years 1999-2000. The electron microscopic studies and serological studies were conducted at the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research, Bangalore and Indian Agricultural Research Institute, New Delhi. The results of the studies are summarized here under. 1. The chlorotic spot virus caused chlorosis of the plant, chlorotic spots and malformations of leaves on J. sambac Ait.,. Where as, symptoms were different viz., chlorosis extending along the veins sometimes with rough circular shape on J. multiflorum. 1. The incidence of JCSVD in parts of the North Kamataka ranged from 3.0 to 95.0 per cent. The incidence was recorded in all the fields of J. sambac Ait. surveyed, with the maximum incidence of 95.0 per cent at New orchard, U.A.S., Dharwad. Symptoms on J. multiflorum Roth., were observed only at Floricultural orchard of K.R.C.C.H., Arabhavi with 30.0 per cent incidence. 3. The DAC-ELISA using polyclonal antibodies of CMV, PVY and Triple antibody ELISA using monoclonal antibodies of TSWV 2B6, TSWV 4E2, INSV 5E11 showed negative results indicating that the NTrus infecting J. sambac Ait., and J. multiflorum Roth., was not related to CMV, PVY, and TSWV groups. 4. Electron microscopic studies only with J.sambac samples revealed presence of abundant elongated flexuous particles of approximately 630 nm in size but, no particles were recorded in J. multiflorum Roth, samples. 5. The elongated flexuous particles did not react with any of the twelve virus antisera of other known elongated viruses belonging to Poty, Potex, Carla and Clostero virus groups indicating a distinct nature of the virus under study. 6. Ultramicrotomy revealed the presence of some laminated rings of virus inclusion bodies from the leaf sample sections of J. multiflorum Roth., only. 7. Mechanical transmission trials failed to transmit JCSV to any of test plants even when different buffers with different additives were tried. 8. The virus was successfully transmitted through approach grafting from donor J. sambac Ait. to healthy J. sambac Ait. test plants in 35 days after grafting, but not to any other Jasminum spp tried. 9. The virus under study was readily transmissible through the vegetative cuttings, but not through soil. 10. Even the different insect vectors Viz.,aphids {Aphis gossypii Glover.); whiteflies {Bemisia tabaci Genn.) and thrips {Thrips orientalis L.) failed to transmit JCSV either from J. sambac to J.sambac or N.tabacum. 11. None of the twenty hosts tried through mechanical sap transmission could be infected by JCSV. But it was found to be transmissible through approach grafting from J. sambac Ait., to J. sambac Ait.,. 12. Based on symptoms, transmission studies, serology, host range and Electron microscopy the virus associated with the jasmine chlorotic spot disease in Kamataka has been caused by a probable member or strain of Carla virus group. 13. JCSV was not affected by hot water treatment at 45°C for 60 min and the treatments above 45°C for 60 min had bad effect as the cuttings lost the ability to establish. Hence, hot water treatment was not an effective method for management of JCSV of J. sambac Ait. 14.Leaf extracts of coconut, maize and mirabilis (5%) showed promising results in inhibiting the JCSV infecting both J. sambac Ait., and J. multifloriim Roth, cuttings. RAMA KRISHNA Dr. M. S. KULKARNI Major Advisor ABSTRACT Jasmine chlorotic spot virus (JCSV) disease, is present in almost ail fields of J. sambac of North Karnataka, and causing considerable damage. The incidence ranged from 3.00 to 95.00 per cent. The JCSV caused chlorosis of the plant, chlorotic spots and malformations of leaves on J. sambac whereas symptoms were different viz., chlorosis extending along the veins sometimes with rough circular shape on J. multiflorum. The other two species J. auriculatum and J. grandiflorum never exhibited symptoms indicating their resistance. The leaf samples of both J. sambac and J. multiflorum showed negative reaction with TSVW, CMV and PVY tested through ELISA. The electron microscopic observations with infected J. sambac leaves revealed presence of elongated flexuous particles of approximately 630 nm size. These particles were not reacting with any of twelve antisera of other known viruses belonging to Poty, Potex, Caria and Clostero virus groups in ISEM test. Ultrathin microtomy revealed the presence of some laminated rings of virus inclusion bodies in leaf sample sections from J. multiflorum only. The Jasmine chlorotic spot causing virus was not sap transmissible, also not transmissible by insects and soil. But, this was transmissible through approach grafting and through vegetative cuttings using infected material in the nurseries. Based on Symptoms, Electron microscopy, Serology, Transmission studies and Host range the virus associated with the Jasmine chlorotic spot disease in Karnataka has been concluded to be a probable member or strain of CarIa virus group. Hot water treatment was not effective for management of JCSV of J. sambac as the temperatures necessary for therapy had deleterious effect on survival of vegetative cuttings. Dipping cuttings in leaf extracts of coconut, maize and mirabilis (5%) showed promising results in inhibiting the JCSV infecting both J. sambac and J. multiflorum.

The generis name has been assigned in the honor of P. A. Micheli, a famous Florentine botanist. The genus has attractive trees. The leaves are simple, whole and alternating, with prominent stipules. It is commonly referred as yellow champaca. There are three species of Michelia available in Malaysia. They are Michelia alba (White chempaka), Michelia champaca (Orange chempaka) and Michelia figo (dwarf chempaka) with Michelia alba being the most popular species within the family (Raja and Koduru, 2014). They are also very fragrant when a Michelia tree flowers, the fragrance produced is noticeable some distance from the tree (Patil et al., 2014). Michelia champaca is grown in moist, deep, well- drained, good quality soil with pH 5.6 to 6.0. In its natural habitat, champaca grows in areas where temperatures are 0 to 47.5℃ and annual precipitation is 2250 to 5000 mm or more. It thrives in a damp climate (Mane et al., 2019). It cannot withstand temperatures below zero or rains of less than 200 mm. Michelia champaca is a very tall tree that grows up to 30m tall. The leaves are ovate in shape and are up to 30.5 cm long and 10.2 cm wide narrowing to a fine point at the apex. The flowers are pale yellow to orange and fairly large growing up to 5.1cm in diameter. The flower has 15 tepals that curve up towards the tips and many stamens (pollen producing structures) (Raja and Koduru, 2014). The tree blooms from May to October and produces abundance of star- shaped flowers with mesmerizing scent (Mane et al., 2019). Michelia champaca is famous for the sweet odour of its blossoms. The flower possesses a scent that can be described as fresh, floral and strong sweet jasmine-like scent. Most of the aromatic compounds encountered have rather strong odors, and especially the esters are regarded as possessing floral notes. Methyl benzoate (heavy-sweet, deep-floral), indole (floral character highly reminiscent of jasmine and orange blossom) and 1,8-cineole (fresh camphoraceous) are contributing significantly to the fragrance of Michelia champaca flowers. (Ibrahim et al., 2008) Michelia (champaka) species is commonly known to produce high value essential oil. The popularity of the fragrance has resulted with many species of Michelia being grown all over the world. It was reported that the essential oil of Michelia has been used as a key top note in Joy and J’adore, which are among the world’s most expensive perfumes (Ibrahim et al., 2008)Champaca flowers are employed in India in the preparation of attars and perfumed hair oil. ‘Joy’ the second best selling perfume in the world which is derived in part from the essential oil of champaca flowers (Desai and Lalitha, 2018). 3 Michelia champaca has several ornamental, commercial and medicinal uses for gardeners. It is an excellent choice as a house plant or companion plant in landscape. Michelia has strongly fragrant flowers in varying shades usually golden – yellow, golden – orange and creamy – white. Especially in India, Michelia are primarily used for worship at temple, at home or out and more generally worn in hair by girls and women as a means of beauty ornament as well as a natural perfume (Mane et al., 2019). Traditionally, Champaca is widely used in both Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. The champaca flower is useful for snake bite and scorpion sting (Tandon et al., 2017). It is being used in fever, colic, leprosy, post-partum protection and in eye disorders. The flower oil is useful in cephalalgia, opthalmia and gout. The bark is useful as a stimulant, expectorant, astringment and febrifugal properties. Root and bark are used as purgative and in the treatment of inflammation, constipation and dysmenorrhea. The flower and fruits are considered stimulant, antispasmodic, tonic, stomachic, bitter and cool remedies and are used in dyspepsia, nausea and in fever (Raja and koduru, 2014). The flowers were reported to contain 26.3 per cent of essential oil (Baslas, 1967). The oil yielded a sesquiterpene champacene (Nigam, 1963). Cineole, isoeugenol, phenylethyl alcohol, benzaldehyde and methyl anthranilate were also reported from the flowers (Rout et al., 2006). 1.2 Importance and Need of the Study The chemicals (elicitors) play a key role in increasing shelf life of loose flowers (florets) where a single day enhancement of shelf life is an important issue to extend the availability for costumers (Chawla et al., 2020). Ascorbic acid is an antioxidant that extends the vase life of flowers by lowering the rate of respiration and ethylene generation. It is essential for plant growth and development, cell division, cell wall metabolism, root development, photosynthesis, florescence regulation, leaf senescence regulation and enzyme activity (Rakesh et al., 2022). It has been suggested that using boric acid as a mineral salt could improve the water balance and longevity of cut flowers by raising the osmotic concentration and pressure potential of the petal cells (Choudhary et al., 2019). In case of sodium benzoate, the shelf life of flowers are increasing due to its action on decreasing the pH (making it acidic) and creating an unsuitable environment for the growth of micro-organisms, especially bacteria and fungi (Kumar et al., 2020). Packaging is a tool for controlling flower quality in the distribution chain. Apart from preventing mechanical damage, the package serves as a barrier between the conditions inside and 4 outside the package. It protects the flowers from unfavourable outside conditions and enables a micro climate to develop inside the package (Nowak and Rudnicki, 1979). It also makes the flowers to look fresh and of good quality. The main principle of packing is to prolong the storage life and keeping quality of flowers by lowering the rate of transpiration, respiration and cell division during transportation and storage. Since flowers are delicate and highly perishable, they need great attention through advanced technologies in packaging to keep them fresh to consumer’s satisfaction. By improving the packaging techniques farmers can get more income by extending the storage life and keeping them fresh for longer time [Bhattacharjee (1997), Rakesh et al.,(2022)]. Near about, 30-50 per cent losses of flowers occur due to improper post harvest handling during entire market chain. Post harvest treatments are aimed at encouraging the process under quality traits, including flower size, shape, colour and longevity (Chander, 2017). The flowers have good demand for export due to its attractive fragrance. But one of the major problems faced by farmers are lack of suitable packaging material, less shelf life of flowers and browning of tepals on the second day of harvest with abrupt loss in fragrance (Choudhary et al., 2019). Therefore, the present investigation is planned to study the effect of different chemical pretreatments, packaging material and low temperature storage impact on shelf life of champaca flower. 1.3 Objectives of the Study 1. To study the effect of chemical pretreatments on the quality attributes of champaca flowers during storage 2. To study the storage behaviour of champaca flowers under low refrigerated conditions 1.4 Hypothesis of Assumptions The present study regarding “Studies on packaging and storage behaviour of champaca (Michelia champaca Linn.)” was carried out with a view to find the best chemical treatment and the packaging material to improve the shelf life of champaca flowers. Pre-treatment with different chemicals and use of various packaging materials with low temperature storage would help to delay respiration, minimize weight loss and increase the shelf life of flower during the post harvest storage of Michelia champaca flowers. 5 1.5 Scope and Limitation The scope of Michelia champaca flowers, also known as Champak flowers, is quite broad, encompassing various aspects like beauty, perfumery industry, cosmetics, religious significance, traditional medicine and pollinators. They boast stunning, cup-shaped blooms with vibrant colors ranging from creamy yellow to orange-yellow, often releasing a sweet, fruity fragrance. These attractive features make them popular choices for landscaping, adorning gardens and parks with their exotic charm. The intense, sweet scent of Michelia champaca flowers is widely appreciated and used in various aromatic applications. In traditional medicine practices, Michelia champaca flowers are used for their purported therapeutic properties. They are believed to possess anti- inflammatory, antibacterial, and anti-anxiety effects, finding use in various remedies. The essential oil extracted from Michelia champaca flowers is highly sought-after in the perfume industry. The essential oil and extracts from the flowers are also utilized in cosmetic products. Michelia champaca flowers attract a diverse range of pollinators, including bees, butterflies, and other insects, playing a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance. In conclusion, the scope of Michelia champaca flowers extends far beyond their aesthetic appeal. The small and marginal farmers living in the remote areas cannot afford the refrigeration system and they are least interested in time consuming post harvest techniques. Thamaraiselvi et al. (2010) studied the storage life of jasmine flowers (Jasminum sambac) under cold room conditions. (2012) treated, the jasmine flowers with 2% sucrose, 4% sucrose, 2% boric acid, 4% boric acid, 25 ppm salicylic acid, 50 ppm salicyclic acid, 50 ppm ascorbic acid, 100 ppm ascorbic acid, 50 ppm NAA, 100 ppm NAA, distilled water and no soaking (control). Raigad, (18º25'35.16312" N, 73º10'45.77484" E) during the year 2022-23. 3.1 Material Required 3.1.1 Chemicals 1. Sodium benzoate 2. Boric acid 3. Ascorbic acid 4. Potassium hydroxide 5. Folin ciocalteau reagent 6. Sodium bicarbonate 7. Toulene 8. Ethanol 9. Gallic acid 10. Phosphoric acid 3.1.2 Instruments and equipments 1. Spectrophotometer 2. Pestle and mortar 3. Colorimeter 4.
