Moisture analyzer 3.1.3 Experimental material The half bloom champaca flowers were plucked during morning hours from PGI- PHTM campus, A/P.: Killa, Taluka: Roha, District: Raigad (MS). Harvested flowers were brought to the department of PHM of FVF laboratory and washed. Fresh flowers was treated with different concentrations of sodium benzoate, boric acid and ascorbic acid as per the treatment and dipped for five minutes in solution. Later on, the flowers were air dried, packed in different packaging material on pre- treatment and stored at refrigerated storage at 7℃. Chemical, glassware, instrument and other material were procured from the Department of Post Harvest Management of Fruit, Vegetable and Flower Crops, Post Graduate Institute of Post Harvest Technology and Management, Killa- Roha, Dist.- Raigad. 3.2 Experimental Details Crop :Champaca (Michelia champaca L.) Cultivar :Champaca - Local Design : Factorial Completely Randomized Design (FCRD) Number of treatment : 7 × 4 = 28 combinations Replications :3 3.2.1 Treatment details a) Main treatments : Different chemical treatments T1 : 100 ppm Sodium benzoate T2 : 150 ppm Sodium benzoate T3 : 1% Boric acid T4 : 2% Boric acid T5 : 100 ppm Ascorbic acid T6 : 150 ppm Ascorbic acid T7 : Control 20 b) Sub Treatment Sub treatment Different packaging material P1 : LDPE bag P2 : Poly propylene bag P3 : Transparent standup pouch P4 : Control 3.3 Methods Adopted 3.3.1 Procedure for chemical treatment and packaging of champaca flowers FLOW CHART : Harvesting of champaca flowers early in the morning Selection of healthy flowers of champaca Quick dipping of flowers in chemical solution as per the treatment Packing in different packaging materials as per the treatment Storage at refrigerated condition (7±1˚C) 21 3.3.1.1 Harvesting of flowers Fresh champaca (Michelia champaca L.) flowers were procured in the morning at (6 to 7 am) at half bloom stage from PGI- PHTM campus, Killa, Taluka: Roha, District: Raigad (MS). 3.3.1.2 Preparation of sodium benzoate solution The sodium benzoate with concentration were prepared by dissolving required quantity of sodium benzoate in distilled water. The champaca flowers were then immersed in the solution for 60 seconds. 3.3.1.3 Preparation of boric acid solution The boric acid solutions of 1 and 2 per cent strength were prepared by dissolving required quantity of boric acid in distilled water. The champaca flowers were then immersed in the prepared solution for 60 seconds. 3.3.1.4 Preparation of ascorbic acid solution The ascorbic acid solution of 100 and 150 ppm strength were prepared by dissolving required quantity of ascorbic acid in distilled water. The champaca flowers were then immersed in the ascorbic acid solution for 60 seconds. 3.3.1.5 Processing and packaging of flowers After dipping flowers in the solution for 60 seconds, the flowers were air dried for short time and packed in the different packaging material (Polyethylene, Polypropylene and Transparent standup pouch) as per treatment and then stored at refrigerated condition. The observation were recorded every day till the end of shelf life. 3.3.2 Changes in the visual and physical quality parameters of the champaca flowers The observations recorded daily were the colour L*, a*, b* value, freshness index (FI), fragrance index, colour retention index and overall acceptability. 3.3.2.1 Colour (L*, a*, b* value) The changes in physical parameter such as colour (L*, a*, b*) values of champaca were determined by using colorimeter (make Konica Minolta, Japan) during storage. 22 3.3.2.2 Freshness index The freshness of champaca flower was measured by visual observations using the following score card developed for the evaluation of champaca flower in Fig 1. This research was aimed to study the effect of chemical pretreatments, combination of packaging and refrigerated condition storage on the physiological change, freshness and colour retention of champaca flowers and chemical changes of these flower after storing in refrigerated condition. Seven treatments comprising different pre chemical treatments and packaging materials as a sub treatments which comprises four packaging material with three replications. The research data was subjected to the statistical analysis with Factorial Completely Randomized Design (F.C.R.D.). The physiological loss in weight of champaca flower packed in different packaging materials exhibited an increasing trend during storage. 5.1.3 Changes in chemical parameters of champaca flower influenced by different chemical treatments and packaging materials during storage 81 5.1.3.1 Carotenoid content (mg/100g) In case of LDPE bags, the 2% boric acid treatment (227.29 mg/100g) recorded maximum mean carotenoid content of champaca flower and control (200.87 mg/100g) recorded minimum mean carotenoid content of champaca flower. As regards the polypropylene bags, the maximum mean carotenoid content of champaca flower (203.63 mg/100g) was observed in the 2% boric acid treatment and minimum mean carotenoid content of champaca flower (182.26 mg/100g) was recorded in the control. As per the data observed in standup pouch, the treatment 150 ppm sodium benzoate treatment recorded the highest (215.66 mg/100g) mean carotenoid content of champaca flower. The lowest (199.90 mg/100g) mean carotenoid content of champaca flower was observed in the control. As concerned with the control (without packaging), the treatment 150 ppm sodium benzoate treatment recorded the highest (195.66 mg/100g) mean carotenoid content of champaca flower. The lowest (174.90 mg/100g) mean carotenoid content of champaca flower was observed in the control. The carotenoid content of champaca flower packed in different packaging materials was decreased during storage. 5.1.3.2 Total phenol content (mg/g) As per the data presented in Table 4.10 and depicted in Fig 4.37 to 4.40, in LDPE bags, the 2% boric acid treatment recorded the highest (18.61mg/g) mean total phenol content of champaca flower. The lowest (15.78mg/g) mean total phenol content was observed in the control (Control). In case of polypropylene bags, the 2% boric acid treatment recorded significantly maximum (17.59 mg/g) mean total phenol content of champaca flower and lowest (14.49 mg/g) mean total phenol content was observed in the control. As regards the standup pouch, the treatment 150 ppm sodium benzoate treatment recorded the highest (20.12 mg/g) mean total phenol content of champaca flower. The lowest (15.90 mg/g) mean total phenol content was observed in the control. In control (without packaging), the treatment 150 ppm sodium benzoate treatment recorded the highest (19.12 mg/g) mean total phenol content of champaca flower. The lowest (14.90 mg/g) mean total phenol content was observed in the control. The total phenol content of champaca flower packed in different packaging materials exhibited a decreasing trend during storage. 5.1.4 Economics of champaca flower As far as the economics of champaca flower is concerned, among all the treatments, the 2% boric acid treatment recorded the highest benefit : cost ratio i.e. 1:1.27 and the lowest in the Control i.e. 1:1.07. 82 5.2. Conclusion An investigation entitled “Studies on packaging and storage behaviour of champaca (Michelia champaca Linn.)” was carried out to assess effect of different chemical treatments and packaging materials on physiological, physical and chemical parameters of champaca flower. The champaca flowers from different treatments were evaluated for changes in their physiological, physical and chemical parameters such as colour L*, a*, b*, physiological loss in weight, freshness, fragrance index, colour retention index, carotenoid content and total phenol content during refrigerated storage. The study revealed that the quality parameters such as colour a* and physiological loss in weight was increased during storage. The colour L*, b* values, fragrance index, freshness index, colour retention index, overall acceptability, carotenoid content and total phenol content was decreased during storage. From the result of present studies, it can be concluded that the flowers treated with 2% boric acid treatment packed in LDPE bag helps in maintaining quality and shelf life of champaca flowers up to 7th day of storage under refrigerated condition. Sawant SK, Shirke GD, Kadam JH and Relekar PP DOI: https://doi.org/10.33545/26174693.2024.v8.i5k.1214 Abstract An experiment entitled, “Studies on packaging and storage behaviour of champaca (Michelia champaca Linn.)” was conducted at the Department of PHM of fruit, vegetable and flower crops, PGI- PHTM, Killa-Roha during the year 2022-23. The experiment was laid out in Factorial Completely Randomized Block Design (FCRD) comprising six treatment combinations of different chemicals along with control viz., Sodium Benzoate (100 ppm and 150 ppm), Boric Acid (1 and 2 percent) and Ascorbic Acid (100 ppm and 150 ppm) and were packed in three different types of packaging material viz., LDPE bags, polypropylene bags, stand up pouches and control were stored in refrigerator at 7 ℃. The quality of the champaca flower could be improved by treating with different chemical at different concentration and packed in various packaging material. From the present investigation, it was observed that the physical parameter such as L* and b* value for colour exhibited an decreasing trend while increasing trend was observed in a* value for colour of the champaca flower irrespective of treatments during storage. From the results of present studies, it can be concluded that the champaca flowers treated with 2 percent boric acid could be stored up to 7 days at low temperature (7± 2 ℃) conditions, when packed in LDPE bags. Keywords: Champaca, packaging materials, boric acid, LDPE bags, refrigerated storage, retention, shelf life Introduction Michelia is a historical genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Magnoliaceae (Mane et al., 2019) [8]. This valuable tree species is found wild in the forests of eastern sub- himalayan zone from Nepal eastwards, along the foothills up to 900 m elevation including West Bengal and Assam. The common names for champaca are Golden champa (English), Sampige (Kannada), Sampangi (Tamil), Chattusampangi (Telugu), Sonachapha (Marathi) (Desai and Lalitha, 2018) [6]. The generis name has been assigned in the honor of P. A. Micheli, a famous Florentine botanist. The flowers are axillary or terminal, trimerous and often enormous. Petal and sepal characteristics are often comparable and deciduous (Shejale and Yeligar, 2019). In India, as per 2nd advanced estimate (2021-22) of area and production of horticultural crops released by The Department of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare, the area and production of loose flower is 2,76,000 hectare and 22,98,000 MT, respectively (Anon., 2021) [1]. Michelia champaca is famous for the sweet odour of its blossoms. Methyl benzoate (heavy-sweet, deep-floral), indole (floral character highly reminiscent of jasmine and orange blossom) and 1,8-cineole (fresh camphoraceous) are contributing significantly to the fragrance of Michelia champaca flowers. Michelia (champaka) species is commonly known to produce high value essential oil. ‘Joy’ the second Best Selling perfume in the world which is derived in part from the essential oil of champaca flowers (Desai, 2018) [6]. The chemicals play a key role in increasing shelf life of loose flowers (florets) where a single day enhancement of shelf life is an important issue to extend the availability for costumers (Chawla et al., 2020) [4]. Ascorbic acid is an antioxidant that extends the vase life of flowers by lowering the rate of respiration and ethylene generation (Rakesh et al., 2022) [12]. It has been suggested that using boric acid as a mineral salt could improve the water balance and longevity of cut flowers by raising the osmotic concentration and pressure potential of the petal cells (Choudhury et al., 2019) [5]. In case of sodium benzoate, the shelf life of flowers are increasing due to its action on decreasing the pH and creating an unsuitable environment for the growth of micro-organisms, especially bacteria and fungi (Kumar et al., 2020) [7]. Apart from preventing mechanical damage, the package serves as a barrier between the conditions inside and outside the package (Nowak and Rudnicki, 1979) [9]. Since flowers are delicate and highly perishable, they need great attention through advanced technologies in packaging to keep them fresh to consumer’s satisfaction. By improving the packaging techniques farmers can get more income by extending the storage life and keeping them fresh for longer time (Bhattacharjee, 1997) [2] (Rakesh et al., 2022) [12]. Near about, 30-50 percent losses of flowers occur due to improper post harvest handling during entire market chain. Post harvest treatments are aimed at encouraging the process under quality traits, including flower size, shape, colour and longevity (Chander, 2017) [3]. The flowers have good demand for export due to its attractive fragrance. But one of the major problems faced by farmers are lack of suitable packaging material, less shelf life of flowers and browning of petals on the second day of harvest with abrupt loss in fragrance (Choudhury, 2019) [5]. Therefore, the present investigation is planned to study the effect of different chemical pretreatments, packaging material and low temperature storage impact on shelf life of champaca flower. Therefore, keeping in mind, the above discussed factors regarding the champaca flowers, the present investigation was planned. Materials and Methods Materials The half bloom champaca flowers were plucked during morning hours from PGI- PHTM campus, A/P.: Killa, Taluka: Roha, District: Raigad (MS). Harvested flowers were brought to the department of PHM of FVF laboratory and washed. Chemical, glassware, instrument and other material were procured from the Department of Post Harvest Management of Fruit, Vegetable and Flower Crops, Post Graduate Institute of Post Harvest Technology and Management, Killa-Roha, Dist.- Raigad. 25g of uniform size, freshly harvested flowers are used for each treatments and observation like colour value (L*, a* and b*), carotenoid content and total phenol content were recorded during storage of flowers at 24 hours of intervals. Methods The colour of champaca flower was measured using Colorimeter (Colour Reader CR-10) and expressed as L*, a*, b* values. The data were statistically analyzed by using Factorial Completely Randomized design (FCRD) described by Panse and Sukhatme (1985) [10]. Pretreatment and packaging of champaca flower Fresh flowers was treated with different concentrations of sodium benzoate, boric acid and ascorbic acid as per the treatment and dipped for few seconds in solution. Later on, the flowers were air dried, packed in different packaging material on pre- treatment and stored at refrigerated storage at 7 ℃. This experiment was laid out in FCRD design with 7 treatments and 3 replication. The treatments are: T1- 100 ppm sodium benzoate, T2- 150 ppm sodium benzoate, T3- 1% boric acid, T4- 2% boric acid, T5- 100 ppm ascorbic acid, T6- 150 ppm ascorbic acid, T7- control and sub treatments are packaging material: P1- LDPE bags, P2- polypropylene bags, P3- standup pouch and P4- control. The flowers were kept in refrigerated storage and stored at 7 ± 2 ℃. Discussion According to the present studies, at the end of storage period, there was significant difference in the mean L* value for colour. The boric acid treatment helped to prevent loss of the champaca flower irrespective of packaging treatment. The L* value showed the decreasing trend with increase in storage time in refrigerated conditions and increased browning during storage. Similar observations were recorded by Qazi et al. (2016) [11] in marigold flower. Varpe et al. (2020) [15] stated that pre chemical treatment with 4 and 6 percent boric acid helped to retain the lightness of colour by preventing browning reactions in jasmine flower. The L* value of champaca flower shows best result when packed in LDPE bags. The champaca flowers packed in standup pouch and control were discarded after 2nd day of storage. Identical trend was noticed in jasmine flower buds by Varpe et al. (2020) [15] in same packaging material. The redness in the champaca flower was determined from a* value for colour of champaca flower. The a* value of champaca observed in treatment T4 (2% Boric acid) packed in LDPE bags was lower than that of T7 (control) when packed in LDPE bags. Redness of flower increased in storage period due to increase in browning and decrease in lightness of flowers during storage. These results are in accordance with the findings of Varpe et al. (2020) [15] and Siriamornpun et al. (2012) [14]. The a* colour value was significantly lower than the other packaging material like standup pouches and polypropylene bags. The champaca flowers were discarded due to loss of their shelf life which were packed in standup pouch and control (without packaging) after 2nd day of storage. The similar results were observed in jasmine flower buds by Varpe et al. (2020) [15] in same packaging material. A continuous decreasing trend with significant difference was observed in mean b* value for colour during storage. On the 1st day of storage, the mean of b* value of colour was highest in treatment T4 and at 7th day of storage and it was decreased as compared to the control when packed in LDPE bags. As regards to the packaging materials, the b* value of champaca flower was lowest in Polypropylene bags. The champaca flowers packed in standup pouch and control were discarded after 2nd day of storage. These observations are in accordance with the findings recorded by Varpe et al. (2020) [15] in jasmine buds and Siriamornpun et al. (2012) [14] in marigold flower for b* value of colour. Conclusion An investigation entitled “Studies on packaging and storage behaviour of champaca (Michelia champaca Linn.)” was carried out to assess effect of different chemical treatments and packaging materials on physical of champaca flower. The champaca flowers from different treatments were evaluated for changes in their physiological, physical and chemical parameters such as colour L*, a*, b*, during refrigerated storage. The present study revealed that the quality parameters such as colour a* was increased during storage. The colour L*, b* values was decreased during storage. From the result of present studies, it can be concluded that the flowers treated with 2% boric acid treatment packed in LDPE bag helps in maintaining quality and shelf life of champaca flowers up to 7th day of storage under refrigerated condition. Retailers 4.10 Producer’s share in consumer rupee in marketing of flowers INTRODUCTION Agriculture has been the backbone of Indian economy. India is a country of villages comprising of 6,40,867 villages. Rural India has 68.84 per cent of the population. This population is dependent on agriculture and allied activities for its livelihood. Agriculture is the primary sector of the Indian economy apart from being the mainstay for nearly three fourth of the population, it contributes 14.2 per cent to the nation’s Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and 8.5 per cent of the total exports from agriculture sector. Importance of flowers in the economy Flowers have their own importance since ancient times and are being used for decoration, worshiping as well as in satisfying the aesthetic feelings. The language of flowers were nurtured and developed in England during 18th and 19th centuries. Flower speaks a language, which could be universally understood by the people across the world and are designated as the best ambassadors of good will. In recent years, the floriculture is emerging as a market demand driver activity throughout the world and considered as a potential money spinner. Under WTO regime, the floricultural sector being recognized as a lucrative profession with much higher margin of returns per unit area when compared to the field and other horticultural crops. Among horticultural crops, cut flowers and ornamentals perhaps do fetch higher value. The words of John Kaetes, “A thing of beauty is a joy forever”, connotes fresh flowers have been one of the best medium of expression of greetings, regards, love and care and respect in enhancing aesthetics of daily décor in human habitations. It is being rightly said “flowers speak a millions of unspoken words…” They fit in all occasions, be it a birth, a marriage or a death ceremonies. Hence, floriculture is fast emerging activity as a major commercial venture in the world. The social and economic aspects of growing flowers are, however, recognized much later. The offering and exchange of flowers on all social occasions, in places of worship and their use for adornment of hair by women and for home decoration have become an integral part of human living. Appreciation of the potential of commercial floriculture has resulted in the blossoming of this field into a viable agri-business option. Availability of natural resources like diverse agro-climatic conditions has helped in producing of wide range of temperate and tropical flowers, almost all through the year in some part of the country or other. Improved communication facilities have increased their availability in every part of the country. The commercial activity of production and marketing of floriculture products is also a source of gainful and quality employment to millions of in the country. Floriculture - World scenario The world cut flower industry is a highly dynamic sector. Product varieties, the origin of the production, production techniques, markets and retailing arrangements are all undergoing continuous changes, challenging the adaptive capacity of the farmers involved. In a slowly, but steadily growing world market, new developing country exporters are gaining market share at the expense of the existing producers. These producers try to stay ahead by raising productivity and through diversification and innovation. The world cut flower trade is characterized by a high degree of concentration by product and sources. Roses are the main traded product and Germany is the main market for imports and the Netherlands is the world’s leading exporter of flowers. The global floriculture trade is estimated to be about area US $ 52 billion and has been growing continuously at the rate of 10 per cent per annum (Anon., 2014). Floriculture – Indian scenario Government of India has identified floriculture as a sunrise industry and accorded it 100 per cent export oriented status. Owing to steady increase in demand for flowers floriculture has become one of the important commercial trade in agriculture. Floriculture in India is being viewed as a high growth industry. Commercial floriculture is becoming important from the export angle. The liberalization of industrial and trade policies paved the way for development of export-oriented production of cut flowers. The new seed policy had already made it feasible to import planting material of international varieties. It has been found that commercial floriculture has higher potential per unit area than most of the field crops and is therefore a lucrative business. Indian floriculture industry has been shifting from traditional flowers to cut flowers for export purposes. The liberalized economy has given an impetus to the Indian entrepreneurs for establishing export oriented floriculture units under controlled climatic conditions. About 190 thousand ha area was under cultivation in floriculture in 2011-12, Production of flowers are estimated to be 1.031 million loose flowers and 690.27 million cut flowers in 2011-12. The country has exported 3,09,26,023 MT of floriculture products to the world for the worth of ` 365.32 crores in 2011-12. USA, Germany, Netherlands, United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and UAE are the major importing countries of Indian flower. The important flower growing states in India are Karnataka (18,439 ha), Tamil Nadu (1775 ha) West Bengal (10050 ha), Andhra Pradesh (8036 ha) and Rajasthan (2035 ha). Among these states, Karnataka alone produces 1, 56,584 tones of fresh flowers annually. Karnataka is one of the major flower growing states in India and flower cultivation has been taken up in almost all districts of the state. The major flower growing districts are Bangalore urban, Chamrajnagar, Kolar, Haveri, Tumkur, Bangalore rural, Gadag, Bellary, Belgaum and Chitradurga. During 2011-12 the total area under major flowers estimated to be 26827 hectares. The total area under marigold (7209 ha), followed by jasmine (5431 ha) and chrysanthemum flower was (4816 ha). Major flowers of India Rose is the principal cut flower grown all over the country, even though in terms of total area, it may not be so. The larger percentage of the area in many states is used for growing scented rose, usually local varieties akin to the Gruss en Tepelitz, the old favorite to be sold as loose flowers. These are used for offering at places of worship, for the extraction of essential oils and also used in garlands. For cut flower use, the old rose varieties like Queen Elizabeth, Super Star, Montezuma, Papa Meilland, Christian Dior, Eiffel Tower, Kiss of Fire, Golden Gaint, Garde Henkel, First Prize are still popular. In recent times, with production for export gaining ground in the country, the latest varieties like First Red, Grand Gala, Konfitti, Ravel, Tineke, Sacha, Prophta, Pareo, Noblesse, Virsilia and Vivaldi are also being grown commercially. Tuberose, a very popular cut flower crop in India is grown mainly in the eastern part of the country i.e. West Bengal and also in northern plains and parts of south. Both single and double flower varieties are equally popular. Tuberose flowers are also sold loose in some areas for preparing garlands and wreaths. The other main cut flower item is orchid. Its production is restricted mainly in the north-eastern hill regions, besides parts of the southern states of Kerala and Karnataka. The main species grown are Dendrobiums, Vanda, Paphiopediliums, Oncidiums, Phalaenopsis and Cymbidiums. Under traditional flowers jasmine flower production contributes greatly to the states fresh flower production. Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) belongs to a family called Oleaceae which is one of the oldest fragrant flowers cultivated by human and known to be the native of subtropical regions and taken to the other parts of the globe. The term jasmine is derived from an Arabic word “Jessamine” and in Persian language it is called as “Yasmin” or “Yasmyn” which means fragrance. As many as 90 species of jasmine are grown in India, out of these, 20 species are cultivated in South India. The most commonly cultivated Jasmine species are Jasminum multiflorum (kakada), Jasminum sambac (gundumallige) Jasminum grandiflorum (Jaji Mallige) and Jasminum auriculatum (Soojimallige). The products of jasmine are important natural raw materials in the perfume industry. Jasmine concrete is the most common of the jasmine extract products. It is used as such in making perfumed hair oil, preparation of absolute and handkerchief perfumes. In addition, it is used in toiletries, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, food essences, chewing tobacco, dental preparations, confectionaries etc. Jasmine is one of the major commercial flower crops of India. Asteraceae] is not only grown as ornamental cut flower and landscape plant, but also as a source of natural carotenoid pigment for poultry feed. The pigment is added to intensify the yellow-orange colour of eggs yolk by adding in the poultry feed. Today, it is one of the most important commercial flowers grown world-over and in India as well, accounting for more than half of the nation’s loose flower production. A native of South and Central America, precisely Mexico by considering its easy adaptability under Indian conditions, it is presumed that T. erecta is of Indian origin though it is an introduction (Nalawadi, 1982). The genus Tagetes comprises about 33 species, of which the commercially cultivated species includes Tagetes erecta L. (African/American tall marigold), T. patula (French/dwarf marigold), T. minuta, T. signeta and T. lucida are referred as perfume marigolds. Amongst these, T. erecta is commonly grown for their exquisite blooms and also natural dye (xanthophyll) extraction. Marigold also has got therapeutic values. The flowers either fresh or dried are much used in stews, soups, mixed with cheese, possets, broths and drinks. Even today, the marigold is used by herbal doctors for simple ailments. The juice extracted from leaves is used for getting relief from boils, carbuncles and earache (Raghava and Saxena, 2001). Marigold can be cultivated easily and their petals are the most concentrated source of xanthophylls, can be extracted either from fresh or after having pressed in silose, to remove water. The resulting cake is dried, pelletized and extracted with hexane. Chrysanthemum is said to be the oldest flower cultivated by man. It was introduced in China as early as in the fourth century B.C. Chrysanthemum means “Golden flower” in Greek. It is often described as “Autumn Queen” as it blooms in November-December. Chrysanthemum is the national flower of Japan and is popularly grown in China, Japan, France, Holland, United States of America and Australia probably enjoying the world wide popularity, perhaps next only to roses. Chrysanthemum belongs to the family Compositae. It is an important herb grown for it’s highly decorative nature and long lasting flowers. It has both annual and perennial species. Chrysanthemum flowers are found either in single or in double attractive colours. Chrysanthemums are very commonly grown in glass houses for cut flowers and their flowering can be manipulated with artificial light and controlled temperature. Much of the fascination of chrysanthemum lies in its wide range of types, shapes, size and a variety of delightful colours. There are thousands of varieties of chrysanthemum now in cultivation in different countries of the world. This phenomenon has made only all the more popular and placed it in great demand. Importance of present study In Haveri district, most of traditional flowers are grown in open fields. The traditional flowers grown in the open include chrysanthemum, jasmine, crossandra, rose, tuberose, aster and marigold. The traditional flowers are grown in all taluks of the district. The traditional floriculture is still predominant in the district in terms of area and production. However, very little information is available on the economics of these flower crops cultivation and problem concerned to its production, harvesting, storage and marketing. Thus, the present study made an attempt to analyse the production and marketing related aspects of three major flowers viz., jasmine, chrysanthemum and marigold grown in the district with the following specific objectives. Specific objectives 1. To estimate the growth in area, production and productivity of major flower in Haveri district 2. To analyze the cost and returns in cultivation of selected flowers. 3. To analyze financial feasibility of investment in cultivation of perennial flower crop (Jasmine). 4. To estimate cost and margins under different channels of flower marketing. 5. To analyze the problems associated with production and marketing of selected flowers to suggest suitable policies to enhance efficiency in production and marketing of flowers. Hypotheses 1. The area of major flower crops in Haveri district is decreasing over the years. 2. Cultivation of flower crops is profitable 3. Investment in perennial flower garden (jasmine) is financially feasible and economically worth. 4. Cost and margin varies in marketing of major flowers. 5. Farmers are facing many problems in production and marketing of flowers in the study area. Chapter – III outlines the features of the study area, sampling design followed, nature and sources of data and analytical tools used in the study. Chapter – IV is devoted highlighting the main findings of the study through tables, graphs etc. Chapter – V discussion of the results of the study. Chapter – VI summarizes the entire study and brings out relevant policy implications and recommendations to improve the flowers production and marketing production. At the end important references have been listed related to the present study. REVIEW OF LITERATURE This chapter deals with a brief review of the research work done in the past and are presented under the following headings based on the objectives of the study. 2.1 Growth in area and production 2.2 Costs and returns structure 2.3 Investment pattern in perennial flowers 2.4 Cost and margin under different channels of marketing of flowers 2.5 Problems in production and marketing 2.1 Growth rates of flower in area and production Nirmal Singh et al. (1987) studied the “Financial feasibility of horticultural development in Kandi area of Punjab”. They found that fruit crops recorded a significant growth rate of 12.95 per cent per annum during the period 1981-85. Species wise, the growth rate of area per annum was significant and positive for all the fruit crops. The growth rate of area was the highest for kinnow (32.20%) followed by ber (14.96%), pear (13.30%), mango (6.75%) and guava (5.44%). Yeledhalli (1987) computed the growth rates of area, production and productivity of dry chillies in Dharwad district by using the compound growth rate of the type Yt = A.Bt. Dry chilli area and productivity growth rates during the study period were observed to be 3.42 per cent and 0.24 per cent respectively and inferred that the growth in dry chilly production in Dharwad district was the combined effect of the growth in area and productivity. Hashmi and Singh (1989) examined the trend of rice production in seven districts of Western Uttar Pradesh by using the compound growth rates for the high yielding varieties under pre and post introduction periods. The results showed that, six districts recorded relatively higher growth rates of production during the post high yielding variety programme (1966-67 to 1985-86) period, due to the increase in rice yield in these districts. Further it was observed in one district higher growth rate in rice production was due to the interaction of the area and yield. Arya and Rawat (1990) examined the compound growth rates of area, production and yields of principal crops in Haryana state over the period from 1966-67 to 1980-81. They observed that, despite inter-district variation, positive area, production and yield growth rates were recorded for wheat, rice and potatoes in all the districts while maize, sorghum, millet, barley, pulses registered declining trend. Sidhu and Sidhu (1991) in their study on “Pulses and oilseeds in India trends and policy suggestions”, observed that the growth rate around one per cent for area, production and yield of groundnut at the national level over the last four decades. The growth in production of groundnut for period 1949-50 to 1964-65 was mainly due to the growth in area. They further noticed that, a significant increase in oilseeds production (15.30%) with respect to Karnataka because of growth in area (130.00%) from 1965-66 to 1988-89. Umesh et al. (1992) examined the “Output growth stability of oilseeds in Karnataka” and found that after green revolution a marginal increase in the growth of groundnut productivity and area led to 1.81 per cent increase in production in the country. Negative growth rates were noticed during pre-green revolution period. Bhowmick and Ahamed (1993) examined the growth in area, production and yield of major oilseed crops in Assam during the pre and post green revolution period by fitting linear function of the type Y = a + bt and exponential function of the type Y = ABt. During the period 1950-51 to 1988-89, rapeseed and mustard registered 3.34 per cent growth in production which was a result of 2.96 per cent and 0.35 per cent growth in area and productivity of the crop respectively. The result indicated that increase in oilseeds production had been related to increased acreage rather than intensification of production. Behura and Naik (1994) while analyzing agricultural performance in Kalahandi district of Orissa worked out compound growth rates for area and productivity of different crops in the district during 1966-67 to 1990-91. Among all crops summer rice recorded the highest growth rate (7.77%) in area during the period. But the compound growth arte of summer rice showed that productivity declined by 2.14 per cent per annum over the years. Although summer rice in the district was at adopting stage which was sharing only 0.30 per cent of the total cropped area under the study period 1986-87 to 1990-91. Further, it was observed that the productivity of summer rice declined during the period due to limited area availability of suitable varieties at farmers front. The results revealed that Karnataka state was found to be highest growth rate in area (2.23%) and production (16.26%) over the period of 13 years (1991-92 to 2004-05) on the contrary Chitradurga market growth rate was found to be negative and non significant with area of (-1.73) and production of (7.27). 2.2 Costs and returns structure of flowers Patil and Hiremath (1985) studied the “production and marketing of chrysanthemum flowers in Dharwad district, Karnataka”. They reported that, per hectare cost of production was ` 19,350 and sales through commission agent was the main channel of marketing. The margin in the case of Belgaum market was slightly higher than that of Hubli market due to higher cost incurred in marketing. Subrahmanyam (1986) estimated the “Economics of production and marketing of chrysanthemum flowers in Karnataka”. He observed that the average total cost of cultivationwas around ` 21,537.59 per ha showing the high capital intensive nature of crop. Among the different items of cost, input cost has accounted for nearly 46 per cent of the average total cost of cultivation followed by marketing cost at 44 per cent showing the heavy expenditure incurred for marketing the crop. Among the different items of costs, human labour consisting of mostly hired labour has accounted for nearly 50 per cent of the total input cost showing the labour intensive nature of the crop. Pappiah and Balakrishnan (1989) in their study observed that the net income of ` 42,885 from the cultivation of red rose in Bangalore with a gross output value of ` 60,000 realised after incurring the total input cost of ` 17,115. The benefit cost ratio was calculated at 1:2.5. Rameshkumar (1989) studied the “Economics of production and investment in Jasmine flowers in Madurai district in Tamil Nadu”. He reported that the total expenditure incurred by Jasmine growers for establishing the Jasmine garden in the first year was ` 13,700 per ha. Among the different items of establishment, planting and plant material has accounted for the major portion i.e., about 31 per cent of establishment cost. The maintenance cost for carrying out various operations was ` 32,184 per ha. Subrahmanyam (1989) studied the “Economics of production in jasmine in Kolar district in Karnataka”. Jasmine was a perennial crop and its economic life varies from 15 to 20 years. In the first year the total cost of cultivation was around ` 18,400 per ha. Out of which around ` 10,900 was incurrred towards cost of inputs. From second year onwards the total cost of cultivation varied from ` 42,000 to ` 52,570 per ha. Out of which, nearly 35 per cent was towards marketing cost, 55 per cent towards cost of inputs and the rest towards fixed costs. Out of the total input cost large amount was accounted by harvesting cost. This was because of the fact that Kakada variety plants bear flowers through out the year. Neeraja Devi (1990) studied the “Economics of production and marketing of Kakada flowers in Bangalore district, Karnataka”. The results revealed that the average per acre establishment cost incurred by the Kakada growers was ` 3,978.16. Of which the labour and material costs accounted for 50.75 and 49.25 per cent respectively. The average labour used per acre for establishment was 71.09, 65.88 and 8.89 men, women and bullock pairs, respectively. The annual maintenance cost for carrying out various operations was ` 6,849.75 per acre. Nagarajan (1992) conducted study on “Cost of cultivation of Soundarya Kanakambaram at Olakkur village in Tindivanam taluk (Madras)”. The results revealed that, it provides a net income of ` 1,59,485 per acre with a gross output value of ` 2,40,000.00 on total input cost of ` 80,575.00. Prabhakar Rao et al. (1992) examined the “costs and returns of jasmine cultivation in Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh”. They categorized the sample into three main age groups of plants based on area under this crop. The per ha maintenance cost of jasmine were ` 43009.88, ` 52597.90 and ` 46842.01 for the age groups of plants in one to three years, four to eight years and nine and above nine year age groups respectively. The gross returns per ha were ` 52,171.70, ` 67,411.50 and ` 57,954.10, in the above age group of plants respectively. Rao et al. (1992) studied the “economic analysis of flower production in Thane district, Maharashtra”. The study revealed that the flower production needs very intensive cultivation and large initial investment. Once the production starts, there was continuous income to the farmers. The generation of employment opportunities was also very high. Study also indicated that, due to the excessive use of inputs resulted into low profit margins. Hiremath (1993) studied the “Pattern of investment in lime orchard in Bijapur district, Karnataka”. He categorized the sample into three main size groups namely small, medium and large orchards based on the area under lime plantation. The study revealed that the per ha total maintenance cost of lime orchard were ` 39,852.38, ` 32,655.13 and ` 30,686.53 on small, medium and large size orchards respectively. It also indicated that gross returns the per hectare for over total cost were found to be ` 33,193.15, ` 25,431 and ` 22,101 on small, medium and large size orchards respectively. METHODOLOGY This chapter presents the agro climatic and economic features of the study area, the nature and source of data collected, the analytical tools and techniques employed for realizing the objectives of the study. These are presented under the following heads. 3.1 Description of the study area 3.2 Sampling procedure 3.3 Nature and sources of data 3.4 Analytical tools and techniques employed 3.5 Definition of terms and concepts 3.1 Description of the study area 3.1.1 Description of the study area Haveri, popularly known for Byadgi chilli variety and its market in South East Asia, is almost in the center of Karnataka. Geographically the district is situated between north latitude 140 28’ to 140 39’ and east longitude 750 07’ to 750 38’. Haveri is one of the newly formed districts of Karnataka, one and a half decades ago (15th August 1997). The district is located in northern semi rainfed and semi malnadu zone bounded on the North by Dharwad and Gadag districts, on the East by Bellary district, on the West by Uttar Kannada district and on the South by Davangere and Shimoga districts. The total geographical area of the district is 4, 85,156 hectare (Table 3.1 and Fig. 3.1). The district has seven taluks with 208 gram panchayats, 691 inhabited and 7 uninhabited villages, The initial provisional data suggest a density of population was 331 in 2011 compared to 298 of 2001 (Haveri district at a glance 2011-12). 3.1.2 Geomorphology and soil types The district is generally a gently undulating plain except for the hilly area on the western most part of the district bordering Uttar Kannada district and ridges on Southern most parts of the district, which forms part of Hirekerur taluk. The landmass of the district is situated between the elevations of 515 to 732 m above Mean Sea Level (MSL). The general slope in the district is in North-East direction. The Tungabhadra River flowing on the eastern boarder of the district is the only perennial river in the district. The Varada and Kumadwati rivers are major tributaries of Tungabhadra and the river Dharma, a major tributary of Varada, drains the district. All the rivers in the district together with their tributaries exhibit dendretic drainage pattern and they form part of Krishna main basin In the major part of the district, around 65 per cent red sandy soil is found, followed by the medium black and deep black soils. Computation of costs and returns procedure of jasmine Jasmine is a perennial flower crop with an approximate economic bearing life span of 15 years. Therefore, expenditure incurred towards cultivation of Jasmine has the important components viz., (a) Establishment cost and (b) Maintenance cost. a) Establishment cost The establishment cost includes all the expenditure incurred during the pre-bearing period for the establishment of jasmine garden. Items like cost of ploughing, leveling and digging of pits, planting material, manures and fertilizers, plant protection chemicals, cost of irrigation, after cultivation practices, earthing up, making of field channels etc., were included. b) Maintenance cost All recurring costs required for maintaining the plants and its health during active bearing period such as expenditure on cultural practices, manures and fertilizers, plant protection chemicals, irrigation, pruning, weeding etc., were considered as maintenance cost. Besides, interest on fixed and working capital, annual depreciation on equipments, land rent and land revenue was also included for working out the cost of cultivation. The following three cost concepts were used for working out the cost of production and net returns. Total cost includes variable cost (input cost + interest on working capital) + fixed cost (rental value of the land, interest on fixed assets, amortized establishment cost over a period of 15 years) + marketing cost. In the present study, the concepts of gross income and net income were used. The gross income from jasmine cultivation was computed by multiplying the total physical quantity of jasmine produced with the weighted average price realized by the farmers per unit quantity. From the gross income two types of net income were calculated, viz., Net income over the maintenance cost, net income over all costs. 3.4.2 Compound growth analysis For computing the growth in area, production and productivity of Jasmine, Marigold and Chrysanthemum in Haveri district, an exponential form of the function was used as shown below Y = abteu Where, Y= Dependent variable (area/production/yield) a = Intercept b = Regression coefficient t = Time period in years eu = error term In the logarithmic form the function is expressed as, log Y = log a + t log b + u Log a and Log b were obtained using the Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) procedures and the R2 was computed for the goodness of fit. The net present worth was ` 739559.98 per hectare at 12 per cent discount rate. 4.4.2 Benefit cost ratio (BCR) This criterion indicates the rate of return per rupee invested in jasmine enterprise. The benefit cost ratio at 12 per cent discount rate was 1.60 which was more than unity and indicated that investment in jasmine enterprise was financially viable. 4.4.3 Internal rate of return (IRR) This criterion measures the rate of return that can be realized by reinvestment of the returns in jasmine gardens. Hence, the IRR indicates an important basis of investment and scores over other criterion of evaluation, which does not consider the reinvestment opportunities. The value of IRR generally depends on the magnitude of returns realized in each year over the economic life period and more particularly in the initial years of jasmine enterprise. It may be noted here that, the IRR was found to be very high (31%), compared to the opportunity cost of capital or rate of interest paid on borrowed capital indicating that the investment in jasmine garden was highly profitable, economically feasible and financially sound. 4.4.4 Payback period (PBP) It is the period required to recover the initial investment incurred in establishing the garden and in the present study the payback period was found to be 2 years. This clearly indicated that it would take around three years to recover the entire investment. However, this criterion neglects the net returns realized by the farmers in the subsequent years which may be more significant in the case of long term enterprise like jasmine. SUMMARY AND POLICY IMPLICATIONS Floriculture in India is being viewed as a high growth industry. Commercial floriculture is becoming important from the export angle. The liberalization of industrial and trade policies paved the way for development of export-oriented production of cut flowers. The new seed policy has already made it feasible to import planting material of international varieties. It has been found that commercial floriculture has higher potential per unit area than most of the field crops and is therefore a lucrative business. Indian floriculture industry has been shifting from traditional flowers to cut flowers for export purposes. The liberalized economy has given an impetus to the Indian entrepreneurs for establishing export oriented floriculture units under controlled climatic conditions. In India the Income realized from the annual cut flower trade nearly observed to be was ` 27585(Lakhs), of this the foreign exchange earned through the export of cut flowers worked out to ` 10005 (Lakhs). This foreign exchange was earned by exporting flowers to destinies viz. USA, Germany, UK, Italy, Saudi Arabia, Netherlands, Spain, Sri Lanka, Japan and United Arab Emirates. Indian cut flower exports include rose, gladiolus, carnation, chrysanthemum, Lilly and jasmine. Thus India with its high potential of skilled labour at relatively low cost can play a major role in the international floriculture business. Karnataka is one of the major flower growing states in India and flower cultivation has been taken up in almost all districts of the state. The major flower growing districts are Bangalore urban, Chamrajnagar, Kolar, Haveri, Tumkur, Bangalore rural, Gadag, Bellary, Belgaum and Chitradurga. During 2011-12 the total area under major flowers estimated to be 26827 hectares. The total area under marigold (7209 ha) followed by jasmine (5431 ha) and chrysanthemum flower was (4816 ha). MUNDINAMANI Major Advisor ABSTRACT The present study was undertaken to analyse the production and marketing of major flower crops in Haveri district of Karnataka. Primary data were collected from 120 flower cultivators in Haveri district. Savanur, Hirekerur and Ranebennur were selected for the study. From each six sampled villages, 20 flower growers were selected randomly. Secondary data were collected from State Department of Horticulture. Multistage sampling technique was adopted in the selection of the district, taluks, villages and cultivators. For analysis of data compound growth rate, financial analysis and tabular presentation were employed. The labour and material costs accounted for 90.43 and 9.56% of the total establishment cost, respectively. The average maintenance cost (` 305442.40) and average total cost of cultivation (` 325502.00) per hectare were worked out for all age groups gardens. Whereas in marigold and chrysanthemum total cost of cultivation worked out was ` 44345.27 and 52613.06 per hectare. The net returns of jasmine, marigold and chrysanthemum was ` 179516.70, ` 115730.70 and ` 229004.00 respectively indicating the profitability of major flowers cultivation. The investment appraisal analysis revealed that the net present value of investment was ` 739559.98 per hectare at 12% discount rate for jasmine enterprise. The producer’s share in consumer rupee was in Channel-I and Channel-II was 70.98% and 75.81% respectively in jasmine. The scarcity of water was ranked II, III and II with the mean score of 70, 67.50 and 70.00 respective to jasmine, marigold and chrysanthemum. Majority of the farmers jasmine, marigold and chrysanthemum expressed delay payment was the major problem in marketing of major flowers with the mean score of 92.5, 60 and 80 respectively. Lack of floriculture grower cooperative marketing society was also one of the marketing problems in all the crops with mean score of 50, 47.5 and 37.5 respectively.

STANDARDIZATION OF FERTIGATION SCHEDULE FOR GROWTH, YIELD AND QUALITY OF JASMINE [Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews] UNDER EASTERN DRY ZONE OF KARNATAKA Varsha A. P ABSTRACT An experiment conducted on “Standardization of fertigation schedule for growth, yield and quality of jasmine [Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews] under Eastern dry zone of Karnataka” was carried out at Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre, UHS campus, Bengaluru during 2014-15. Experiment was laid out in Factorial Randomized Complete Block Design (FRCBD) comprising of four levels of fertigation (control - soil application of 60:120:120 g NPK per plant, 30:60:60 g NPK per plant (50%), 45:90:90 g NPK per plant (75%) and 60:120:120 g NPK per plant (100%) through fertigation and two levels micronutrients (no micronutrients and ZnSO4, CuSO4, MnSO4, FeSO4 and Borax @ 0.72 g each/plant). Results reveals that, application of 60:120:120 g NPK per plant plus ZnSO4, CuSO4, MnSO4, FeSO4 and Borax at 0.72 g each per plant through fertigation resulted in increased plant height (84.60 cm), plant spread (103.40 cm), number of branches (13.79) and number of suckers (10.97). Same treatment has influenced in early bud initiation (42.40 days), 50 per cent flowering (50.52 days), increased flower diameter (42.07 mm), corolla tube length (14.92 mm). Also, highest flower yield per plant (88.32 g), cumulative yield (288.23 g) and yield per hectare (6.00 t) and shelf life (46.49 hr) has been recorded from same treatment. 100% RDF with micronutrients has resulted highest soil (N, P, K, Zn, Cu, Mn, Fe and boron), leaf nutrient content (N, P, Zn, Cu, Mn and B) and benefit cost ratio (2.04). Whereas, highest soil K content, leaf Fe content was recorded in 100% RDF without micronutrients and 75% RDF with micronutrients, respectively. Higher, water (0.175 kg/m3) and fertilizer use efficiency (82.09 kg/kg) was scored by 60:120:120 g NPK per plant plus micronutrients and 30:60:60 g NPK per plant, respectively. INTRODUCTION Floriculture is one of the fast growing segments of horticulture, having potential for providing enhanced returns to the farmers. The area coverage under flower crops in India is 232.74 thousand hectares with a production of 1.729 MT of loose flowers and 76.73 MT cut flowers (Anon, 2013). Karnataka plays a key role in loose flower production in South India with 201.6 MT on area of 27,000 hectares (Anon., 2013). Among different loose flowers grown in Karnataka, jasmine is one of the commercially cultivated crops. The term jasmine is probably derived from the persian word „Yasmin‟ meaning „fragrance‟. Jasmine is widely grown in warm parts of southern Asia, Europe, Africa and the Pacific regions. It is the national flower of the Philippines adopted by its government in 1937 and in 1990; Indonesian government also adopted it as the national flower. Although more than 2,000 species are known, 40 species have been identified in India and 20 are cultivated in South India (Bhattacharjee, 1980). Jasmine can be grown in a variety of climate and soils. Generally, it prefers mid tropical climate for proper growth and flowering. Commercially grown important Jasminum species are J. sambac Ait., J. auriculutum Vahl., J. grandiflorum L. and J. multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews. In India, jasmine species are cultivated throughout the country. However, the largest area under jasmine flower production is in Tamil Nadu followed by Karnataka and the largest chunk of areas are districts of Bengaluru, Tumkur, Chitradurga, Mysore, Bellary, Davanagere, Dharwad and Gadag in Karnataka. Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews is one of the important traditional flower crops of South India and popularly known as Kakada. Jasmine flowers are used for making garlands, veni and for religious offerings. The jasmine tea is used for balancing the body affected by sun stroke. It belongs to the family Oleaceae. Jasminum multiflorum is popular due to its special characteristics such as, i. Production of attractive pure white flowers which can be mixed with other varieties while preparing garlands ii. Assurance of regular income to farmers as it is a perpetual bearer producing flowers throughout the year except for a short span about two months during summer (March-April) iii. Transportation of flowers to distant markets as they are very hardy compared to other species and varieties of jasmine Application of fertilizers through surface irrigation may be wasteful and a significant amount of fertilizer, notably nitrogen, may be lost in tail water and in deep percolation or seepage. According to one estimate, in India, there is depletion of at least 28-30 million tonnes of nutrients annually whereas, only 20 million tonnes of nutrients are being replenished to the soil, leaving a nutrient deficit of 8-10 million tonnes annually (Anon., 2004). To alleviate the ill-effects of over and under usage of inputs like fertilizes, a new technology called fertigation has emerged. Fertigation is the application of fertilizers, soil amendments or other water- soluble products through irrigation water. Fertigation has got benefits over conventional or drop-fertilizing methods including; increased nutrient absorption by plants, reduction in fertilizer, chemicals and water needed, reduced leaching of chemicals to ground water, reduction in water consumptions due to the plant's increased root mass ability to trap and hold water. Application of nutrients can be controlled at precise time as they are needed and at the rate they are utilized, minimizes the risks of the roots contracting soil borne diseases through the contaminated soil water, eliminates the soil erosion issues as the nutrients is pumped through the water drip. By introducing fertigation, it is possible to increase the yield potential by three times with the same quantity of water, by saving about 45 to 50 per cent of irrigation water and increasing the productivity by about 40 per cent. When fertilizer is applied through fertigation, it was observed that the yield has been increased and about 30 per cent of the fertilizer could be saved (Sivanappan, 1998). Proper plant nutrition is essential for successful production of floricultural crops in open and also under protected conditions. Integrated supply of micronutrients with macronutrients in adequate amount and suitable proportions is one of the most important factors that control the plant growth in flower crops. Micronutrients are involved in all metabolic and cellular functions. The importance of micronutrients in Indian floriculture is truely well recognized and their use had significantly contributed to the increased productivity of several crops. The nutrient elements which are required comparatively in small quantities are called as micro or minor nutrients or trace elements. Micronutrients are essentially as important as macronutrients to have better growth, yield and quality in plants. In the past, there was no need of micronutrients because these trace elements were naturally supplied by soil and organic manuring. But due to intensive cultivation, increase in salinity and soil pH in most of soils, these nutrients are present but are not available to plants. Micronutrients taken up by the plants from soil are to be necessarily replenished through fertilization or supplemented through fertigation for good growth and yield of crops and maximizing the efficient use of applied N, P and K. In the absence of these micronutrients, the plants are known to suffer from physiological disorders which eventually lead to imbalanced growth and low yield. Nowadays, micronutrients are gradually gaining momentum among the flower growers because of their beneficial nutritional support and at the same time they ensure better harvest and returns. The demand for increasing flower production will require a thorough knowledge on the relationship between micronutrients and crop growth. The available information regarding the impact of micronutrients on Jasminum multiflorum is scanty. Since, Kakada jasmine performs better in Eastern dry zone of Karnataka and water and nutrients has to be efficiently utilized with increased productivity to get good returns to the jasmine growers. Research work done on fertigation studies for Jasminum multiflorum that suits to our region is scanty. There is always demand for Kakada flowers in local market. In this background, the present work was compiled to study the influence of micronutrients with different macronutrients levels on Jasminum multiflorum through fertigation. Study has been made to standardize fertigation for their qualitative and quantitative parameters and finally recommend the suitable schedule of fertigation for Eastern dry zone of Karnataka with the following objectives: 1. To study the effect of different NPK levels with combinations of micronutrients through fertigation on growth and yield 2. To assess the water and fertilizer use efficiency 3. Dabonoir (Kawarkhe et al., 2001). 30 g nitrogen m-2 and 20 g P m-2 application significantly increased the durability of first floret (2.94 days) and whole spike (11.12 days) in the same crop (Rajivkumar et al., 2003). Maximum plant height, number of leaves, leaf length and spike length with 10:10:5 g NPK per pot, whereas, emergence of spike, opening of first and last floret, flower diameter and flower weight were maximum with 5:5:5 g NPK per pot in Gladiolus hortulanus L. cv. Wind Song (Khan et al., 2004). Application of nitrogen @ 40 g m-2 increased the plant height and spike length (Das et al., 2005), application of 60 kg phosphorous ha-1 resulted in maximum leaf area (Haokip and Singh, 2005) and application of potassium @ 150 kg ha-1 increased the plant height and weight of the corms in gladiolus (Barman et al., 2005). Plant height and spike number in gladiolus cv. Lunaria were improved by the application of 30 g phosphorous m-2 (Khan et al., 2005). 2.1.1.3 Marigold Increased weight of flowers per plant (286.55 g) was recorded with the application of 10 g N m-2 and 20 g P m-2 in african marigold (Mohanty et al., 2002). Application of 300 kg nitrogen per ha increased the number of leaves and plant height in marigold (Baboo et al., 2005). Application of nitrogen @ 400 kgha-1 increased the growth characters in french marigold were reported by Karuppaiah and Krishna, 2005. Application of 200 kg N ha-1 increased the flowering in african marigold (Sharma et al., 2006). Yield and flower quality of african marigold was increased by the application of 100 kg nitrogen ha-1 (Sreekanth et al., 2006). Among various levels of nitrogen and vermicompost, 160 kg nitrogen per ha with 10 tonnes per ha respectively minimized days to 50 per cent flowering, increased the number of flowers, flower yield, flower diameter and keeping quality in african marigold cv. Sierra Yelllow (Patel et al., 2011). 2.1.1.4 Chrysanthemum The closer spacing of 30 × 20 cm and application of 150 kg nitrogen ha-1 resulted in the highest yield per ha (35.78 tha-1) in chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum coronarium L.) cv. Effect of fertigation on water and fertilizer use efficiency Fertigation reduces the water and nutrient loss that would normally occur with conventional methods of fertilizer andwater application and thus permits better availability and uptake of nutrients by crops, leading to higher yield with high water and fertilizer use efficiency. Efficiency of phosphorous fertilizer could be increased to 45 per cent by drip irrigation compared to only 10-20 per cent achievable by conventional method of application (Satisha, 1997). 2.2.1 Jasmine Highest nitrogen and potassium fertilizer use efficiency (48.65 kg ha-1 kg of N-1) and (75.74 kg ha- 1 kg of K-1) were recorded through fertigation with the application of 75 per cent RDF with mulch in J. grandiflorum (Vijayselvaraj, 2007). 2.2.2 Rose Optimal fertigation scheduling is very important to save water and nutrients, while efficient use of water by drip irrigation is becoming increasingly important. Accurate supply of nutrients and water will result in better water use efficiency, avoid stress situations and control production in rose (Raviv and Blom, 2001). Drip fertigation is an effective way which supplies any water soluble fertilizer in precise amounts, as and when required to match the plant needs or any other agronomic management thereby enhancing the nutrient use efficiency. Thus, fertigation proved a promising technique for increasing the water and nutrient use efficiency in the rose production (Suganya et al., 2007). 2.2.3 Other flower crops Unlike surface irrigation and conventional fertilizer application, fertigation makes uniform distribution of nutrient solution in the root zone and thereby increases the fertilizer use efficiency, since the uptake of nutrients by the plant roots depends on their availability to the root system (Rao, 1996) in chrysanthemum cv. “Kasturi”. Nitrogen use efficiency was registered to be 25.42 per cent in the treatment received nitrogen @ 120 Kg ha-1 followed by 17.7 per cent in N @ 220 kg ha-1 and 13.93 in treatment received N @ 320 kg ha- 1 in tuberose (Rathore and Singh, 2009). 2.2.4 Tomato Nutrient solution along with irrigation water brought about a high nutrient recovery and appeared to be a superior method for supplying nutrient and water (Fujiyama and Nagal, 1987) in tomato. Higher plant height, fruit size and yields of tomato were obtained with drip irrigation when compared to furrow irrigation. Also, the water use efficiency (WUE) and irrigation application efficiency values were found greater in drip system (Yohannes and Tadesse, 1988). In tomato crop, the fruit yield was increased linearly upto 50 kg P ha-1 applied through broadcasting, but in fertigated treatment, equal yield was achieved with 25 kg P ha-1 and 50 per cent of P was saved through fertigation due to increased FUE (Carrijo, 2000). In tomato, application of nitrogen through drip irrigation with equal splits at eight days interval saved 20 to 40 per cent nitrogen compared to furrow irrigation (Singandhupe et al., 2002). III. MATERIALS AND METHODS The present investigation “Standardization of fertigation schedule for growth, yield and quality of jasmine [Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews] under Eastern dry zone of Karnataka” was carried out at Floriculture section, Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre, UHS campus, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra post, Bengaluru during 2014-15. The details of the materials used and the techniques adopted during the course of the experiment are furnished in this chapter. 3.1 MATERIALS 3.1.1 Experimental location The experiment was carried out on two year old jasmine plants of Floriculture section, Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre, UHS campus, GKVK, Bangalore, Karnataka. The research plot is situated between 13° 05' N latitude and 77° 33' E longitude at an altitude of 924 m above mean sea level. 3.1.2 Climate Climate of the area is mild with mean annual rainfall of about 898.40 mm with about 61 rainy days. Monthly rainfall measured during the experimental period (2014-2015) is given in Appendix-I. The mean maximum temperature varied from 26.60°C to 32.20°C and the mean minimum temperature varied from 15.20°C to 19.50°C. The mean maximum relative humidity of 94 per cent and the mean minimum relative humidity of 37 per cent were observed during the month of August 2014 and March 2015 respectively. 3.1.3 Details of Experimental set up The research work entitled “Standardization of fertigation schedule for growth, yield and quality of jasmine [Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews] under Eastern dry zone of Karnataka” was taken up during the year 2014- 2015. The experiment was laid out in the field following the recommended package of practices for jasmine except for irrigation and fertilization. 3.1.4 Soil The soil in the experimental field was red sandy loam in texture. The composite soil samples were collected initially from 0 to 30 cm depth before implementation of experiment and analyzed for physical and chemical properties. 3.1.5 Brief description of crop Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews is an evergreen branching vine that can be trained as a shrub or as a spreading vine like shrub. It usually appears as an open, spreading and weeping mound. The stems and leaves are covered with a downy pubescence that gives the plant an overall greyish-green appearance. The leaves are ovate, rounded at the base and opposite. The white, clustered, star-shaped flowers appear nearly round the year and are not as fragrant as other jasmines. The plant is commercially propagated by rooted cuttings. The fully developed unopened flower buds should be picked in early morning and on an average, 5.0 tonnes per hectare can be obtained from two year old plants. 3.2 METHODS 3.2.1 Experiment: 3.2.1.1 Design and experimental layout The experiment was laid out by adopting Factorial Randomized Block Design (FRCBD). Along the laterals, emitters with a discharge rate of 2.0 lph were fixed at a spacing of 1.2 m. Fig. 1. The split doses were applied at fortnightly intervals through fertigation during the study period. 3.2.4 Soil application of fertilizers Recommended dose fertilizers were applied manually (60:120:120 g NPK/plant/year) in two splits for control plots. The fertilizer sources of supplying NPK were Urea (46% N), SSP (16% P205) and MOP (60% K2O) respectively. 3.3 CROP MANAGEMENT The normal cultural practices such as pruning, irrigation, weeding and plant protection measures followed are briefly described here under. 3.3.1 Pruning In the beginning of the experiment, during the second week of August, the plants were pruned by removing dead, diseased and excess branches by cutting back all the bushes to a height of 40-60 cm from the ground level. 3.3.2 Weeding and irrigation The plot was kept free from weeds by periodic hand weeding and mulching with black polythene. Irrigation was provided at an interval of seven to ten days throughout the period of experimentation, depending on the soil moisture status and climatic condition. 3.3.3 Plant protection Timely and suitable plant protection measures were taken to protect the plants from pests and diseases. Before pruning, mosaic viral disease was noticed with mites as vector and it was controlled by spraying pegasus 0.25 g/l. Red mites were seen during growth period and kelthane 3 ml/l was sprayed as a measure. During flowering leaf webbers damaged the leaves and flower bud and they were controlled by spraying chloropyriphos 20 EC in combination with dichlorovas 76 EC at the rate of 2 ml/l each. 3.3.5 Harvesting White buds were harvested whenever appeared. The first picking was in last week of September month and continued up-to March month. Yield obtained in each picking was weighed, accounted and summed up to obtain the total flower yield per plant from which the yield per hectare was estimated. 3.4 COLLECTION OF DATA 3.4.1 Sampling procedure The observations on various parameters of vegetative growth and flowering were recorded at six stages of plant growth starting immediately after pruning (zero stage, I stage, II stage, III stage IV stage V stage) at monthly intervals from the date of pruning. 3.4.2 Observations on growth parameters 3.4.2.1 Growth parameters 3.4.2.1.1 Plant height Height of the plant was measured in cm from the base of the stem to the tip of the stem in twenty randomly tagged plants in each treatment and the mean values were worked out. 3.4.2.1.2 Plant spread Spread of the foliage in cm both in East-West and North-South directions were measured from labelled five in each replication plants and the mean value was worked out. 3.4.2.1.3 Number of branches The total number of primary and secondary branches were counted after pruning and at different stages of growth and the average was computed. 3.4.2.1.4 Thickness of stem The thickness of branch was recorded with the help of digimatic caliper on thick primary branch at a point just above the ground and expressed in mm 3.4.2.1.5 Leaf area Leaf area was measured at all stages using leaf area meter and expressed as square centimetres by selecting three leaves per plant (young, middle and old leaf) and average was calculated. 3.4.2.1.6 Number of suckers per plant The total number of suckers per plant araised around tagged plants were counted at different stages of growth. 3.4.2.2 Flowering characters 3.4.2.2.1 Days to first bud initiation Observations were recorded from each randomly selected tagged plant by counting the number of days from the date of pruning to the stage at which the first flower bud formation was started and mean was worked out in days. 3.4.2.2.2 Time taken to first flowering Observations were recorded from each randomly selected tagged plant by counting the number of days from the date of pruning to the stage at which the first flower bloomed in each plant and mean was worked out in days. 3.4.2.2.3 Days to 50 per cent flowering Observations were recorded from each randomly selected tagged plant by counting the number of days taken for 50 per cent of the flowering in each treatment plant was recorded and mean was worked out in days. 3.4.2.3 Quality parameters 3.4.2.3.1 Diameter of flower Diameter of the flowers in millimetre was measured at the point of maximum breadth, from three flowers/tagged plant and the average was computed with the help of digimatic calipers. 3.4.2.3.2 Corolla tube length Length of the corolla tube was measured in millimetre from the lower end of the corolla tube to the junction of the free petals, from three flowers/tagged plant and the average was computed with the help of digimatic calipers. 3.4.2.3.3 Flower bud length The length in centimetre from tip of the bud to the tip of corolla tube end, from three flowers/tagged plant and the average was computed with the help of digimatic calipers. 3.4.2.4 Yield parameters 3.4.2.4.1 Flower yield per plant per picking Flower buds were harvested from five tagged plant in each replication and weighed per plant per picking and expressed in grams. 3.4.2.4.2 Hundred flowers weight per picking The weight of 100 flower buds collected from the randomly selected ten plants in each treatment was recorded in grams and average values were worked out. 3.4.2.4.3 Flower yield per plant (cumulative yield) The yield of flowers harvested from each treatment recorded regularly in terms of weight in grams/plant and the cumulative yield for each month during the experimental period. 3.4.2.4.4 Flower yield per hectare From cumulative yield obtained, from first harvest to last harvest yield per hectare was estimated and expressed as flower yield in tonnes per hectare. 3.4.2.5 Shelf life of flowers Randomly selected flowers in each treatment were kept in polyethylene trays. Shelf life of the flowers was assessed by recording the number of hours up to which 50 per cent or more flowers maintained freshness without exhibiting brown pigmentation. 3.4.2.6 Soil physical, chemical properties and plant nutrient content. It includes soil Bulk Density (BD), soil texture, soil type, soil moisture content, soil pH, soil Electric Conductivity (EC), Organic Carbon (OC), Bulk Density (BD), available NPK and micronutrients (Zinc, Copper, Manganese, Boron and Iron) in soil and total nutrient content (NPK, Zn, Cu, Mn, B and Fe) in plant‟s leaves at zero and 150 days after pruning. 3.4.2.6.1 Soil analysis for physical properties, NPK and micronutrients Soil samples were collected immediately after pruning of plants and before imposing treatments to the plants at zero and 150 days after pruning. These samples were analysed for chemical properties such as pH, EC, OC, BD, available nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and micronutrients (Zn, Cu, Mn, B and Fe) by using standard methods as presented in Appendix- III. 3.4.2.6.2 Plant chemical analysis Plant samples from the experimental site were collected at two stages of the experiment (initial and 150 days after pruning). Collected plant samples were dried, ground and were digested by using Di- acid digestion method (9:4 mixture of HNO3: HClO4). These digested samples were used for the determination of amount of nitrogen, phosphorus, potash and micronutrients using standard methods (Appendix III). 3.5 Water and fertilizer use efficiency 3.5.1 Water use efficiency (kg / m3) Water use efficiency was calculated using the formulae, WUE (kg/m3) = Yield (kilo grams) Unit of soil water used (cubic meter) 3.5.2 Fertilizer use efficiency Water use efficiency was calculated using the formulae, FUE (kg/kg) = Yield (kg) Unit fertilizer input (kg) 3.6 Benefit cost ratio (BCR) 3.6.1 Cost of cultivation The cost of cultivation was worked out based on prevailing market rates of various inputs and wages paid to the labours on early basis. 3.6.2 Gross return Total income obtained from the crop was worked out considering the prevailed market price during the experimentation. The benefit cost ratio was worked out by using the formula suggested by Palaniappan (1985). BCR = Gross return (Rs. / ha) Total cost of cultivation (Rs. / ha) 3.7 Statistical Methods Data pertaining to the various vegetative and floral parameters were tabulated and statistically analyzed using Factorial Randomized Complete Block Design (FRCBD). After analysis, Fisher and Yates‟ tables were referred for obtaining the tabulated „Y‟ values and the inference was drawn after comparing the calculated „F‟ values with the table „F‟ values at 5 per cent (P= 0.05) level of significance. Interpretation of data was followed as outlined by Panse and Sukhatme (1967). IV.
