DISCUSSION The results of the field experiments on “Standardization of fertigation schedule for growth, yield and quality of jasmine [Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews] under Eastern dry zone of Karnataka” was carried out at Floriculture section, Regional Horticultural Research and Extension Centre, College of Horticulture, UHS campus, Gandhi Krishi Vignana Kendra, Bengaluru at 2014-15 are discussed in this chapter. The availability of irrigation water becomes dwindling day-by-day as such adoption of conventional methods of irrigation to crops lead to an acute scarcity of water and result in reduced production and productivity of crops. Micro irrigation in the form of drip irrigation has led to revolutionary changes in crop production, resource conservation and resource use efficiency in many crops. There is considerable saving in water by adopting this method since water could be applied almost precisely to the root zone. By introducing fertigation, it is possible to increase the yield potential by three times with the same quantity of water, by saving about 45 to 50 per cent of irrigation water and increasing the productivity by about 40 per cent. It was observed that yield could be increased in addition to saving of fertilizer up to 30 per cent through fertigation. Jasmine requires balanced fertilizer management strategies for the better growth and development of the crop. Since it is a heavy feeder of nutrients, high yield can be obtained only through the application of nutrients at optimum doses in balanced proportion. Optimum use of major and micronutrients not only improve the yields but also benefit various quality aspects of the crop. In order to economize water and fertilizer use efficiency, both can be combined at the right proportion and applied to the crop. Integrated supply of micronutrients with major nutrients in adequate amount and suitable proportions is one of the most important factors that control the plant growth in flower crops. Micronutrients are involved in all metabolic and cellular functions. Plants differ in their need for micronutrients. With this background, the present investigation was designed to assess the impact of different levels of fertigation with micronutrients combination on growth, yield and quality parameters at different growth stages in Jasminum multiflorum and conclusion drawn based on wide range of observations on different aspects are discussed here under. 5.1 Effect of fertigation and micronutrients on growth parameters of J. multiflorum 5.1.1 Vegetative characters Growth and development in plants are the result of co-ordination of several processes operating at different stages of plant growth. Growth, development and ultimate yield of any crop are regulated through series of biological events involving biochemical, physiological and morphological changes which takes place at its development in accordance with the supply of light, water, temperature and nutrients (Donald, 1962). Enhancement in crop productivity in many vegetable crops due to the supply of nutrients through drip irrigation was reported by Papadopoulos (1992). The results of the present investigation revealed that out of four different levels of fertigation, fertigation level 60:120:120 g NPK per ha showed better results. Among micronutrients treatments and control (without micronutrient application), micronutrients application proved best and out of eight interactions, 60:120:120 g NPK per ha + micronutrients resulted in enhanced growth in J. multiflorum. It is evident from the data on plant height, plant spread, number of stem, stem thickness, number of suckers and leaf area, which were significantly influenced by method of fertigation and micronutrients application. 5.1.1.1 Plant height Highest plant height of 81.71 cm was obtained in F3 -60:120:120 g NPK per ha through fertigation (Table 1). It might be due to the fact that frequent irrigation cum fertilization maintained at the root zone with well aerated condition and adequate soil moisture content that did not fluctuate between wet and dry extremes (Patil and Janawade, 1999). Under fertigation, frequent application of fertilizers at opportune intervals, increases the available nutrient status in the root zone thus increasing the uptake of nutrients. Sufficient supply of nutrients might have shown stimulatory action, in terms of cell elongation and thus resulting in increased plant height. The present findings are in accordance with those of Bankar and Mukhyopadhyay (1990) in tuberose, Gopinath (2001) and Krishna (1998) in carnation. In 2010, Thamara et al. opined that, Increased plant height in fertigation treatments might be due availability of nutrients near the root zone, efficient uptake and utilization of nutrients. Split application might have enhanced the uptake and mobilization of nutrients in china aster var. Kamini. Increased plant height was observed with higher level of NPK application at all the stages of growth. Among the three major nutrients N played an important role in increasing the plant height (Rahman et al., 1996) in rose. The increase in growth may be due to increased cell division and cell elongation by utilization of applied nitrogen in protein synthesis and increased level of auxin and gibberellins activity. The increase in plant height by nitrogen may be due to the synergistic interaction of N with available endogenous auxin resulting in increased cell wall plasticity and cell elongation. The favourable influence of nitrogen on plant height was quiet evident as much as it being a constituent of phosphonucleotide which helps for increased cell division and expansion thus resulting in increased plant height (Kumaresan, 2008). Pafli (1965) suggested that nitrogen, being the chief constituent of chlorophyll, protein and amino acids, is accumulated in the shoot through increased supply of nitrogen to the plants at appropriate time. The increase in height of the plant with enhancement of nitrogen levels could be attributed to rapid meristametic activity in plants due to nitrogen or enhanced cell division. This result corroborates with the findings of Sehrawat et al. (2003) in African marigold. Increased plant height with the highest levels of nitrogen was also reported by Muhilarasi (2008) in chrysanthemum. Similar reports were also given by Prince et al. (1990) and Rao et al. (1992) in chrysanthemum, Hugar and Nalawadi (1994) in J. auriculatum, Jain and Gupta (2004) in gladiolus, Solomon and Singh (2004) in rose, Devi et al. (2005) in carnation and Sreekanth et al. (2006) in African marigold. Phosphorus being a basic element, also stimulated the growth of plant. Application of phosphorus favourably influenced the growth and development of plants through its synergistic influence on uptake of other nutrients (Sharma et al., 2006 in African marigold). Increased plant height in kakada observed in the present study may also be attributed to the micronutrients application. At 150 DAP, the plants with the treatment (M1) ZnSO4, CuSO4, MnSO4, FeSO4 and Borax at 0.72 g each / plant resulted maximum height of 77.67 cm. This might be attributed to availability of micronutrients. Significant differences were obtained due interaction effect between fertilizers X micronutrients in the treatment (F3M1) 60:120:120 g NPK per ha + ZnSO4, CuSO4, MnSO4, FeSO4 and Borax at 0.72 g each / plant (84.60 cm). This might be due to synergetic interactions between two factors. Similar results were obtained by Rose and Hao (1999) in Rhododendron. 5.1.1.2 Plant spread Regarding the spread of plants in all four directions there is a direct relationship between levels of fertilizers and micronutrients. The nitrogen content was little lower in leaves at 0 days after pruning and later started to increase in almost all the treatments. Nutrient uptake was maximum under the highest level of nutrients (60:120:120 g NPK per ha) and decreased with the decrease in nutrients level in both soil and plant parts. A gradual increase of nutrient contents and uptake was recorded with increasing the nitrogen fertilizer rate in chrysanthemum (Joshi et al., 2012). This might be due to increased nutrient uptake which would have contributed to the higher relative growth rate of the plants (Pan et al., 1999). Increased nutrient status in different plant parts are due to accumulation of carbohydrates, which may take place gradually with the advancement of crop growth. Similar findings were reported by Papadopoulos (1987), Shirguge et al. (1999), Petillo (2000) and Colla et al. (2001). Phosphorus is an important nutrient in the plants which participate in energy transfer system. Drip fertigation increases the concentration of phosphorus in the plant. These results are in accordance with the findings of El-Gizawy (1992), Balasubramaniam (2008) and Swapna (2010). Potassium being a protoplasmic factor is an essential plant nutrient which is involved in photo and oxidative phosphorylation thus augmenting the energy required for flower growth. In the present study plants under fertigation of different levels of fertilizers with micronutrients exhibited higher potassium content over the other treatments (Table 13 and 15). These results are in accordance with the findings of El-Gizawy (1992) in tomato. Fertigation with 60:120:120 g NPK per has enhanced the uptake of potassium at all stages of crop growth. Fantes et al. These transformation reactions might have led to greater availability of potassium in the soil and consequently resulted in the better utilization by the plant. WSF might have activated the physiological processes for the rapid absorption and utilization of the nutrient for primary metabolic processes. Similar finding was reported by Ghanta and Mitra (1993) in banana, Singh et al. (1995) in french bean and El -sherif et al. (1993) in tomato. Nutrient uptake is due to continuous availability of soil moisture content which might have helped to solubilize the plant nutrient near the root zone and favoured easy absorption of plant nutrients by the crop. This resulted in increased production of dry matter and yield under fertigation treatments. In other words, due to the improved growth characters, the plant tend to take up more nutrients from the soil since it is available nearer the root zone at required level. This was in conformity with the findings of Black (1969) who reported increased nutrient uptake under high frequency irrigation, due to increased plant growth. Higher nutrient uptake in chilli under fertigation was also reported by Tumbare and Nikam (2004). Fertigation of WSF allows application of nutrients directing to the rhizosphere which start to absorb and match with the physiological needs of the crop for better root development and for better vegetative growth and flower development as suggested by Shivashankar (1999). The application of micronutrients also increased the nutrient status of the soil and in plants and increased the nutrient availability throughout the period of growth and resulted in higher uptake of nutrients from the soil and higher contents in leaves (Table 14 and 18). This might be due to the application of micronutrients, so increase the accumulation of micronutrients in the leaf and soil. 5.7 Effect of fertigation and micronutrients on water and fertilizer use efficiency Fertigation system supplies water and nutrients in close proximity to the zone of maximum root density, resulting in enhanced crop growth and more efficient use of water and nutrient inputs. The attributes like water and fertilizer use efficiencies were positively influenced by the levels of fertilizers and micronutrients application. 5.7.1 Water use efficiency The water use efficiency was higher (0.215 kg /m3) for the treatment F3M1 (60:120:120 g NPK per ha + ZnSO4, CuSO4, MnSO4, FeSO4 and Borax at 0.72 g each / plant) which is given in the Table 18. More efficient water use reflects lower surface evaporation losses (Phene et al., 1987). Water use efficiencies might have been improved without affecting crop yield by more optimal drip fertigation management (Feigin et al., 1982; Hoffman et al., 1984; Khan et al., 1997). This might have been achieved by applying less water at each irrigation event, thereby reducing the amount of water lost from the root zone and the number of fertigation events Micro and major nutrients like N, K, B and manganese indirectly affects the plant growth by stomatal regulation and significantly improves relative water content and solution uptake, as well as longevity and electrolyte leakage (Mortazavi et al., 2010). Increased boron applications may promote root elongation in acidic and high-aluminium soils which might have helped to uptake of nutrient solution (Blevin and Lukaszewski, 1998). 5.7.2 Fertilizer use efficiency Application of 50 per cent RDF (F1M0) increased (82.09 kg/kg) fertilizer use efficiency. These lower efficiencies are due to significant losses of nutrients by leaching, run-off, gaseous emission and fixation by soil (Table 19). Higher FUE by the treatment F1M0 might be due to reduced fertilizer input and decrease in the rate of nutrient losses. These findings are in conformity with Beyaert et al., 2006. Fertilizer efficiency in these soils is profoundly influenced by fertilizer placement and timing. Salinity, acidity, elemental deficiencies, toxicities and low organic matter content are some of the major chemical constraints. Physical constrains such as high bulk density layers or pans, poor structure and texture, surface sealing and crusting, high or low water holding capacity, water logging and extreme drying or poor aeration can also reduce NUE. Among other nutrient dynamics, these factors can affect mineralization and immobilization, fixation by adsorption and precipitation mechanisms, leaching, runoff and gaseous losses via denitrification and ammonia volatilization which was lesser in the treatment 30:30:60 g per plant compared to others (Beyaert et al., 2006).. S0· '11.f INTRODUCTION i Jasmines are one of the most important group of flowering plants which caught the imagination of mankind for domestication since time immemorial. The use of flowers has a central place in Indian culture and religious practices. Religious worship does not take place without offering of flowers . In addition, women in some parts of the country adore themselves with flowers daily. Arrangements of expensive flowers are inherent part of interior decoration in luxury hotels and affluent homes. Flowers are increasingly gifted on happy occasions and sorrowful events. No other commodity either natural or man-made in the world has unique distinction of bringing joy and happiness to all race of people and ethnic origin as flowers. Flowers "speak" a language which universally understood by people of all countries, they are considered to be the best "ambassadors" of goodwill . The variety of agro-climatic conditions prevalent in India offers a vast scope for growing wide range of flower crops. The potential of growing floricultural crops in enhancing the India's economy especially in the field of foreign trade has been realised of late only. This can be seen from the observations made by the 'National Commission on Agriculture'. "In our opinion the need of the hour is to explore the various avenues by which floriculture could be expanded and made lucrative". Efforts in this direction have already been made and 100 per cent exporb· oriented project mooted by the "All India Schedule Caste Cooperative Society" for cultivation of flowers in Karnataka which has already begun (Subrahmanyam, 1988). Jasmine flowers command themselves as highly valued ornamental plants for home gardens as well as for commercial cultivation. Jasmine flowers are used for making garlands for ceremonial offering, for adoring hair by ladies and for production of 'attar' and 'concrete' in cosmetic industry. The different plant parts such as leaf, stem, bark, root, seed and fruit are also used for medicinal purposes (Jayanthi, 1988). As many as 200 species of genus Jasminum are known to occur in tropical and subtropical reg'ions throughout the globe (Lendle, 1925 antl Bailey, 1958) of which 40 are found in Indian sub-continent (Hooker, 1882). Large number of species are however, concentrated around the area comprising the Himalayas, China and Malaysia. Some of the countries growing jasmine on a commercial scale are France, India, Italy, Algeria, Morocco, North Africa, Spain and Egypt. India is the home of many jasmine species and it is cultivated throughout the country over an extent of about 8,000 hectares, both in plains and on hills upto 3,030 meters. The most commonly cultivated ones are Jasminum sambac (Gundumalle), Jasminurn auriculatum (Jajimalle) and Jasminurn grandiflorum (Vasanthamalle). India produces flowers worth rupees eight to ten crores annually and contributing substantially to the national economy. In Andhra Pradesh Guntur ranks third in area of jasmine cultivation. 1.1 THE PROBLEM The Guntur district occupies the first position in area under flower cultivation in the coastal Andhra region of Andhra Pradesh. Very few studies have been done on the economic aspects of jasmine cultivation. There were greater variations in the cost of cultivation in different age groups of jasmine gardens. There is every need to know the factors that are contributing for the variations in yields. The fluctuations in price had become quite common in recent years. Despite these price fluctuations, there seems to be no support price policy in respect of jasmine crop by the Government. The general characteristics of many agricultural products are not found in case of flowers. Firstly, flowers are highly perishable. Hence, they require careful handling and also speedy disposal. Therefore, the market remains a localised one. For the same reason flower cultivation has necessarily been confined to places very close to the markets in big cities where the demand pronounced is more. Apart from the location, perishability makes the flower trade more complicated and risky. Secondly, the demand for flowers is not uniformly steady and it has very little relationship to the supply of flowers. Factors like location, season and socio-religious festivals affect the demand and supply relationship in the flower marketing. The flowers also undergo form utilities before they reach the ultimate consumer. All these factors call for specialised knowledge and skills where the gardens can not have necessitating the entry of various intermediaries in the flower trade which will finally affects the income of the cultivators. Hence, the flower cultivation is a risky enterprise, so that it is taken up on a small scale by a few cultivators only. Besides, flowers like jasmine are perennial in nature requiring high cost of cultivation. Thus, the entire production and marketing of flowers is confronted with the various types of problems 9 which calls for an indepth and systematic study on the investment, economic aspects of production, resource use efficiency and marketing of flowers. The present study is an attempt in this direction on jasmine flowers in Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh to know the present status and to suggest measures thereof for increasing returns from the cultivation of this crop. 1.2 OBJECTIVES The specific objectives of the present study are: 1. REVIEW OF LITERATURE A clear cut knowledge of the various concepts is very important for any research work. The concepts identify the objects and phenomenon and bring clarity in making inferences and permit comparison with other studies dealing similar concepts .v--Review of concepts used in earlier studies help to adopt, modify and improve the conceptual frame work and provide link with past studies ~ In this chapter an attempt is made to review the various concepts used in the earlier studies and to specify the concepts used and adopted in the study . ..,.,.....For better exposition, the review of literature have been organised under the following headings~ 1. Studies on marketing costs and marketing problems of producers. 2.1 TECHNIQUES OF INVESTMENT EVALUATION Prest and Turvey (1965) indi cated that the cost benefit analysis as a practical tool in assessing the /,5 desirability of projects. The benefit-cost analysis is considered as a complete enumeration and evaluation of all relevant costs and benefits from the projects over a period of time. Upton (1966) compared the discounted returns per acre of the tree crops with that of annual crops in West Nigeria. He discounted the expected future margins per acre from new varieties of cocoa, oil palm and rubber over a period of 32 years, 35 years and 30 years, respectively and the present worth was compared with returns of crops like cotton, rice, maize and tobacco. The results of the study lead to a conclusion that with the expansion of rubber the returns from the tree crops were lower than that of annual crops. Dalton (1967) indicated that the discounted cash flow technique could be used as a guiding aid for deciding investment. The method has an advantage as the future variable cashf low are reduced to single sum at a point of time and thus facilitating comparison between various alternatives for proper decision. Persad ( 1967) while using the discounted cash flow methods to calculate the present value of tree crops stressed the need for proper estimation of life period as it influences the present worth of crops. The /f appropriate length is one which gives maximum average annual margins. Peters (1970) contended that the choice of discount rate should be used on the rate at which the capital could be raised and project could be accepted only when the internal rate of return exceeds the interest rate or which the net present value of project is positive or when benefit-cost-ratio exceeds unity. Cracknel (1971) realised that the project appraisal techniques help in establishing priorities among investment alternatives. It is a continuous process and should be applied at every successive level of decision making. The author felt that analysis is more of subjective nature due to lakh of quantification of social factors and is more of an art than sciences. Gittinger (1974) suggested two types of discount rates to be chosen for the purpose of evaluation in agricultural projects. They are (1) the opportunity cost of capital and (2) the borrowing rate of capital. Though there were practical problems in establishing the opportunity cost of capital, the borrowing rate of capital will be influenced by the financing terms. Venkataram (1979) evaluated the Karnataka Agricultural Credit Project which provides long term 1(. loans to farmers for miner irrigation, land development and tractorization in Karnataka. He observed that most of the cultivators (92 per cent) in Chickaballapur taluk sold their produce through commission agents, whereas in Malur taluk most of the cultivators contractors. (81 per cent) sold to pre-harvest The main reason for Chickaballapur taluk farmers selling through commission agent was nearness of important market like Bangalore. Subrahmanyam (1988) studied the flower marketing in Karnataka for important flowers like jasmine, rose, chrysanthemum and marigold. He found that different channels followed by flower cultivators for disposing their produce. The flower culti vators had followed mainly two types of marketing channels viz., (1) Selling through commission agent at the market, and (2) selling to pre-harvest contractors. In case of jasmine and rose most of the cultivators have sold through commission agent i.e., 96 per cent and 36 per cent respectiv~ly. Sales through pre-harvest contractors was negligible i . e., 2 per cent in case of jasmine while it was 14 per cent and 41 per cent in case of marigold and chrysanthemum respectively . The use of other channel viz. , sale to wholesaler at market, sale to wholesalers at the field and sale to retailer was noticed only in case of rose. He also indicated that field sales to wholesaler was the most undesirable channel of sales as it will result in lowest income compared to other channels and selling through retailer eliminating both commission agent and wholesaler at the market gives highest share to the producer . The discounted cash flow method of evaluating long term projects is based on the fact that a rupee invested today is worth more than a rupee in future years. It is a process of finding the present worth , of an amount received or paid in the future. This technique has on advantage that future cash flows are reduced to a s.ingle sum at one specific point of time and this facilitates comparison between alternatives investment choices, if any. The discounted cash flow measures used in the analysis were, net present worth, benefit cost ratio and internal rate of returns. Besid~s these the undiscounted measures like pay back period of the jasmine garden and simple rate of return were also calculated. Simple rate of returns: Simple rate of return expresses the net value added per year by an investment, expressed as a percentage of total investment. Here the returns from entire life period of the project is taken into consideration. Higher the simple rate of returns better will be the project. Hence, the cost incurred can be classified into two categories viz., (1) Establishment cost and ( 2) Maintenance cost. Eastablishment cost: The establishment costs include all the expenditure incurred during the pre-bearing period for the establishment of jasmine garden. Items like preparing the land, cost of ploughing, digging pits, cost of planting material, cost of manures and fertilizers, cost of plant protection chemicals, cost of irrigation, cost of inter cultural practices etc., are considered as establishment cost. Besides, other input costs, fixed costs like rental value on land, land revenue, interest on working and fixed capital and depreciation upto bearing age were also considered as a part of establishment cost done in first year. Maintenance cost: All recurring costs required for maintaining the plants during active bearing period such as expenditure on cultural practices, manures and fertilizers, plant protection, irrigation, pruning, weeding, etc., were considered as maintenance cost. Besides, these usual costs such as interest on fixed and working capital, annual depreciation on equipments, land rent and land re'enue were also considered for working out the cost of cultivation. The discounted cash flow technique is considered to be the most appropriate. This technique has been indicated as important and scores over other techniques of evaluation, since it considers the reinvestment opportunities which are absent in other criterion. The internal rate of return usually depends on the magnitude of net returns realised in each year over the economic period and more particularly in the initial years of economic life period which may not have an impact on the net present worth and the benefit-cost ratio techniques. In the present study the internal rate of return that can be obtained by investment was found to be 39. 44 per cent. Since the internal rate of return was greater than 15 per· cent over the cost of capital, it satisfied the World Bank standard and thus the investment was found feasible in jasmine gardens. In the past, flowers were not of much economic importance. One would grow flowers to fulfill his or her aesthetic desire. At times, flowers were offered for sale to meet the special requirements of people. With the passage of time drastic changes have come about in the life style of people leading to commercialized cultivation of flowers. Today, flower plants are no longer meant for only window garden but play an important role in the decoration of the living houses and office establishments. Floriculture is a fast emerging and highly competitive industry. Floriculture may be defined as an art, science and business of growing and marketing flowers. Flowers are fast emerging as a potential money-spinner for many third world countries. Globally 145 countries are involved in the cultivation of ornamental crops and the area under these crops is increasing steadily. The production of flower crops has increased significantly and there is a huge demand for floricultural products in the world, resulting in growing international flower trade. Floricultural products consist of a wide variety of different types of plants and plant materials. The country has exported 22,485.21 MT of floriculture products worth of ` 455.90 crores in 2013-14 and the major export destinations were USA, Germany, Netherlands, United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and UAE during the same period but the Indian floriculture products account for only around 0.18 per cent of the global trade in flowers and serious efforts are being made to capture at least one per cent of the total market. Indian floriculture industry has been shifting from traditional flowers to cut flowers for export purposes. The liberalized economy has given an impetus to the Indian entrepreneurs for establishing export oriented floriculture units under controlled climatic conditions. The major flower growing states in India are Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh in the south, West Bengal in the east, Maharashtra in the west and Rajasthan, Delhi and Haryana in the north. Presently about 60,000 hectare is under floriculture in country with an estimated production of 2,00,000 tonnes of loose flowers and 500 million cut flowers. In Karnataka, the production of loose flowers increased from 2,33,000 million tonnes to 5,09,193 million t and that of cut-flowers increased from 5,555 lakh numbers to 10,388 lakh numbers during 2013. The major traditional flowers grown are marigold, jasmine, rose, aster crossanda and the cut-flowers with stem include rose, gladiolus, tuberose and carnation, hibiscus, china aster, several annuals as gonphera, cocks, comb, golden rod, dahlia, zinnia, It plays a lead role in the cut flower exports from the Country. Bengaluru, the capital city of Karnataka is one of the largest flower trading centres in the country for marketing of flowers for southern states, especially Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. In 2003, the International Flower Auction, Bengaluru (IFAB), the operating company controlled by growers, has taken over the operations of the flower auction centre run by the State-owned Karnataka Agro Industries Corporation (KAIC). Jasmine (Jasminum spp.) belongs to the family “oleaceae”, which is one of the oldest fragrant flowers cultivated by humans and known to be the native of subtropical regions and taken to other parts of the globe. The term jasmine is derived from an Arabic word “Jessamine” and in Persian language it is called as “Yasmin” or “Yasmyn” which means fragrance. As many as 90 species of jasmine are grown in India, out of these most commonly cultivated jasmine species are jasminum multiform (kakada), jasminum samabac (dundumaliige) and jasminum auriculatum (soojimallige). Jasmines are widely grown in warm parts of Southern Asia, Europe, Africa and the Pacific region. It is the national flower of the Philippines adopted by its government in 1937 and in 1990, Indonesian government adopted as the national flower. Although more than 2,000 species are known, 40 species have been identified in India, and 20 species are cultivated in South India (Bhattacharjee, 1980). Jasmine can be grown in a variety of climate and soils. Generally, it prefers mid tropical climate for proper growth and flowering. In India, jasmines are cultivated throughout the country. However, the largest area under Jasmine flower production is in Tamil Nadu followed by Karnataka. The annual production of flowers in India is worth more than ` 120 million. Apart from internal trade, fresh flowers of jasmine are exported to Malaysia, Singapore and Srilanka. It has its special place in South Indian flower crops. It is mainly used for extraction of scented oil. India exports this oil mainly to England, United States of America, Holland, Sweden, Japan, Norway and European Union. The products of jasmine are important natural raw materials in the perfume industry. Jasmine concrete is the most common of the jasmine extract products. It is used in making perfumed hair oil, preparation of absolute and hand kerchief perfumes. Jasmine oils are used extensively in the manufacture of cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, soaps, confectionary perfumes, perfumed tobacco, syrups, aerated water, ointments, disinfectants and detergents. France and Italy are the major producers of jasmine concrete (semi solid mass) and also have largest markets for the products. The different plant parts like leaf, stem, bark, root, seed and fruit are also used for medicinal purpose. The fragrance of jasmine flower cannot be imitated by any of the known synthetic aromatic chemicals. The bulk of the flowers are used as such in garlands and decorative bunches for religious offerings and a small quantity for the production of oils and attars. It ranks next to rose in the order of importance. The annual production of jasmine concrete is more than 15 tonnes in India, the largest producer being Egypt followed by Morocco, India, Italy, France and China. Jasmine oil blends well with every floral scent imparting smoothness and elegance to the perfume composition. The essential oil in flowers is extracted through effleurage which is widely used for production of jasmine attars in India. The usual yields are 0.30-0.35 per cent concrete and 45-55 per cent absolute. Among the flower crops grown in Karnataka jasmine ranks second in terms of area (3,634 ha) and third in terms of production (20,765 t) followed by chrysanthemum ranks third in terms of area and second in terms of production. In Karnataka, the jasmine flower cultivation has been taken up in almost all the districts, particularly in Bengaluru urban, Chamarajnagar, Kolar, Haveri, Tumakuru, Bengaluru rural, Gadag, Raichur, Ballari, Belagavi and Chitradurga. The total area in Karnataka under jasmine cultivation is 3,634 ha with a total production of ` 20,765 tonnes. The productivity is about 6 t per hectare and value is 4,268 lakhs. In NEK region the demand for cut flowers is increasing day by day but the production of jasmine is not met. As jasmine cultivation is highly profitable and there is a bright prospect for expansion of area, it is essential to address the marketing problem of jasmine flower crop in NEK region. The results will be useful to identify the lacunae in marketing, reasons for non cultivation of the crop on a wide area which would further help in increasing the area and profitability of the crop in the region. With this background, the present study is taken up on economics of production and marketing of jasmine in North Eastern Karnataka region with the following specific objectives 1. To study the growth in area, production and productivity of jasmine. 2. To study the economics of jasmine production. 3. To study the marketing efficiency of jasmine. 4. To identify the constraints in production and marketing of jasmine. Hypothesis 1. There is a increasing trend in area, production and productivity of jasmine in NEK region. 2. The cultivation of jasmine is economically viable. Fixed costs: The costs which do not vary with the level of operations like rental value of land, land revenue, interest on fixed capital and depreciation on implements and machineries. DISCUSSION Results of investigation presented in earlier chapter are discussed in detail in this chapter. The main focus here is to throw a light on some of the causes responsible for the major trends observed in the findings. This kind of analysis is helpful to identify such of the policy measures and execute corrections that can be implemented to overcome the constraints encountered by jasmine flower growers. Keeping the objectives of the study in view, the results are discussed under the following headings: 5.1 Demographic characteristic of sample farmers 5.2 Trends in area, production and productivity of jasmine 5.3 Economic aspects of jasmine production 5.4 Financial feasibility of investment in jasmine gardens 5.5 Marketing of jasmine flowers 5.6 Problems faced by the farmers in production and marketing of jasmine 5.1 Demographic characteristic of sample farmers The family size and educational status of the sample farmers as presented in Table 4 revealed that the average age of the sample farmers was 38, 42 and 36 years in Koppal, Ballari and Raichur districts. This showed that the sample respondents belonged to productive age group and were dynamic, capable of risk bearing and open to new ideas for improvement in the profitability of jasmine flower cultivation. The average family size of sample jasmine flower growing farmers was 6 members in Koppal, 5 members in Ballari and 7 members in Raichur districts. It was interesting to note that majority of the families were large and they were also involved in jasmine flower cultivation as it is a labour intensive enterprise. As far as the literacy was concerned, majority of the respondents were literates in Koppal (73.33 %), Raichur (70 %) and Ballari (53.33 %) having their education ranging from primary to college level. Jasmine flower being a little high investment enterprise has been perceived by these respondents mostly due to their education, which might have enabled the respondents to allocate the manageable size of the area under jasmine flower cultivation to get higher returns over other crops. 5.2 Trends in Area, production and productivity of jasmine The growth rate of area, production and productivity for the period 1999 to 2012 for study districts, NEK region and Karnataka state as a whole are depicted in Table 5. The positive and significant growth in area and production of jasmine flower was observed in NEK region, as well as for Karnataka state as a whole. This trend may be due to the increasing popularity of this flower in the study area and also, higher prices of flower in the recent past as well as increased demand for jasmine flower in the domestic market and for its better income opportunities over other flowers. Though the area under jasmine flower is increasing at a rate of 5.22 per cent per annum in NEK region but for Karnataka state as a whole the growth in area was less (3.30 %). This is due to high fluctuation in area of jasmine flower in other parts of the state over the years. The productivity of jasmine flower in Karnataka (-0.41 %) was found to be negative. This negative growth in productivity of jasmine flower may be due to poor management practices by the producers. Among the districts of study area, the growth in area under the cultivation of jasmine flower was high in Koppal at 7.79 per cent which was due to the increased popularity of this flower in the study area and also, higher prices in the recent past as well as continuous demand for jasmine flower in the local market. Among the three districts, Raichur registered a positive and significant growth in production (23.20 %) and productivity (14.32 %). Hence, the hypothesis of increasing trend in area, production and productivity of jasmine in NEK region has been accepted. 5.3 Economic aspects of jasmine production 5.3.1 Establishment cost of jasmine garden Jasmine is a perennial flower crop which continues to bear flower upto 15 years. The total costs incurred for growing jasmine in the first year till its time of bearing constitute the establishment cost. It has been observed from the tables that the average establishment cost incurred per acre in kakada, soojimallige and dundumallige were ` 45,880.36, ` 41,281.59 and ` 43,440.26 respectively during the first year (Table 6, 7 and 8) which seems to be lower compared to return from the investment. The same was apportioned among the number of years of economic yielding to estimate the annual cost of cultivation. A study conducted by Vanishree (2007) supported the findings of the present study. It was clearly indicated in Table 7, 8 and 9 that the major item of labour cost was irrigation and weeding as jasmine crop required frequent irrigation and weeding. Flowers were packed in gunny bags. Better packing always helped in maintaining the quality and in reducing the losses during transit on account of spoilage. 5.5.2 Marketing channels Three distinct channels were identified for jasmine in the study area. A particular channel prevailed in a particular district/market as jasmine production was concentrated in a few pockets which followed a single marketing system. In channel-I the producer himself took the produce to the market and sold to the retailers through commission agent cum wholesaler to create competition among the buyers which prevailed in Koppal district/market for kakada species. Similarly in channel-II, producer sold the produce to retailers through commission agent to wholesaler and finally retailer in Ballari district /market for soojimalligr species. Channel-III for dundumallige species that prevailed in Raichur market consisted the sale of produce by the producer to the contractor cum-wholesaler on the farm itself. Then, the contractor cum-wholesaler sold the produce to the retailer’s and then to consumers. 5.5.3 Marketing costs incurred by the producers in sample markets The total marketing cost per kg of jasmine was estimated at ` 2,246.86 (Koppal) and ` 2,089.85 (Ballari). Out of which, the significant item of cost was the commission charges accounting for ` 2,172.64 in Koppal and ` 2,026.7 in Ballari per q, followed by transportation cost. There was no marketing cost incurred by farmers in Raichur district of the study area as the farmers had sold their produce directly to the contractor cum wholesalers (Table 19). The foregoing discussion indicated that commission charges and transportation were the major items of marketing costs. This calls for intensive control measure on part of government to regulate the activities of commission agents and to reduce the commission charges to safeguard the interest of the farmers, besides creating infrastructure facilities for transport of jasmine flower to markets on time. The results are in line with the previous study conducted by Deepika Shekhawat (2012). 5.5.4 Marketing costs incurred by the intermediaries in the sale of jasmine It could be observed from the Table 20 that, the marketing cost incurred in case of retailers in Koppal market (kakada), Ballari market (soojimallige) and Raichur market (dundumallige) was ` 235.56, in ` 226.62 and in ` 223.05. This was mainly due to the difference in transportation charges and costs like packing, wages for garland preparation and spoilage etc. Significant item of marketing cost in Ballari market were transportation charges, contributing to the extent of 51.38 per cent. This was due to the fact that the commission agent was expected to move from one village to the other for assembling the flowers, for which he had to incur cost on transportation and other expenses incurred towards, packing charges, loading and unloading charges. In Raichur market the contractor cum-wholesaler had a main role in assembling the produce and major item of marketing cost was transportation charges (45.33 %). The main reason behind this was that the contractor cum-wholesaler purchased the produce from the farmers field on an agreed price. 5.5.5 Marketing cost and margins of jasmine in different markets Price spread is one of the important measures of marketing efficiency which indicated the share of producer in the consumer’s rupee. Besides this, it also indicated the share of various market intermediaries in the consumer's rupee in return to their services as the commodity moved from the producer to consumer (Table 21). Producer’s share in consumer’s rupee was higher in Ballari market (43.35 %) followed by Koppal (39.64 %) and Raichur market (26.19 %). This was mainly due to the higher net price received by the farmers in Ballari market for soojimallige. 5.5.6 Marketing efficiency of jasmine flower Marketing efficiency is essentially the degree of market performance. Market efficiency is the ratio of output (satisfaction) to market input (cost of resources). An increase in the ratio represents improved efficiency and a decrease denotes inefficiency of marketing channels. The efficiency of selected markets in the study area as presented in Table 22 indicated that, the Ballari (1.77) market was found to be more efficient than Koppal (1.66) and Raichur (1.35) markets for jasmine crop again because of higher price realized in Ballari market. 5.6 problems faced by the farmers in production and marketing of jasmine The problems faced by the producers of jasmine flower in production and marketing as presented in the previous chapter (Table 23) have been briefly discussed as follows. 5.6.1 Problems faced in production All the jasmine growers in Koppal, Ballari and Raichur districts expressed the problem of pest and disease with a mean score of 77 followed by non-availability of labour on time and lack of technical guidance. This was mainly due to reason that the jasmine flowers were susceptible to pest and disease at the time of bud formation which affected the quality and quantity of flowers and jasmine flower cultivation is a labour intensive enterprise and there was a problem of availability of the labour especially during the peak time of harvesting and during other operations in study area. The jasmine flower growers opined that the harvesting season of jasmine flower clashed with other agricultural operation resulting in scarcity of labour for harvesting of jasmine flowers. 5.6.2 Problems in marketing The problems faced by the farmer in marketing of jasmine flower presented in the previous chapter (Table 24) have been briefly discussed below. In Koppal and Ballari markets major problems observed were higher commission charge with a mean score of 69.59 and 73 followed by fluctuation in market prices. This was due to the fact that commission agents charged 10 per cent commission to the producer, which ultimately reduced the producer’s net price and also farmers expressed that there was an understanding among commission agents and wholesalers. So there is a need to establish regulated market for flower in flower growing regions. In Raichur the price fluctuation was the major problem with a mean score of 69. This was due to the reason that good harvest season fetched lower price and vice versa even with predetermined prices which often fluctuated. VI. SUMMARY AND POLICY IMPLICATIONS Floriculture is a lucrative line of business and it has identified as a sunrise industry, accorded it 100 per cent export oriented status. India is endowed with varied agro climatic conditions suitable for growing a number of flowers. The country is known for growing the traditional flowers such as rose, jasmine, marigold, chrysanthemum, tuberose and many more. Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, West Bengal, Maharashtra, Jammu and Kashmir, Sikkim and Andhra Pradesh are major flower growing states. Jasmine is one of the oldest fragrant flowers cultivated by man. The flower is used for various purposes viz., making garlands, bouquet, decorating hair of women, religious offering etc. It is also used for production of Jasmine concrete which is used in cosmetic and perfumery industries. More than 80 jasmine species are found in India, of which only two species are used for commercial cultivation. They are Jasminum sambac (Gundumalli / Madurai Malli), J. auriculatum (soojimallige) these are mainly cultivated for selling as fresh flower. Several countries consider jasmines as a national symbol they are Indonesia, Philippines and Pakistan. In India about 232.74 thousand hectares area was under cultivation in floriculture in 2012-13. Productions of flowers are estimated to be 1.729 million tonnes loose flowers and 76.73 million tonnes cut flowers in 2012-13. The country had exported 22,485.21 MT of floriculture products to the world for the worth of ` 455.90 crores in 2013-14. Major export destinations were United States, Netherlands, Germany, United Kingdom, United Arab Emirates, Japan and Canada were major importing countries of Indian floriculture during the same period. Thus, India with its high potential of skilled labour at relatively low cost can play a major role in the international floriculture business. As jasmine cultivation is highly profitable and there is a bright prospect for expansion of area, it is essential to address the marketing problem of jasmine flower crop in NEK region. The results will be useful to identify the lacunae in marketing, reasons for non cultivation of the crop on a wider area which would further help in increasing the area and profitability of the crop in the region. JOSHI Major Advisor ABSTRACT The study was conducted to analyze growth in area, production and productivity, cost and returns, marketing efficiency and price spread in jasmine marketing using both primary and secondary data. Tabular analysis, marketing efficiency techniques were employed as analytical tools. The positive and significant growth in area and production of jasmine flower was observed in NEK region, as well as for Karnataka state as a whole (1999-12). The area and production of jasmine flower registered a positive and significant annual growth rate in Koppal district, but the productivity was non significant. In the case of Ballari, the growth in jasmine area was non significant and production and productivity was negative and non-significant. Similarly in the case of Raichur district. The growth in area was non- significant but production and productivity were positive and significant. The average establishment cost incurred was ` 45,880.36, ` 41,281.59 and ` 43,440.26 for kakada, soojimallige and dundumallige per acre respectively during the ‘first year’. The labour and material costs accounted for 39.85 and 35.72 per cent for kakada, 35.94 and 34.74 per cent for soojimallige and 36.95 and 34.12 per cent for dundumallige respectively. The average maintenance cost for kakada, soojimallige and dundumallige were high, which was worked out to be ` 1,99,073.14, ` 1,96,782.05 and ` 1,38,160.84 per acre for ‘above five year’ gardens respectively. The marketing efficiency was high in the case of Ballari (1.77) followed by Koppal (1.66) and Raichur (1.35). Regulation of jasmine marketing is required to reduce the higher commission charges and orderly marketing of jasmine by bringing jasmine under the list of notified commodities and Proper infrastructure facilities need to be developed in the study area for marketing of jasmine.

CHINNIAH Professor Department of Agricultural Entomology Agricultural College and Research Institute, Madurai – 625 104. 2008 The present investigation was undertaken on seasonal incidence and the impact of abiotic factors / weather parameters on the population dynamics of erineum mite on jasmine, assessment of the efficacy of basal application of organic amendments in combination with foliar application of entomopathogenic fungi, bioefficacy of certain newer acaricides, insecticide molecules and medicinal herbal extracts to suppress the incidence of erineum mite of jasmine A. jasmini. It was evident from the survey that the severity of incidence, egg and mite population of eriophyid mite was at the maximum in Dindigul, Madurai and Dharmapuri districts compared to those in Erode, Theni, Coimbatore, Ramanathapuram and Salem districts. Over 70% of the samples had severe to very severe infestation by A. jasmini. The assessment of damage potential of Aceria jasmini indicated that the intensity of eriophyid infestation had a significant impact on reduction of jasmine flower yield. An absolute yield reduction of 95.33 % was noticed when the bushes had 76-100 % erineum infestation. The incidence of erineum mite of jasmine, A. jasmini was maximum during August 2007. Attempts made to establish the correlation between weather parameters and erineum mite population dynamics, revealed that maximum temperature, minimum temperature and rainfall had a negative correlation on population dynamics, whereas relative humidity had a significant positive correlation on the population build up of mite. Other abiotic factors viz., sunshine hours and wind velocity did not have any significant impact on mite population dynamics. For every 10C increase in maximum temperature the mite population decreased by 0.71%, where as for every 10C increase in minimum temperature the mite population decreased by 0.02%, so also for every 1 mm increase in rainfall there was a reduction of 0.01% in mite population. Nevertheless for every one per cent increase in relative humidity, the mite population increased by 0.27%. Basal application of neem cake @ 100 g/ plant + foliar application of (two rounds) Hirsutella thompsonii (1 X108 colonies per ml) was found to be the best and effective in reducing the mite population which also recorded 64.74% increased flower yield over untreated control with higher cost benefit ratio, next only to the standard i.e. carbofuran compared in this study. Hence, it can be construed that application of neem cake in combination with either foliar application of Hirsutella thompsonii (1 X108 colonies per ml) /Beauveria bassiana (1 X108 colonies per ml) may be a better alternative to the application of conventional synthetic acaricides, in the context of environmentally benign management tactics so also in order to mitigate the adverse effect on the total environment. This would not only trigger an idea of increased dependency on biologicals for better suppression of this notorious pest of jasmine in near future but also the slow and gradual elimination of the highly dangerous chemical molecules in the years to come. From the investigations, it is also evident that the application of profenophos @ 2ml / lit. or spiromesifen @ 0.7ml / lit. exerted an excellent suppression of jasmine erineum mite in field condition with increased flower yield and cost benefit ratio. These newer acaricidal molecules with novel mode of action should be popularized so that the existing older acaricides may be phased out eventually. From the survey in jasmine ecosystem for the prevalence of possible alternate host plants, Jasmine species (Jasminum auriculatum) is the only one main host for the erineum mite, no other flora exhibited infestation by A. jasmini. Natural occurrence of predatory fauna like phytoseiid mites (several spp of Amblyseius); Stigmaeidae (Agistemus sp.) and an abundant population of coccinellid predators (Micraspis discolor Fab.) which would probably exert a natural check over the pest mite population and it will not lead to an out break situation in any circumstances. CHAPTER -I INTRODUCTION Jasmine, Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. (Tamil-Mullai; Hindi-Juhi) is one of the major traditional flower crops of India. The genus Jasminum belongs to the family Oleaceae under the order Oleales. which is a climbing, trailing, erect, shrubby flowering, evergreen and deciduous plant. Jasmine buds are used for making garlands, bouquets, religious offerings and for the extraction of perfumed oils and attars. Jasmine is known in India as the "Queen of the Night" because of its perfume. The flowers and parts of this plant are also used for the preparation of several ayurvedic medicines (Ramadas et al., 1985). The commercial cultivation of jasmine is confined to certain traditional areas of Tamil Nadu viz., Madurai, Dindigul, Theni, Salem, Coimbatore, Erode, Dharmapuri and Ramnathapuram districts of Tamil Nadu; Bangaluru, Bellary, Mysore, and Kolar (Karnataka); Pune, Aurangabad and Ahmednagar (Maharashtra); Ahmedabad, Anand and Vadodara (Gujarat); Ambala, Gurgaon and Faridabad (Haryana); Kannauj, Jaunpur and Gazipur (Uttar Pradesh); Delhi; Ludhiana, Jalandhar, Patiala and Amritsar (Punjab);Ranaghat, Kolaghat, Panskura and 24-Parganas (West Bengal); Udaipur, Ajmer, Jaipur and Kota (Rajasthan); Hoja, Jorhat, Alnugarh (Assam) (Jayachandran, 2001). However, largest chunk of area under jasmine flower production is in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka (57.97%). The annual production of flowers is worth more than Rs. 120 million. Apart from domestic trade, the fresh flowers of jasmine are exported to Malaysia, Singapore and Sri Lanka for various uses, thus it earns considerable foreign exchange also. A number of jasmine species are grown in India. Some of the commercially important species are Jasminum sambac Ait., Jasminum auriculatum Vahl., Jasminum grandiflorum Linn., Jasminum multiflorum (Burm. f.) Andrews. At present, about 29,288 ha of land is under cultivation of jasmine in India which is spread over the states like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh (Dadlani, 2007). Tamil Nadu accounts for about 9360 ha with an annual production of 77247 tonnes of fresh flower buds. Of late, there is an increasing demand for high-grade perfumes. There is also a tremendous scope for the development of essential oil industry with considerable foreign exchange by way of export of various jasmine based products. Nevertheless, this popular commercial crop is ravaged by a number of insect pests and mite viz., Erineum mite Aceria jasmini Chann., Bud worm Hendecasis duplifascialis Hmpsn., the gallery worm Elasmopalpus jasminophagus Hmpsn., the leaf web worm Nausinoe geometralis Guen., the blossom midge Contarinia maculipennis Felt., the red spider mite Tetranychus cucurbitae Rah., and root knot nematode Meloidogyne incognita Chitwood. apart from several diseases and deficiency symptoms. The occurrence of the eriophyid mite, Aceria jasmini Chann. was first noticed in Tamil Nadu (David, 1958). on Jasminum sambac Ait. (Gundu malli) and Jasminum flexile Vahl. Later Channabasavanna (1966) reported its occurrence on Jasminum pubescens Wild. from Karnataka state. Colonisation by the mites results in the formation of felty outgrowths (erinea), resulting in malformation of vegetative and floral parts and consequent reduction in growth and yield. Sunder Raj et al. (1967) have reported that the infestation of this mite brought about severe damage to Jasminum auriculatum (J) in Coimbatore district. The long and pointed budded type is found be highly susceptible to the erineum mite.Parimullai which belongs to the species Jasminum auriculatum (J). (Medium round bud; with a flowering duration of nine months/year) is resistant to erineum mite. Farmers depend mostly on chemical pesticides for managing these pests, because of the immediate and spectacular knockdown effects, often leading to indiscriminate use of broad spectrum pesticides culminating in reduction of biodiversity of natural enemies (Balasubramani and Swamiappan, 1993).Outbreak of secondary pests (David et al., 1991), development of insect resistance to pesticides (Regupathy et al., 1994), pest resurgence (Mitra et al., 1999), dermal toxicity to the labours exposed in the field (Kuttalam and Regupathy, 1995), environmental pollution through accumulation of pesticides in soil, water and air and residues in agricultural products (Buttu et al., 1999). In order to mitigate these problems, concerted efforts in evolving an alternate strategy for pest management in recent years indicated a great potential for harnessing organic amendments, botanicals and biocontrol agents for the management of erineum mite of jasmine. Therefore, the present investigation was undertaken to evolve an IPM strategy for the management erineum mite on Jasminum auriculatum with the following objectives, 1. To conduct survey on the occurrence and abundance of jasmine erineum mite, Aceria jasmini Chann.in the traditional jasmine growing tracts of Tamil Nadu. 2. To study the population dynamics/seasonal incidence of Aceria jasmini on jasmine to assess the influence of abiotic factors on temporal distribution. 3. To evolve an IPM strategy, incorporating the ecofriendly pest management methods against jasmine erineum mite. 4. To evaluate the bioefficacy of certain new acaricide / insecticide molecules and medicinal herbal extracts against A. jasmini. 5. To identify the alternate hosts and natural enemies of erineum mite of jasmine. CHAPTER-II REVIEW OF LITERATURE Jasmine (mullai), Jasminum auriculatum Vahl. Eriophyid galls The family Eriophyidae is extremely important, as much by virtue of its high number of cecidogenous species as by virtue of the diversity of cecidogenous effects. Of the approximately 500 gall- inducing species of Eriophyidae in the world (Mani, 1964), 350 are from Central and Northern Europe (Buhr 1964). Nalepa (1929), Roivainen (1953) and Keifer (1971) reported the occurrences of eriophyids in California. Jeppson, Keifer and Baker (1975) reported the works in California. Mathez (1965) mentioned the details of the monographs of Eriophyes vitis Pgst. on grapevine. Noteworthy works on the morphology of acarocecidia was reported by Thomas (1877) and Schlechtendal (1916). A fairly complete catalogue was published from North America by Keifer, Baker, Kono, Delfinado and Styer (1982).The anatomy was studied by Fockeu (1896). Cytological studies were reported by Molliard (1897), Nemec (1924), Kendall (1930), Garrigues (1951) and Westphal (1977). Westphal (1977a) reported the morphogenesis and ultrastructural cytology of various types of acarocecidia. Westphal (1977b) reported the sequence of cecidogenetic processes occurring at early stages of induction of pouch galls on the leaf of Prunus padus L. by Phytoptus padi Nal. 2.2.2. Morphology and anatomy of eriophyid galls Host reactions are mainly species- specific to the eriophyids. All the young aerial parts can be attacked, especially the vegetative and floral buds, as well as the leaves. 2.2.2. 1. Organoid galls Morphogenetic action produced organoid galls. The role of eriophyids for inducing virescences was well demonstrated by Peyeritsch (1888). The virescences caused by Eriophyes lycopersici (Wolff). (= E. cladophthirus Nal.) and E. peucedani Can. was reported by Molliard (1905) and Westphal (1968). Westphal (1968) reported that, in addition to organoid action, eriophyids can stimulate the tissues and transform into well- differentiated nutritive tissues and E. lycopersici (Wolff) is not very specific in its host selection. Organoid effects also have been obtained experimentally by introducing individuals coming from Solanum dulcamara L. to other species, including S. capsicastrum and S. luteum Mill., and even different genera, like Nicandra physaloides and Petunia hybrida. Arnold (1968) reported that, Eriophyes loewi Nal. causes witches‟ brooms on lilac. and apical transformations on Nothofagus, Clianthus and Plagianthus. Arnold (1970) reported that, cecidogenetic action can even lead to more or less total suppression of leaves. 2.2.2. 2.Histoid Galls The attacked buds remain closed but greatly enlarged, as in the gall of Cecidophyopsis psilaspis Nal. on Taxus baccata L., the bud scales and young leaves are transformed and exhibit excrescences on their surface. Cecidogenetic action on leaves is extremely variable. Initially the “erinea” which occur in the form of mats of nutritive hairs. Erinea are extremely common in Europe on certain trees, particularly Maples lindens, beeches and alders. The nutritive hairs vary greatly, which are often species- specific with respect to the mite. Kuster (1952) reported that, in case of erineum on Acer campestre, the hairs arise after brief induction by feeding of the mite. Nutritive hairs can sometimes arise in the larval cavities of pouch galls. Saravanan and Umapathy (2003) also reported an yield loss of even 100 per cent in severe case of infestation. The copra yield loss in Central and South America and the Caribbean and West Africa due to A. guerreronis Keifer. was recorded to be 30 per cent (Hernandez, 1977). Mariau (1977) estimated an yield loss of copra as high as 25 per cent in the Caribbean Islands of Africa and America due to coconut perianth mite attack. Moore et al. Ramaraju et al. (2002) found that the copra content was 1.6 kg copra per 10 healthy (uninfested) nuts, as against 1.16 kg in case of 10 infested nuts and the estimated loss of copra in Tamil Nadu was 27.5 per cent. 2.4. BIOLOGY Channabasavanna (1966) recorded several biological observations on Aceria jasmini. Further, the structural and behavioral features of Aceria jasmini find a parallel in other eriophyids such as Eriophyes ficus (Baker, 1939), Aceria sheldoni (Boyce and Korsmeir, 1941), Eriophyes vitis (Kido and Stafford, 1955), Aceria litchi (Alam and Wadud, 1963). The life cycle of mite consists of egg, nymph, and adult stages. The eriophyid mite, Aceria jasmini is found to colonise several vegetative and floral organs of the jasmine plant. Egg laying is mostly inside the unopened leaf and leaf axils and there are three nymphal instars, with quiescent period occurring between the first and second instars. Eggs are laid singly, close to the base of hairs on the leaves. They are oval, transparent when fresh, turning to pearly white prior to hatching. The mean length and breadth being 45.9 and 38.8 microns respectively. Incubation period ranges between 2 and 5 days, averaging 3.6 days. In between I and II instar, a short quiescent period intervenes. The nymphs pass through three instars to reach the adult stage. The nymphal stage lasts for 8-11 days (Letchoumanane and Subramaniam, 1981). The adult is vermiform, with its cylindrical body gradually tapering towards the caudal end. The mean length and width measures 190.1 microns and 51.9 microns respectively. The body is white with the gnathosoma being much reduced and set off from the rest of the body. The chelicerae are short and below these is the rostrum with a fine, slender and highly reduced stylet. Two pairs of six segmented legs are seen, being borne on the propodosoma. The tarsus is wedge shaped with its pointed, possessing a strong and thick three rayed feather claw. The total life cycle of the mite lasts for about 18.7 days ranging between 17 and 20 days (Letchoumanane and Subramaniam, 1981). According to Saravanan and Umapathy (2003) the different life stages of Jasmine mite, A. jasmini indicated that the mean incubation period was 2.95 days, total nymphal period last for 6.7 days, where as the total longevity lasts for 14.40 days. 2.5. BIOSYSTEMATICS AND BIODIVERSITY The earliest record of an eriophyid mite in this country was by Green (1890) who made certain observations on Calacarus carinatus (Green), the purple mite of tea. The pink mite of tea, Acaphylla theae (Watt, 1988) was also recorded towards the end of the last century (Watt and Mann, 1903). Later Das and Sengupta (1963) reported the occurrence of pink mite of tea in North East India and on the biology and management of the purple mite. In the early decades of the nineteenth century, there were stray reports on the incidence and distribution of eriophyid mites (Misra, 1920; Massee, 1927; Cherian, 1931; Saksena, 1942; Muthukrishnan, 1956). The first elaborate systemic account on Indian eriophyidae was published by Channabasavanna (1966) who recorded 61 species of mites under 18 genera. Later in the 1970‟s, the Indian eriophyid studies had a fillip due to contributions by Mohanasundaram (from 1979 to till date) who recorded hundreds of new taxa from South India. West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands eriophyid mite species have been reported by Chakrabarti, Ghosh, and Mondal (1981), also have reported several new taxa from Northern and North eastern states of our country. 2.6. VARIETAL SCREENING FOR RESISTANCE AGAINST JASMINE ERINEUM MITE The study by Sunder Raj et al. (1967) revealed that the long and pointed budded variety was highly susceptible (94%) to the erineum mite while the medium and pointed budded selections recorded a negligible infestation (3.5%). Rajagopal (1968) proved that out of 15 species and 36 varieties of jasmine evaluated for the degree of mite injury, based on the assessment of erineum, Jasminum auriculatum blood were infested severely. Rajagopal et al. (1970) reported that the physiological mechanisms of resistance in jasmine was due to the feeding injury of mite on the plant surface, the epidermal cells became meristematic, producing multicellular uniseriate rows of hairs which later formed erineum. The resistant varieties were found to have a larger number of vascular bundles with highly ramifying veins in the mesophyll, whereas the susceptible varieties had comparatively fewer vascular bundles with lesser ramification of the veins in the mesophyll. 2.7. INFLUENCE OF ABIOTIC FACTORS ON THE INCIDENCE OF ERINEUM MITE 2.7.1. Effect of temperature, relative humidity, and rainfall on mite infestation Letchoumanane and Subramaniam (1981) studied the seasonal fluctuations of the erineum mite, A. jasmini at various temperature- humidity combinations. The incidence was above 75 per cent (77.7% to 96.7%) during April to October and this part of the year experienced relatively lower humidity (84 to 90% RH) coupled with a higher maximum temperature (29 to 36 ºC). There was a gradual reduction in infestation during November and February. The period between October and December also experienced considerable precipitation, and the minimum temperature was lower (15-20 ºC) during this period of decline. The highest mite incidence (97.1%) observed in July and lower humidity levels (84% RH). Further, the two peaks in maximum temperature, one in May (37 ºC) and the other in September (32 ºC), were apparently marked by corresponding peaks in mite infestation. EFFECT OF ORGANIC AND INORGANIC SOURCES OF NUTRIENTS ON JASMINE MITE 2.8.1. Effect of organic sources of nutrients Organic manuring was found to have slow release effects on nutrients providing a balanced growth, thus making the plants less prone to pests and diseases. In India, neem (Azadirachta indica A. Juss.) and pungam (Pongamia glabra L.) are commonly available and they have been exploited as botanical pesticides. The oil cakes are invariably used as soil amendments and further play a multirole as organic fertilizer, antifeedant and insecticide. In addition to deterrent action, neem seed cake (NSK) residue contained a greater concentration of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium and magnesium than farmyard manure and might economize the use of fertilizers (Basu, 1989). Neem cake has been recognized as potent organic fertilizer as it combines the properties of fertilizer as well as pesticide (Sidhu et al., 2002). Rani and Mohan (1994) reported that, soil application of neem cake @100g / plant and foliar application of neem oil 2% significantly suppressed the damage by Aceria jasmini on Jasminum auriculatum. Chinniah and Mohanasundaram (1995) reported that, the superiority of neem formulation viz., NSKE 10% and neem oil 3% caused 90.0 and 87.7 per cent mortality respectively of A. cajani on pigeon pea. Ramarethinam and Marimuthu (1998) recommended Neem oil formulation at 25 to 30 ml per liter of water for the control of the coconut mite, A. guerreronis K. Muthiah and Baskaran (2000) recorded 63 per cent population reduction of mite using Neem oil 2 per cent + Garlic extract ( 2 per cent ). Soil application of neem cake @ 250kg/ha combined with foliar application of NSKE 10% was found be effective in controlling erineum mites (Umapathy and Rajendran, 1999). Muthiah and Bhaskaran (2000) reported that, the coconut perianth mite mean damage grade index in the chemical fertilizer treatment was the highest (50%).While the least damage (29%) was observed in the treatment of neem cake @2 kg + bone meal 0.5 kg + mill ash 4 kg (per tree/Year). The studies conducted by Chakrabarti (2004) revealed that the application of neem cake @ 3 kg \ m2 effectively controlled yellow mite population on chilli. The investigations on the influence of organic based sources of nutrients and biofertilizer against red spider mite, T. urticae (Koch) on okra revealed that application of farm yard manure @ 12.5 t/ha and biofertilizer (Azophos @ 2 kg/ha) with any of the oil cakes viz., neem cake @ 600 kg/ha or pungam cake @ 800 kg/ha as basal was found to be effective in reducing the mite population significantly (Balaji and Chinniah, 2006). The various organic sources of nutrients evaluated as basal application of farm yard manure @ 6.25 t/ha + neem cake @ 300 kg/ha + Azophos @ 1kg/ha was found to be significantly effective in reducing the chilli yellow mite,P. latus, egg and mite population (Ambika and Chinniah, 2007). Soil application of neem cake effectively checked the infestation of mango mealy bug, Drosicha mangiferae (Green) (Tandon and Lal, 1980). The development of BPH nymphs was significantly reduced on TN 1 rice seedlings when 2 per cent neem cake was mixed with water soaked seeds for 48 hours (Abdul Kareem et al., 1987). Mallik and Lal (1989) reported that, deoiled neem cake application @ 5 kg per plot reduced the incidence of the fruit borer in okra. Rajendran (1993) observed that neem cake @ 250 kg/ha along with 20 kg N was found to be superior than pungam, illuppai and castor cakes against sucking pests of okra. The populations build up of Nilaparvata lugens (Stal.) was found to be low in rice, applied with 3: 10 neem cake – urea mixture than in control plots (Saxena et al., 1984). Velusamy et al. (1987) stated that neem cake blended urea @ 75 kg N / ha recorded less population of green leaf hopper compared to control. Neem cake + carbofuran mixture (1:1 w/w) effectively checked the population of rice GLH, Nephotettix virescens (Distant.) and in turn rice tungro virus infection (Abdul Kareem et al., 1989). Geetha and Gopalan (2001) reported the reduction of BPH population in neem cake treated plots. Dayakar et al. (1995) recorded the least incidence of pod borer on pigeon pea treated with Farm Yard Manure @ 6000 kg/acre. EFFECT OF ORGANIC AND INORGANIC SOURCES OF NUTRIENTS ON SOIL MICROFLORA Microbes continuously added to soils as biofertilizers increased soil organic carbon, microbial polysaccharides and in turn improved soil properties. The repeated application of microbes through biofertilizers increased the availability of N, P, K and other micronutrients to the crops (Dubey, 2001). Although microbial biomass accounts for only about 1 to 3 per cent of the soil organic matter, it exhibits a rapid turnover and can be considered as a driving force of major nutrient cycles. 2.9.1. Farm yard manure Vemana et al. (1999) observed maximum increase in the fungal and bacterial population in farm yard manure treatment. Higher bacterial population, available nitrogen and organic carbon content were observed in FYM treated plots (Sriramachandrasekaran, 2002). Farm Yard Manure @ 12.5 t/ha in combination with neem cake @ 600 kg/ha, pungam cake @ 800 kg/ha and Azophos @ 2 kg/ha, registered more fungal and bacterial population (Balaji and Chinniah, 2006). Combination with biofertilizer, basal application of farm yard manure @ 6.25 t/ha + neem cake @ 300 kg/ha + Azophos @ 1kg/ha was found to have maximum bacterial colonies 126.50 x 106 and fungal colonies 20.75 x 103 in soil (Ambika and Chinniah, 2007). 2.9.2. Neem cake Goswamy and Bhattacharya (1989) reported greater frequency of fungi in neem cake amended soils. Maximum soil fungal colonies and maximum plant growth were recorded in plots amended with neem cake (Pandey and Singh, 1990). There was a marked predominance of Aspergillus spp. in neem amended soil. Increased fungal population during the decomposition of oil cakes could be due to the release of acids and other chemicals from decomposing oil cakes which changed the soil environment in favour of dormant fungal bodies present in soil originally. These dormant bodies on getting suitable environment and organic carbon as food from decomposing oil cakes multiply fast and increase quantitatively as well as qualitatively. Neem cake @ 600 kg/ha + B. bassiana (1x108 colonies per gram) registered more fungal and bacterial population (Balaji and Chinniah, 2006). Application of neem cake @ 600 kg/ha + Ocimum sanctum (20% aqueous leaf extract as foliar spray) recorded the maximum number of bacterial (128.63 x 106) and fungal colonies (28.25 x 103) in the rhizosphere soil (Ambika and Chinniah, 2007). 2.9. 3. Pungam cake Pungam contained more nitrogenous matter and favoured the production of urease by soil microorganisms (Balasubramanian et al., 1972). The positive effect of neem and pungam cakes on the rhizosphere microflora of groundnut was proved and found to have no detrimental effect on beneficial microbial biomass (Abdullah et al., 1999). Further it was proved to be superior in improving the rhizosphere mycoflora. 2.10. EFFECT OF HOST PLANT RESISTANCE ON MITE INFESTATION Rajagopal et al. (1970) reported that the high yielding Mullai selection, medium long and pointed budded variety (Jasminum auriculatum Vahl.), is highly resistant to the erineum mite, Aceria jasmini Chann. Mariau (1986) reported that cultivars varied in their susceptibility to coconut mite infestations and trees of cultivars from Cambodia suffered no attack. This may be due to the fact that tepals were more tightly adpressed to the fruits in rounded nuts than in elongated ones (Moore, 1986; Howard and Rodriguez, 1991). Upto 90 per cent of the trees were attacked in varieties Atlantic tall as against lower infestation in Malayan Yellow Dwarf in Costa Rica (Schliesske, 1988). 2.11. EFFECT OF CULTURAL PRACTICES ON MITE INFESTATION Pruning of jasmine shoots reduced the infestation of Aceria jasmini Chann., so as the population of A. litchi Keifer. was significantly reduced on litchi when the affected shoots were pruned (Kumar, 1992). Long periods of drought resulted in greater yield losse due to the coconut perianth mite (Mariau, 1977 and 1986), because the fruit development was very slow during dry periods. Well maintained trees, with appropriate fertilizer application, were found to suffer less from coconut perianth mite attack. 2.12. EFFECT OF INSECTICIDES FOR THE MANAGEMENT OF ERIOPHYID MITES Management of eriophyid mites has become challenging on account of its potent damage to some important crops. Evaluation of soil application of four insecticides at four doses (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 kg a.i / ha) indicated that aldicarb at the highest dose could provide the best control of Jasmine mite, Aceria jasmini followed by carbofuran and phorate, while disulfotan was the least effective chemical (Letchoumanane and Subramaniam, 1981). Fortnightly application of monocrotophos @ (0.5 kg a.i per ha), Phosalone (0.7 kg a.i per ha) or Wettable sulphur (1 kg a.i per ha) was found to be effective in controlling Aceria jasmini (Mohan and Udhayagiri, 1984). Mallikarjunappa et al., (1991) reported that a mixture of ethion 0.05 % and dimethoate 0.03 % effectively reduced the incidence of Jasmine mite in Karnataka. Spraying of Wettable sulphur 0.3% or triazophos 0.06% with the onset of monsoon at 14 days interval, when repeated 2-3 times, provided effective control of A. jasmini (Shivaramu and Jhansi Rani, 1996). Application of carbofuran at a higher dose (2 kg/ ha) resulted in substantial reduction of Aceria jasmini population on jasmine (Umapathy and Rajendran, 1997). Jose et al. (1999) reported that diafenthiuron (0.1 %) was the most effective chemical followed by bromoprophylate (0.1 %), dicofol (0.1 %) and monocrotophos (0.1 %) in controlling Aceria jasmini Chann.
