COMPOSTING OF ORGANIC WASTE Composting is a method of solid waste management whereby the organic component of solid waste is biologically decomposed and stabilized under controlled conditions to a state where it can be handled, stored and / or applied to the land without adversely affecting the environment (Golueke, 1977). During the composting process the readily decomposable substrates are utilized by microorganisms as energy sources and for conversion to microbial tissue and products. The composting is therefore simply a means of converting raw waste organic matter into usable humus (Gray and Biddlestone, 1971). Composting of animal wastes is a spontaneous bio-oxidative process to produce more uniform, concentrated, and safe final products compared to fresh manure, allowing for easy spreading in the soil and also significant elimination of pathogens (Bernal et al., 2009). Generally, it is a fast biodegradation process, which takes 4–6 weeks of microbial action to break down organic materials to stable and usable organic substances called compost. 2.3.1. Factors influencing composting process The process of composting is typically divided into four main phases based on temperature and active microbial community: mesophilic, thermophilic, cooling and maturation phases (Ryckeboer et al., 2003). It is influenced by a number of factors. Among them the major factors include particle size of the matter to be composted, pH, air supply, moisture content, temperature and some chemical characteristics. 2.3.1.1. Particle size The smaller the size of the particles of organic material, the greater is the surface area available for adsorption by the microorganisms. Very small particles, however, pack tightly together so that the spaces between them are small which prevents the movement of CO2 from going out. If the particle size is very large, the surface area for attack by the microbes is markedly reduced and the reaction proceeds slowly or stops. A compromise on particle size thus is necessary. 2.3.1.2. Temperature Temperature is a critical factor/parameter for sanitization, degradation and stabilization of organic matter during composting. The maximum decomposition occurs between 35-45°C while the decomposition rate falls below 20°C. Temperature rises from 30-35°C to 55-60°C depending upon the air supply, moisture content and chemical characteristics of waste. Guang et al. (2010) found that increase in temperature during composting was due to biological and biochemical degradation of organic materials by microorganisms. During composting, the initial organic matter is decomposed and humified through various biological processes. Similar results during composting were observed by Ogunwande et al. (2008). Hachicha et al. (2006) also proved that, composting mixtures rapidly achieved thermophillic temperatures (>45°C) and maximum temperature reached during composting was 62°C. In thermophillic (high temperature) phase, the microorganisms decompose the easily degradable organic substances, producing heat due to intense microbial activity. However, high temperatures are essential for the destruction of pathogenic organisms and weed seeds. 2.3.1.3. Moisture content and C/N ratio Moisture is necessary for microorganism growth, but excessive moisture displaces the air that is necessary for microorganism growth. The ideal moisture content for composting is between 40% and 60%; the upper limit depends upon the material being composted. Moisture and C/N ratio have a major influence on a successful composting process. For poultry waste, a low C/N ratio contributes to large ammonia losses (Gray et al., 1971). The high moisture content, of more than 75%, inhibits a quick start to the composting process. The moisture content (or the degree of material drying) is a major influence on the decomposition rate and the tendency to stabilise, since the metabolic heat generation during decomposition drives evaporation. Factors that contribute to moisture loss include evaporation, leaching and aeration, natural or forced. Rynk et al. (1991) reported that moisture content should be maintained between 40% and 60% during the composting process. The extent and speed of the composting cycle are affected by moisture content, particle size, aeration temperature and initial carbon- nitrogen ratio (Livestock Waste Facilities Handbook, 1985). 2.3.1.4. Air Supply Aeration is necessary during thermophilic aerobic digestion in order to produce high quality compost and to avoid nuisance conditions during composting. Aeration can also be used to overcome an initial moisture content that is too high. If a compost pile becomes anaerobic as indicated by odors or by a temperature drop during the first 7 to 10 days, then turning is required. No matter how anaerobic a compost pile may become, frequent turning and aeration will handle the situation. 2.3.1.5. Compost The composted material is odorless and fine textured with low moisture content and can be used as an organic fertilizer. Finished compost is generally more concentrated in nutrients than the initial combination of raw materials used and can serve as an effective means of building soil fertility (Brady and Weil, 1999). Mature compost (finished compost) provides a stabilized form of organic matter and has the potential to enhance nutrient release in the soil more than the raw organic waste (Adediran et al., 2003). Composted organic materials are not only a source of macro and micronutrients, but they also improve the soil characteristics like aeration, water holding capacity, bulk density, aggregation, cation exchange capacity and activity of beneficial micro flora (Chaudhry et al., 2013; Jilani et al., 2007). 2.4. COMPOSTING OF POULTRY WASTE Composting is one of the most versatile and remunerative techniques for handling biodegradable solid wastes by biological stabilization into a safer and more stabilized material called as compost (Gajalakshmi and Abbasi, 2008) , which can be used as a source of nutrients and soil conditioner in agricultural applications (Gabhane et al., 2012). It can be considered as an important source of organic matter (Szilveszter et al., 2012). Composting has been proved to be an effective method to produce organic fertilizers in order to treat the ever-increasing volume of poultry wastes (Tiquia and Tam, 2002), which converts the soluble nutrients to more stable organic forms, thus increasing their bioavailability while reducing their susceptibility to loss when applied to agricultural land. The quality of compost itself vary with type of raw materials used, management of composting processes, stage of decomposition processes, type of nutrients applied to enrich the compost and/or to enhance decomposition. After complete decomposition, the household waste compost also contain significant proportion of plant nutrients and soil properties amending constituents (Mrabet et al., 2012). Nutrient-rich ecofriendly compost can be prepared by composting poultry waste with rock phosphate and elemental sulphur. This can be used as a valuable nutrient source especially for organic farming practices. Addition of small amount of elemental sulphur reduces the pH of the compost, thereby reducing the volatilisation losses of ammonia (Mahimairaja et al., 1993). It also enhances the dissolution of rock phosphate and enriches the compost with P and S nutrients (Mahimairaja et al., 1995b). In poultry manure a large proportion on nitrogen is present in the form of uric acid and urea. The uric acid and urea are rapidly hydrolyzed to ammonia and carbon dioxide by the enzymes urease and uricase and more than 60% of ammonia can be subsequently lost through volatilization. Not only does the loss of ammonia reduce the nutrient value of the manure, but levels of ammonia exceeding 25 ppm in the poultry shed may lead to various respiratory and other problems which would affect the bird’s growth. The nitrogen in the poultry manure can be conserved either by inhibiting the hydrolysis of uric acid to ammonia or by reducing the ammonia volatilization. Mixing poultry manure with carbon rich waste materials will also reduce the ammonia loss by temporary immobilization of NH4 ions. In an earlier study, it was reported that the bedding material viz., paddy straw, wood chips and peat were found to be efficient in reducing the ammonia loss during composting. The volatilizing ammonia can be easily trapped and conserved by the process of immobilization by organic materials such as coir pith with low nitrogen content and high cation absorption capabilities into organic molecules. Ammonia binds tightly with the components of the bulking agent and therefore N losses are reduced during composting (Mahimairaja et al., 1994). The study conducted by Vinod Kumar et al. (2014) indicated that windrow composting of poultry wastes with coir pith as co-composting material can be considered as biologically and environmentally safe disposal option, with recycling nutrients in the form of compost. The work carried out by Sakthivadivu et al. (2015) also supported that composting of poultry waste along with coir waste sounded ecofriendly. Prasanthrajan and Boomiraj (2012) reported that coir pith mixed poultry compost recorded high nitrogen and potassium content, whereas, coir pith and rock phosphate (RP) mixed poultry compost recorded high phosphorus content. Chaudhry et al. (2013) concluded that composting of poultry litter/manure along with plastic sheet cover provides the best storage condition to conserve nutrients. 2.4.1. Amendments for composting of poultry waste Various amendments were added to the poultry manure including two natural zeolites, clay, coir (mesocarp of coconut fruit), CaCl2, CaSO4, MgCl2, MgSO4 and Al2+SO4 3+. The zeolite and coir amendments were therefore proposed to be the most successful for reducing NH3 losses during composting of poultry manure. Co-composting of coir pith having low nitrogen content and wide C : N ratio with poultry manure having high nitrogen content and narrow C : N ratio has been hypothesized to solve the current problems in coir pith composting. PELLETIZATION OF POULTRY MANURE Pelletization increases the bulk density and particle size uniformity of litter (McMullen, 2005) allowing a more nutrient dense litter to be transported and thus more area to be utilized for land application (Moore, 1998). One of the possible way to increase the economical hauling distance of broiler litter is pelletization. Pelletization will likely affect the dynamics of nutrients in poultry litter. Pelletization of broiler litter proved to benefit its marketability by adding value through safer handling, greater nutrient density, and more uniform spreading (Suppadit et al., 2002). Pelletized broiler litter enriched with nitrogen(N), phosphorus(P), and potassium (K) has been shown to be a more effective fertilizer than unprocessed broiler litter and resulted in similar N uptake and plant yield when compared to ammonium nitrate (NH4NO3) (Hamilton and Sims, 1995). Pelletized poultry manure can be an effective nutrient source for corn production. Pelletization of manure has been shown to yield more rapidly mineralizable N, resulting in higher concentrations of NH4 in the soil (Hadas et al., 1983). Pelletization may constitute an improved method for handling broiler litter with the determined change in nutrient concentration from pelletizing broiler litter (Hammac, 2007). 2.5.1. Fertilizer efficiency of compost pellets The fertilizer efficiency of pelletized compost does not differ essentially from that of the compost which is used as the raw material. Therefore, the pellets can be applied to crops according to the standard application rates for organic fertilizer. The pellets expand and their shape becomes distorted when they are soaked in water (Hara, 1998). However, the effect on crops of the pellet is rather different than that of ordinary compost. The shape of the pellet persists in soils for a comparatively longer time. The breakdown of pellets in soil is slower than that of ordinary compost. Therefore, even if the compost used as the raw material is immature, the negative effect on the plant caused by the rapid decomposition of easily decomposable organic matter is limited. Hara (2001) stated that compost pellets are leached of their bases and release nitrate nitrogen several weeks later than ordinary compost. Therefore, an anaerobic state is maintained inside the pellets, so that nitrification increases. These characteristics are more pronounced in larger pellets, in pellets containing an additional material, and in pellets made from immature compost. On the other hand, molding into pellets has no effect on the mineralization rate over time of nitrogen. The fertilizer efficiency of compost pellets seems to vary according to the nature of the compost used as raw material and the soil conditions. 2.6. Application of poultry manure alone was effective in increasing the pH, organic C, and available P content of the soil. A common and traditional practice has utilized manure as an organic fertilizer or soil improver due to its contribution of organic matter and nutrients, mainly N and P (He et al., 2004). The organic materials, such as farmyard manures, agro-industrial by-products and composts can be used as amendments to enhance and sustain the overall soil fertility Diacono and Montemurro (2010). Researchers like Berova and Karanatsdis (2009) and Fernandez-Luqueno et al. (2010) studied the effect of organic fertilizers on the amount of chlorophyll pigments and rate of photosynthesis. They concluded that the application of organic fertilizers not only enhances the synthesis and amount of chlorophylls but also increases the rate of photosynthesis. 2.6.1. (2013) reported that the application of enriched poultry manure compost on equal N basis (2.3 t.ha-1) recorded higher yield attributes and grain yield of rice (4675 kg.ha−1 in 2007 and 4953 kg.ha−1 in 2008), in comparable with composted poultry manure. The residual effect of enriched poultry manure compost and composted poultry manure applied to preceeding rice crop improved yield attributes and yield of succeeding blackgram (42.8% and 47.7%). Improved rice grain quality, in terms of chemical composition, cooking quality and high score of sensory evaluation was achieved under organic manures application. The higher concentration of macro and micronutrients in the enriched poultry manure compost and composted poultry manure and higher and steady nutrient release compared to other organic manures. The poultry waste had both urinary and fecal excretion, hence the fertilizer value was nearly three times higher than farmyard manure. The enhanced and continuous supply of nutrients by the enriched organics leads to better tiller production and filled grain of rice (Ghosh and Sharma, 1999; Mohandas et al., 2008). The supremacy of enriched poultry manure compost lies in the fact that it can supply the nutrients in soluble form for a quite longer period by not allowing the entire soluble form into solution, to come in contact with soil and other inorganic constituents, thereby minimizing fixation and precipitation from the enriched manures, the plant roots can very well compete with loss mechanisms and absorb more nutrients leading to better yield. Bhuiyan et al. (2015) showed that average concentration of phosphorus (as P2O5) were 3.6%, 2.5%; Total N were 1.6%, 1.7%; Ammonium (NH4-N) were 0.4%, 0.8% and Potassium (as K2O) were 1.5%, 1.3% in broiler and layer poultry litter respectively which were in standard level of organic fertilizer. This relates to the residual effect of compost and manure resulted in high soil microbial biomass C, potentially mineralizable N and high pH (Ginting et al., 2003). ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT OF POULTRY WASTE Poultry manure can also become a serious environmental pollutant (Gao et al., 2006) and contributor to greenhouse gases (Zhou et al., 2007). In addition, air quality has become a major environmental concern of the poultry industry. There are environmental and health issues linked to bio-aerosols (e.g. microbes, endotoxins and mycotoxins suspended in air) generated at production, manure storage facilities and during land spreading of poultry litter (Bolan et al., 2010). The environment in the poultry housing is a combination of physical and biological factors which interact as a complex dynamic system of social interactions, husbandry system, light, temperature and the aerial environment (Hobbs et al., 2004). The production and emission of gases in poultry or any livestock facilities involve complex biological, physical and chemical processes. The rate of emission is influenced by many factors, such as diet composition and conversion efficiencies, manure handling practices and environmental conditions (Ellen, 2005; Gates et al., 2008). 2.7.1 Ammonia Ammonia (NH3) is the primary basic gas in the atmosphere. Animal production produces a significant component of anthropogenic NH3 emissions. Ammonia is also a component of odour. Ammonia volatilisation from manure materials within poultry barns can adversely affect production, and also represents a loss of fertiliser value from the spent litter. It is generated during bacterial decomposition of protein and urea in housing areas and during storage and application of excreta under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (Kristensen et al., 2000). The main source of NH3 is urine of animals. Seventy percent of nitrogenous substances in excrement originate from urine and 30% from feaces. Poultry feaces contain 60−65% of uric acid, 10% of ammonia salts, 2−3% of urea and remaining of creatinine. Especially uric acid is rapidly changed by the microbes to NH3 (Groot Koerkamp, 1994). 2.7.2 Nitrous oxide N2O can be produced in soils following inorganic and organic fertilizer application and also from manure storage surfaces (Redding, 2013). Nitrous oxide is generated by the microbial conversion of nitrates in excreta during their storage and applications (Oenema et al., 2005). The production of N2O from poultry manure depends on feaces composition, microbes and enzymes involved and the conditions after excretion. 2.7.2. Carbon dioxide The main source of carbon dioxide in livestock is animal respiration, combustion of natural gas for heating and cooking, and decomposition of organic matter (Knizatova et al., 2010). The high emission from propane use in broiler and pullet houses due to heating the houses during brooding and cold weather (Calvet et al., 2011). There is also a link between metabolism and animal production of CO2 (Mihina et al., 2012). Carbon dioxide production by birds is proportional to their metabolic heat production, and thus to the metabolic body weight of the birds, which in turn is affected by the temperature and bird activity. The animal CO2 production under normal farm conditions has normally a diurnal variation of ±20% (Pedersen et al., 2008). Materials and Methods

Materials and Methods CHAPTER III MATERIALS AND METHODS Large-scale accumulation of poultry wastes will continue to pose a serious disposal and pollution problems unless eco-friendly management technologies are evolved. Such technologies will not only help in sustaining agriculture, but also minimizes the adverse environmental impacts. In the current study, a series of laboratory experiments were conducted and based on the results, an organic fertilizer product was developed by blending of poultry waste and low grade rock phosphate with elemental sulphur (So). The effectiveness of the fertilizer product on soil and crops was further evaluated by conducting a pot experiment. The materials used and methods adopted in various experiments are presented in this chapter. 3.1 COLLECTION AND CHARACTERIZATION OF POULTRY MANURE 3.1.1. Sample collection and characterization The poultry manure was collected from the Poultry Unit of the Department of Veterinary and Animal Science, TNAU, Coimbatore. The poultry droppings were collected from the broiler and layer (cage) system. The samples collected were immediately transferred to a polythene bags, closed tightly to avoid any loss of moisture from the sample and used for various analysis. The samples were analyzed for important characteristics. 3.1.2. Loss of nitrogen from poultry manure Incubation experiment was conducted to examine the loss of nitrogen (N) during the composting/storage of poultry manure. Two hundred grams of poultry manure, collected from the broiler and layer units, was placed in 500 cm3 plastic containers. Wherever necessary required quantity of distilled water was added to achieve a final moisture content of 60 percent. The plastic container was covered with a polyethylene bags containing small pin-sized holes to permit aeration. Three replicates of each treatment were prepared and randomly placed. One set of treatments was kept in the laboratory at 25o C (± 2 o C) and another in the open air outside the laboratory. Based on the weight loss distilled water was added to the container to maintain the moisture content uniformly throughout the incubation experiment. The samples were taken after 15, 30 and 60 days and determined pH, N and organic carbon content of manure. The moisture factor was computed and applied to express the results on oven dry basis. 3.1.3. Dissolution of rock phosphate during composting of poultry manure A laboratory closed incubation experiment was conducted to examine the dissolution of rock phosphate during 30 days storage of poultry manure. About 2g of poultry manure was placed in a 50 cm3 polypropylene centrifuge tube and the moisture content was adjusted to 60 percent by adding distilled water. The rock phosphate (Starphos, 18%P2O5) was added at a rate equivalent to 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0 and 5.0 of P2O5 and mixed thoroughly with the manure. The tubes were covered with lids loosely and incubated at 25oC (±2oC) under laboratory condition for 30 days. The treatments were: T1 : Poultry manure (PM) T2 : PM + Rock phosphate (RP) 1% T3 : PM + RP (2%) T4 : PM + RP (3%) T5 : PM + RP (4%) T6 : PM + RP (5%) Periodically manure samples were removed. The dissolution of added rock phosphate was determined by a sequential fractionation procedure. The changes in soluble and exchangeable-P (∆NaCl+ TEA-P), adsorbed and exchangeable-P (∆NaOH-P) and residual P (∆HCl-P) were calculated. The dissolution of added rock phosphate was calculated as follows (Mahimairaja et al., 1995b). Moisture content The moisture content in the poultry manure sample was determined by drying a known quantity of sample in an electric oven at 105° C for 8 hrs and the loss in weight was found out. The moisture content was expressed on oven dry basis. 3.4.1.2. pH and electrical conductivity The pH was measured using a combined electrode pH meter. The pH of poultry manure was measured in water (1:5) after half an hour equilibrium. The electrical conductivity (EC) of the supernatant suspension was measured using a conductivity bridge (Jackson, 1973). 3.4.1.3. Organic carbon Total organic content of the samples were determined by the wet digestion method (Walkley and Black, 1934). 0.5 g of sample was taken in a 500 ml conical flask. To this, 10 ml of 1N K2Cr2O7 and 20 ml of conc. H2SO4 were added. The contents were allowed to stand for 20-30 minutes and then 200 ml of distilled water, 10 ml of orthophosphoric acid and 1 ml of diphenylamine indicator was added. This was titrated against 0.5 N Ferrous Ammonium Sulphate to get the endpoint of a bright green colour. 3.4.1.4. Total Nitrogen The total nitrogen content of the samples was determined by following Bremner method (Jackson, 1973). 0.5 g of sample was added with 15 ml diacid mixture (sulphuric acid and perchloric acid at 5:2) in a conical flask and kept for digestion until a clear solution was obtained. The digested content was transferred to a 100 ml volumetric flask and the volume made up to 100 ml. To 10 ml of diacid extract taken, 25 ml of 40% NaOH was added, 25 ml of 2% boric acid with double indicator (Bromocresol green and methyl red) was titrated against 0.1 N H2SO4 and N content was calculated. 3.4.1.5. Total Phosphorus Total P content of the samples were determined by a calorimetric (Vanadomolybdate) method (Jackson, 1973). A 0.5 g of manure sample was digested using 15 ml of triple acid mixture (nitric acid, sulphuric acid and perchloric acid in the ratio of 9:2:1) on a sand bath until a clear solution was obtained and the volume made up to 100 ml. To a 5ml of triple acid extract taken in a 25 ml volumetric flask 5 ml of Bartons reagent (ammonium molybdate and ammonium metavanadate) was added. Then the volume was made up to 25 ml and kept for colour development. The yellow colour developed was read at 470 nm in a UV spectrophotometer. 3.4.1.6. NaHCO3-P NaHCO3-P was determined by a colorimetric method (Olsen et al, 1954). A 5g of sample was taken in a polycarbonate shaking bottle. Fifty ml of 0.5 M NaHCO3 and a pinch of activated carbon were added to the sample and shaken for 30 min. The extract was filtered using Whatman No. 40 filter paper. A 5 ml of filtrate was pipetted out into a 25 ml volumetric flask and 4 ml of Reagent B was added and made up to 25 ml. After 30 min, the absorbance value of the colour developed in the sample was read at 660 nm in a spectrophotometer and the available phosphorus was calculated from the standard curve. 3.4.1.7. Phosphorus (P) fractions The different P fractions in compost were determined following a modified P fractionation technique which involves both alkaline and acid extractants (Bolan and Hedley, 1989) Two gram poultry manure was added with 30 ml distilled water and shaken for 2 hrs in a 50 ml centrifuge tube. After centrifuging at 8000 rpm for 10 min, the supernatant solution was filtered and analysed for easily available P. The sample residue was subsequently shaken with 30ml 0.5 M NaCl+ 0.5 M TEA (Triethanol amine) for 16 hrs. After centrifuging and filtering, the solution was analysed for available P which included both adsorbed and exchangeable P. The sample residue was subsequently shaken with 1M NaOH (at 1:30 sample solution ratio) for 16 hrs. After centrifuging and filtering, the solution was analysed for available P which included both adsorbed and exchangeable P. To the residue in the tube, 30ml of 1M HCl was added and shaken for further 16 hrs and centrifuged and filtered. The P was determined in the solution as acid soluble P (Residual P). The manure residue was digested using 10-15 ml of triacid at 260 °C for 45 min and the concentration of P in the extract was subsequently measured. 3.4.1.8. Total Potassium The sample was digested with triacid mixture and then filtered. With the filtrate the total potassium was determined using a flame photometer (Jackson, 1973). 3.4.1.9. Based on the results an organic fertilizer product was developed. The effectiveness of the fertilizer product on soil and crops was evaluated. The results of the experiments are presented in this chapter. 4.1 CHARACTERISTICS OF POULTRY MANURE Samples of manures collected from broiler and layer system differed markedly in their characteristics (Table 4.1). The mean pH of the broiler manure was 7.51, whereas, it was 8.59 for the layer manure. The electrical conductivity (EC), an index of salt loading, varied between 8.3 and 13.2 dSm-1. The manure collected from the layer birds recorded higher values of EC than the manure from the broiler birds. Marked difference was also observed in the N content. The broiler manure had relatively lesser amount of N (22400 mg kg-1) than the layer manure (36400 mg kg-1). Large amount of phosphorus (P) was observed in the layer manure (15109 mg kg-1) than the broiler manure (5524 mg kg-1). Only a small difference was observed in potassium (K) content of the manure samples, which ranged between 14200 and 15100 mg kg-1. The carbon (C) content of manure samples varied between 46.2 and 35.9 percent and the broiler manure recorded the highest value. Marked variations in calcium (Ca), magnesium (Mg) and sulphur (S) were also observed between the samples. The layer manure had relatively higher amount of Ca (40600 mg kg-1), Mg (23500 mg kg-1) and S (12340 mg kg-1) contents than the broiler manure. 4.2 LOSS OF NITROGEN FROM POULTRY MANURE Laboratory experiment was conducted under two different environments to examine the loss of N from broiler and layer manures. Therefore, the dissolution of rock phosphate during composting/storage of poultry manure was examined by conducting a laboratory closed incubation experiment for 30 days. This helps to enrich the organic fertilizer with the maximum amount of rock phosphate. The dissolution of added rock phosphate was measured by a sequential fractionation procedure. The changes in the concentration of different fractions of phosphorus viz., soluble and exchangeable-P as extracted in NaCl+TEA and exchangeable and adsorbed-P as extracted in NaOH were determined. To enhance the solubility of rock phosphate, an acid producing material viz., elemental sulphur (S°) was introduced. Upon oxidation, S° produces sulphuric acid (H2SO4) which should dissolve the rock phosphate. Therefore, to optimize the level of S° addition, an incubation experiment was conducted for 30 days and examined the oxidation of S°, by measuring the pH and sulphate (SO4) production. The results on pH and the concentration of SO4 produced are presented in Table 4.7. Irrespective of the treatments, the pH was found decreased during the incubation. The pHs ranged from 7.05 to 9.22 at 14th day, whereas, it ranged from 6.44 to 8.58 at 30th day of incubation. The highest pH was recorded in the manure alone treatment (T1) and the lowest pH in the manure treated with S° (2%, T4). Increase in the rate of S° addition decreased the pHs of the manure up to 2 percent addition of S°, thereafter the pH was found decreased. After 30 days, the manure amended with S° (2%) had shown the lowest pH of 6.44. Due to the oxidation of S° large amount of SO4 was produced in the poultry manure during incubation. From the initial concentration of 8.2 mg kg-1, the SO4 concentration was found increased in all the treatments. At 14th day the SO4 concentration ranged between 142 and 1332 mg kg-1, whereas, at 30th day it ranged between 315 and 5510 mg kg-1. Characteristics of fertilizer products Some important characteristics of the fertilizer products viz., Phospho-Fertilizer and Sulpho-Fertilizer developed are given in Table 4.11. Discussion CHAPTER V DISCUSSION Large amount of poultry manure is produced in India which contains a relatively high proportion of plant nutrients than other animal manures. In the current study, the poultry manure was enriched with nutrients and a nutrients rich fertilizer product suitable for organic farming, was developed by blending poultry manure, rock phosphate and elemental sulphur (S°). The effectiveness of fertilizer products on soil and crops was evaluated. The results obtained from various experiments are discussed in this chapter. 5.1. CHARACTERISTICS OF POULTRY MANURE The manures collected from broiler and layer system showed marked difference in their nutrients content. Significant variation was observed in pH and EC of manures, both were higher in layer manure. In general the manure collected from layer birds had shown greater amounts of N, P, K, Ca, Mg and S, than the manure collected from broiler units. The variation might be due to the loss of N and dilution effect due to bedding materials used in the broiler system. Fresh poultry manure generally contains about 20 to 30 percent dry matter, which is rich in cellulose, lignin, nitrogenous compounds and minerals. As manure directly or indirectly originates from plant source (feeds contain mostly cereals), it contains all the plants nutrients (Mahimairaja et al., 1994; Kelley et al., 1996; Chan et al., 2008). The nutrient content vary considerably with the species and age of birds, the composition of feed and the manure storage and handling system. Amongst different manures (cattle, sheep, pig, horse), poultry manure generally contains the greater amount of N, P and Ca. Besides, appreciable amount of macro and micro nutrients, the poultry manure also contained a high level of carbon (C) which could replenish the supply of humus and improve the physical properties of soils. The nutrients contents were comparable to values previously reported (Mahimairaja et al., 1994; Kirchmann and Witter, 1989; Bitzer and Sims, 1988). Nitrogen in the manure is of primary concern because of its role in plant growth and its impact on environmental pollution (Sharpley et al., 2007). It is estimated that about 70 to 90 percent of N in the feed is excreted by the birds in the solid and liquid portions of manure. Three major fractions of N identified in manure are : i) Inorganic-N (NH4 and NO3) and easily mineralizable-N (uric acid and urea), ii) easily decomposable organic N with a low C/N ratio (protein and amino acid) and iii) ‘resistant’, slowly mineralizable organic N with high C/N ratio (lignocellulosic fibre complex). Large variation in total P content was observed between the broiler and the layer manure. Phosphorus in poultry manure is present mainly as solid- phase inorganic P and the amount of P varies considerably due to variation in dry matter content and composition of feed. In fresh manure, the inorganic P constitutes up to 95 percent of total P whereas, the organic P constitutes only 1 to 5 percent, and only a small fraction of the total P in manure solution is present as dissolved organic P (Mahimairaja, 1993; Sharpley and Smith, 1995; Yuquan et al., 2015). Both broiler and layer manures contain an appreciable amount of K, Ca and S. The K in manure is considered to be as available as its fertilizer equivalent. The macro and micro nutrients present in poultry manure make this manure a valuable source of nutrients and organic matter. 5.2 LOSS OF NITROGEN FROM POULTRY MANURE Nitrogen loss from broiler and layer manure was examined in a laboratory experiment. Results have shown that significant loss of N occurred from the manures kept under different environmental conditions. In general the manures that were kept open (both inside and outside the laboratory) lost significantly greater amount of N than the manures that were kept covered, resulting in reduced N content of the manures. The summary of the study, salient findings and conclusion drawn are presented in this chapter. 6.1 CHARACTERISTICS OF POULTRY MANURE AND NITROGEN LOSS Poultry manures (Broiler manure and Layer manure) were characterized for their nutrient potential. The loss of N was assessed in laboratory experiment. The following are the results.  The nutrient contents vary considerably between the manures. The layer manure had shown greater amounts of plant nutrients (N, K, Ca, Mg and S), than the broiler manure.  Large variation in total P content was observed between the broiler and the layer manure. The amount of P was about three times higher in layer manure than the broiler manure.  The macro and micro nutrients present make the poultry manure a valuable source of plant nutrients and organic matter.  Significant amount of N was lost from poultry manure kept under different environmental conditions. The manures that were kept open (both inside and outside the laboratory) lost significantly larger amount of N than the manures that were kept covered.  The N loss was approximately 43.8 to 62.5 percent from the broiler manure and 50.1 to 73.1 percent from the layer manure during 60 days of incubation.  The bedding material of the broiler unit was found to have reduced the N loss from the broiler manure.  Due to rapid decomposition large amount of C was found lost from poultry manure. The C loss was approximately 32.5 to 47.2 percent (of initial C present) in broiler manure and 54.1 to 68.5 percent in layer manure.  The C loss was the greatest from the layer manure that was kept open outside the laboratory and the lowest from the manure that was kept covered.  There exists a positive correlation between C loss and N loss from poultry manure during the 60 days of incubation. 6.2 DISSOLUTION OF ROCK PHOSPHATE To enrich the poultry manure with adequate level of P, firstly, the dissolution of rock phosphate during composting of poultry manure was examined in a closed laboratory incubation experiment conducted for 30 days. The following are the salient findings.  The dissolution of rock phosphate-P, measured from the ∆ NaCl+TEA-P (soluble and exchangeable-P) plus ∆NaOH-P (adsorbed and organic-P), was found increased progressively up to 3 percent addition of rock phosphate-P, thereafter, the dissolution was found decreased. The rate of dissolution ranged from 6.8 to 12.8 percent only. 6.3 OXIDATION OF ELEMENTAL SULPHUR AND ITS IMPACT ON DISSOLUTION OF ROCK PHOSPHATE The result of the previous experiment had shown that only low rate (<13%) of rock phosphate dissolution occurred during the incubation of poultry manure with rock phosphate. The dissolution of rock phosphate could be improved by enhancing the supply of protons (H+). This could be achieved through addition of some acidifying materials like elemental sulphur (So). Therefore, the oxidation of So in poultry manure and its impact on the dissolution of rock phosphate was examined by conducting incubation experiments. The results showed the following:  Significant reduction in pH of manure was observed due to the oxidation of S°. Increase in the rate of (S°) addition decreased the pHs of manure up to 2 percent addition of S° and thereafter the changes were not significant.  The oxidation of S° produced large amount of SO4 in the manure during the 30 days of incubation.  Both, the decrease in pH and increase in SO4 contents indicate that large amount of S° should have oxidized in the poultry manure.  Addition of S° to the manure had significant influence on the dissolution of rock phosphate during the 30 days of incubation.  Addition of S° produced large amount of H+ upon oxidation. These H+ ions help in the dissolution of rock phosphate. Due to the addition of S°, the dissolution of rock phosphate varied between 6.8 and 74.4 percent. 6.4 DEVELOPMENT OF FERTILIZER PRODUCT The previous experiments showed that the maximum dissolution of rock phosphate could be achieved with the addition of rock phosphate-P (3%) and So(2%) during composting of poultry manure. Addition of So not only provides H+ for the dissolution of rock phosphate, but also helps in reducing the NH3 volatilization and thus conserves N in the manre. Based on these results – the following two organic fertilizer products were developed. i) Phospho-Fertilizer : by blending poultry manure and rock phosphate (at a rate equivalent to 3% of the composting manure). ii) Sulpho-Fertilizer : by blending poultry manure, rock phosphate (3%) and S° (2%). After mixing, the materials were composted for 12 weeks (three months). The composts thus produced were subjected to granulation and coating. Irrespective of crops grown, application of Sulpho-Fertilizer resulted in significantly greater amounts of available N, P and K in soil.  The biomass yield of paddy and ragi was significantly greater due to the application of Phospho-Fertilizer than Sulpho-Fertilizer and NPK (chemical) fertilizers.  Surprisingly, the application of Sulpho-Fertilizer produced only a small amount of biomass of paddy, which could be attributed to the toxicity of hydrogen sulphide (H2S) produced due to addition of S° under submerged condition of paddy soil.  The performance of Sulpho-Fertilizer was found better in influencing the biomass and fruit yield of tomato plants. The biomass yield of tomato plants increased by about 15 percent and 63.1 percent, respectively over Phospho-Fertilizer and NPK (chemical) fertilizer. The fruits yield was also significantly greater due to the Sulpho- Fertilizers than the Phospho-fertilizer (by 70.1%) and NPK (chemical) fertilizer (by 63.3%).  The uptake of NPK by paddy, ragi and tomato plants as influenced by the organic and inorganic fertilizers closely followed the trend in biomass yields. Therefore showed a strong correlation between nutrients uptake and biomass yield.  Like biomass yield, the uptake of NPK by paddy was trivial due to the Sulpho- Fertilizer. The toxicity of H2S resulted in poor biomass production and low amount of nutrients uptake by paddy. In ragi, the Sulpho-Fertilizer resulted in significant higher uptake of N (by 15%)and P(by 4%) than the NPK(chemical) fertilizer. The performance of Sulpho-Fertilizer was more pronounced on tomato crop. The uptake of N, P and K was found increased by 53.5, 36 and 43.5 percents, respectively, due to the Sulpho-Fertilizer than the NPK (chemical) fertilizers.  Comparing the two organic fertilizers, the Sulpho-Fertilizer was found superior as it resulted in higher uptake of N (24.2%), P (60.7%) and K (40%) by tomato crops than the Phospho-Fertilizer. The greater yield and uptake of nutrients by crops supplemented with Sulpho-Fertilizer could be attributed to the multiple role of So. As illustrated in Figure 6.1, it is evident that the increase in availability of N due to the conservation of N in poultry manure, enhancement of P availability due to the dissolution of rock phosphate and improvement in S nutrition are achieved by the addition of So. The enrichment of N, P and S by the addition of S° to the poultry manure might have enhanced the availability and subsequent release of nutrients in soil. Furthermore, the decomposed organic matter in the form of humus present in the organic fertilizers might have also favoured the microbially mediated nutrients (N, P and S) mineralization in soil. Thus, the Sulpho-Fertilizer was more effective than the Phospho-Fertilizer and chemical fertilizers. The study perceptibly demonstrated that an environment friendly organic fertilizer could be developed by blending poultry manure, rock phosphate (3%) and So (2%) that would be more effective than the chemical fertilizers. ABSTRACT ABSTRACT STUDIES ON THE FLOWERING AND PRODUCTIVITY OF GUNDUMALL1 (Jasminum samhac. Ait) AS INFLUENCED BY NUTRIENT MANAGEMENT TECHNIQUES BY B SENTHAMIZH SELV1 DEGREE MASTER OF SCIENCE (HORTICULTURE) CHAIRMAN SANBU, Ph D(Hort) PROFESSOR AND HEAD Horticultural Research Station Kodaikanal - 624103 2000 Investigations were undertaken to study the effect of modified NPK fertilization, micronutrients and the method of application of micronutrients on growth, flowering and yield of jasmine (Jasminum samhac Ait) cv. Gundumalli under Periyakulam conditions. The experiment was laid out in a factorial randomised block design with three replications Three levels of modified NPK fertilization viz , 120:240:240 g of NPK per plant in the months of November and June (N|), in the months of October and April (N2) and in four splits during the months of October, January, April and July (N3) in the form of urea, super phosphate and muriate of potash, three levels of micronutrients viz, 4g per plant and 0 5 per cent spray of Zn, 8 g per plant and 0 5 per cent spray of Fe and Zn + Fe combination in the months of December and June in the form of ZnS04 + FeS04, four method of application viz., water spray (Tf) soil (T2), foliar (T3) and soil + foliar (T4) were tried in all possible combinations. This study revealed that four split application of 120:240:240g of NPK per plant significantly increased the plant height, number of primary and secondary branches, number of shoots produced one month after pruning and during the crop growth, plant spread, leaf area, early flower bud emergence, early flower bud picking, number of cymes per plant, number of buds per cyme, flower bud length, corolla tube length, bud diameter, yield per plant, yield per ha and reduction in number of pink buds per cyme Four split application of NPK increased the chlorophyll content and the soil and plant nutrients like NPK, Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn Advanced application of NPK nutrients in the months of October and April to that of the existing recommendation had similar effect as that of four split application of NPK nutrients Combined application of 4g of ZnS04 and 8 g of FeS04 per plant through soil and 0.5 per cent each of ZnS04 and FeS04 through foliage in the months of December and June exerted significant increase in plant height, secondary branches, number of shoots produced during crop growth, plant spread, leaf area, flowering behaviour, flower bud length, corolla tube length, yield per plant and yield per ha. Soil + foliar application of ZnS04 + FeS04 in combination increased the soil nutrients like NPK and Mn Application of ZnS04 increased the soil Zn and Cu, while FeS04 had positive influence on soil Fe content whereas, plant nutrients like N, K, Fe, Mn, Cu and Zn increased with ZnS04 + FeS04 application and very least influence was observed on leaf P content Soil + foliar method of micronutrient application expressed significant influence on all growth characters, flowering behaviour, flower bud characters, yield per ha and soil and plant nutrients. Among different treatment combinations, application of NPK nutrients in four splits, ZnS04 + FeS04 combined with soil + foliar method of application increased growth, flowering, yield attributing characters and yield/ha (4400 kg ). The highest net return of Rs 2,20,500 and the highest benefit-cost ratio of 2 56 were also obtained in the combination. Zinc and iron applied plant 148 INTRODUCTION CHAPTER I INTRODUCTION Jasmines, one of the leading traditional flowers of India constitute an important group of high value commercial crops especially in Tamil Nadu. Along with other flower crops jasmines are cultivated in over 4203 hectares in Tamil Nadu with an estimated production of Rs 10-15 crores worth of fresh loose flowers (Kolavalli, 1991). Jasminum samhac Ait. cv. Gundumalli (F; Oleaceae) is the most commercially important cultivar of jasmines as sources of fresh flowers and products. Jasmines have received a boon in view of the potentialities of south Indian jasmines as sources of essential oil Therefore, a considerable portion of flowers are being used for the extraction of essential oil Different plant parts like leaf, stem, bark, root etc. are also very useful in pharmaceutical preparations (Bhattacharjee, 1995) The cultivation of jasmine including post harvest management is highly labour oriented. However, it offers substantial returns both as fresh flowers and as products Jasmine cultivation has a drawback that temperature controls transition from vegetative phase to reproductive phase, besides influencing the growth of plants (Nedumaran and Shanmugavelu, 1978) Being a semiperennial flower crop jasmine has different growth phases with seasonal variations during growth and development Bhattacharjee (1980) reported that J.samhac blooms freely from summer through rainy season and in Tamil Nadu flowering occurs freely throughout the year and for convenience pruning is taken up during the fag end of the North-East monsoon since the flower production is less intense during this period 2 Srinivasan el al. (1989) and Bhattacharjee (1995) observed that the yield of flowers was greatly influenced by vegetative and reproductive phases as a consequence of changes in nutritional status of jasmine plants. Hence, proper regulation of nutrient supply is indispensable in order to make essential nutrient elements available during various growth stages and is necessary to go in for split application, an efficient fertilizer management Recently, multinutrient deficiencies have become a common occurrence in Tamil Nadu because of continuous growth period with higher flower yield and the nutrient depletion is not properly replenished Incidence of chlorosis affecting the plant growth and yield has been reported in J.samhac (Kannan, 1988) threatening the essential oil industries in Coimbatore district of Tamil Nadu Correction of these deficiencies through sprays of certain micronutrients have been only a temporary remedy. Therefore, it is important to go in for balanced nutrient application including macro and micronutrients for optimum growth and development Strategies such as combination of nutrients, split application of fertilizers, soil and foliar application of nutrients and judicious nutrient management are essential to regulate the available nutrient status in the soil continuously (Ranade, 1993) These methods are useful to mitigate the effect of adverse climatic conditions during the crop growth. Since information on these aspects is scanty, the present investigation was takenup to study the flowering and productivity of cv Gundumalli as influenced by nutrient management techniques With a view to elicit and elucidate informations on the above, the investigations were conducted with the following specific objectives; To evaluate the efficacy of various nutrient management techniques by means of soil and / or foliar applications with split doses of NPK, To study the influence of different nutrient elements on the growth and development To examine the effect of micronutrients on the yield and quality of flowers To asses the influence of essential nutrient elements on the period of availability of flowers. Flowering In ./ grandiflorum, Natarajan and Madhava Rao (1983) recorded a linear response of flower bud length to increased levels of nitrogen Parthiban and Khader (1991) observed more number of spikes per plant and flowers per spike in tube rose with nitrogen at 100 kg per hectare 2.1.3. Yield 6 In jasmine, higher yield was registered with nitrogen at 60g per plant and 120 g per plant was also found to increase the yield (Natarajan and Madhava Rao, 1979). According to Bhattacharjee (1988) improved floral and higher yield in J.grandiflorum was recorded with nitrogen at 33,3 g per plant each in December, April and August. Significant increase in flower yield with nitrogen at 30g per plant was also noticed by Kumar and Gill (1988) in J.sambac cv, Gundumalli 1 Increasing levels of nitrogen upto 43,43 kg per hectare was found to increase the number and fresh weight of flowers in chrysanthemum (Bik, 1972). Similar results were also obtained (Jhonson, 1975) with the application of nitrogen at 330 kg per hectare, Peter Vedanayagam (1985) recorded highest flower yield with organic and inorganic forms of nitrogen. Whereas, Mohammed Yassin (1987) observed higher flower yield with the combined application of nitrogen at 25 kg per hectare through sheep manure and 75 kg per hectare of nitrogen through urea In tuberose, Parthiban and Abdul Khader (1991) recorded highest number of flowers with an increased flower bud diameter when applied with nitrogen at 100 kg per hectare. 2,2. Red gold and the lines IIHR-Sel 7 and IIHR-Sel 8 were found to be resistant and tolerant respectively Foliar application of iron 0.0075 per cent significantly increased the number of leaves per branch (Mostafa et al, 1997) 2.4.2. Bhattachaijee (1982) reported that the foliar application of 0,05 per cent zinc sulphate during February, April and June gave highest percentage (34,5) of increase in flower production. Soil Analysis 3.2.1. Soil sampling and processing The soil samples were collected from the field 10 days before treatment for the analysis of initial soil characteristics of the experimental field . The soil samples were also collected from the field during the growth stages of jasmine. The soil samples were collected for analysis at a depth of 15 cm and 30 cm away from the base of the plants at different locations from all treatment plots. The samples were than shade dried , ground with wooden mallet and passed through 2 mm sieve and bagged in cloth bag and used for analysis of NPK and micronutrients, 3.2.1.1. pH and Electrical Conductivity (EC) The pH and EC of 1:2 soil and water suspension was determined by using pH meter and conductivity bridge respectively (Jackson, 1973). 3.2.2. Macro nutrients 3.2.2.1. Available nitrogen The available nitrogen content of the soil sample was estimated by the alkaline permanganate method (Subbiah and Asija 1956) and expressed in kg/ha. 3.2.2.2. Available phosphorus The available phosphorus content of the soil sample was estimated by the 19 extraction with sodium bicarbonate (Olsen et al., 1954) and expressed in kg/ha. 3.2.2.3. Available potassium The available potassium content of the soil sample was extracted with N N NH4OAC and estimated by the flame photometer (Stanford and English, 1949) and expressed in kg/ha. 3.2.3. Micronutrients 3.2.3.1. DTPA Soil test Ten grams of soil was taken in a 200 ml polypropylene shaking bottle and 20 ml of DTPA solution was added and shaken for 2 hrs Then this was filtered through Whatman No.l filter paper The extract was collected and fed into atomic absorption spectro­ photometer (ASS) Varian Tehran Model AA 10/20 BQ for determining the concentrations of iron, manganese, copper and zinc (Lindsay and Norvell, 1978). 3.3. Leaf nutrient concentration Fully expanded third pair of leaf from the top of the shoot was selected for sampling. Twenty pairs of leaves were collected at random The leaves were thoroughly washed with 0 1 N HCLfolIowed by double distilled water. The plant samples were shade dried and then dried in hot air oven at 60°C The dried leaves were chopped with stainless steel knife and then used for analysis 3.3.1. Macro nutrients 3.3.1.1. Nitrogen The nitrogen content of the leaf sample was estimated by microkjeldahl method of Piper (1966) and expressed as percentage. 3.3.1.2.Phosphorus The phosphorus content of the leaf was estimated by adopting Vanado phosphoric yellow method (Jackson, 1973) and expressed as percentage. 3.3.1.3. Potassium The potassium content of the leaf sample was estimated by flame photometric method (Jackson, 1973) and expressed as percentage. 3.3.2. Micronutrients One gram of plant sample was weighed and put in 250 ml conical flask and I2ml of triple acid mixture was added and kept overnight for cold digestion. On the next day it was digested over sand bath for one hour until clear white solution was obtained. After the digestion was over, the content was made up to 50 ml with distilled water and to conical vials and fed into AAS for micronuinent analysis (Jackson, 1973). 3.3.3.SPAD - 502 Measurements SPAD - 502 measurements were made as described by Peng et at.. (1993s using a chlorophyll meter (SPAD - 502, Soil Plant Analysis Development (SPAD) section. Minolta Camera Co. Ltd.. Japan). The readings were recorded on the upper most fully expanded leaves in 10 randomly chosen plants. The average were worked out for each plot and expressed as SPAD readings. 3,4. Biometrical Characters Two uniform plants were selected randomly in each replications for recording the following observations and the mean was calculated. Observations on biometric characters were recorded during vegetative and flowering stages for growth, yield and floral characters. 3.4.1. Growth characters 3.4.1.1. Plant height Height of the plant was measured from the^hase of the stem to the axil of the youngest fully unfolded leaf. 30 days after pruning and expressed in cm 3.4.1.2. Number of primary branches The shoots arising from the base of the plants were observed as primary branches and expressed in number. 3.4.1.3. Number of secondary branches The shoots arising from the primary branches were observed as secondary branches and expressed in number, 3.4.1.4. Number of shoots produced one month after pruning The shoots produced one month after pruning were observed and expressed in number 3.4.1.5. Number of shoots produced in a year The primary secondary and tertiary shoots produced in a plant during the crop growth were observed and presented in number. 3.4.1.6. Plant spread Plant spread was measured in North-South direction and East-West direction and expressed in m2. 3.4.1.7. Leaf area The leaf area was calculated by the graphical method and expressed in cm2 23 3.4.2. Flowering behaviour / 3.4.2.1. Days taken for first flower bud emergence Number of days from pruning to visible flower bud appearance were observed and expressed in number. 3.4.2.2. Days from pruning to first flower picking The dates on which the flower buds were ready for picking and the number of days from pruning to commencement of picking were recorded. 3.4.2.3. Number of cymes per plant The number of cymes produced during the flowering period were recorded and expressed in number. 3.4.2.4. Number of flower buds in a cyme at the time of harvest The number of flower buds present in a cyme at the time of harvest was counted and expressed in number. 3.4.2.5. Number of pink buds in a cyme The number of pink buds in a cyme were counted and expressed in number. 3.4.3. Flower bud characters 3.4.3.1. Flower bud length The length of the flower buds was measured from the lower end of the corolla tube to the distal end of the bud and expressed in cm. 3.4.3.2. Corolla tube length The length of the corolla tube was measured from the lower end of the corolla tube to the junction of the bud and expressed in cm 3.4.3J. Yield of flower buds The total yield of the flower buds per plant in all the three flowering stages (1, 2, 3) were recorded as weight of the flower buds in all the treatments. Monthly yield was also recorded , The yield was expressed in g. From the yield per plant per year, yield per hectare per year was estimated. 3.4.4.2. DISCUSSION CHAPTER V DISCUSSION Production of jasmine (J.sambac Ait. cv, Gundumalli) flowers is presently on the increasing trend. However, the production does not match the increasing demand of loose flowers and perfume industries. To promote the jasmine flower production, it is essential to establish strategies such as balanced use of fertilizers and inclusion of micronutrients in fertilizer schedule. The integrated supply of micronutrients and macro nutrients in splits in adequate amounts and in suitable proportions is one of the most important factors that controls the growth of plants (Zende, 1996). The importance of split application of fertilizers and micronutrients in jasmine crop is fairly well recognised and their use had significantly contributed to the increase in crop productivity. It is necessary to recognise that micronutrients are as essential as macronutrients and they are to be necessarily taken up by plants from soils supplemented through soil or foliage for achieving maximum use of efficiency of applied nutrients. Information regarding combined application of macronutrients, micronutrients and their method of application is scanty. Hence the present study was undertaken with a view to stimulate productive potential of jasmine. Data collected on growth and yield attributes, flowering behaviour, nutritional status and soil fertility level are critically analysed and discussed 5.1. Growth characters Based on the growth and development, traits such as plant height, number of primary branches, number of secondary branches, number of shoots produced one month 114 after pruning, number of shoots produced during crop growth and plant spread showed a linear increase with the nutrients use. Application of NPK nutrients in four splits enhanced the growth attributes of jasmine. Split application of NPK nutrients during the cropping period might have minimised the nutrient loss due to the restricted leaching and fixing. The data corroborated with the findings of Bhattacharjee (1988) and Srinivasan et al. (1989) in jasmine, Bankar and Mukhopadhyay (1990) in tuberose and Somani (1996) Application of 120;240;240g NPK in four splits during the months of October, April, January and July increased the plant height, number of primary and secondary branches. This is in line with the previous findings of Nanjan . (1979) in rose; Natarajan and Madhava Rao (1980) in jasmine The number of shoots produced one month after pruning and the total number of shoots produced during the crop growth increased that commensurate with the application of NPK nutrients in four splits This might be attributed to the enhanced vegetative growth, as the availability of nutrients suitably compensated the demand during the crop growth Bhattacharjee (1988) reported that the increased vegetative growth of the plants supplied with split application of nitrogen resulted from the enhanced photosynthetic efficiency of the plants As a consequence of increased meristematic growth, the shoot length and the shoot number had increased in the treatment receiving split application of nitrogen Bhattacharjee (1985), Jayaprasad and Sulladmath (1978) reported increased plant height and number of branches due to split application of fertilizers. 115 The larger plant spread recorded with the four split application of NPK nutrients might be attributed to the cumulative effect of increased plant height, number of primary and secondary branches and number of shoots produced. This positive influence of the growth attributes on plant spread was in confirmation with the findings of Rajamani and Sundaram (1997) in rose. Advancing the NPK fertilization in the months of October and April also showed remarkable increase in the growth characters compared to the existing recommendation in the months of November and June This might be due to the fact that the application of nutrients prior to pruning assists in maintaining the healthy conditions of the crop, thus flushing with increased plant height, primary and secondary branches, numbers of shoots and plant spread. Combined application of micronutrients, ZnS04 (4g per plant, 0.5 per cent) + FeS04 (8g per plant, 0.5 per cent) increased all the growth characters. Similar trend of response has been reported earlier by many authors in several horticultural crops (Patel and Patel, 1985, Rajkumar, 1994; Singh and Bhattacharjee, 1997). The ZnS04 + FeS04 applications had a profound influence on the vegetative growth (Suchetha, 1989) The growth promoting effect of zinc on plant growth may be due to its involvement in auxin biosynthesis (Skoog, 1940 and Tsui, 1948), The importance of iron on vegetative growth could be related to its effect of iron in chlorophyll formation, to form amino lenulinic acid (ALA) in the biosynthetic pathway. Zinc plays a vital role in the active synthesis of tryptophan which is the precursor of IAA The growth stimulating substances would have assisted in the stimulated growth 11C of zinc applied jasmine plants. Similarly in crossandra, Abdul Khader et al. (1985) showed enhanced growth due to Zn application. Iron participates in the synthesis of chlorophyll in plants and thus helps in greater photosynthetic activity and growth. With regard to the different methods of micronutrient application, soil + foliar fertilisation greatly increased the growth characters such as plant height, primary and secondary branches, number of shoots produced one months after pruning and during crop growth and plant spread This agrees with the findings of Rajkumar (1994). Foliar application of micronutrients was better in terms of growth characters than the soil application Similar response has been reported earlier (Kannan, 1988). Accordingly foliar spray appears to be the most effective method of application as the effect is rapid, timely and induce efficient absorption in plant system. From the present study, the data revealed that under improved NPK fertilization practices (N2 and N3), soil and foliar application of micronutrients was found to be the best in increasing the plant height, the growth attributing factor. But under normal NPK fertilization (N|), either soil or foliar application of micronutrients was found to be performing better. In contrast, the combined soil + foliar application of micronutrients increased the plant spread under normal NPK fertilization (Ni) and split application of NPK nutrients (N^), Whereas, on advancing the application of NPK nutrients in the months of October and April, the plant spread was better even with soil application alone or foliar spray alone 117 Split application of micronutrients (N3) combined with ZnSCL + FeSO* (M3) applied through soil + foliar methods (T4) was the best treatment combination in increasing the growth and development traits like plant height, primary and secondary branches, number of shoots produced one month after pruning and during the crop growth and plant spread. Loss of soil nutrients has been reported mostly due to leaching and fixation However, split application of nitrogen and application of micronutrients would efficiently circumvent the nutrient losses and enhance growth attributes. Especially nitrogen which is readily available in a few days after application may be leached immediately if not depleted by plants. 5.2. Nitrogen, along with phosphorus and potassium is the most recognised basic element required for most metabolic activities of the plant resulting in the synthesis of chlorophyll and cytochromes which are essential for photosynthesis and respiration processes of the plants. Flowering behavoiur In the present study, improved NPK fertilization practices had a favourable effect on flower characters viz., days to first flower bud emergence and days to first flower bud picking from the day of pruning. Early flowering and flower bud picking in this study was in line with the findings of Von Hentig (1959) in chrysanthemum; Garibaldi (1964) in gladiolus and Bankar and Mukhopadhyay (1990) in tube rose. Earliness in flower bud emergence and flower bud picking was observed with four split application of NPK nutrients (Nr,) This was not in line with the findings of Bhattacharjee (1988), according to whom split application of NPK nutrients did not have significant influence on flowering characters However, Srinivasan el al (1989) reported positive response with the split application of nutrients. Earliness due to the application of nitrogen and phosphorus in four splits might be due to the availability of nutrient in phases at optimum level during the initial stages of growth and development, which was conducive for induction of flowering Application of ZnSC>4 + FeSC>4 advanced the days to first flower bud emergence and first flower bud picking , FeS04 and ZnS04 might have favoured the storage of more carbohydrates through photosynthesis as improved photosynthetic product, which might be the attributing factor for the positive effect of FeS04 on flowering This was confirmed with the results of Som Dutt and Bhambota (1971) and Singh and Bhattacheijee (1997) 120 In the present study, it is evident that application of NPK nutrients in the months of October and April (N2) enhanced the early flower bud emergence and flower bud picking. With the advancement in application of NPK (N2) and application of NPK in four splits (N3) going in for FeS04 alone was the best for early flower bud emergence. Under the combined application of ZnS04 + FeS04, advancing the NPK nutrients in the months of October and April is the best in improving the flowering characters. This was in line with the explanation of Som Dutt and Bhambota (1971) 5.4. Yield and yield attributes Application of NPK nutrients in four splits and advancing the NPK application in the months of October and April had 82.5 and 44.9 per cent increase in the yield respectively over normal application of NPK nutrients in the months of November and June Modified NPK fertilization practices improved the yield attributes such as number of cymes per plant, number of buds per cyme at the time of harvest, reduced number of pink buds per cyme, flower bud length, corolla tube length, bud diameter and hundred bud weight. All these had positive correlation with the yield per plant and yield per hectare of jasmine Similar views were already expressed by Bhattacharjee (1988), Srinivasan et al. (1989) in J.sambac, Ram Singh (1996) in calendula, Singh (1996) in African marigold, Sunil Kumar and Singh (1998) in tuberose. Increased yield with improved NPK fertilization practices might be due to the substantial availability of the nutrients throughout the growing season Increased yield with the split application of NPK nutrients during the months of October, January, April 121 and July might also be due to the increased carbohydrate synthesis in the plant in a phased manner (Barooh and Ahmed, 1983, Das etal., 1987, Bhattachaijee, 1988 and Srinivasan etal, 1989). Combined application of ZnS04 + FeS04 in the months of December and June increased the yield and yield attributing characters except the flower bud diameter. The results obtained are in line with the findings of Chaturvedi et al. (1980) in gludiolus; Rajkumar (1994) in jasmine; Mostafa et al (1997) in chrysanthemum and Moretti et al (1998) in rosemary. The chlorophyll content significantly increased with four split application of NPK nutrients and FeS04 applied through soil + foliar methods. First flower bud emergence was early when the plants were supplied with NPK nutrients in the months of October and April, 8 g per plant; 0.5 per cent of FeS04 through soil + foliar method of application First flower bud picking was earlier with the application of FeS04 in the months of December and June. Yield of jasmine flower buds was the highest with NPK application in four splits during the months of October, January, April and July Application of ZnS04 + FeS04 in combination increased the yield markedly. Nitrogen plays an important role for enhancing yield and quality in jasmine. Nitrogen is one of the major components of nucleic acid, co-enzymes and cell membranes and it is involved in many of the metabolic processes viz., cell division, photosynthesis, protein synthesis and expansion of shoot and root growth in plants and has active role during vegetative growth. Nitrogen is responsible for the healthy green colour of stem and leaves, vigorous growth, branching, leaf production and size enlargement, it drives plant growth. Plants deficient in Nitrogen are stunted and yeljowish green. In case of severe deficiency, leaves turn brown and die. Yield as well as protein content is reduced. Organic fertilizers provides nitrogen in a usable form, which will help improve plant growth while neither burning roots nor destroying beneficial micro-organisms in the soil. Organic and inorganic nitrogen is the most important components to obtain sustainable crop production. It implies the most efficient use and management of organic, inorganic sources of major nutrients to attain higher levels of crop productivity and to maintain the fertility of the soil. Intensive agriculture, with the extensive use of chemical fertilizers, which is the resultant of green revolution, boosted up the production to meet the increasing population. But, there was no thought about hazardous adverse effects in the long run on the soil health in general and environment in particular. In view of the escalating cost of chemical fertilizers & their harmful polluting effects on the environment, there is growing awareness in the farming community about the alternative agricultural system. Integrated systems of agricultural production are less dependent on high inputs of energy & synthetic chemicals & more dependent on intensive management rather than conventional mono- cultural systems. The strategy of integrated nutrient management (INM) is receiving increased attention, aimed at reducing the dependence of chemical fertilizers and at the same time increasing the effectiveness of organically supplied nutrients. Total organic farming may be a desirable proposition for improving the quality of agricultural produce. It may not be possible to maintain the quality of the produce in commercial agriculture, where mostly the stress will be given mainly on yield. It is impossible to meet the nutrient requirement of the crops, exclusively through the organic fanning. Under these circumstances, integrated soil fertility management practices involving judicious combination of organic manures and chemical fertilizers seems to be a feasible option for sustainable agriculture on a commercial and profitable scale. In addition, they are eco-friendly, easily available and cost effective. Plants were sprayed with 0.1% copper ox chloride soon after pruning. And there was a mild attack of thrips on crop. These pests were controlled by spraying monocrotophos 0.1 per cent at a 15 days interval throughout the period of experimentation. 3.12 Harvesting The buds were harvested daily in the morning. The first picking was in march-April month and continued up to June month. 3.13 Field observation Technique of random samples was adopted and five plants selected from each treatment in all replication for the detailed studies on growth, flower and yield parameters and shelf life. 3.13.1 Growth parameter Following characters were studied during the growth phase of the crop. t 3.13.1.1 Length of shoot (cm) Length of shoot was recorded at 30 days interval starting from 30 day after application of fertilizers up to 150 days of crop growth. Lengths of shoots were measured by meter scale, from initiation point of shoot to the growing tip. 3.13.1.2 Spread of the plant (cm) The spread of plant was measured in both the direction east west and north south at 30 days interval from 30 days after application of fertilizers to 150 days of crop growth with the help of meter scale. 3.13.1.3 Number of leaves per plant To find out die average number of leaves plant'1 under various treatment all the leaves of observational plants were counted and the average per plant was worked out. 21 3.13.1.4 Leaf area (cm2) The leaf area was calculated with the help of leaf area meter machine. For this, 3 leaves were group in 3 categories i.e. small, medium and large size and average leaf area calculated. 3.13.1.5 Number of primary shoots To find out average number of primary shoot plant"1 all primary shoots of observational plants were counted and average number of shoots per plant per treatment was calculated. 3.13.1.6 Number of secondary shoots To find out average number of secondary shoots per plant all secondary shoots of observational plant were counted average number of shoots per plant per treatment was calculated. 3.13.2 Flower parameter 3.13.2.1 Diameter of flower (cm) The diameter of fully opened flowers was measured in on two perpendicular axis and values were average as centimeter. 3.13.2.2 Fresh weight of flower (g) The weight of 100 flowers harvested during the period of flowering was recorded and total number of flowers calculated at all picking. 3.13.2.3 Shelf life of flower buds Unopened flower buds of mogra were kept in open condition having ventilation at room temperature, according to various treatments. The end of shelf life was decided when flowers start fading and according to shelf life days was recorded. 3.14 Yield parameter 3.14.1 Flower yield per plant (g) The randomly selected five plants of each treatment per plot were used for this purpose. The cumulative weight at each harvesting was calculated for yield per plant. 22 3.14.2 Flower yield per plot (kg) and per hectare (q) The weight of the flowers harvested was recorded from the first to last harvest per plant and flower yield per plot was calculated. The flower yield per hectare was calculated on the basis of yield per plot. 3.15 Soil analysis The soil samples were used for estimation of pH, EC and available nitrogen. 3.15.1 Effect on available nutrients 3.4.1.1 Available Nitrogen Available nitrogen was determined by the potassium permanganate method given by Subbiah and Asija, 1956. 3.15.2 Soil physic-chemical properties 3.15.2.1 Soil pH It was determined in soil: water suspension (1:2.5) using glass electrode pH meter. 3.15.2.2 Electrical conductivity Electrical conductivity was estimated in (1:2.5) soil: water suspension after settlement of solids using Conductivity Bridge and expressed in dSm1. 3.16 Statistical analysis The analysis of variance was carried out according to simple randomized block design. 23 Chapter IV RESULTS In the present investigation entitled “Effect of different levels of organic and inorganic nitrogen on growth and yield of Mogra (Jasminum sambac L.) cv.
